**Feed output.** Vietnamese feed mills made about 22 Mt of livestock and poultry feed in 2025, after 21.5 Mt in 2024 [@MAC-01; @MAC-28] {VN-direct|Medium}. This official figure excludes aquafeed. Aquafeed estimates disagree: industry estimates by species sum to about 3.9 to 4.8 Mt for 2025 (our sum), while USDA's post estimates 6.5 Mt [@MAC-06; @MAC-01] {VN-direct|Low}. We do not average them (see [[app-s6-feed-market]] and [[app-r2-disagreements]]).

**Imports of the two ingredients that set feed cost:**

| Ingredient (2025) | Imports | Share of domestic supply imported | Main origins | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Maize | 11.91 Mt, USD 2.95 bn | about 74% | Argentina 46.5%, Brazil 34.8%, United States about 13% | [@MAC-08; @MAC-01] {VN-direct\|High} |
| Soybeans | 2.61 Mt, USD 1.21 bn | 98.4% of imports plus domestic production (our calculation) | Brazil 45.8%, United States 43.6% | [@MAC-04; @MAC-09] {VN-direct\|High} |
| Soybean meal | 5.70 Mt | 79% of meal (imports over imports plus domestic crush); about 99% of soy protein (domestic crush uses imported beans); both our calculations | Mostly Argentina (origin shares not re-checked) | [@MAC-04; @MAC-09] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Wheat (all uses) | 5.45 Mt, USD 1.46 bn | 100% (derived) | Australia, Brazil, United States | [@MAC-10] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| DDGS | 1.5 Mt | 100% (inferred) | United States 72% | [@MAC-01] {VN-direct\|High} |

Vietnam grew only 42,000 to 43,000 t of soybeans in 2025 on about 26,000 ha, and domestic maize output was flat to falling at about 4.1 Mt [@MAC-04; @MAC-01] {VN-direct|High}. Even if every domestic soybean were crushed, it would supply about 2% of the crush (our calculation from [@MAC-04]). Domestic crushing capacity is expanding, led by one Bunge and Wilmar plant at Phu My in Ho Chi Minh City (former Ba Ria-Vung Tau) with 2.6 Mt a year of capacity [@VCO-16] {VN-direct|Medium}. But crushing imported beans at home shifts imports from meal to beans; it does not reduce protein import dependence.

**The import bill.** Adding four customs lines (maize, soybeans, wheat and the "animal feed and ingredients" group) gives about USD 10.2 billion of imports in 2025 (our calculation from [@MAC-07; @MAC-08; @MAC-09; @MAC-10]). This includes some milling wheat and food soybeans. The livestock department's narrower 2024 figure for feed ingredients is 22.4 Mt and USD 7.7 billion [@MAC-28] {VN-direct|Medium}. USDA's 2025 feed-ingredient table shows 23.57 Mt imported out of 28.62 Mt used, about 82% [@FS-23] {VN-direct|High}.

{{chart:chart-feed-import-dependence}}

> **Correction.** Earlier drafts of this project cited soybeans as "41,000 t produced against 3.2 Mt imported". Those were forecasts for 2026 mixed with 2025 actual figures. The 2025 actuals are 42,000 to 43,000 t produced and 2.61 Mt imported (98.4% of imports plus domestic production, our calculation), with 5.70 Mt of soybean meal imported and 7.2 Mt fed [@MAC-04]. See [[app-m5-changelog]].

## 1.3 Exposure: prices, disease and policy shocks

A protein supply chain that depends on imports transmits external shocks directly into Vietnamese farm costs.

- **Feed is most of the cost.** Industry sources put feed at 60% to 70% of livestock production cost, and above 70% for pigs [@MAC-24; @MAC-43] {VN-direct|Low}. For shrimp, 2026 trade press puts feed at 50% to 60% of production cost [@FM-10] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **2022.** During the post-Ukraine price spike, wheat import prices reached USD 424/t in September 2022, 37% above a year earlier [@MAC-44] {VN-direct|Medium}. A review estimates that price pressure forced about 30% of small farmers to stop farming in recent years [@MAC-43] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **2026.** Feed prices rose 10% to 14% between January and April 2026 (poultry association estimate), which the association attributed to the Middle East conflict. Farm-gate egg prices fell below production cost [@MAC-24] {VN-direct|Medium}. Shrimp feed makers raised prices by VND 1,200 to 1,500/kg in June 2026 [@FM-10] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Fishmeal.** The World Bank fishmeal price reached USD 2,500/t in August 2026, 43% above a year earlier and the highest in the 2020 to 2026 series [@FM-01; @FM-02] {general|High}. The fishmeal-to-soybean-meal price ratio widened from 3.8 in 2024 to 6.2 in August 2026 [@GT-15] {general|High}.
- **Disease.** African swine fever killed or forced the culling of about 6 million pigs in 2019, more than 20% of the herd, and returned in 2025, reaching most provinces by the third quarter; about 1.2 million pigs were culled that year [@MAC-37; @MAC-01; @MAC-12] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Tax.** Animal feed became "not subject to VAT" from 1 July 2025, so feed makers can no longer deduct VAT paid on inputs [@COST-24; @MAC-25] {VN-direct|High}. This matters for any new feed-protein producer (see [[ch09-economics]]).

{{chart:chart-fishmeal-price}}

## 1.4 Growth ahead, and where it will come from

- USDA expects total feed demand (livestock, poultry and aquafeed) to rise from 28.6 Mt in 2025 to 31.2 Mt in 2027 (August 2026 forecast, up from 30.6 Mt in April), and raised its forecast of maize imports for 2026/27 to 15 Mt [@MAC-01; @MAC-03] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- The national livestock strategy targets 30 to 32 Mt of industrial feed output and 6.0 to 6.5 Mt of carcass meat by 2030 [@MAC-23] {VN-direct|High}. If the feed target covers livestock and poultry feed only, it implies growth of about 6% to 8% a year from 2025 (our calculation; see [[app-f1-outlook]] for the scope question).
- Vietnam's population is projected at 104.3 million in 2030 and 106.5 million in 2035 (UN medium variant) [@GT-12] {VN-direct|Medium}. Population will rise only about 5% between 2025 and 2035, so protein demand growth will come mostly from income and diet.
- We found no numerical target for localising feed raw materials in the published strategies. The livestock strategy encourages domestic feed from by-products such as brewer's grain and cassava pulp, and biological products that replace antibiotics, but sets no localisation number [@MAC-23; @REG-54] {VN-direct|High}.

On current trends, every additional tonne of feed demand will be met by imports.

## 1.5 An exporter of animal protein and an importer of the plant protein behind it

Vietnam exported USD 11.3 billion of seafood in 2025 (+12.4%), including about USD 4.6 billion of shrimp and USD 2.2 billion of pangasius [@MAC-15; @MAC-01] {VN-direct|High}. In January to August 2026 seafood exports reached USD 8.0 billion, with China and Hong Kong now the largest market [@MAC-34] {VN-direct|Medium}. Vietnam also exported about USD 1.4 to 1.5 billion of animal feed in 2025 [@MAC-01; @MAC-12] {VN-direct|Medium}, and it is a net exporter of fishmeal by value (USD 430 million exported, USD 260 million imported in 2023) [@FM-37; @FM-38] {VN-direct|Medium}.

The shape of the economy is therefore clear: **Vietnam imports plant protein and energy, converts them into animal and aquatic protein, and exports a large share of the result.** Its competitive strength is processing. Its vulnerability is the input.

A second, related pattern appears on the carbohydrate side. Vietnam supplied about 39% of China's cassava starch imports by value in 2024 (1.56 Mt, USD 757 million, China-reported), but only about USD 0.16 million of glucose [@RGN-51; @RGN-55] {VN-direct|High}. In 2025 Vietnamese starch exports to China rose to about 2.28 Mt in 11 months, and Vietnam became China's largest cassava starch supplier [@FS-01; @FS-13] {VN-direct|High}. The step that turns starch into fermentable sugar, and sugar into higher-value products, mostly happens after the starch leaves Vietnam. [[ch04-asset-map]] and [[ch03-regional]] return to this.

## 1.6 What the case for alternative protein rests on, and what it does not

For readers deciding whether Vietnam belongs in an alternative-protein strategy, four arguments carry different weight.

1. **Supply security and the import bill (strong).** About 99% of soy protein in feed and about 74% of maize supply are imported, feed demand is growing, and the 2022 and 2026 shocks show the exposure. Any domestically made protein that can match imported protein on price for a defined use reduces that exposure. This is the argument with the most evidence behind it.
2. **Industrial value added (strong, but conditional).** Vietnam already processes cassava, rice, sugar, soy and seafood at scale, and exports much of the carbohydrate as starch. Converting more of it to protein or fermentation feedstock at home is an industrial-policy argument that aligns with Resolution 36 on biotechnology and the 2026 high-technology priority list (see [[ch07-rules]]). It is conditional on costs ([[ch09-economics]]) and on a legal route to market.
3. **Environment (real, but narrower than often claimed).** Agriculture's 2020 emissions under the NDC business-as-usual projection were 104.5 MtCO2e, 19.8% of the projected national total (our calculation) [@MAC-32] {VN-direct|High}. But in the 2016 inventory, livestock (enteric fermentation plus manure) was 18.5 MtCO2e, 5.8% of the national total, against 49.7 MtCO2e from rice cultivation [@MAC-33] {VN-direct|Medium}. In our judgement, the environmental case for alternative protein in Vietnam therefore rests more on the land footprint of imported feed, manure pollution and antimicrobial use than on national methane totals. About 71.7% of antimicrobials used in Vietnam in 2015 went to animals [@MAC-36] {VN-direct|Medium}.
4. **Animal welfare (a motivation for some actors, including the publisher of this report).** The scale is large: tens of millions of pigs and hundreds of millions of poultry on farms at any time, and billions of farmed fish and shrimp. Proteins that displace animal products in food, or that displace forage fish in feed, reduce these numbers. Proteins that make aquaculture cheaper could also expand it. This report does not model welfare effects; the sign depends on the use (see [[ch26-plays]]).

A fifth argument, consumer demand, is outside this report's scope. We note only that the traditional *đồ chay* (vegetarian) category already exists in every supermarket we visited, and that the first thing it lacks is protein, not shelf space ([[ch02-alt-protein-today]]).

## 1.7 What this means for each reader

- **Investors:** the addressable demand is B2B (feed mills and food manufacturers), large, concentrated and price-disciplined by duty-free imports of soybean meal and maize (0% MFN duty since March 2025 [@REG2-21] {VN-direct|Medium}). Size theses on specific uses, not on total feed tonnage.
- **Policy makers:** the protein import dependence is structural and unmeasured in policy targets. A feed-and-protein security indicator (share of feed protein from domestic inputs) would make it visible.
- **Startups:** your first customers are among about 10 to 15 feed groups and a similar number of food manufacturers. The import price is your ceiling.
- **Manufacturers:** input-cost volatility (2022, 2026) is the business reason to qualify a second source of protein, even at parity.
- **Researchers:** the missing basic data (feed balances, Vietnam-specific fishmeal inclusion rates, aquafeed volumes that match output statistics) are cheap public goods.
- **International bodies:** Vietnam's feed-security exposure is a regional issue; the same import chains supply its neighbours.

**Related:** [[app-s6-feed-market]] (all feed and fishmeal data), [[app-f1-outlook]] (projections), [[ch09-economics]] (the prices to beat).

data.title: The alternative-protein economy today
data.summary: Vietnam's real non-animal protein economy is incumbent: soy milk, tofu and industrial đồ chay made by meat and frozen-food processors. Most of it is low in protein, and every locally made high-protein product runs on imported textured soy or wheat gluten, much of it from China. Modern plant-based brands are nearly absent. The most advanced alternative-protein market is feed, where insect meal is already sold and Chinese microbial protein is already imported.
data.body:
# 2. The alternative-protein economy today

**In one paragraph.** Vietnam already eats and makes a great deal of non-animal protein, but almost none of it comes from the technologies the global alternative-protein sector talks about. The real economy is soy milk (one firm holds about 80% of it), tofu, and industrial *đồ chay* (traditional vegetarian food) made by meat and frozen-food processors on the same lines as meat. Our September 2026 audit of 186 products in 11 stores found that most "alt-protein" shelf products are low in protein, and that every locally made product with 10 g or more of protein per 100 g runs on imported textured soy, soy concentrate or wheat gluten (partly inferred from labels), much of it from China. Modern plant-based meat brands are nearly absent. The most advanced alternative-protein market in Vietnam is animal feed, where a Vietnamese-built insect-meal plant sells to a major seafood exporter and Chinese microbial protein is already imported.

---

## 2.1 The incumbent non-animal protein economy

| Segment | Scale and leaders | Main protein input | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Soy milk | Vinasoy (Quang Ngai Sugar): more than VND 4,100 billion of soy-milk revenue in 2024, about 80% market share (self-reported); 390 million L/yr capacity (2022) | Whole soybeans (imported) | [@ECO-41; @IND-48; @IND-50] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Tofu and tofu skin | Mostly artisanal; a few industrial makers (ToFu House, capacity 150 to 500 t/month); craft villages for *tàu hũ ky* | Soybeans (mostly imported) | [@IND-51; @FORM-14] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Industrial *đồ chay* | Meat and frozen-food processors (Vissan, CJ Foods Vietnam with Cau Tre and bibigo, SG Food, Cholimex), specialists (An Nhien, Au Lac, Thoai An, LC Foods), retailer private labels | Mung bean, vegetables and starch; or imported textured vegetable protein (TVP), soy concentrate and wheat gluten | [@ECO-30; @ECO-33; @FORM-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Plant milks and yoghurts | Vinamilk (11 plant-milk products, several blended with cow's milk), TH true NUT (contains fresh milk), Nutifood, Vinasoy's Veyo; imports such as 137 Degrees (Thailand) and Oatside | Imported soybeans, oats, nuts; imported pea protein in high-protein lines | [@ECO-43; @ECO-45; @FORM-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Microalgae | Small spirulina producers selling health supplements | Spirulina | [@ECO-52; @ECO-53] {VN-direct\|Low} |

This incumbent economy operates under existing food law without difficulty ([[ch07-rules]]). It is also the natural first customer for any new protein ingredient made in Vietnam.

## 2.2 What the shelf is made of: the September 2026 retail audit

AltProtein Vietnam logged 186 products (SKUs) in 11 modern and premium stores in Nha Trang (6 September 2026) and Ho Chi Minh City (16 and 20 September 2026), with ingredient lists for 120 and protein values for 78 [@FORM-01]. It is a convenience sample, not a market survey: no wet markets, dedicated chay shops, online-only brands or food service. Full method and tables are in [[app-s2-retail-audit]].

**Most of the shelf is not a protein product.** The two largest groups are plant milks (27% of SKUs) and filled wrappers such as spring rolls, dumplings and buns (25%). Across 43 unique ready-to-eat or ready-to-cook foods with a label value, **median protein is 4.7 g per 100 g; 53% have under 5 g and only 16% reach 10 g** [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|High}.

**Two tiers, little in between.**
- *Tier 1:* starch-and-vegetable filled wrappers with mung bean filling, 1.5 to 5.7 g protein per 100 g (median 4.0 g). CJ's current *há cảo chay* and *chả giò rế chay* labels list no soy protein among the ingredients, though the allergen line declares wheat (gluten) and soy; mung bean is the main protein ingredient [@FORM-22; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|High}.
- *Tier 2:* gluten- or TVP-based analogues (base inferred from protein level for three) at 12 to 25 g per 100 g hydrated (median 19 g), and dried TVP or gluten slices at 53 to 67 g as sold [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|High}.

{{chart:chart-retail-protein-archetypes}}

**High protein means imported protein.** All 10 locally made products with 10 g or more protein per 100 g use (or, for three, almost certainly use) soy protein, TVP, soy concentrate or wheat gluten. Local foods with no imported protein ingredient (8 products) top out at 4.6 g [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|High}. Of the 170 SKUs whose main protein ingredient could be identified, **77% rely on an imported protein ingredient and a further 11% partly do** (soybeans count as imported, since about 98% are) [@FORM-01; @FORM-09] {VN-direct|Medium}.

**China is a major supplier of the concentrated ingredients.** China reported exporting to Vietnam in 2023 about 7,957 t of protein concentrates and textured protein (HS 2106.10), 10,028 t of protein substances including soy isolate (HS 3504) and 10,338 t of wheat gluten, at about USD 1.6 to 1.7 per kg [@FORM-05; @FORM-06; @FORM-07] {VN-direct|High}. By 2025 textured protein shipped at USD 1.24 per kg FOB and landed at about USD 1.29 to 1.38 per kg duty-free (our calculation, assuming freight of 3% to 8% and port costs of USD 15 to 40 per t; [[ch09-economics]]) [@TIC-12; @BUY-02; @FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}. Vietnam-reported quantities for these codes are estimated by the database and should not be used; values are more reliable (for example USD 31.1 million of wheat gluten imported in 2023) [@FORM-03] {VN-direct|High}. These codes also supply meat processors (for sausages and *giò chả*), so they are not a measure of the alternative-protein market.

**No domestic TVP.** We found no commercial TVP extrusion in Vietnam, and the country's soybean crushing is feed-grade only ([[ch05-industrial-base]]) [@FORM-10; @FORM-11; @FORM-35] {VN-direct|Medium}.

**Price per gram of protein.** Protein is cheapest in the least processed formats: tofu (median about VND 66,000 per 100 g of protein) and dried TVP slices (median about VND 65,000), then hydrated gluten or TVP analogues (median about VND 112,000). Filled wrappers cost a median of about VND 369,000 per 100 g of protein. The only imported "modern" analogues on shelf (an Italian soy burger and sausage) cost VND 542,000 to 622,000 per 100 g of protein, about five times local gluten or TVP analogues [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. For comparison, eggs and chicken breast retail at about VND 34,000 to 45,000 per 100 g of protein [@COST-40; @COST-41] {VN-direct|Medium}.

{{chart:chart-retail-price-per-protein}}

**Chay versus meat.** In the one high-confidence same-brand pair, Vissan's *chả giò rế chay* cost 38% less per 100 g than Vissan's meat version [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. Other pairs rest on low-confidence price reads. Because most chay wrappers hold 3 to 5 g of protein, a cheaper pack is not cheaper protein. The audit did not capture protein values for the meat equivalents, so price per gram of protein cannot yet be compared.

**Other supply-side observations.**
- "Chay" is not the same as vegan: five SKU rows contain or may contain egg or dairy [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|High}.
- Korean-owned CJ Foods Vietnam accounts for 20 of 186 rows; imported finished products are concentrated in premium stores, while mass retailers carry almost only Vietnamese-made products [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|High}.
- No label showed high-moisture extrusion, mycoprotein, precision-fermented or cultivated ingredients. Apart from one imported nutritional-yeast SKU and yeast extract used as flavouring, fermentation appears only in plant yoghurts and cultured cashew cheeses [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|High}.

**What this means for supply.** The largest concrete gap visible on Vietnamese shelves is a domestic protein ingredient: textured soy or soy-gluten granules and slices, and a protein that can lift the 4 g-protein wrapper category. The natural first customers are named in [[ch26-plays]] and [[app-s2-retail-audit]].

## 2.3 Modern plant-based meat: nearly absent

- The Mintel launch database, as reported by GFI APAC, logged **no plant-based meat launches in Vietnam from 2022 to the second quarter of 2023** [@ECO-23] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- GFI's global company database lists only two Vietnamese companies, both plant-based, founded in 2019 and 2023 [@VCO-21] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- Imported brands arrived through restaurants and gourmet shops, not mass retail: Beyond Burger at BiaCraft in Ho Chi Minh City in August 2019; OmniFoods on a Starbucks Vietnam menu in summer 2023; Next Meats, Heura and others through gourmet importers [@ECO-15; @ECO-16; @ECO-20] {VN-direct|Medium}. No brand announced a formal national entry, so there were no formal exits either.
- The only products labelled "Plant Based" in mass retail were Chinese canned soy luncheon meats, at about three times the price per 100 g of Vissan's Vietnamese canned chay beef [@FORM-01; @ECO-40] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- Domestic startups are few and small: Emmay (Ho Chi Minh City, mushroom and mycelium products, about 1.5 to 2 t a month in 2023), Kashew (cultured cashew cheese, 2020), Ong Tempeh, and a handful of others with no confirmed current scale [@ECO-12; @ECO-13; @ECO-49; @ECO-51] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- Published market-size figures for Vietnamese plant-based meat ("about VND 1,000 billion", "USD 500 million within several years") give no traceable method and should not be used [@ECO-17; @ECO-18; @ECO-19] {VN-direct|Low}.

## 2.4 Fermentation, algae, duckweed and cultivated meat: almost nothing yet

- **Fermentation for food.** We found no Vietnamese company making koji protein, mycoprotein or precision-fermented ingredients. Tempeh (Ong Tempeh, which also sells *Rhizopus* starter) is the only commercially made fungal-fermented protein food we could verify [@ECO-51] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Microalgae and duckweed.** Spirulina is small and sold as a supplement; one source claims more than 70% of spirulina-derived products sold in Vietnam are imported (2023) [@ECO-53] {VN-direct|Low}. No commercial duckweed producer was found [@ECO-57] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Cultivated meat and seafood.** Vietnam has no cultivated-meat company or facility. The links are corporate and outward:
  - Vinh Hoan (the pangasius exporter) holds a minority stake in Avant Meats through Vinh Technology, and joined Shiok Meats' 2021 round [@ECO-58; @ECO-59; @ECO-60] {VN-direct|Medium}.
  - Minh Phu (shrimp) signed a memorandum with Shiok Meats in July 2022 for a joint R&D centre in Vietnam; we found no sign it went further, and UMAMI Bioworks merged with Shiok in 2024, taking over its assets; UMAMI's partner list names no Vietnamese firm [@ECO-60; @ECO-61; @ECO-63; @VCO-22; @VCO-23] {VN-direct|Medium}.
  - VinaCapital Ventures invested in Korea's INNOHAS (plant-based meat) in July 2024 to help it enter Vietnam; INNOHAS shows no Vietnam activity two years later [@ECO-65; @VCO-31] {VN-direct|Low}.

## 2.5 Feed: the most advanced alternative-protein market in Vietnam

| Actor | What | Scale and status | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entobel (Singapore holding; plants in Vietnam) | Black soldier fly larvae meal (H-Meal, at least 53% crude protein), oil, frass | 1,000 t/yr in Dong Nai (2019); 10,000 t/yr in Ho Chi Minh City (former Ba Ria-Vung Tau), opened 23 November 2023; Heineken Vietnam by-products as feedstock; more than 200 staff. Output not disclosed. | [@ECO-01; @ECO-02; @ECO-03; @ECO-06; @VCO-18] {VN-direct\|High} |
| Vinh Hoan offtake | At least 15,000 t of Entobel insect protein over 2025 to 2027 (about 5,000 t a year) | Announced February 2024 | [@ECO-05] {VN-direct\|High} |
| Skretting Vietnam (Nutreco) | Commercial shrimp feed containing Entobel insect meal, described as the first in Vietnam | From November 2025; inclusion and volume not disclosed | [@VCO-28] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Cricket One | Cricket farming and processing, Dong Nai (former Binh Phuoc) | 1,000 t/yr processing capacity claimed (2023); last evidence of activity October 2024 | [@ECO-09; @ECO-11] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Chinese microbial protein (imported by CK Vietnam / V-Group) | Bacterial biomass from glutamic-acid (MSG) fermentation, at least 70% crude protein, sold as "Mycoprotein" | For pig, poultry, fish and shrimp feed; price not published | [@ECO-69; @FM-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Western single-cell protein (FeedKind, Unibio) | Methanotroph bacterial protein | Not found in Vietnam; covered in Vietnamese media as a global trend | [@ECO-66; @ECO-67] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Functional yeast products | Yeast derivatives trialled in shrimp | Trials at ShrimpVet (Ho Chi Minh City) | [@ECO-70] {VN-direct\|Low} |

Two lessons stand out. First, **a Vietnamese novel-protein-into-feed business already exists**, built with local private equity, development finance and a seafood exporter's offtake (see [[ch08-capital]]). Every new feed protein will be benchmarked against it. Second, **the import counterfactual is already here**: Chinese microbial protein, a by-product of amino-acid fermentation, is sold into Vietnamese feed today. A Vietnamese single-cell protein would compete with it, not only with fishmeal.

## 2.6 The support ecosystem is thin

GFI APAC includes Vietnam in regional consumer surveys but has no Vietnam-specific programme [@ECO-24; @ECO-73] {VN-direct|Medium}. GFI's database lists no Vietnamese research actors [@VCO-21] {VN-direct|Medium}. The support we found for founders was generic (for example, women-entrepreneur programmes that backed Emmay) [@ECO-13; @ECO-14] {VN-direct|Medium}. We did not verify the activity of NGOs, vegetarian associations or plant-based events in Vietnam; this is a gap, not a finding of absence (see [[ch30-unknowns]]). The demand research found the organised vegan movement small and mainly online, and no national vegetarian association with a public membership figure ([[ch12-chay-baseline]]).

{{chart:chart-timeline}}

## 2.7 Reading the market

1. **The protein gap is inside the existing categories.** The biggest near-term supply opportunity in food is not a new category but more, and more local, protein in existing ones: textured protein for specialist chay makers, and cheap protein to lift 4 g wrappers.
2. **Incumbents are the customers and the co-packers.** An Nhien, Au Lac, Thoai An, LC Foods, Cholimex, CJ Foods Vietnam, Vissan and private-label makers already buy imported protein ingredients; Vinamilk and Vinasoy buy imported pea protein and soybeans.
3. **Feed leads food.** Novel protein in feed is already legal, funded and bought in Vietnam. Novel protein in food has no Vietnamese producer to test the rules.
4. **Price anchors are low.** Chay sells at or below meat prices; tofu and dried TVP deliver protein at about 1.5 to 2 times the price of egg and chicken protein. A new ingredient must fit that structure.

**For each reader.**
- **Investors:** there is almost no plant-based venture deal flow; the investable scale is in ingredients and feed. A "protein upgrade for đồ chay" thesis sells to incumbents, as suppliers or acquirers.
- **Startups:** your first customers can be named today; start there, not with a consumer brand.
- **Manufacturers:** a domestic TVP or soy-gluten supplier would reduce dependence on a single import origin; clearer protein labelling is a competitive opening.
- **Researchers:** measured (not label) protein and amino-acid data for common chay products are missing and cheap to produce.
- **Policy makers and international bodies:** a Vietnam company census and a chay nutrition audit are low-cost public goods.

**Related:** [[app-s2-retail-audit]], [[app-s1-directory]], [[ch26-plays]]. Part III re-reads this chapter's retail audit for demand ([[app-d3-retail-demand-signals]]) and asks who buys what ([[ch13-consumers]], [[ch16-business-buyers]]).

data.title: Vietnam in the region
data.summary: Vietnam ranks near the top in Asia on production cost and at the bottom on rules. Singapore approves, Thailand and Korea have routes but few approvals, and China builds at scale. Vietnam already supplies the region's bio-industries with cassava starch, but the starch it exports is turned into fermentation sugar in China. The regional lesson is that a published procedure with a fixed timeline matters more than cheap labour.
data.body:
# 3. Vietnam in the region

**In one paragraph.** The only published regional comparison, the GFI APAC and Hawkwood Biotech "Where to Build" study (October 2025), scores Vietnam 100 on labour cost, 97 on utilities and 93 on construction, and 0 on regulatory readiness. Indonesia is as cheap, and Thailand is nearly as cheap with far better rules and sugar supply. The study's own cost models show that labour and power are a small share of fermentation cost, so cheap inputs alone will not bring plants. Singapore has approved 18 novel foods but has stepped back from producing alternative protein at home. Thailand and Korea have approval routes but, as of September 2026, no approvals of cultivated meat. China is building yeast-protein and mycoprotein plants of 11,000 to 20,000 tonnes a year and sets the price any Vietnamese microbial protein must beat. Vietnam's real regional role today is as a feedstock supplier: it shipped 2.15 million tonnes of cassava starch in 2023, mostly to China, while China imported only USD 0.16 million of glucose syrup from Vietnam in 2024. Keeping the starch-to-sugar step at home and publishing a novel-food procedure are the two moves the region points to.

---

## 3.1 How the region scores Vietnam

The GFI APAC and Hawkwood Biotech study scored nine Asia-Pacific countries from 0 to 100 on seven drivers of biomanufacturing location (100 = best in the group) [@RGN-01; @RGN-02] {VN-direct|High}.

| Driver | Vietnam input | Vietnam score | Best in region |
|---|---|---|---|
| Labour | USD 342 a month (manufacturing wage) | 100 | Vietnam and Indonesia (100) |
| Utilities | USD 0.08 per kWh | 97 | Indonesia (99) |
| Construction cost | USD 1,672 per m² | 93 | Indonesia (100) |
| Business environment | World Bank Doing Business, about 70 | 30 | Singapore (100) |
| Sugar capability | 1.35 Mt produced, 0 exported, 110 kt imported (2024) | 26 | Thailand (100) |
| Talent | 779 researchers per million people | 26 | Korea (68) |
| Regulatory readiness | No framework, no approvals | 0 | Singapore and Australia (100) |

Source: [@RGN-01] {VN-direct\|High}.

{{chart:chart-hawkwood-scores}}

Three readings matter more than the ranks.

1. **Vietnam is not unique on cost.** Indonesia scores the same or better on labour, utilities and construction. Thailand scores 81 to 99 on cost and much higher on sugar (100), business environment (74) and rules (50). No country in the study combines low cost with regulatory readiness; Thailand comes closest [@RGN-01] {VN-direct|High}.
2. **Cost advantage acts on a small share of cost.** In the study's representative plant models, labour is 5% (biomass, 80,000 t a year) and 4% (precision fermentation, 10,000 t a year) of production cost, utilities 7% and 17%, and capital depreciation 10% and 18%. Feedstock, at 56% and 37%, is the largest line. The models were run for a US Midwest plant on corn glucose, not an Asian site [@RGN-01] {general|High}. The same report also cites other studies in which feedstock is 30 to 65% of cost; either way, labour and power together are only about 12 to 21% of cost ([[ch09-economics]]).
3. **The sugar index understates Vietnam.** It counts only cane sugar and ignores cassava starch, Vietnam's main fermentable carbohydrate ([[ch04-asset-map]]). But that starch is already sold abroad (section 3.5).

> **Correction.** In v0.6 this said labour was 7% and 17% of production cost and capital depreciation 37 to 56%; the source gives labour 5% and 4%, utilities 7% and 17%, depreciation 10% and 18%, and feedstock 56% and 37%.

The study's three recommendations for Vietnam are all about rules and delivery: fund Resolution 36 on biotechnology through programmes with named agency mandates; clarify incentive eligibility and timelines for biomanufacturing sites; and "publish regulatory procedures and statutory timelines for novel food approvals" [@RGN-01] {VN-direct|High}. It also finds that a 50% capital grant, a 10% cut in feedstock cost or a loan guarantee does more for project value than a tax holiday [@RGN-01] {general|High}.

**Our critique.** The index uses a World Bank indicator discontinued in 2021, gives no cost per kilogram for any country, and ranks countries against each other rather than against an investment threshold. It is a useful map of relative position, not a site-selection model [@RGN-01] {VN-direct|Medium}.

## 3.2 Rules: who approves what

| Country | Novel-food route | Cultivated meat | Approvals of novel proteins (Sept 2026) | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Singapore | Pre-market approval since 2019; codified in the Food Safety and Security Act, novel-food provisions in force 28 Nov 2025 | Yes | 18 items on the SFA list | [@RGN-04; @REG-63] {VN-adjacent\|High} |
| Thailand | Ministry of Public Health Notification 376 (2016); safety assessment by FDA-recognised assessment units; mycoprotein guideline; approved list updated Sept 2026 | Dossiers accepted; first filed Dec 2024 | No cultivated approval found | [@REG2-26; @RGN-32] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| South Korea | "Temporary standards" for new food ingredients, extended to cell and microbial culture Feb 2024; Food Tech Industry Promotion Act in force Dec 2025 | Yes (fee reported KRW 45 million; review up to 270 working days) | None found | [@RGN-19; @RGN-21; @RGN-34] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| Japan | Food Sanitation Act, case by case | Draft safety checkpoints May 2026 | None found | [@RGN-33] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| China | New food raw material approvals (NHC); cultivated framework expected from late 2026 | Not yet | Mycoprotein and yeast protein reported (dates not verified) | [@RGN-24; @RGN-25] {general\|Low} |
| Australia and New Zealand | Novel food standards plus new cell-cultured food standards | Yes | Vow quail (2025) | [@RGN-18; @RGN-20] {general\|Medium} |
| Malaysia | General novel-food provision; no fermentation or cultivated guidance | No | None found | [@RGN-19; @RGN-20] {VN-adjacent\|Low} |
| Indonesia, Philippines | No novel-food category | No | None | [@RGN-01; @RGN-19] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| **Vietnam** | **No novel-food category** ([[ch07-rules]]) | **No** | **None** | [@RGN-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} |

**Singapore's list** (dated 14 August 2026) has 6 cultivated meats (including Parima's duck, 10 April 2026, and Aleph Farms' beef, 22 July 2026), 6 fungal or bacterial biomass proteins (including Solar Foods' Solein, 2022), 3 precision-fermented ingredients, 2 microalgae and 1 synthetic compound [@RGN-04; @RGN-29] {VN-adjacent|High}. In the United States the FDA completed its review of Wildtype's cultivated coho salmon on 28 May 2025, the first cultivated seafood cleared there [@RGN-03] {general|High}.

{{chart:chart-regional-approvals}}

**A route is not an approval.** Korea opened applications in February 2024 and Thailand received its first cultivated dossier in December 2024; neither had approved a cultivated product by September 2026 [@RGN-20; @RGN-21; @RGN-32; @RGN-34] {VN-adjacent|Medium}. Staff, assessor capacity and published review times matter as much as the legal text.

**Halal.** In December 2025 Malaysia became the first Muslim-majority country to rule that cultivated meat can be halal, and Singapore's Islamic authority has set out a path. Aleph Farms plans to use capacity in Penang to supply the region [@RGN-20; @RGN-28; @RGN-30] {VN-adjacent|Medium}. This matters for any Vietnamese fermentation or cultivated product aimed at Malaysian, Indonesian or Middle Eastern buyers.

## 3.3 Strategies and state money

| Country | Instrument | Money found | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Singapore | Singapore Food Story 2 (Nov 2025) replaced "30 by 30"; 2035 local targets (30% of protein as eggs and seafood, 20% of fibre) exclude alternative protein "given the nascency of the sector" | S$144 M R&D programme (2019); S$42 M for 11 future-food projects (2025) | [@RGN-08; @RGN-09; @RGN-22] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| Thailand | Biotechnology Industry Development Framework 2026 to 2035 (NXPO, Nov 2025): "future food and alternative proteins" one of four target sub-industries; proposed GMP upgrade of a precision-fermentation pilot plant; proposed CDMO network | Proposed target of 500 M baht a year for 10 years for synthetic biology research | [@RGN-35] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| South Korea | Food Tech Industry Promotion Act; Gyeongbuk regulation-free zone for cell-cultured food; public cultivated-meat research centre in Uiseong (2027) | KRW 14.5 bn (about USD 10 M) for the Uiseong centre | [@RGN-19; @RGN-21] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| China | 2021 plan to reduce corn and soybean meal in feed names single-cell protein; 2024 State Council document on a diversified food supply ("new types of food"); Shanghai novel-food plan | About USD 1 bn from SDIC into biotech facilities (2025, per GFI) | [@RGN-22; @RGN-24; @RGN-25; @RGN-43; @RGN-56] {general\|Medium} |
| Vietnam | Resolution 36-NQ/TW (2023) on biotechnology; high-tech incentives ([[ch07-rules]]) | No alternative-protein line found | [@RGN-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} |

Two regional moves are directly relevant to Vietnam.

- **Thailand is responding to the same ranking.** Its new framework cites the GFI and Hawkwood study, and plans public pilot and contract-manufacturing capacity [@RGN-35] {VN-adjacent|Medium}. If Thailand delivers, a Vietnamese project competes with a neighbour that has cheaper sugar, a working approval route and public pilot plants.
- **Singapore has stepped back from production.** It now acts as regulator, research hub and financier rather than a manufacturing base [@RGN-08; @RGN-09] {VN-adjacent|Medium}. That leaves room for lower-cost neighbours to host manufacturing for Singapore-approved products, if their plants meet Singapore's import rules (not yet checked; see [[ch30-unknowns]]).

## 3.4 Pilot and contract capacity a Vietnamese company can use

| Facility | Country | What | Food status | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ScaleUp Bio | Singapore | Up to 10,000 L fermentation plus downstream processing; new shareholder announced March 2026 (Fusionopolis Ventures to join ADM) and widened scope beyond food | SFA food manufacturing licence (May 2024) | [@RGN-10; @RGN-11; @RGN-12; @RGN-13] {VN-adjacent\|High} |
| EECi Biorefinery Pilot Plant | Thailand | 12 fermenters, including 2 × 15,000 L; contract manufacturing and tech transfer | Not stated | [@RGN-36] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| Esco Aster | Singapore | Licensed for cultured animal cells (2021); now mostly cell therapy | Licensed (cells) | [@RGN-15; @RGN-16] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| Chinese pharma and food CDMOs | China | Largest and cheapest; client keeps strain, CDMO may own process improvements | Varies | [@RGN-24] {general\|Medium} |
| BBGI biotech plant | Thailand | Termination notice filed 22 September 2026 (title only read) | n/a | [@RGN-38] {VN-adjacent\|Low} |

Vietnam has no equivalent open food-grade pilot plant ([[ch05-industrial-base]], [[app-s8-labs-talent]]). A Vietnamese precision-fermentation or biomass startup today scales up abroad: in Singapore (food-licensed, dearer), Thailand (larger tanks, food status to confirm) or China (largest and cheapest, with more exposure of know-how).

**China sets the price.** Angel Yeast makes about 11,000 t a year of yeast protein; Fushine is expanding mycoprotein from 1,200 to 20,000 t a year; a 20,000 t a year mycoprotein plant (More Meat with Guangzhou Shuangqiao, a starch-sugar maker) began commercial runs in June 2026. One foreign client said scale-up in China took half the time and half the cost of alternatives [@RGN-24] {general|Medium}. Chinese gas-fermentation protein made from steel-mill off-gas is in feed trials [@RGN-57] {general|Medium}. Any Vietnamese microbial protein, for food or feed, will be priced against these plants.

## 3.5 Trade: Vietnam sells starch, not fermentation sugar

**Food-protein ingredient imports are small.** Vietnam reported 2023 imports of USD 22.2 million under HS 3504 (protein substances, including soy protein isolate; China 45%) and USD 34.0 million under HS 2106.10 (protein concentrates and textured protein; United States 46%, China 27%), about USD 56 million in all [@RGN-45; @RGN-46] {VN-direct|Medium}. China's mirror data show larger tonnages (25,267 t under HS 3504 in 2024) at USD 1.0 to 1.6 per kg, a price that suggests much of this is feed-grade rather than isolate [@RGN-47; @RGN-48; @RGN-49; @RGN-50] {VN-direct|Medium}. The retail audit found the same pattern at shelf level: textured soy, soy isolate and gluten mostly from China ([[ch02-alt-protein-today]]).

**Carbohydrate exports are large.** Vietnam exported 2.15 Mt of cassava starch worth USD 1.06 billion in 2023, 93.5% of it to China [@RGN-53] {VN-direct|High}. In 2024 Vietnam supplied 39% of China's cassava starch imports (1.56 Mt, USD 757 million), second to Thailand. China also bought USD 104 million of dried cassava and USD 114 million of modified starch from Vietnam, but only USD 0.16 million of glucose syrup [@RGN-51; @RGN-52; @RGN-54; @RGN-55] {VN-direct|High}.

{{chart:chart-cassava-starch-trade}}

**Reading.** For exported carbohydrate, the conversion of starch to glucose, the feedstock of every fermentation plant, happens in China. Glucose is made in Vietnam, but for captive or domestic use: Vedan alone built a glucose syrup plant of about 140,000 t a year in 1995 [@VCO-03] {VN-direct|Medium}. Some of that glucose may already feed Chinese yeast-protein or mycoprotein plants: the 20,000 t mycoprotein joint venture's partner is a starch-sugar maker. We could not confirm whether it uses Vietnamese starch [@RGN-24] {general|Low}. Moving part of that step to Vietnam, for Vietnamese or foreign fermenters, is the most direct way for Vietnam to "plug in" to the regional build-out ([[ch26-plays]], play T4).

## 3.6 Regional companies with a Vietnam foothold

| Company | Alternative-protein activity | Vietnam link | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ajinomoto | Partner of Solar Foods; Solein products launched in Japan (2025) and Singapore (Dec 2025) | Large MSG and seasoning fermentation in Vietnam ([[ch05-industrial-base]]) | [@RGN-40; @RGN-60; @IND-10] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| Thai Union | Early investor in Aleph Farms | Took a majority stake in Vietnamese seafood canner Yueh Chyang (2008) | [@RGN-32; @RGN-58] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| CJ CheilJedang, Daesang | Korean majors developing cultivated meat and partnering startups | Daesang runs an MSG fermentation plant and a starch plant in Vietnam; CJ runs food operations (CJ Foods Vietnam) and sold its feed business to De Heus in March 2026 | [@RGN-19; @RGN-34; @IND-11; @VCO-08; @FORM-24] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| Guangzhou Shuangqiao | Starch-sugar partner in a 20,000 t mycoprotein JV | Possible buyer of Vietnamese starch (not established) | [@RGN-24] {general\|Low} |

These firms already own fermentation, feed or seafood assets in Vietnam. They are the most likely hosts for a first tolling or pilot arrangement ([[ch26-plays]], play T5).

## 3.7 How neighbours built their rules

| | Singapore | Thailand | South Korea |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Import dependence above 90%; new food agency (2019); early applicants | Bio-circular-green agenda; foreign applicants; national science agency leadership | Industrial policy; provincial cluster push; conglomerate R&D |
| Instrument | New pre-market approval, later written into law | Ministerial notification plus recognised assessment units | Amendment of an existing rule (about nine months), then a promotion law |
| Time to first approval | About 2 years (first cultivated approval Dec 2020) | None for cultivated by Sept 2026 | None for cultivated by Sept 2026 |
| Tool worth copying | Public list with specifications; pre-submission help | Borrowing an existing science body as assessor | Published fee and review time; demonstration zone |

Sources: [@RGN-04; @RGN-19; @RGN-32; @RGN-34; @RGN-44; @REG2-26] {VN-adjacent\|Medium}.

**Transferable lessons (our assessment).** {VN-adjacent|Medium}
1. **A new law is not needed.** Korea added a new-ingredient assessment step to an existing instrument in about nine months. Vietnam's equivalent is a delegation clause in the Food Safety Law now in drafting and a procedure in its implementing decree ([[ch07-rules]], [[ch27-policy-options]]).
2. **Borrow assessors.** Thailand designated existing bodies as assessment units instead of building a new agency. Vietnamese candidates include the National Institute for Food Control.
3. **Rely on others' work.** Singapore's published specifications let later regulators rely on its assessments. Vietnam already uses a five-country reliance lane for GM food under Decree 43/2026 ([[ch07-rules]]); the same logic can apply to novel foods.
4. **Publish the timeline.** The study's single most specific ask of Vietnam is a published procedure with statutory timelines. Korea's fee and review period give applicants something to plan around, even before the first approval.

## 3.8 What this means

- **Investors:** Vietnam is a cost story without a food approval route. Until one exists, a Vietnamese novel-protein plant is justified only for feed, or for export under another country's approval. Price any microbial protein against Chinese plants of 11,000 to 20,000 t a year.
- **Policy makers:** the region's clearest message is to publish a novel-food procedure with a statutory timeline and pair it with capital grants rather than tax holidays. Thailand is already acting on the same study.
- **Startups:** plan scale-up in Singapore, Thailand or China and use a Singapore approval as the regional credential. Budget 9 to 12 months or more after a complete dossier [@RGN-17] {VN-adjacent|Low}.
- **Manufacturers:** food-grade protein ingredient imports are small (about USD 56 million), with the United States and China the largest suppliers. The bigger lever is the starch Vietnam already ships to China each year.
- **Research bodies:** Chinese cassava-to-protein and gas-to-protein feed work, and Thai pilot capacity, are the fastest partnerships for catching up.
- **International bodies:** help draft the procedure (through SFA's regulator agreements or FAO's food-safety work) and consider a Thailand-Vietnam pilot-plant access arrangement.

**Related:** [[app-s3-regional]] (full country tables, approval list, trade flows, study details), [[ch07-rules]], [[brief-international]].

data.title: What Vietnam has: raw materials and side streams
data.summary: Vietnam is rich in fermentable carbohydrate (cassava, rice, sugar) and poor in protein-rich side streams. The carbohydrate is mostly already traded, often to China, and nobody measures the residues. The asset map points to microbial conversion of carbohydrate with added nitrogen, sited where the residues are made.
data.body:
# 4. What Vietnam has: raw materials and side streams

**In one paragraph.** Vietnam's biological raw materials are dominated by carbohydrate: about 10 Mt of cassava roots grown and roughly 8 Mt more imported for processing, 43.5 Mt of paddy rice, and a sugar industry in surplus. Protein-rich side streams (brewer's spent grain, okara, seafood by-products) are small next to a feed sector that uses 7.2 Mt of soybean meal a year. The largest single residue is cassava pulp at starch factories, which we estimate at about 6 Mt wet a year (about 1.2 Mt dry matter), clustered in Tay Ninh. But the pulp has almost no protein, cassava roots rose about 50 to 90% in price, depending on province, in the year to April 2026, and a new fuel-ethanol mandate now competes for the crop. Three rules follow: residues are traded, not free; wet residues must be used where they are made; and any protein route from Vietnamese carbon must buy nitrogen.

{{kn:kn-cassava-pulp}} {{kn:kn-tay-ninh-starch}} {{kn:kn-cassava-price-rise}}

---

## 4.1 The shape of the asset base: carbon-rich, protein-poor

The streams that could become protein, or feed a protein process, fall into four groups. Full data sheets for 34 streams are in [[app-s4-feedstocks]].

| Group | Largest streams (2025 unless stated) | Protein content | What it is today | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Starch and sugar | Cassava roots 10.24 Mt grown [@FS-01]; cassava pulp about 6 Mt wet (derived) [@FS-05; @FS-06]; paddy 43.5 Mt [@FS-25]; broken rice (0.87 Mt of 100% broken exported) [@FS-23]; sugarcane 13.3 Mt crushed, 1.30 Mt sugar (2025/26) [@FS-31; @FS-33] | Very low (pulp 1.55% to 2.6% of dry matter) | Traded commodities or low-value feed | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Protein-bearing residues | Brewer's spent grain up to 0.8 to 0.9 Mt wet (derived) [@FS-38; @FS-40; @FS-41]; okara up to 0.6 to 0.66 Mt wet (derived) [@FS-44; @FS-24]; rice distillers' grain (volume unknown) [@RD-22]; seafood by-products (about 68% of the fish, derived from 3.1 kg of pangasius and tilapia per kg of fillet in Vietnam and Brazil) [@FS-48] | 20% to 80% of dry matter | Cattle and pig feed, fishmeal, some export | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Oil and nut crops | Peanut about 380 kt, only 35 kt crushed; copra 31 kt crushed (USDA forecasts for MY2025/26) [@FS-24]; cashew processing (volumes not established) | Press cakes 35% to 50% | Small, scattered, mostly food | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Aquatic and fungal biomass | Seaweed, spirulina, duckweed, mushrooms: we found no reliable national volumes | About 28% (straw mushroom); 35% to 40% (duckweed) [@FS-55; @SCI-36] | Health food, research collections | {VN-direct\|Low} |

For scale: the entire protein content of Vietnam's brewer's spent grain (at most about 35 kt a year) and okara (at most about 40 kt a year) is about 2% of the protein in the soybean meal the feed sector uses (derived from [@FS-38; @FS-40; @FS-41; @FS-44; @MAC-04]). **Local protein-rich residues cannot replace imported soybean meal at scale.** Only microbial conversion of carbohydrate streams, or new protein crops, have the volume to matter.

{{chart:chart-feedstock-volumes}}

## 4.2 Cassava: the largest processable carbohydrate, now contested

**The crop.** Vietnam harvested 10.24 Mt of fresh cassava roots from 499,100 ha in 2025, down 18,600 ha from 2024 [@FS-01] {VN-direct|High}. Annual cassava supply exceeds 18 Mt, about 42% of it (roughly 8 Mt) imported, mainly from Laos and Cambodia [@FS-14] {VN-direct|Medium}. About 85% of roots go to industry: starch, ethanol, monosodium glutamate (MSG) and others [@FS-08] {VN-direct|Medium}.

**The factories.** Estimates of the number of industrial starch factories range from about 100 (Vietnam Cassava Starch Association, reported by the Ministry of Industry and Trade, 2021) to about 120 in 27 provinces (ASEAN Cassava Centre, reported January 2023) and "150+" (Vietnam Cassava Association, 2025) [@FS-04; @FS-02; @FS-07] {VN-direct|Medium}. The ASEAN Cassava Centre gives 11.3 Mt of design capacity and 8.62 Mt of actual root capacity (data year not stated) [@FS-02]. **Tay Ninh alone has 65 to 68 factories and 6.4 Mt a year of root capacity** [@FS-03; @FS-07] {VN-direct|Medium}. Tay Ninh now includes the former Long An province (see [[app-s10-admin-map]]).

**Exports to China.** Vietnam exported about 2.28 Mt of cassava starch to China in the first 11 months of 2025 (+70%), becoming China's largest supplier [@FS-01; @FS-13], and 3.99 Mt of cassava products worth USD 1.27 billion over the year [@FS-01] {VN-direct|High}. China took about 93% [@FS-01] {VN-direct|High}.

**The pulp.** Nobody publishes the national tonnage of cassava pulp (*bã sắn* or *bã mì*). Using a Thai factory material balance (4.4 t of roots and 2.5 t of wet pulp per tonne of starch, at about 80% moisture) and Vietnam's 2025 starch output, we estimate **about 6 Mt of wet pulp in 2025, range 4 to 8 Mt, or about 0.8 to 1.7 Mt of dry matter** (our calculation from [@FS-05; @FS-06; @FS-53; @FS-01]) {VN-adjacent|Low}. Pulp volume moves with starch exports: the 2024 equivalent was only about 3.7 Mt wet.

> **Correction.** Earlier drafts gave 1.7 to 2.1 Mt of wet pulp, which is too low unless it refers to pressed or partly dried pulp. The ratios in circulation disagree mainly because they use different moisture bases. See [[app-s4-feedstocks]] and [[app-m5-changelog]].

**Composition.** Pulp is about 54% to 70% starch and only 1.55% to 2.6% crude protein on a dry basis [@FS-18; @FS-19; @FS-20] {VN-adjacent|High}. All the pulp in Vietnam holds only about 20 to 35 kt of protein (our calculation). It is a **carbon source, not a protein source**: any microbial protein grown on it needs nitrogen bought in.

**Price.** No current gate price is published. The only 2024 signal is an implied value of about VND 1,700/kg from one Tay Ninh factory's pulp revenue [@FS-03] {VN-direct|Low}. Pulp is already sold to cattle and pig farms, dried for feed mills, pelleted, or digested for biogas [@FS-03; @FS-17; @FS-22] {VN-direct|Medium}.

**Cassava is no longer cheap.** By April 2026 fresh-root prices were VND 3,000 to 3,550/kg (30% starch) in Tay Ninh, Dak Lak, Quang Ngai and Gia Lai, about 50 to 90% above April 2025, depending on province. Starch rose from USD 405 to 415/t FOB in January 2026 to USD 520 to 540/t in April [@FS-01; @FS-11; @FS-12] {VN-direct|Medium}. Vedan, the largest cassava-based fermenter, reported that cassava prices "rose sharply" from the fourth quarter of 2025 through the first half of 2026 [@VCO-02] {VN-direct|High}.

**A new competing buyer.** E10 gasoline has been mandatory nationwide since 1 June 2026 [@GT-10] {VN-direct|High}. Three fuel-ethanol plants (Dung Quat in Quang Ngai, the Quang Nam plant now in Da Nang, and Tung Lam in Dong Nai) have a combined design capacity of 830 m3 a day, and Dung Quat plans to switch its feedstock from cassava to maize [@FS-09] {VN-direct|High}. About 80% of E10 ethanol was still imported in mid-2026 [@IND-20] {VN-direct|Medium}. Any plan that assumes cheap cassava roots should be stress-tested against this.

## 4.3 Rice: large, concentrated, and already sold

- **Paddy and bran.** Vietnam harvested 43.5 Mt of paddy in 2025 [@FS-25] {VN-direct|High}. Bran is about 4.35 Mt a year at 10% of paddy (derived from [@FS-27]). In 2025, 1.2 Mt of bran was exported (double 2024) and about 2.8 Mt of bran plus broken rice went into domestic feed [@FS-23] {VN-direct|High}. Bran sold for VND 7,300 to 7,650/kg in An Giang on 19 September 2026 [@FS-26] {VN-direct|Medium}. Full-fat bran is about 11% protein [@FS-56] and 12% to 24% oil [@FS-57] {general|Medium}.
- **Broken rice.** Vietnam exported 0.87 Mt of 100% broken rice in 2025 [@FS-23]. On 19 September 2026, fragrant 100% broken rice sold at USD 368 to 372/t FOB against USD 440 to 445/t for fragrant 5% broken [@FS-26] {VN-direct|Medium}. Broken rice is a food-grade starch at a commodity price, and the total volume is not published.
- **Rice distillers' grain.** Vietnamese research shows dried distillers' grain from rice ethanol and rice liquor holds 55% to 80% protein on a dry basis [@RD-22]. Alkaline extraction recovered 54% to 55% of it in one study [@RD-22] and 90% in another [@RD-23] {VN-direct|Medium}. The national volume of this stream is unknown. It is one of the few protein-rich residues with published Vietnamese extraction data.

**Reading.** Rice bran and broken rice are not free residues. They are traded feed and food commodities with export demand. A rice-protein business in Vietnam buys its raw material at market prices.

## 4.4 Sugar: a surplus, and a cheap clean carbon source

The 2025/26 crop crushed 13.3 Mt of cane for 1.298 Mt of sugar [@FS-31; @FS-33]; about 25 mills were operating in 2024 [@FS-34] {VN-direct|High}. The average domestic sugar price was about VND 16,505/kg in mid-2026, a three-year low and below prices in China, Indonesia and the Philippines [@FS-31; @FS-33] {VN-direct|Medium}. Molasses volume is not published; we estimate 0.55 to 0.72 Mt a year from Indian yield ratios [@FS-37] {general|Low}. Earlier drafts treated Vietnam as short of sugar for fermentation. On 2026 prices, surplus domestic sugar and broken rice are both clean, food-grade carbon sources worth comparing against residues that need pre-treatment.

## 4.5 Protein-bearing side streams: real, but small

- **Brewer's spent grain (*bã bia*).** Beer output of more than 4 billion litres a year (2022) to 4.4 billion litres (2019) implies at most 0.8 to 0.9 Mt of wet spent grain, about 32 to 35 kt of protein assuming about 20% dry matter and 20% protein in the dry matter (derived from [@FS-38; @FS-40; @FS-41]) {VN-adjacent|Low}. Two groups dominate: Heineken (43%) and Sabeco (33.9%) held about 77% of the 2023 beer market [@FS-41] {VN-direct|Medium}. Entobel's insect plant in Ho Chi Minh City (former Ba Ria-Vung Tau) uses Heineken Vietnam by-products [@ECO-01; @ECO-03] {VN-direct|High}. Fresh spent grain spoils in two to three days [@FS-42] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Okara (*bã đậu nành*).** Vietnam uses about 550 kt of soybeans for food a year [@FS-24]. At 1.1 to 1.2 kg of wet okara per kg of beans, that gives at most 0.6 to 0.66 Mt of wet okara (derived from [@FS-44; @FS-45]) {general|Low}. It is scattered across many tofu and soy-milk makers, and its protein was already imported as soybeans.
- **Seafood processing by-products.** Filleting uses about 3.1 kg of pangasius or tilapia per kg of fillet in exporting countries such as Vietnam and Brazil, so about 68% of the fish becomes by-product (derived) [@FS-48] {VN-adjacent|Medium}. Shrimp processing side streams (heads and shells) carry 40% to 65% protein on a dry basis [@FS-49] {general|Medium}. These are animal-origin streams: benchmarks and competitors for alternative protein in feed, not alternative-protein feedstocks. Vietnam exported USD 430 million of fishmeal in 2023, 93.5% to China [@FM-38] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Fermentation co-products.** Vedan's "fertiliser and feed" segment earned USD 27.1 million in 2025 [@VCO-01], and Ajinomoto Vietnam sells liquid and solid feed ingredients, with a permitted liquid capacity of 30,000 m3 a year rising to a proposed 50,000 [@IND-08] {VN-direct|Medium}. Chinese single-cell microbial biomass from glutamic-acid fermentation, at least 70% crude protein, is already imported and sold as a feed protein in Vietnam [@FM-12; @ECO-69] {VN-direct|Low}. Whether Vietnamese MSG plants make a similar protein-rich biomass stream is an open question worth one phone call.

## 4.6 Crops for plant protein

Vietnam has no large protein crop of its own.

- **Soybean:** about 43,000 t on 26,300 ha in 2025, falling [@FS-24] {VN-direct|High}.
- **Peanut:** about 380 kt (USDA forecast for MY2025/26; 388 kt in 2025), of which only 35 kt is crushed (forecast) [@FS-24] {VN-direct|High}.
- **Coconut:** only about 24 to 31 kt of copra crushed a year (USDA 2025 estimate to MY2025/26 forecast) [@FS-24] {VN-direct|High}.
- **Mung bean (*đậu xanh*):** national production was not established. Vietnam imported USD 138 million of dried mung and black gram beans in 2023, 65% from Myanmar [@FORM-08] {VN-direct|Medium}. Mung bean is the main protein ingredient in mass-market *đồ chay* fillings ([[ch02-alt-protein-today]]), so even "domestic" chay protein is partly regional imports.
- **Cashew:** Vietnam is the world's largest cashew processor, largely from imported raw nuts. Broken-kernel tonnage was not established.
- **Coffee pulp:** about 450 kt of dried pulp a year (reported in a 2020 paper, which describes it as exported), mostly burned in dryers or used as fertiliser; caffeine limits its use as feed [@FS-46] {VN-direct|Low}.

**Reading.** A domestic plant-protein ingredient industry cannot rest on a Vietnamese protein crop today. It would process imported beans (as soy-milk and tofu makers already do), or use rice and mung bean at a cost premium, or grow a new crop.

## 4.7 Aquatic and fungal biomass: promising, unmeasured

- **Seaweed:** 827 recorded species; the commercially important genera (Caulerpa, Sargassum, Gracilaria, Ulva, Kappaphycus) are farmed and harvested commercially, including in Khanh Hoa (including former Ninh Thuan). No production volume was found [@FS-51] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Spirulina:** small health-food producers. Vinh Hao in Lam Dong (former Binh Thuan) reports more than 12,000 m2 of cultivation area and about 17 t a year (2013 figure); VN Vastcom in Nghe An about 5 t of biomass a year (2023) [@ECO-52; @ECO-53] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Duckweed:** Vietnamese researchers hold a collection of more than 100 wild duckweed samples (*Spirodela*, *Lemna*, *Wolffia*) [@RD-44] {VN-direct|Medium}, but we found no commercial cultivation, only feed trials [@FS-54] {VN-direct|Low}. Duckweed (*bèo*) is already on the permitted livestock feed list ([[ch07-rules]]). Planning yields should use a conservative 10 to 30 t of dry matter per hectare per year (our assumption; reported averages are about 30 t and maxima up to 100 t) until Vietnamese field data exist [@SCI-36; @SCI-37] {general|Medium}.
- **Mushrooms:** a large smallholder sector on rice straw and sawdust; national output and spent-substrate volumes were not verified in this study [@NOV-78] {VN-direct|Low}.

Any plan built on these streams starts with primary data collection.

## 4.8 Energy and gases

Industrial power costs about USD 0.073 to 0.081/kWh for a plant running around the clock [@COST-01; @COST-03] ([[ch09-economics]]). The grid emits about 0.66 kg of CO2 per kWh (2023 official factor) [@COST-08] {VN-direct|High}, so power-intensive processes carry a high carbon footprint unless they buy renewable power. The revised national power plan targets 28% to 36% non-hydro renewable electricity by 2030 [@GT-11] {VN-direct|High}. Biogas from cassava starch wastewater is used at some starch factories but unquantified, and one ethanol plant plans research on low-carbon methanol from biogenic CO2 [@FS-04; @FS-09] {VN-direct|Low}. Gas-fermentation routes therefore have feedstocks in principle, but no measured supply.

## 4.9 Five rules from the asset map

1. **Carbon is abundant; nitrogen and protein are scarce.** Microbial protein from Vietnamese carbohydrate needs purchased nitrogen (Phu My urea was VND 553,100 per 50 kg bag in March 2026, about USD 425/t at 26,000 VND per USD, and world urea spiked to USD 726/t [@COST-33; @COST-30] {VN-direct|Medium}).
2. **Residues are traded, not free.** Bran, broken rice, pulp, spent grain and okara all have buyers. Model them at a positive price per tonne of dry matter.
3. **Wet residues must be used where they are made.** Pulp, spent grain and okara spoil in days (pulp ensiles well in pits [@FS-18]). This argues for co-location with a starch factory, brewery or soy plant.
4. **Volumes swing with China.** Cassava pulp in 2024 was about 60% of the 2025 volume because starch exports to China jumped. Supply contracts need several factories or storage.
5. **Nobody measures by-products.** No agency publishes national data on starch output, pulp, spent grain, okara, molasses or seafood by-products. A one-page annual return from starch factories, breweries, sugar mills and seafood processors would make the circular-economy case investable (see [[ch27-policy-options]]).

{{chart:chart-feedstock-map}}

**For each reader.**
- **Investors:** the volume thesis for "cheap cassava residue" holds; the price thesis is weaker than earlier drafts assumed. Stress-test for cassava price cycles and E10.
- **Startups:** for pulp-based fermentation, start in Tay Ninh; negotiate on dry-matter basis; budget nitrogen. For spent grain, plan one plant next to one brewery.
- **Manufacturers:** domestic protein-rich residues are too small to replace soybean meal; they suit niche or functional products.
- **Policy makers and international bodies:** a public Vietnam by-product atlas (volume, location, price, composition), updated yearly, is a cheap and missing public good.
- **Researchers:** priority measurements are a Vietnamese pulp material balance across factories and seasons, and duckweed and seaweed productivity on Vietnamese sites.

**Related:** [[app-s4-feedstocks]], [[ch05-industrial-base]], [[ch09-economics]].

data.title: The industrial base: fermentation, feed and food processing
data.summary: Vietnam has large, modern feed, food and brewing industries, but its aerobic fermentation capacity is captive inside three amino-acid makers, and there is no food-grade contract fermentation, open pilot plant, protein-isolate plant or domestic textured-protein extruder. A new venture can borrow feed-mill trial capacity, frozen-food co-packers and GMP-trained people, but must bring its own process equipment or negotiate with an incumbent.
data.body:
# 5. The industrial base: fermentation, feed and food processing

**In one paragraph.** Vietnam's industrial base is large where alternative protein needs buyers and co-packers, and thin where it needs process equipment. Feed mills run at about half their capacity, about six firms make most shrimp feed, and frozen-food processors already make vegetarian lines next to meat. But the sterile, aerated fermentation tanks that biomass and precision fermentation need sit almost entirely inside three amino-acid producers (Vedan, Ajinomoto and Daesang), none of which publicly offers contract manufacturing. We found no food-grade contract fermentation, no open pilot fermenter, no protein-isolate or concentrate plant, and no Vietnamese maker of textured vegetable protein. Soybean crushing is growing fast, but only to make feed.

---

## 5.1 Fermentation: large in volume, captive in practice

**Aerobic fermentation** (stirred, aerated, sterilisable tanks, the kind used for amino acids, yeast and precision fermentation) is concentrated in three groups:

| Group | Location | What it makes | Capacity signals | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vedan Vietnam (Taiwan) | Dong Nai (Long Thanh) | MSG and glutamic acid, lysine, starch, glucose syrup, feed and fertiliser co-products | Glutamic acid nameplate raised to 180,000 t/yr in 2004 (last published); 700 m3 per fermentation tank (tank count not disclosed); Vietnam revenue USD 154.3 M in 2025 (down 7%); capex for equipment replacement only | [@VCO-03; @IND-01; @VCO-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Ajinomoto Vietnam (Japan) | Dong Nai (Bien Hoa) | MSG by fermentation of cassava starch and cane molasses; liquid and solid feed ingredients as co-products | MSG 150,000 t/yr (2023 environmental assessment); liquid feed ingredients 30,000 m3/yr proposed to rise to 50,000 | [@IND-08; @IND-09] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Daesang Vietnam (Miwon, Korea) | Phu Tho (Viet Tri); starch in Tay Ninh | MSG (Miwon) and starch | Over 35,000 t/yr of Miwon seasoning (2020 Korean press, which places the plant in Bac Giang, now part of Bac Ninh) | [@IND-11; @IND-13] {VN-direct\|Low} |

> **Correction.** Earlier notes used Vedan's 1995 glutamic acid nameplate of 36,000 t/yr. The last published nameplate is 180,000 t/yr (2004) [@VCO-03]. Neither is confirmed as current.

Our modelled estimate of installed aerobic, aseptic fermentation volume in Vietnam is **about 11,000 to 34,000 m3**, almost all inside these three groups. Adding anaerobic volume (fuel ethanol about 38,000 to 58,000 m3, brewing about 170,000 to 410,000 m3) gives roughly 220,000 to 500,000 m3 of fermentation vessels in total (modelled estimate from published capacities; see [[app-s5-facilities]] and `fermentation_volume_estimate.csv`) {VN-direct|Low}.

**Other fermentation assets:**
- **Baker's yeast:** AB Mauri at La Nga, Dong Nai (6,000 t/yr in 2019, when it was suspended for a pollution incident; current status not re-checked) and Saf-Viet (Lesaffre), site not confirmed by our sources, capacity undisclosed [@IND-15; @IND-16; @IND-17] {VN-direct|Medium}. Yeast is the closest existing process to yeast single-cell protein, and it is small.
- **Fuel ethanol:** six or seven plants with about 450,000 to 490,000 m3 a year of design capacity; only three ran in mid-2026, and E10 demand is now pulling idle plants back to fuel [@IND-18; @IND-19; @IND-20] {VN-direct|Medium}. Ethanol fermenters are not aerated, so converting one to protein would need a retrofit, and the conversion would compete with E10 economics.
- **Breweries:** Sabeco runs 26 breweries with 2.4 billion litres a year of design capacity (about 60% used in 2024); Heineken's Vung Tau plant has 1.1 billion litres approved to rise to 1.6 billion; Carlsberg planned to raise its Phu Bai plant in Hue from 360 to 600 million litres [@IND-23; @IND-26; @IND-27] {VN-direct|Medium}. They matter for side streams (spent grain, spent yeast) and trained staff, not for aerobic capacity.
- **Biologics:** Vietnam has 12 GMP-WHO veterinary vaccine plants, and Vabiotech makes a recombinant hepatitis B vaccine [@IND-34; @IND-37] {VN-direct|Medium}. A 100-million-dose human vaccine plant (VNVC, technology from Sanofi) is due in Tay Ninh (former Long An) at the end of 2027 [@IND-31; @IND-32] {VN-direct|Medium}. These are sources of GMP skills and quality systems, not tank volume.

**No contract fermentation.** We found no Vietnamese company offering food-grade contract fermentation at pilot or commercial scale, and no public facility that publishes an open pilot-fermentation service [@IND-01; @IND-08; @INF-02; @INF-04; @INF-05] {VN-direct|Medium}. The Food Industries Research Institute's (FIRI) pilot centre in Hanoi lists soy-milk, tofu, juice and powder processes but no fermenters [@INF-02] {VN-direct|High}. This is absence of evidence from published sources and should be tested by direct enquiry. Vedan's falling Vietnamese MSG sales and replacement-only capex [@VCO-01] suggest that the incumbents could have both idle capacity and a motive to talk. That is a hypothesis, not a finding.

## 5.2 Feed: big, half-used, and consolidating

- **Scale and utilisation.** In 2023 there were 269 industrial feed mills with 43.2 Mt a year of design capacity. They produced 20.8 Mt in 2022, about 48% utilisation. Foreign-invested firms owned 90 of the mills, 51.3% of capacity and 62.5% of output [@IND-39] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Aquafeed.** Up to 5.5 Mt of installed capacity at 60% to 70% utilisation in 2025. Six firms (Sheng Long, owned by Haid; C.P.; Uni-President; Tongwei; Grobest; Gromax) supplied about 640 kt of shrimp feed, about 70% or more of a shrimp-feed market of up to 920 kt (our calculation) [@IND-41; @IND-43] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Consolidation in 2025 and 2026.**
  - Royal De Heus bought CJ's regional feed business, CJ Feed & Care (announced 1 October 2025, closed 3 March 2026), covering 17 mills across five countries [@VCO-07; @VCO-08] {VN-direct|High}. De Heus Vietnam now lists 21 plants: 14 livestock, 6 aquafeed and 1 premix [@VCO-09] {VN-direct|Medium}.
  - De Heus opened a marine and cold-water fish feed mill in Vinh Long in July 2026, 84,000 t a year in its first phase (168,000 t a year at design capacity) [@IND-45; @VCO-10] {VN-direct|Medium}.
  - Cargill left aquafeed in May 2025; C.P. opened a 124,800 t/yr shrimp-feed plant in Ca Mau in August 2026 [@IND-42; @IND-43] {VN-direct|Medium}.
  - Skretting Vietnam (Nutreco) and Entobel announced a partnership on 26 November 2025 and began what they describe as Vietnam's first commercial shrimp feed containing insect meal [@VCO-28] {VN-direct|Medium}.

> **Correction.** Earlier notes said De Heus took over 17 CJ plants in Vietnam. The 17 mills are across five countries; the Vietnamese share was not disclosed [@VCO-07].

**What this means.** A new feed protein has relatively few, sophisticated buyers. Spare pelleting capacity is widespread, so feed trials are easy to host. The new plants target high-protein marine and shrimp feeds, which is where fishmeal substitutes earn the most ([[app-s6-feed-market]]).

## 5.3 Soy and protein-ingredient processing

- **Crushing.** VAL (Bunge and Wilmar) at Phu My 1 Industrial Park, Ho Chi Minh City (former Ba Ria-Vung Tau), can crush 2.6 Mt of soybeans a year after a USD 100 million second line in December 2025; city leaders expect it to supply about 30% of domestic soybean meal [@VCO-16; @FORM-10] {VN-direct|Medium}. USDA forecasts national crush rising to 3.0 Mt in 2027 [@MAC-04] {VN-direct|Medium}. **No food-grade defatted flake or soy-protein line is on record.**
- **Protein isolates and concentrates.** We found no soy, pea or rice protein isolate or concentrate plant in Vietnam [@FORM-11] {VN-direct|Medium}. Distributors sell Chinese soy protein and Chinese wheat gluten in 20 to 25 kg bags [@FORM-11; @FORM-13] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Textured vegetable protein (TVP).** No Vietnamese TVP extruder was identified. Chinese extrusion lines of 100 to 2,000 kg/h are marketed in Vietnam, and at least one chay maker says it imports food from partners in the United States, Australia and Canada [@FORM-34; @FORM-35] {VN-direct|Medium}. The only extrusion we documented is feed-grade (for example, Haid's aquafeed plants, including Hai Dai Vinh Long) [@IND-43] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Soy milk and tofu.** Vinasoy (owned by Quang Ngai Sugar) has had 390 million litres a year of soy-milk capacity since its third plant opened in 2017, the figure still given in 2022 [@IND-49; @IND-50], and claims about 80% of the soy-milk market [@IND-48] {VN-direct|Medium}. Tofu is mostly artisanal. One industrial maker, ToFu House in Hung Yen, states a capacity of 150 to 500 t a month and is building model fields of domestic soybeans [@IND-51] {VN-direct|Medium}. Tofu skin (*tàu hũ ky*) comes from craft villages such as My Hoa in Vinh Long, mostly from imported beans [@FORM-14] {VN-direct|Medium}.

## 5.4 Food processors and co-packers

- **Meat and frozen-food processors with vegetarian lines:** Vissan (Ho Chi Minh City; about two-thirds owned by the state trading group SATRA, about a quarter by Masan MEATLife) [@VCO-13; @BUY-04]; CJ Foods Vietnam (Cau Tre and bibigo brands, owned by CJ CheilJedang) [@VCO-12]; Cholimex and SG Food (both in Vinh Loc Industrial Park) [@FORM-27; @FORM-31] {VN-direct|Medium}. These firms make *đồ chay* on the same lines as meat products and are the most plausible co-packers for plant-based products.
- **Private labels:** Saigon Co.op's Coop Select vegetarian lines are made under contract (one line by GN Foods in Tay Ninh) [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. Retail private labels show that chay contract manufacturing already works.
- **Dairy:** Vinamilk, TH and Nutifood all sell plant-based milks; several are blended with cow's milk [@ECO-43; @ECO-45; @AIB-10] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Starch and glucose:** Vedan built 140,000 t a year of glucose syrup capacity in 1995 and sells glucose to third parties; Daesang has run a starch plant in Tay Ninh since 2005 [@VCO-03; @VCO-05; @IND-11] {VN-direct|Medium}. Glucose syrup from cassava is the obvious local carbon source for fermentation, and it already exists.
- **Spray drying:** available in instant-coffee and dairy plants; toll drying for third parties was not documented.

## 5.5 Shared infrastructure and services

- **Parks:** Saigon Hi-Tech Park covers 913 ha with 165 projects and an incubator, an R&D centre and a biotech centre [@INF-06] {VN-direct|High}. Hoa Lac Hi-Tech Park in Hanoi has a 263 ha R&D zone [@INF-25] {VN-direct|Medium}. A 2026 decree lets provinces create high-tech agriculture zones [@INF-23] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Testing:** FIRI's NACEFA laboratory is ISO/IEC 17025-accredited (VILAS 259) and designated to test imported feed ingredients; NIFC is the Ministry of Health's reference food laboratory; QUATEST 3 opened a transaction office in Dong Nai in September 2026 [@INF-03; @INF-10; @INF-13] {VN-direct|High}. No laboratory page we read lists a protein-digestibility assay, which a protein-quality claim or a novel-food dossier needs; NACEFA lists amino-acid analysis by HPLC only (scope and accreditation unconfirmed) ([[ch06-knowledge-talent]]).
- **Feed trials:** the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment (MAE) merged its livestock trial centre, which runs feed trials, with its veterinary-drug testing centre in Hanoi (from 1 October 2026), and reorganised its aquatic centre, which runs aquafeed trials, into one national centre with regional centres in Can Tho and Ho Chi Minh City (2025); both may sell services [@INF-18; @INF-28] {VN-direct|High}.
- **Engineering:** plants are typically designed by foreign firms (Rieckermann designed the VNVC vaccine plant) and fitted out by local contractors (HTG Engineering built utilities and cleanrooms for Ajinomoto) [@IND-31; @IND-64; @INF-24] {VN-direct|Medium}. We found no local maker of sanitary fermenters, extruders or spray dryers.

## 5.6 What an alternative-protein venture can and cannot borrow

{{chart:chart-capability-matrix}}

| Capability | Exists in Vietnam? | Who | Open to third parties? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aerobic, sterile fermentation at scale | Yes (about 11,000 to 34,000 m3, modelled) | Vedan, Ajinomoto, Daesang | No published offer; JV or tolling would need negotiation |
| Food-grade contract fermentation (pilot or commercial) | Not found | n/a | n/a |
| Glucose from cassava starch | Yes | Vedan, others | Yes (Vedan sells glucose) |
| Feed pelleting and extrusion | Yes, about 48% utilised | 269 feed mills | Trials easy to host |
| Food extrusion (TVP, high-moisture) | Not found | n/a | n/a |
| Protein isolate or concentrate | Not found | n/a | n/a |
| Food-grade soy flakes | Not found (crushing is feed-grade) | VAL could in principle | Unknown |
| Frozen chay co-packing | Yes | Vissan, CJ Foods, Cholimex, SG Food, GN Foods | Yes (private labels exist) |
| UHT plant-milk filling | Yes | Vinasoy, Vinamilk, TH, Nutifood | Not documented |
| GMP biologics skills | Yes | Vaccine and veterinary plants | People, not tanks |
| Accredited testing (proximate, contaminants) | Yes | NACEFA, NIFC, Eurofins, QUATEST 3 | Yes |
| Amino-acid profile and digestibility testing | Digestibility not found on laboratory pages; NACEFA lists amino-acid analysis by HPLC (scope and accreditation unconfirmed) | NACEFA (amino acids only) | Likely overseas for now |
| Official feed and aquafeed trials | Yes (state centres, reorganised 2025 to 2026) | MAE centres | Yes (services allowed) |

**For each reader.**
- **Investors:** do not underwrite a thesis that assumes rentable aerobic fermentation in Vietnam. Treat Vedan and Ajinomoto as possible strategic partners (they have tanks, glucose, feed co-product businesses and falling or flat MSG sales), not as vendors.
- **Startups:** the shortest paths to scale are (a) tolling or JV talks with an amino-acid producer; (b) frozen-food co-packers that already make chay; (c) feed-mill trials, since mills have spare capacity. Bring your own extruder or fermenter otherwise.
- **Manufacturers:** a food-grade soy stream from the growing crush sector is the obvious feedstock for Vietnamese TVP; nobody makes it yet.
- **Policy makers and international bodies:** a shared, food-grade pilot facility (fermentation of about 50 to 3,000 litres, extrusion and spray drying) with open-access rules is the clearest missing public good. Saigon Hi-Tech Park or FIRI are natural hosts ([[ch27-policy-options]]).

**Related:** [[app-s5-facilities]] (plant-level data), [[app-s8-labs-talent]] (pilot and testing facilities), [[ch26-plays]].

data.title: Knowledge, talent and shared infrastructure
data.summary: Vietnam's research base sits next to alternative protein rather than inside it: strong in aquafeed trials, yeast protein expression, stem-cell culture, koji genetics and microalgae; near zero in texturisation, mycoprotein, precision fermentation and food cell lines. Its novel-food research intensity is about a quarter to a third of Thailand's.
