The binding gap is shared infrastructure: no open pilot fermentation, no food extrusion line and no protein-digestibility testing.
data.body:
# 6. Knowledge, talent and shared infrastructure

**In one paragraph.** Vietnam is not starting from zero in the sciences that feed alternative protein, but it is starting from almost zero in the technologies that turn them into food. Its universities and institutes publish fish and shrimp feeding trials at regional levels, express proteins (including growth factors used in cultivated-meat media) in yeast, culture human stem cells in serum-free media, engineer the koji mould, and grow microalgae. They publish almost nothing on texturisation, mycoprotein, precision-fermented food proteins or food-grade fish cell lines, and Vietnam's research intensity on novel foods is about a quarter to a third of Thailand's (a quarter on OpenAIRE; about 31% on a broader OpenAlex basket [@HSC-01] {VN-direct|Medium}). The binding constraint is not ideas but shared infrastructure: we found no open pilot fermentation facility, no food extrusion line and no laboratory offering the accredited amino-acid and digestibility tests a protein-quality claim or a novel-food dossier needs.

---

## 6.1 Research output: small in novel food, regional-level in feed

We counted Vietnam-affiliated publications from 2015 to September 2026 in the OpenAIRE scholarly database and compared them with Southeast Asian peers (OpenAlex was rate-limited; method in [[app-s7-research]]). All counts are lower bounds and include some off-topic records.

| Topic (2015 to Sept 2026) | Vietnam | Thailand | Malaysia | Philippines | Singapore |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plant-based or cultivated meat, records (per 10,000 publications) | 9 (0.37) | 49 (1.58) | 61 (1.02) | 10 (0.62) | 112 (2.94) |
| Fishmeal replacement in aquafeed | 10 (0.42) | 14 (0.45) | 28 (0.47) | 11 (0.68) | 6 (0.16) |
| Spirulina / *Arthrospira* | 87 (3.62) | 164 (5.29) | 178 (2.98) | 36 (2.23) | 28 (0.74) |

Source: [@BIB-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. Indonesia is excluded from the intensity comparison because the database indexes many Indonesian national journals.

{{chart:chart-research-benchmark}}

**Reading.** Vietnam's weakness is specific to novel food technologies; in algae and in aquafeed protein replacement it is at the regional level (and the aquafeed count is certainly an undercount; broader term searches found at least 10 and up to about 20 Vietnamese replacement studies [@BIB-06; @RD-01] {VN-direct|Medium}). After reading titles, Vietnam has **zero or near-zero** published work in precision fermentation or recombinant food proteins, mycoprotein, fish or shrimp cell lines for food, and cultivated meat (one 2024 legal analysis), and at most one study on meat-analogue extrusion [@BIB-01; @RD-43] {VN-direct|Medium}. About six Vietnamese papers address plant-based meat products (reviews, a soy-burger shelf-life study, a partly meat-free sausage) [@BIB-01; @RD-26; @RD-27] {VN-direct|Medium}.

> **Correction.** Earlier drafts said no Vietnamese study had reported RNA reduction, mycotoxin testing or protein digestibility. That was too strong: nucleic-acid reduction in spent brewer's yeast (2018), aflatoxin testing in traditional fermented soy (2025) and in vitro digestibility of rice distillers'-grain protein (2025) are all published. What remains true is that none has been applied to a novel microbial biomass, and **no Vietnamese DIAAS or PDCAAS study was found** [@RD-31; @RD-61; @RD-23] {VN-direct|Medium}.

## 6.2 Five adjacent strengths

1. **Aquafeed nutrition trials** (Can Tho University; Research Institute for Aquaculture No. 2; An Giang University). Measured Vietnamese benchmarks include: soy protein concentrate replacing 40% of fishmeal protein in snakehead with no loss of growth; fermented soybean meal with 88.8% protein digestibility in whiteleg shrimp; spent brewer's yeast replacing up to 60% of fishmeal protein in giant freshwater prawn [@RD-46; @RD-47; @RD-48] {VN-direct|Medium}. These are tank trials, but they are exactly the evidence a feed-first play needs.
2. **Recombinant protein expression in *Pichia*** (VNU-HCM University of Science), including three growth factors used in cultivated-meat media (FGF-2, KGF and PDGF-BB) and an alkaline phytase aimed at aquafeed [@RD-36; @RD-37; @RD-38; @RD-35] {VN-direct|Medium}. None of this work has targeted food proteins such as dairy, egg or heme proteins.
3. **Stem-cell culture** (Vinmec), including tests of serum-free and xeno-free media, where only one of four commercial kits worked for cord-blood cells [@RD-39; @RD-40] {VN-direct|Medium}.
4. **Fungal genetics for koji mould and *Cordyceps*** (VNU Hanoi University of Science): transformation systems and gene-deletion tools in *Aspergillus oryzae* [@RD-33; @RD-34] {VN-direct|Medium}.
5. **Microalgae cultivation** (VAST Institute of Biotechnology), including a lab-scale salt-tolerant spirulina strain reaching 48.7% protein (of dry cell weight) [@RD-21] {VN-direct|Medium}.

Two further assets are specific and under-used:
- **Hanoi University of Science and Technology (HUST)** has recovered 90% of the protein from rice distillers' grain (55% to 80% protein on a dry basis) and made protein products from spent brewer's yeast [@RD-22; @RD-23; @RD-32] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **A duckweed research collection** of more than 100 wild samples and a duckweed genome with a Vietnamese first author; we found no protein work on either [@RD-44; @RD-71] {VN-direct|Medium}.

## 6.3 Research gaps Vietnam is well placed to fill

Each of these combines a Vietnamese raw material, species or skill with an absence of published work (detail in [[app-s7-research]]):

1. Food-grade adaptation of striped catfish (*tra*) and shrimp cells. Continuous striped-catfish lines exist in India, but they are serum-dependent virology lines [@SCI-10] {general|High}, and we know of no true continuous shrimp line (the "PmLyO-Sf9" line is part insect) [@SCI-12] {general|Medium}.
2. Low-cost *Pichia*-made growth factors tested on fish cells.
3. Fungal biomass from cassava pulp and peel with a food-grade safety package (cyanide, mycotoxins, RNA, digestibility).
4. Characterised Vietnamese *A. oryzae* (*tương*) strains as biomass-protein hosts, with the strain safety data regulators will ask for (cyclopiazonic acid and 3-nitropropionic acid) [@SCI-19] {general|High}.
5. Texturisation of rice distillers'-grain and broken-rice protein.
6. Protein extraction and feeding trials with Vietnamese duckweed clones.
7. Protein ingredients from salt-tolerant spirulina.
8. Seaweed protein for food and feed.
9. Bacterial protein from pig-farm and cassava-starch biogas.
10. **A DIAAS or PDCAAS reference dataset for Vietnamese protein ingredients** (mung bean, rice, spirulina, catfish side-stream isolates, spent yeast). Pig-based DIAAS values exist abroad (mung bean 86, soy isolate 97, brown rice concentrate 42), but human digestibility of mung bean measured in children was about 20% lower than the pig estimate [@SCI-40; @SCI-41; @SCI-42] {general|High}.
11. Bacterial single-cell protein and fungal meal in pangasius and whiteleg shrimp diets.

## 6.4 Shared infrastructure: the binding constraint

- **Pilot fermentation.** We found no Vietnamese facility that publishes an open, food-grade pilot fermentation service. FIRI's pilot centre in Hanoi lists soy-milk, tofu, juice and powder processes but no fermenters; the HCMC Biotechnology Center lists agriculture and aquaculture technology transfer, not contract fermentation [@INF-02; @INF-04; @INF-05] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Extrusion.** We found no food extruder listed by a Vietnamese university or institute [@RD-01; @INF-02] {VN-direct|Medium}. A team at the Industrial University of Ho Chi Minh City (IUH) published high-moisture meat-analogue work in 2026, so IUH should be checked first [@TIC-21] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Testing.** FIRI's NACEFA laboratory (VILAS 259) lists proximate, contaminant, mycotoxin and microbiology tests and HPLC equipment for amino-acid analysis; the NIFC page we read shows no test scope. No laboratory page we read lists accredited amino-acid profiles or protein digestibility (DIAAS) testing [@INF-03; @INF-10; @INF-11; @INF-13; @INF-14] {VN-direct|Medium}. PDCAAS and DIAAS work will probably need an overseas laboratory for now.
- **Feed trials.** MAE has restructured its state trial centres (a merged livestock and veterinary-drug testing centre in Hanoi, covering feed trials, from 1 October 2026; an aquatic-products centre based in Hanoi with regional branches in Can Tho and Ho Chi Minh City), and both may sell services [@INF-18; @INF-28] {VN-direct|High}. University wet labs (Can Tho, Nha Trang) and private contract labs (ShrimpVet) complement them.
- **Parks.** Saigon Hi-Tech Park (913 ha) has an incubator, an R&D centre and a biotech centre [@INF-06] {VN-direct|High}. A 2026 decree lets provinces create high-tech agriculture zones with R&D and interest-subsidy incentives [@INF-23] {VN-direct|Medium}.

## 6.5 Talent

Degrees in food technology, biotechnology and aquaculture are offered at several universities. Can Tho University alone has a 2026 quota of 860 places in these three programme groups (300, 240 and 320), within a total quota of 11,850 [@INF-15] {VN-direct|High}. We could not sum a national intake (several admissions sites failed or showed quotas only as images) [@INF-15; @INF-21] {VN-direct|High}. The skills gap is specialist rather than general: the literature shows almost no Vietnamese work in extrusion, food-grade downstream processing of microbial biomass, sensory and structure work on meat analogues, protein-quality scoring, or cell culture of fish and livestock cells for food [@RD-01; @BIB-01] {VN-direct|Low}. Startups in those areas will import know-how and people, which adds cost and key-person risk. We found no salary survey for food or biotech engineers.

## 6.6 Research funding

- **NAFOSTED** (national science foundation) and VINIF are both frequently acknowledged in relevant Vietnamese papers; typical grant sizes were not established [@RD-05; @RD-06; @RD-12] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **VINIF** (Vingroup) mainly funds people: about 1,300 master's and doctoral scholarships, 180 postdoctoral fellowships and 117 projects in 2018 to 2023 [@RD-05] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **International:** ACIAR spends about AUD 5.4 million across 23 Vietnamese projects in 2025/26, none on alternative protein [@RD-04] {VN-direct|High}; the GFI research grant programme lists no featured grantee in Vietnam or elsewhere in Southeast Asia on the page we read, and is closed [@RD-02; @RD-03] {general|Medium}; the largest recent open call (Coefficient Giving's alternative-protein R&D request, up to USD 30 million, international applicants welcome) closed on 15 September 2026 [@CAP-57] {general|High}.
- **Law 93/2025** allows acceptance of research risk and liability exemption when procedures are followed, which a national protein-research programme could use [@RD-08; @REG-48] {VN-direct|Medium}.

## 6.7 What this means

- **Researchers:** the fastest route to a visible track record is to point existing tools at food protein: *Pichia* for a food protein, *A. oryzae* biomass on cassava residue, spirulina protein extraction, duckweed protein from the research collection, a DIAAS dataset. Publish in indexed journals with DOIs; much applied Vietnamese work is invisible abroad.
- **Policy makers:** three pieces of shared kit would unlock most gaps: a food-grade pilot fermentation train (about 50 to 3,000 litres with downstream processing), a pilot extrusion line, and amino-acid and digestibility methods added to an accredited laboratory's scope. A directed call on "protein from Vietnamese side streams and species" would turn scattered groups into a network ([[ch27-policy-options]]).
- **Investors and startups:** credible trial partners exist for feed (Can Tho, Nha Trang, the state aquafeed centre) and for side-stream protein (HUST); ask founders for their trial data. Do not assume any Vietnamese partner owns an extruder or a 100-litre-plus food-grade fermenter until confirmed.
- **International bodies:** the GFI research grant page we read lists no featured grantee in Vietnam; the most fundable public goods are a food-grade catfish or shrimp cell-line adaptation project, a Vietnamese protein-quality database and duckweed germplasm protein screening.

**Related:** [[app-s7-research]], [[app-s8-labs-talent]], [[app-s13-science]].

data.title: Rules of the game: routes to market, incentives and reforms
data.summary: Vietnam has no novel-food gate: new protein foods enter through self-declaration, under legal uncertainty and with no way to get an ingredient positively cleared, while feed rules are more open. The new Food Safety Law, due for first comments in October 2026 and considered for passage in May 2027, is a one-off window to add a proportionate new-food procedure.
data.body:
# 7. Rules of the game: routes to market, incentives and reforms

**In one paragraph.** For food, Vietnam has an open door but no gate: there is no novel-food category, so a new protein food is sold through the same self-declaration as tofu, yet the Food Safety Law also treats "new-technology food not yet permitted for circulation" as recallable, and no procedure exists to obtain that permission. The result is legal uncertainty, not prohibition. Precision-fermented proteins now probably count as "products of a GMO" under a January 2026 decree. For feed, the picture is clearer and more open: insects, duckweed, algae and several yeasts are already permitted livestock feed materials, and a trial route exists for new ones, though the aquafeed list has a drafting gap and using unlisted feed materials now draws fines. Labels are mostly settled already: a new goods-label decree (Decree 37/2026) keeps the old rules, voluntary standards set protein and vegetarian claims, and no rule reserves meat or milk words. Incentives favour biotechnology in general and recombinant proteins in particular, but the largest cash support is out of reach, and tariffs give no shelter: Chinese and ASEAN protein ingredients enter duty-free. The new Food Safety Law, due for first comments at the October 2026 National Assembly session and for a vote at the May 2027 session, is the one near-term window to write a proportionate new-food procedure; a clause needs to be in the draft revised between the two sessions, in practice by early 2027. This chapter is a summary; the full register is in [[app-s9-regulation]]. It is not legal advice.

---

## 7.1 Who owns what after the 2025 restructuring

On 1 March 2025 Vietnam cut its ministries to 14. The Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development and the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment merged into the **Ministry of Agriculture and Environment (MAE)**; the Ministry of Science and Technology absorbed the Ministry of Information and Communications; the Ministry of Finance absorbed the Ministry of Planning and Investment [@GT-04; @GT-05; @GT-06] {VN-direct|High}. From 1 July 2025 the country also moved from 63 to 34 provinces and abolished the district tier ([[app-s10-admin-map]]) [@GT-01; @GT-02] {VN-direct|High}.

| Topic | Who decides now | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| Processed food declarations, additives, health supplements, the Food Safety Law revision | Ministry of Health (Vietnam Food Administration) | [@REG-08] |
| Livestock feed (lists, trials) | MAE, Department of Livestock Production and Animal Health; many procedures now with provinces | [@REG-42; @REG-35; @REG-41] |
| Aquafeed (lists, trials) | MAE, Department of Fisheries and Fisheries Surveillance; trial recognition with provinces | [@REG-42; @REG-41] |
| GMO biosafety and genetic resources | MAE | [@REG-18; @REG-60] |
| High-tech lists, standards, sandbox law, IP | Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) | [@GT-06; @REG-47; @REG-48] |
| Tax incentives | Ministry of Finance | [@REG-45] |

After the mergers, one ministry (MAE) holds feed, aquafeed, GMO biosafety, genetic resources and the carbon market, and one (MOST) holds standards, the sandbox, high-tech status and IP. That makes a coordinated approach to new proteins administratively simpler than before 2025.

## 7.2 Food: an open door with no gate

**The law.** The Law on Food Safety (55/2010, amended 2018) prohibits "using raw materials not of the type used for food to process food" (Art 5(1)) and lists "food that is a new-technology product not yet permitted for circulation" among foods subject to recall (Art 55(1)(c)). No implementing text defines a new-technology product or says how permission is obtained [@REG-01] {VN-direct|High}.

**The procedure in force.** Market entry still runs on Decree 15/2018 [@REG-02; @REG-06] {VN-direct|High}:
- *Self-declaration* (Art 4 to 5) for processed pre-packaged food, additives and processing aids: the firm files its own product specification with a lab test report and may sell immediately. Ingredients made or imported only for a firm's own production are exempt.
- *Registration* (Art 6 to 8) for health supplements (21 working days at MOH), medical and special-diet foods, products for children under 36 months, and additives with new uses or not on the permitted list (7 working days).
- **No provision covers foods with no history of use or new ingredients.**

**The suspended replacement.** Decree 46/2026 (January 2026) and Resolution 66.13/2026, designed to replace much of Decree 15/2018 and tighten declarations and import inspection, caused port congestion and were suspended in February and April 2026 until a new Food Safety Law takes effect [@REG-05; @REG-06; @REG-08] {VN-direct|High}.

**The new law.** The Ministry of Health's draft revised Food Safety Law, as notified to the WTO as G/SPS/N/VNM/187 on 3 August 2026, had 71 articles in 8 chapters, with a stated approval target of October 2026 and entry into force on 1 January 2027 [@REG-12; @REG2-04] {VN-direct|Medium}. Under the 2026 legislative programme, the National Assembly will review it at the second 2026 session, as a press report of 22 September 2026 noted [@REG-14] {VN-direct|Medium}. On 24 September 2026 the National Assembly Standing Committee settled the timetable: first comments at the October 2026 session and consideration for passage at the May 2027 session, on a draft that now has 76 articles in 9 chapters [@APR-07] {VN-direct|Medium}. The law will therefore pass in two readings, and the 1 January 2027 start date in the WTO notice cannot hold (our reading). The window to add a new-food clause runs from the October session into early 2027, while the draft is revised between readings. The new draft adds risk-based classification, traceability for high-risk foods, duties for collective meal providers and conditions for online food delivery; the press report does not mention new foods [@APR-08] {VN-direct|Medium}.

{{kn:kn-food-law-window}}

Government press describes two product groups: foods that must register a declaration or declare an applied standard before sale, and foods needing no declaration, both under post-market surveillance. The drafters rejected making all pre-packaged foods register [@REG2-05; @REG2-06] {VN-direct|Medium}. **None of the summaries, submissions or stakeholder comments we read mentions novel food, new ingredients, history of use or a sandbox.** We could not read the full draft text [@REG2-04; @REG2-05; @REG2-06; @APR-07] {VN-direct|Medium}.

**What this means.** Ordinary plant-based and fermented foods from known ingredients face no pre-approval, now or (as described) under the new law. A genuinely new ingredient, such as a fungal biomass from a strain with no food history, can be self-declared, but an inspector could treat it as "not a food-type raw material" or a "new-technology product not yet permitted", and there is no way to get it cleared in advance. Investors should price this as enforcement-discretion risk. Founders should talk to the Vietnam Food Administration in writing before launch.

## 7.3 Precision fermentation and the GMO rules

Decree 43/2026 (effective 26 January 2026) overhauled the GMO rules [@REG-18; @REG-21] {VN-direct|High}:
- one MAE procedure now certifies a GMO for both food and feed use, with 67 working days of expert review, or 17 working days if at least five developed OECD or G20 countries already allow it [@REG-18; @REG-23] {VN-direct|Medium};
- gene-edited organisms without foreign DNA are self-assessed and notified;
- a new **certificate for GMOs used in closed production** (Art 37a), with conditions on donor and recipient safety, containment and waste treatment, filed on Forms 32 and 33 with MAE; the review time, fee and validity were not published in the texts we read [@REG2-11; @REG2-12] {VN-direct|High};
- "product of a GMO" now means a product made from a GMO that contains GM genetic material **"or protein from the modified gene"** [@REG2-11] {VN-direct|High}.

A purified recombinant protein is, literally, protein from a modified gene. **A precision-fermented protein is therefore probably a "product of a GMO" in Vietnam, even if no DNA remains.** GM labelling applies only when a GM ingredient exceeds 5% of total ingredients, and not where neither the modified gene nor its product can be detected (Decree 15/2018 Art 10; Joint Circular 45/2015 Art 1) [@REG-02; @LBL-10; @REG-18] {VN-direct|High}. A low-dose use such as lactoferrin at about 0.08% of an infant formula is far below the trigger (our calculation) [@LBL-25] {VN-direct|Medium}, so the label question bites on high-inclusion uses and on whether "non-GMO" claims stay lawful. Making it in Vietnam needs the closed-production certificate. No text says whether the purified protein also needs a GMO food-use certificate, which is written for organisms rather than products. This is the single most important open legal question for precision fermentation in Vietnam, and a joint MAE and Ministry of Health clarification would settle it ([[ch27-policy-options]]).

## 7.4 Labelling, claims, fortification and halal

- **The label decree changed; the rules did not.** Decree 37/2026 (23 January 2026) replaced the goods-label Decree 43/2017 and its amendment, Decree 111/2021 [@LBL-07; @LBL-08] {VN-direct|Medium}. Its text keeps the two rules that matter most for new proteins: a product name must not mislead about the nature or composition of the goods, and any ingredient used in the name must be quantified on the label (Art 11 and 13(4) of Decree 43/2017, carried over) [@LBL-06; @LBL-09] {VN-direct|Medium}. We could not read the new label chapter, so its article numbers are unknown.
- **Protein is on every label.** Since 1 January 2026 every non-exempt pre-packaged food must declare energy, protein, carbohydrate, fat and sodium. Circular 30/2026/TT-BYT replaced Circular 29/2023/TT-BYT on 10 July 2026 with the same core rules; foods made by small food businesses are exempt [@LBL-01; @LBL-02] {VN-direct|High}.
- **Claims are set by voluntary standards.** TCVN 14429:2025 (from Codex) allows "source of protein" at 5 g and "high protein" (*cao đạm*) at 10 g per 100 g, or 2.5 g and 5 g per 100 kcal (our calculation from the 50 g reference value in TCVN 7088:2025) [@LBL-03; @LBL-04] {VN-direct|High}. A content claim needs no registration and no advertising approval [@REG-02; @LBL-19] {VN-direct|High}. TCVN 13625:2023 defines vegetarian and vegan claims, but its "vegetarian" allows egg, milk and honey and it says nothing on alliums, so it is broader than Buddhist *chay* (vegetarian food) [@LBL-15] {VN-direct|High}.
- **No reserved names.** No rule reserves *thịt* (meat), *sữa* (milk) or *phô mai* (cheese) for animal products; a name must only not mislead, and makers already qualify meat words, as in *Heo hầm chay* (chay stewed pork) [@FORM-01]. The new dairy regulation QCVN 28:2026/BCT covers dairy only, and TCVN 12443:2018 sets a floor of 2.0 g of protein per 100 ml for the name *sữa đậu nành* (soy milk) [@LBL-16; @LBL-17; @FTR-06; @BUY-05] {VN-direct|Medium}. No standard sets a minimum meat content for processed meats (TCVN 7049, 7050 and 7048:2020), so a product with a plant extender keeps its meat name, with the named meat's share printed [@LBL-11; @LBL-12; @LBL-13] {VN-direct|High}.
- **No allergen list.** Vietnam has no mandatory allergen list; labels need only generic "warning information" [@REG2-24; @REG2-25] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Fortification reaches no protein food.** Decree 09/2016 makes iodised salt, iron and zinc in wheat flour used in processing, and vitamin A in cooking oil, mandatory; tofu, textured soy and soy milk are not vehicles [@NQR-02] {VN-direct|Medium}. A 2025 draft amendment concerned iodised salt in fish sauce, and we found no amending decree [@NQR-03] {VN-direct|Low}. Processed pre-packaged food self-declares (Decree 15/2018 Art 4) unless it falls under Art 6 (health supplements, medical foods, special-diet foods and products for children up to 36 months), which must register; that a fortified food follows the same rule is our inference [@NQR-04] {VN-direct|High}.
- A voluntary national halal framework has been in force since 1 June 2026 (Decree 127/2026); it is silent on fermentation-derived or GM-derived ingredients [@REG-27] {VN-direct|High}.

## 7.5 Feed: more open, with two traps

**Livestock and poultry feed.** The permitted raw-material list (Circular 21/2019 Appendix VI as amended by Circular 31/2022) already includes **insects**, aquatic plants including **duckweed (*bèo*) and algae**, and since February 2023 **inactive yeasts** (Torula or Candida yeast, yeast grown on molasses, and by-products of amino-acid production) [@REG-32; @REG-33] {VN-direct|High}. These need no feeding trial, only a certified factory, a conformity declaration against the feed contaminant standard QCVN 01-190:2020 and a label [@REG-36; @REG-29; @REG-32] {VN-direct|High}. We found no amendment to the list since the yeast entries were added in February 2023, and it has no entry for bacterial single-cell protein or filamentous fungal biomass [@REG-33; @REG2-07; @REG2-09] {VN-direct|Medium}.

**A new material needs a trial.** Feed containing a "new substance" must be trialled under the Law on Animal Husbandry (Art 37) and Circular 94/2025. The livestock department approves the trial protocol (15 plus 5 working days) and recognises the result (15 plus 5 working days); the recognised result is the basis for adding the material to the list, which is updated annually [@REG-29; @REG-34; @REG-32] {VN-direct|High}. Agency time is about 40 working days; the trial itself and the wait for the list update come on top. **Our estimate of the total is 6 to 18 months; that is an estimate, not a documented timeline.** Results of recognised state research projects are exempt from a separate trial (Art 37(2)) [@REG-29] {VN-direct|High}.

> **Correction.** Earlier drafts attributed feed trials to Article 11 of Decree 13/2020 and quoted a 12 to 18 month timeline. Article 11 covers factory inspections; trials come from the Law on Animal Husbandry and Circular 94/2025, and no text gives a total duration [@REG-30; @REG-34].

**Trap 1: the aquafeed list.** Aquafeed has its own permitted list (Circular 16/2026 Appendix II) and its own trial rule: under the Law on Fisheries (Art 35(1)), aquafeed containing any raw material "not on the list" must be trialled [@REG2-01; @REG2-02] {VN-direct|High}. **The appendix has no raw-material section at all.** It lists chemicals, bioactives, 30 microorganisms (including *Candida utilis*, *Pichia farinosa*, *Saccharomyces* and *Aspergillus oryzae*), vitamins and enzymes, but not insect meal, single-cell protein, microalgae, duckweed or fermented soybean meal [@REG2-01] {VN-direct|High}. Read literally, the law catches every raw material, including fishmeal; practice evidently differs. A startup cannot tell from the texts whether its ingredient needs an aquafeed trial. A written opinion from the Department of Fisheries is the cheapest fix.

**Trap 2: fines.** Since 5 August 2026, using a feed raw material not on the permitted list costs VND 10 to 20 million per material, plus a one-to-three-month suspension of feed production and forced repurposing of the material, or destruction if that is impossible (Decree 211/2026) [@REG2-10] {VN-direct|High}. Running the trial first is now clearly worth its cost.

**Provinces decide more.** Since July 2025 and January 2026, provincial chairs handle feed-factory certificates, supplement-feed reviews (15 working days), import licences for unlisted feed (10 working days), import inspection, and recognition of aquafeed trial results [@REG-35; @REG-41] {VN-direct|High}. The choice of province now affects time to market.

## 7.6 Routes to market at a glance

{{chart:chart-route-to-market}}

| Product | Route today | Documented agency time | Main open risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plant-based food from known ingredients | Self-declaration | Immediate | Transition to the new law (vote considered May 2027); no allergen list or reserved names |
| Koji or traditional mould fermentation on food substrates | Self-declaration | Immediate | Strain and mycotoxin documentation |
| Fungal biomass or mycoprotein food | Self-declaration; no pre-clearance possible | Immediate, with legal risk | "Not a food-type raw material" or "new-technology product" |
| Microalgae food | Self-declaration, or health-supplement registration | Immediate or 21 working days | New species as for fungal biomass |
| Precision-fermented protein, imported | Self-declaration or own-use exemption; GM label above 5% of ingredients | Immediate | Whether a GMO food-use certificate is also needed |
| Precision-fermented protein, made in Vietnam | Closed-production GMO certificate, then food route | Not published | Timeline, fee, issuing level |
| Cultivated meat or seafood | No national route; Hanoi sandbox is the most concrete option | Not published | Whether a city sandbox can set aside national food law |
| Insect meal, duckweed or algae meal, yeast protein: livestock feed | Listed: factory certificate and conformity declaration | Factory about 35 working days | Heavy metals if grown on effluent |
| Same materials: aquafeed | Not on the aquafeed list; a trial may formally be required | 20 days + trial + 10 working days | Ask the Department of Fisheries in writing |
| Bacterial single-cell protein or new microbial biomass | New substance: trial, recognition, annual list update | About 40 working days plus trial | Unlisted use now fined |

Sources: [@REG-02; @REG-29; @REG-30; @REG-32; @REG-34; @REG-35; @REG-36; @REG-37; @REG-38; @REG-40; @REG-41; @REG2-01; @REG2-02; @REG2-10; @REG2-11; @REG2-16; @REG2-17] {VN-direct|Medium}. The full table with legal bases is in [[app-s9-regulation]] and `routes.csv`.

## 7.7 Incentives

- **Corporate income tax.** The Law on Corporate Income Tax 67/2025 (effective 1 October 2025) gives 10% for 15 years plus four years' exemption and nine years at 50% to high-tech enterprises and new projects applying listed high technology; agricultural and aquatic processing gets preferential rates [@REG-45] {VN-direct|Medium}. The guiding Decree 320/2025 adds two tests that matter here: agricultural processing exemptions need agricultural or aquatic raw materials of at least 30% of production cost (a cassava-based fermentation plant probably passes; one on imported refined sugar may not, our interpretation), and products made with technology applied for the first time in Vietnam get three years of exemption once the novelty is confirmed [@REG2-18] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **The high-technology list.** Decision 23/2026 (effective 1 July 2026) lists synthetic biology, new-generation microbial technology, tissue and cell technology in agriculture, and **"technology for producing recombinant proteins, enzymes and monoclonal antibodies"** as priority high technologies, and recombinant proteins and microbial products among encouraged products. There is no item for alternative protein, food or feed as such [@REG-47] {VN-direct|High}.
- **The Investment Support Fund is out of reach.** Decree 182/2024 requires at least VND 12,000 billion of capital or VND 20,000 billion of annual revenue for high-tech product projects, and VND 3,000 billion for R&D centres [@REG-46] {VN-direct|High}. No alternative-protein project in Vietnam is near these sizes.
- **VAT works against new feed proteins.** Feed is "not subject to VAT" since 1 July 2025, so a feed-protein producer cannot reclaim VAT paid on equipment, power and inputs; a food-ingredient producer can [@COST-24] {VN-direct|High}. We estimate this adds about 5% to 10% to taxed input costs (see [[ch09-economics]]).
- **Tariffs give no shelter.** Soybean meal and feed maize have been duty-free since March 2025; fishmeal and soybeans were already at 0% [@REG2-21; @REG2-23] {VN-direct|Medium}. Food protein ingredients carry small most-favoured-nation (MFN) duties: wheat gluten 10%, full-fat soy flour 8%, protein concentrates and textured protein 5%, protein substances 3%, active yeast 10%, inactive yeast and dead single-cell organisms 7% [@REG2-20; @REG2-23; @FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}. These rates apply only to origins without a trade agreement, chiefly the United States. Chinese and ASEAN product pays 0% on all of these lines (HS 1109, 1208.10, 2106.10, 3504, 2102.10, 2102.20 and 2304) under ACFTA and RCEP in 2025 to 2027 and at 0% under ATIGA, and Korean product pays 0% on the protein lines under AKFTA, with a certificate of origin [@FTR-32; @FTR-33] {VN-direct|Medium}. So a domestic textured-protein, isolate or single-cell-protein maker has no tariff edge over Chinese product. {{kn:kn-fta-duty-china}}

## 7.8 Sandboxes

The Law on Science, Technology and Innovation (93/2025, effective 1 October 2025) allows controlled testing of technologies and products "not yet regulated or differing from current law" for up to three years, extendable once, with liability exemptions for regulators and implementers who follow the rules [@REG-48; @REG2-13] {VN-direct|High}. **No national implementing procedure exists yet**; the four decrees guiding the law do not set one up [@REG2-14; @REG2-15] {VN-direct|High}. Hanoi does have one: Resolution 29/2025 sets the procedure under the Capital Law, and Decision 6150 (December 2025) lists biotechnology and high-tech agriculture as priority fields, approved by the Hanoi People's Committee [@REG2-16; @REG2-17] {VN-direct|High}. Hai Phong (Decision 248/2025) and Da Nang (Resolution 20/2026) have issued controlled-testing rules too [@REG2-16] {VN-direct|Low}. The Hanoi sandbox is the most concrete route we found for a supervised cultivated-meat or precision-fermentation pilot, though whether a city sandbox can set aside national food law has not been tested.

## 7.9 Strategies: biotechnology yes, alternative protein by name no

- Resolution 36-NQ/TW (2023) targets a biotechnology industry worth 7% of GDP by 2030 and replacement of at least 50% of imported biotech products [@REG-51] {VN-direct|High}.
- Resolution 57-NQ/TW (December 2024) targets R&D spending of 2% of GDP by 2030 and pilot mechanisms for firms to test new technology under state supervision [@REG-50] {VN-direct|High}.
- The livestock strategy (Decision 1520/2020) targets 30 to 32 Mt of industrial feed by 2030 and encourages biotech feed materials and by-products such as brewery waste and cassava residue to replace imports [@REG-54] {VN-direct|High}.
- The food-systems transformation plan (Decision 300/2023) targets a 10% cut in food-system greenhouse gas emissions against 2020 [@REG-55] {VN-direct|Medium}.

**None of these names alternative, novel or microbial protein** [@REG-51; @REG-54; @REG-55] {VN-direct|High}. The policy language supports the category without committing to it.

## 7.10 Genetic resources and strains

Commercial use of Vietnamese genetic resources, including microorganisms isolated from Vietnamese fermented foods or cassava waste, needs an access licence (a council review of up to 90 days, then a decision within 15 days) and benefit sharing of at least 1% of annual product revenue or 2% of the value of an IP transfer (Decree 59/2017) [@REG-60] {VN-direct|High}. Any "indigenous strain" business model must budget for this.

## 7.11 How neighbours built their routes

- **Singapore:** pre-market approval for foods without 20 years of use as food; supplying an unapproved novel food has been an offence since 28 November 2025 [@REG-63] {VN-adjacent|High}. Singapore approval gives no legal status in Vietnam.
- **Thailand:** a novel-food notification (2016) with safety assessments done by FDA-recognised assessment units, separate forms for cultivated meat and "non-novel" foods, and a published approved list [@REG2-26] {VN-adjacent|Medium}.
- **South Korea:** amended an existing instrument (temporary standards for new food ingredients) in about nine months (May 2023 to February 2024) to open applications for cell-cultured ingredients in February 2024 [@RGN-19; @RGN-21; @RGN-34] {VN-adjacent|Medium}.
- **Vietnam's own model:** the 2026 GMO decree already contains a reliance lane (17 working days if five developed countries approve). A similar lane for new foods approved by reference regulators would not be a foreign import.

See [[ch03-regional]] and [[app-s3-regional]].

## 7.12 What this means

- **The binding constraint depends on the pathway.** Food from known ingredients: none. New food ingredients: legal uncertainty, with no positive clearance. Precision fermentation: GMO product status. Cultivated: no route. Feed: relatively open for listed materials, with the aquafeed ambiguity and new fines for unlisted ones.
- **The window is now.** A one-line delegation clause in the new Food Safety Law ("the Government shall regulate new foods and new food ingredients"), with the detail in the implementing decree, is cheap and only possible while the draft is before the National Assembly: from first comments in October 2026 to the vote considered in May 2027, so in practice until early 2027 [@APR-07] {VN-direct|Medium}. Without it, the next chance may be years away ([[ch27-policy-options]]).
- **Investors:** ask for written regulator opinions (Vietnam Food Administration; Department of Fisheries; MAE on GMO status) as diligence items.
- **Startups:** choose products whose inputs are already listed (feed) or have food history (food); choose your province deliberately; budget for benefit sharing if you commercialise a Vietnamese strain.
- **International bodies:** technical help for a Thai-style assessment-unit model and a reliance lane fits the 2026 to 2027 drafting window.

**Related:** [[app-s9-regulation]], [[ch27-policy-options]], [[app-s10-admin-map]].

data.title: Capital
data.summary: Only one alternative-protein deal in Vietnam has exceeded USD 5 million: Entobel's insect-meal plant, financed by local private equity, a small development-finance ticket and a seafood exporter's offtake. Agritech venture capital in Vietnam was about USD 1 million in 2025. New state venture funds exist but are small. Globally, alternative-protein investment is at a cyclical low and has shifted towards fermentation and ingredients.
data.body:
# 8. Capital

**In one paragraph.** Disclosed investment in Vietnamese alternative protein amounts to one real deal: Entobel's USD 32.5 million insect-meal project, financed by Mekong Capital, Dragon Capital and the IFC, with a seafood exporter as anchor buyer. We found no disclosed institutional venture round for any Vietnam-based plant-based, fermentation, microalgae or cultivated company. Vietnamese strategic money has gone abroad instead. Vietnam's venture market raised about USD 509 million in 2025, of which agriculture took about USD 1 million, and there have been no VC- or PE-backed technology IPOs in 2025 or the four years before, so exits run through trade sales to strategic buyers. New state venture funds (national, Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi) can now accept losses but are small. Globally, alternative-protein investment fell to USD 881 million in 2025 and is shifting towards fermentation and upstream ingredients, which is the part of the value chain where Vietnam's advantages lie.

---

## 8.1 The deal record in Vietnam

| Date | Company | What | Round | Amount | Investors | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019 to 2023 | Cricket One | Cricket protein (food and feed) | Seed (2019), pre-Series A (2020), Series A (2023) | Undisclosed; pre-Series A (Corecam) and Series A each described as "seven-figure" | 500 Startups, Masik, Corecam, others | [@CAP-11; @CAP-12; @CAP-13] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| 2022 to 2023 | Entobel | Black soldier fly insect meal | Series B plus IFC upstream agreement | About USD 32.5 M: Mekong Enterprise Fund IV USD 25 M, Dragon Capital USD 5 M, IFC USD 2.5 M | Mekong Capital, Dragon Capital, IFC | [@CAP-01; @CAP-02; @CAP-03; @CAP-04; @VCO-20] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| 2017 to 2021 | Emmay | Mushroom-based protein foods | Three angel rounds plus two grants from US funds | About USD 0.25 M across the three angel rounds; grants undisclosed (company claim) | Undisclosed | [@CAP-15] {VN-direct\|Low} |
| 2021 | Shiok Meats (Singapore), Avant Meats (Hong Kong/Singapore) | Cultivated seafood | Strategic minority stakes | Undisclosed | Vinh Hoan (Vietnam) | [@CAP-16; @CAP-17] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| 2024 | INNOHAS (Korea) | Plant-based meat | Undisclosed stake | Undisclosed | VinaCapital Ventures | [@CAP-18] {VN-direct\|Medium} |

> **Correction.** Earlier drafts said Entobel raised "about USD 36 million" and that the IFC invested about USD 10 million. The documented total is about USD 32.5 to 33 million, and the IFC's ticket was USD 2.5 million, structured as an "Upstream Collaboration Agreement" (project 46903). A USD 10 million IFC equity proposal from January 2022 does not appear to have closed at that size [@CAP-03; @CAP-04; @VCO-20] {VN-direct|Medium}.

**We found no disclosed institutional venture round for any Vietnam-based plant-based meat, plant-based dairy, precision-fermentation, microalgae or cultivated-meat company** (coverage was limited by our search tools; absence in our log means "not found"). Emmay, a mushroom-based protein maker, reported three angel rounds totalling about USD 250,000 by 2021 (company claim) [@CAP-15] {VN-direct|Low}. Vietnamese strategic money has gone outward: Vinh Hoan into Singapore and Hong Kong cultivated-seafood companies, VinaCapital Ventures into a Korean plant-based company [@CAP-16; @CAP-17; @CAP-18] {VN-direct|Low}.

## 8.2 The Entobel template

Entobel is the only proven financing template for an alternative-protein asset in Vietnam [@CAP-01; @CAP-04; @ECO-05; @VCO-28] {VN-direct|Medium}:
1. **A feed product**, sold business-to-business into aquafeed, not a consumer brand.
2. **A local side-stream feedstock** (brewery by-products) next to the plant.
3. **Local private equity** as lead (Mekong Capital), with a local co-investor (Dragon Capital).
4. **A small development-finance ticket** to de-risk and signal (IFC, USD 2.5 million), with a second DFI, Proparco, backing the lead fund as a limited partner in Mekong Enterprise Fund IV [@CAP-01; @CAP-04; @CAP-47] {VN-direct|High}.
5. **A strategic offtake** from a seafood exporter (Vinh Hoan, at least 15,000 t over 2025 to 2027) and, later, a feed-major partnership (Skretting, November 2025).

The IFC noted in 2023 that private investors remained cautious because insect meal had not yet proved it could compete with fishmeal and soy on scale and price [@CAP-06] {VN-direct|Medium}. Replicating the template needs a company that can show a path to about USD 20 million or more of capital expenditure and a named anchor buyer.

## 8.3 Vietnam's venture and private-equity market

| Year | Venture capital | Agriculture VC | Climate-tech VC | Private equity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | USD 529 M | USD 8 M | USD 25 M (4 deals) | n/a |
| 2024 | USD 398 M | USD 74 M (mostly one deal) | USD 23 M (10 deals) | about USD 1.7 B of buyouts |
| 2025 | USD 509 M (103 deals) | USD 1 M (about 0.2% of VC) | USD 35 M (7 deals) | USD 3.96 B (46 deals, a record) |

Sources: [@CAP-20; @CAP-21; @CAP-22] {VN-direct|Medium}. Definitions differ between reports; a separate climate-tech report counts about USD 98 to 100 million in 2024 because it includes a USD 70 million agrifood supply-chain deal (Techcoop) as climate [@CAP-25; @CAP-19] {VN-direct|Medium}.

{{chart:chart-vn-vc-agritech}}

- Consumer-staples private equity reached a ten-year high of about USD 1.2 billion in 2025, while there were **no technology IPOs in 2025 or the four years before** [@CAP-21; @CAP-22] {VN-direct|Medium}. A food or ingredient company's realistic exit is a trade sale to a strategic buyer or a private-equity buyout.
- Plausible strategic acquirers by fit (not verified as interested) include Masan, Vinamilk, TH, Nutifood, Vinasoy/Quang Ngai Sugar, C.P. Vietnam, De Heus, Vinh Hoan, Minh Phu, Ajinomoto and Vedan. Revealed interest is verified only for Vinh Hoan, CJ CheilJedang (co-investor in Shiok) and VinaCapital [@CAP-16; @CAP-17; @CAP-18] {VN-direct|Low}.

## 8.4 Development finance

The IFC is the only development finance institution we found with a direct Vietnamese alternative-protein ticket (Entobel, USD 2.5 million). Its other Vietnamese agribusiness deals we found run from about USD 20 million to 40 million (for example a USD 40 million warehouse-finance facility for TTC AgriS in 2023, which it helped arrange with SMBC), and it supported Vietnam's first blue bond (SeABank, USD 25 million, 2024) [@CAP-04; @CAP-41; @CAP-43] {VN-direct|High}. ADB Ventures (tickets of USD 0.1 million to 4 million, climate lens) has backed insect protein and microbial oils elsewhere in Asia but has no Vietnamese agrifood deal [@CAP-45; @CAP-46] {VN-direct|High}. Proparco reaches Vietnamese food businesses as an LP in local funds, for example Mekong Enterprise Fund IV, Entobel's lead investor [@CAP-47; @CAP-01] {VN-direct|High}. Other DFIs (FMO, DEG, BII, JICA, KfW, Finnfund, Norfund) were not verified.

## 8.5 State capital: new rules, small funds

- **Decree 264/2025** (in force 14 October 2025) lets national and local venture funds invest directly or as funds-of-funds, accept losses of up to 50% of charter capital per investment cycle, run cycles of up to 10 years (15 for strategic technology), and exempts managers from liability for "objective risk" losses [@CAP-29; @CAP-30] {VN-direct|High}. The national fund (at least VND 500 billion of initial state capital) was still at proposal stage in June 2026 [@CAP-30; @CAP-31] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Ho Chi Minh City's venture fund** has VND 500 billion (about USD 19 to 20 million; 40% state), lists biotechnology as a priority and planned its first one or two investments for the fourth quarter of 2026 [@CAP-32; @CAP-33] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Hanoi's venture fund** was established in April 2026 with VND 230 billion (47.8% state) and a cap of 5% of the fund per investment (about USD 0.45 million); high-tech agriculture and biotechnology are among its priorities [@CAP-34; @CAP-35] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **NATIF** (National Technology Innovation Fund) subsidises up to 50% of loan interest for up to five years on loans from partner banks, with priority for profitable, low-risk borrowers; Round 1 of 2026 closed on 20 September [@CAP-37; @CAP-38] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Credit:** Decree 156/2025 gives organic and circular agriculture credit treatment similar to high-tech agriculture (unsecured loan limits, risk handling) [@CAP-39] {VN-direct|Medium}.

These tickets fit pilot plants, not production plants. The state has not yet named alternative protein or biomanufacturing as a fund priority.

## 8.6 Grants and philanthropy

- **Coefficient Giving's alternative-protein R&D request** (up to USD 30 million across two rounds; USD 0.1 million to 5 million per award; for-profits and international applicants eligible) closed on 10 August and 15 September 2026, with decisions due by the end of 2026. Its topics included fish flavour, off-flavours, fat alternatives and egg replacement [@CAP-57] {general|High}.
- The **GFI Research Grant Program** is closed with no reopening date [@CAP-50] {general|High}; we found no Navigation Fund alternative-protein request on its pages [@CAP-58] {general|Medium}.
- The **Bezos Earth Fund** has committed USD 1 billion to its Future of Food programme, including grants on AI for alternative protein, with no open call found [@CAP-61] {general|Medium}. Its Bezos Centre for Sustainable Protein at the National University of Singapore cites potential impact for "East and South-East Asia's 2.3 billion consumers" [@AFN-15] {general|Medium}.
- **Nova Vista Foundation's Protein Innovation request for proposals** (USD 10 million; announced 7 August 2026, closed 15 September 2026) funds policy and market shaping: public procurement of innovative protein products, advance market commitments and retailer protein-ratio targets. It excludes whole-food plant-based work, culture change, individual diet change and shifts to smaller animals. Its priority geographies for added policy staff are "high-innovation Asian economies (including but not limited to Japan and South Korea)", Germany and the Nordics; Vietnam is not named [@AFN-04; @AFN-05] {general|High}.
- **No major alternative-protein funder names Vietnam as a priority.** GFI APAC's 2025 report card does not mention Vietnam and its team page lists no one covering it; the 2026 ReRoot Asia diet-change fund published no Vietnam-specific application guide; ACE's July 2025 Movement Grants had no Vietnamese grantee [@AFN-11; @AFN-12; @AFN-29; @AFN-28] {VN-direct|Medium}. See [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]] for which routes fit which funder.
- **ACIAR** funds 23 Vietnamese projects (AUD 5.4 million in 2025/26), commissioned through Australian partners, none on alternative protein [@CAP-67] {VN-direct|High}.
- **Accelerators:** Better Bite Ventures (USD 100,000 to 200,000 cheques) and Big Idea Ventures (USD 200,000 through its programme) are the regional early-stage specialists; the ProVeg Incubator offers up to USD 300,000 including in-kind support [@CAP-63; @CAP-62; @CAP-59] {general|Medium}.

Grant windows are episodic, and none of the current alternative-protein programmes treats Vietnam as a priority. Vietnamese groups need an international co-applicant, a proposal that fits the funder's stated scope and a ready draft before windows open.

## 8.7 The global and regional context

- Global alternative-protein investment was **USD 881 million in 2025** (plant-based 450, fermentation 357, cultivated 74) and USD 359 million in the first half of 2026. In the second quarter of 2026, fermentation took about USD 132 million of roughly USD 197 million [@CAP-51] {general|High}. Synthesis Capital's managing partner says valuations "have reset" [@CAP-64] {general|Low}.
- Global agrifood-tech funding was flat at USD 16.2 billion in 2025, with upstream categories (farm, food production and biological systems) up 7% [@CAP-53] {general|Medium}.

{{chart:chart-global-altprotein-investment}}

**Reading.** Money that still flows goes to fermentation [@CAP-51] and to upstream ingredients with what AgFunder calls "tangible science, real unit economics and clear paths to revenue" [@CAP-53]. That is the part of the value chain where Vietnam's advantages (feedstock, feed demand, processing skills) lie, and the opposite of a consumer-brand play.

## 8.8 What this means

- **Investors:** there is no venture track record in Vietnamese alternative protein. A thesis must rest on B2B feed or ingredient revenue, a named strategic buyer, and a structure like Entobel's (private-equity lead, DFI support, offtake). Expect to underwrite capital intensity, not consumer growth ([[ch09-economics]]). A domestic textured-protein line is the exception that proves the rule: its equipment is cheap (Chinese lines listed at USD 11,000 to 100,000) and its main need is USD 0.6 to 3.5 million of working capital, so it suits bank debt and trade finance for an incumbent or SME, not venture equity (our calculation; [[ch26-plays]]) [@TIC-02; @TIC-03] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Startups:** realistic first cheques are angels and family offices, regional seed specialists (USD 0.1 to 0.3 million), ADB Ventures (up to USD 4 million, climate lens), and from late 2026 the Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi funds. A Singapore holding company, as Entobel used, eases foreign investment.
- **Policy makers:** naming "alternative protein and biomanufacturing" as a priority in the rules of the national and local venture funds would cost little. A grant or first-loss window for pre-revenue pilot plants would fill the gap between research grants and private equity that NATIF's priority for profitable borrowers leaves open.
- **International bodies:** the IFC and ADB Ventures precedents transfer directly; a pooled first-loss tranche for a first Vietnamese fermentation-feed plant, or DFI co-investment with a local fund, would target the gap.

**Related:** [[app-s11-capital]] (full deal, investor and programme tables), [[ch26-plays]], [[brief-investors]].

data.title: Economics: what it costs and what it must beat
data.summary: In fermentation, Vietnam's cheap power and labour matter less than capital: on indicative numbers, fungal feed protein made in Vietnam costs USD 4,050 to 14,700 per tonne of protein, against USD 2,625 to 3,846 for fishmeal protein, so it competes as a functional aquafeed ingredient, rarely as bulk protein. For plant-based foods, factory cost is not the barrier.
data.body:
# 9. Economics: what it costs and what it must beat

**In one paragraph.** Vietnam's operating inputs are cheap: power at about USD 0.075 per kWh for a plant running around the clock, a minimum wage of about USD 204 a month, factory rent of about USD 5 per m² a month. But in fermentation those inputs are a small part of cost. On our indicative Vietnamese cost stack, capital charges and maintenance are 54 to 67% of the cost of fungal feed protein, which comes to USD 4,050 to 14,700 per tonne of protein. Fishmeal protein costs USD 2,625 (2025 average) to USD 3,846 (August 2026) per tonne, and soybean meal protein about USD 880. So a Vietnamese microbial protein sold only on protein content is marginal against fishmeal and far from soy. It becomes plausible as a functional shrimp or fish-feed ingredient used at 1 to 5% of the diet, where buyers pay for survival and feed efficiency. For plant-based food the arithmetic runs the other way: textured soy protein costs roughly 3,800 to 7,900 VND per 100 g of protein to make, against 34,000 to 71,000 VND at retail for eggs, chicken and pork. Quality, demand and distribution decide that market, not factory cost. A domestic textured-soy line is also cheap to equip: Chinese lines are listed at USD 11,000 to 100,000. Its problem is the import it would replace, Chinese textured soy that enters duty-free and lands at USD 1.29 to 1.38 per kg, inside the domestic cost range. So the delivered price of food-grade soy flour, 63 to 85% of cost, decides whether the line earns a margin.

> **Read with care.** The cost stacks in this chapter are indicative. They combine sourced Vietnamese prices with stated engineering assumptions and are meant to show orders of magnitude and which lines matter. They are not feasibility studies.

---

## 9.1 Input costs in Vietnam

| Input | Value | Note | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Electricity, manufacturing, 22 to 110 kV | Off-peak 1,190, normal 1,833, peak 3,398 VND/kWh | Unchanged since 10 May 2025 | [@COST-01; @COST-03] {VN-direct\|High} |
| Electricity, blended for a 24/7 plant | 1,905 to 2,110 VND/kWh (USD 0.073 to 0.081); 1,952 at 22 kV | Our calculation with the April 2026 peak hours | [@COST-01; @COST-03] {VN-direct\|High} |
| Grid emission factor | 0.66 t CO2 per MWh (2023, latest official) | Power-heavy processes carry a high footprint without renewable supply | [@COST-08; @COST-09] {VN-direct\|High} |
| Minimum wage, Region I | 5,310,000 VND a month (about USD 204) from 1 January 2026 | Average employee income 9.0 million VND (Q2 2026); employer contributions add about 23.5% (assumed statutory rate) | [@COST-19; @COST-20] {VN-direct\|High} |
| Industrial land | USD 186 per m² for the lease term (south); USD 138 (north) | Q2 2026 | [@COST-21; @COST-22] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Ready-built factory | USD 4.9 to 5.1 per m² a month | Q2 2026 | [@COST-21; @COST-22] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Production water | 16,625 VND per m³ all-in (Ho Chi Minh City) | Park wastewater treatment USD 0.28 to 0.40 per m³ | [@COST-10; @COST-13; @COST-14] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Steam from rice-husk pellets | About 420 to 590 VND per kg of steam (fuel only) | Industrial LPG about 46,100 VND/kg (48 kg cylinder, Ho Chi Minh City) | [@COST-15; @COST-16; @COST-17] {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Urea (nitrogen) | About USD 425 per t equivalent (Phu My, VND 553,100 per 50 kg bag, retail, March 2026); world price spiked to USD 726 | Every microbial route on Vietnamese carbohydrate buys nitrogen | [@COST-30; @COST-33] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Cassava starch | USD 520 to 540 per t FOB (April 2026), up from 405 to 415 in January | Roots up about 50 to 90% in a year, by province | [@FS-01; @FS-11; @FS-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Sugar, domestic average price | About 16,505 VND/kg (mid-2026), a three-year low | Surplus year | [@FS-31; @FS-33] {VN-direct\|Medium} |

**Three rule changes add risk.** A decree now lets the power utility adjust the average price by 2% to under 5% after a ministry review; a two-part tariff with a capacity charge was planned for large users from 1 January 2026, after parallel billing to the end of 2025 [@COST-04; @COST-05] {VN-direct|Medium}; and direct renewable power purchase is allowed but its savings (about 11% in one worked example) are unproven [@COST-06; @COST-07] {VN-direct|Low}.

**Feed is VAT-exempt, which is a hidden cost.** Under the VAT Law in force since July 2025, animal feed is "not subject to VAT" [@COST-24] {VN-direct|High}. A plant selling a feed protein therefore cannot reclaim the VAT it pays on equipment, power and inputs. We estimate this adds about 5 to 10% to its taxed input costs; a food-ingredient plant can reclaim input VAT {VN-direct|Low}.

## 9.2 Fermentation: capital is most of the cost

**Published benchmarks** (full list in `tea_benchmarks.csv`; read in full, in part or as abstracts, as recorded there) [@COST-43; @COST-44; @COST-45; @COST-46; @COST-47] {general|Medium}:

| Technology | Benchmark | Capex | Study |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mycoprotein (food) | USD 3.55 per kg wet; USD 29.6 per kg protein | About USD 108 M for 2 t/h wet | Risner et al. 2023 |
| Bacterial SCP from industrial off-gas (feed) | USD 4.15 per kg (2.78 if intensified) | USD 320 M for 20 kt a year | Vlaeminck et al. 2023 |
| SCP from hydrogen and CO2 (feed) | Minimum selling price USD 2,070 per t | n/a | Jean and Brown 2024 |
| SCP with renewable power | EUR 5.5 to 6.1 per kg protein (2028), falling to EUR 2.1 to 2.3 (2050) | n/a | Fasihi et al. 2025 |
| Cultivated meat | USD 37 to 51 per kg of wet cells | USD 663 M for 6.9 kt a year (perfusion) | Humbird 2021 |

**Capex varies seven-fold.** Per cubic metre of reactor, the off-gas SCP study implies about USD 51,000 and the mycoprotein study about USD 350,000; per annual tonne, USD 16,000 to 23,000 for SCP and mycoprotein and about USD 48,000 to 96,000 for cultivated meat (fed-batch to perfusion; our derivation) [@COST-43; @COST-44; @COST-47] {general|High}. Design, hygiene grade and estimating method explain the spread. A Vietnamese plan needs its own equipment-level estimate, not a borrowed ratio.

{{chart:chart-capex-per-tonne}}

**Cooling in the tropics.** Aerobic fermentation releases about 12 to 18 MJ of heat per kg of dry biomass. In southern Vietnam, we assume cooling-tower water arrives at about 31 to 33 °C, too warm to hold a broth at 30 °C, so most cooling must come from chillers. Our indicative estimate of the penalty is USD 70 to 180 per tonne of dry biomass, about 2 to 4% of the cost of fungal feed protein. Strains that grow at 40 to 45 °C avoid most of it [@COST-50; @COST-51] {general|Low}. Earlier drafts said cooling "may offset" Vietnam's power advantage: that is partly true for the power bill, but because power is a small share of cost, the overall effect is modest.

### Cost stack A: fungal biomass protein for aquafeed, 10,000 t a year

| Line | USD per t product (low to high) | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Carbon (2.0 to 2.2 t glucose-equivalent) | 600 to 1,100 | Assumed USD 300 to 500 per t |
| Nitrogen (0.17 to 0.20 t urea) | 72 to 145 | [@COST-30; @COST-33] |
| Minerals, vitamins, antifoam, enzymes | 50 to 150 | Assumption |
| Electricity, excluding cooling | 58 to 117 | Tariff [@COST-01] × assumed 0.77 to 1.56 MWh per t |
| Cooling electricity | 7 to 117 | Section 9.2 |
| Steam | 78 to 218 | [@COST-16; @COST-17] |
| Water and wastewater | 18 to 58 | [@COST-10; @COST-13; @COST-14] plus assumed 20 to 40 m³ per t and COD surcharge |
| Labour (60 to 100 staff) | 44 to 124 | [@COST-19; @COST-20] plus assumption |
| Land (5 to 8 ha) | 99 to 185 | [@COST-21] |
| Capital charge (capex USD 8,000 to 20,000 per annual t; 12 to 18% a year) | 960 to 3,600 | Below the verified benchmarks, allowing for cheaper local build |
| Maintenance and insurance | 240 to 800 | Assumption |
| **Total per t of product** | **2,227 to 6,612** | 58,000 to 172,000 VND/kg |
| **Total per t of protein (45 to 55% protein)** | **4,050 to 14,700** | |

Source: AltProtein Vietnam calculation from sourced prices and stated assumptions [@COST-01; @COST-19; @COST-21; @COST-33; @COST-43; @COST-44; @COST-47] {VN-direct\|Low}.

{{chart:chart-cost-stack-fungal}}

**Reading.** Capital charges and maintenance are 54% of cost at the low end and 67% at the high end. Labour and power together are under 10%. Two lines deserve attention:
- **Carbon.** At April 2026 cassava starch prices (USD 520 to 540 per t), the carbon line sits at or above the top of the assumed range once conversion to glucose is added. A near-free side stream such as cassava pulp would cut it, but needs pre-treatment and has almost no protein ([[ch04-asset-map]]). Domestic sugar at a three-year low is a clean alternative in surplus years.
- **Capex.** The product nears fishmeal parity only if capex falls below about USD 6,000 per annual tonne, which is well under any verified benchmark. Tolling on existing tanks ([[ch05-industrial-base]]) is the main way to get there.

## 9.3 The prices to beat in feed

Fishmeal (Peru 65%, the World Bank series) averaged USD 1,706 per tonne in 2025 and reached USD 2,500 in August 2026, the highest in the 2020 to 2026 series. Soybean meal was about USD 403 [@FM-01; @FM-02] {general|High}. On a protein basis, that is USD 2,625 to 3,846 per tonne for fishmeal and about USD 880 for soybean meal (our calculation).

| Target | Price to beat (USD per t protein) | Indicative Vietnamese cost (USD per t protein) | Gap at the low-cost end | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bulk fishmeal replacement in shrimp feed | 2,625 to 3,846 | 4,050 to 14,700 | 1.54× (2025 price) to 1.05× (Aug 2026 price) | Marginal. Needs low capex, cheap carbon and a lasting fishmeal spike |
| Functional ingredient in pangasius feed, 1 to 2% inclusion | Buyer can pay about USD 1,000 to 4,250 per t of product for a 3 to 5% performance gain | 2,227 to 6,612 per t of product | Overlaps | Plausible with repeatable trial data; small volumes (20 to 50 kt a year at full uptake) |
| Functional-plus-protein ingredient in shrimp feed, 2 to 5% inclusion | Fishmeal parity plus USD 1,280 to 4,800 per t of product | as above | Overlaps | Most plausible entry point |
| Soybean meal replacement in pig and poultry feed | 796 to 876 | 4,050 to 14,700 | 4.6× to 5.1× | Not plausible for fermentation protein |

Source: [@FM-01; @FM-04; @FM-10; @FM-31] and cost stack A {VN-direct\|Low}. Arithmetic for the functional case: maximum ingredient price = soybean meal price + (performance gain × feed price) ÷ inclusion rate.

{{chart:chart-price-to-beat}}

**The real competitor is imported microbial protein, not fishmeal list prices.** Mills already buy microbial ingredients: Vietnam imported about 9,200 t of inactive yeast and dead single-cell organisms (HS 2102.20) for food and feed together in 2025, 2.4 times the 2019 tonnage, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg [@FBA-17] {VN-direct|Medium}. Chinese and ASEAN product of this kind pays no import duty [@FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}. That USD 1,100 per t [@FBA-17] is the revealed price a Vietnamese functional microbial ingredient must beat, unless head-to-head trials show a gain worth the difference. A bacterial biomass from Chinese glutamic-acid fermentation, with at least 70% crude protein, is already imported and sold into Vietnamese pig, poultry, fish and shrimp feed [@FM-12; @ECO-69] {VN-direct|Medium}. Calysseo's 20,000 t a year FeedKind plant operates in Chongqing [@FM-13] {general|Medium}. By-product protein has near-zero marginal feedstock cost and can be priced anywhere between soybean-meal and fishmeal parity. Our working assumption is that a Vietnamese feed protein should plan to realise 70 to 90% of fishmeal-protein parity {VN-direct|Low}.

**Buyer economics.** Feed is 50 to 60% of shrimp production cost [@FM-10] {VN-direct|Medium}. At 15% inclusion, fishmeal adds about USD 256 per tonne of shrimp feed at the 2025 price and USD 375 at the August 2026 price (our calculation from [@FM-01]). Shrimp feed prices rose by VND 1,200 to 1,500 per kg in June 2026 [@FM-10] {VN-direct|Medium}. Mills are motivated to cut fishmeal, but they already use established substitutes (poultry by-product meal, fermented soy, soy protein concentrate) [@FM-04] {general|Medium}.

## 9.4 Plant-based food: factory cost is not the problem

### Cost stack B: textured soy protein on a Chinese-equipped extrusion line

| Line size and utilisation | Output, t a year | Full cost, USD per t (low to high) | VND per 100 g of protein (52% protein) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 t/h at 50% | 2,000 | 858 to 1,573 | 4,290 to 7,860 |
| 0.5 t/h at 90% | 3,600 | 793 to 1,382 | 3,970 to 6,910 |
| 1 t/h at 70% | 5,600 | 774 to 1,337 | 3,870 to 6,680 |
| 1 t/h at 90% | 7,200 | 761 to 1,294 | 3,800 to 6,470 |
| Of which raw material (food-grade defatted soy flour delivered at USD 627 to 925 per t) | | 646 to 990 (63 to 85% of cost) | |
| Of which capital charge (Chinese equipment) | | 5 to 91 | |

Source: AltProtein Vietnam calculation, full table in [[app-s12-costs]] and `t1_cost_per_kg.csv` [@TIC-12; @TIC-13; @COST-01; @COST-16; @COST-17; @COST-19; @COST-20; @COST-21; @TIC-02; @TIC-03; @TIC-07] {VN-direct\|Low}. Full cost includes utilities, labour, rent, QA, delivery, maintenance, a capital charge and working-capital interest; it excludes VAT, sales and profit. This replaces an earlier single case (3,000 t a year on a 1 t/h line with assumed European-scale equipment, USD 792 to 2,065 per t), which also included a dearer soy-concentrate blend; that blend is a separate product.

**Equipment is cheap; flour and working capital are not.** Shandong makers list complete textured-protein lines of 0.2 to 1.5 t/h, with dryer, at USD 11,000 to 100,000 a set (list prices), and a Ho Chi Minh City dealer sells Chinese soy lines [@TIC-02; @TIC-03; @TIC-07; @FORM-34] {general|Low}. Installed in a rented Vietnamese factory, with fit-out, utilities, certification and contingency, a line costs about USD 0.28 to 1.38 million; working capital for three to four months of revenue, USD 0.6 to 3.5 million, is the larger need (our calculation) {VN-direct|Low}. A European-grade line remains unpriced: on the earlier equipment assumption it would cost USD 2.0 to 5.6 million installed.

{{kn:kn-tvp-line-capex}}

**Retail protein prices to beat** (per 100 g of protein): at a national grocery chain on 23 September 2026, eggs 34,000 to 40,000 VND, chicken breast 39,500 to 45,500 and lean pork about 70,900 [@COST-39; @COST-40; @COST-41] {VN-direct|Medium}; in our retail audit on 16 and 20 September 2026, tofu 39,000 to 121,000 (five plain tofu products), dried soy mock meat about 51,000 and an imported plant-based burger about 542,000 [@COST-42; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium}.

{{chart:chart-retail-price-per-protein}}

**Reading.** Textured protein costs between about one-eighteenth and one-quarter of the retail price of meat and egg protein to make (our calculation). The gap is taken by distribution, brand and retail margins and by product quality.

**Flour decides the margin against imports.** In 2025 China shipped textured protein and concentrates (HS 2106.10) to Vietnam at USD 1.24 per kg FOB, its lowest price to any of eight Asian and US partners (world average USD 1.95) [@TIC-12; @TIC-14] {VN-direct|Medium}. With freight, port and inland costs it lands at about USD 1.29 to 1.38 per kg (our calculation), and it pays no duty under ACFTA or RCEP [@FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}. India shipped at USD 0.98 per kg [@BUY-02] {VN-direct|Medium}. That landed price sits inside the domestic full-cost range of USD 0.76 to 1.57 per kg (cost stack B). Raw material is 63 to 85% of cost and comes from the same countries that export the finished product: Vietnam crushes soybeans for feed meal [@FORM-10] {VN-direct|Medium}, and we found no food-grade defatted flake stream. Because Chinese product pays no duty, a domestic line's natural shelter is only the freight and port cost on the finished product, about USD 50 to 140 per t (our calculation, `t1_landed_competitor.csv`), less the freight on its own imported flour {VN-direct|Low}. To earn a 15% margin at Chinese parity, a 1 t/h line running 70% of the time needs food-grade flour delivered below about USD 700 to 940 per t (our calculation). The observed flour anchors, USD 627 to 925 per t, straddle that line [@TIC-12; @TIC-13] {VN-direct|Low}.

{{kn:kn-t1-flour-breakeven}}

Chinese lines are sold in Ho Chi Minh City, yet we found no Vietnamese textured-protein extruder, which suggests food-grade flour does not reach Vietnam at the low end of that range (our inference). A domestic plant competes on freshness, customisation for local dishes and supply security; it fits a chay maker, co-packer or ingredient distributor financed with debt better than a venture-backed startup ([[ch26-plays]] play T1; [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).

**Chicken and eggs set the floor.** Any plant-based product aimed at mass-market Vietnamese consumers is priced against chicken and eggs at about 34,000 to 45,000 VND per 100 g of protein [@COST-40; @COST-41] {VN-direct|Medium}. A wider check across three retailers on 24 September 2026 gives VND 34,000 to 45,000 for eggs and chicken and about 70,900 for lean pork ([[ch11-protein-diet]]). Imported premium analogues sit an order of magnitude above that.

## 9.5 Precision fermentation and cultivated meat

- **Precision fermentation.** We could not verify a peer-reviewed cost model for food proteins this round. The logic from the regional study still applies: in a 10,000 t a year precision-fermentation plant model, labour was 4% and utilities 17% of cost, and feedstock (37%) was the largest line, ahead of depreciation (18%) [@RGN-01] {general|High}. For Vietnam, this favours high-value, low-dose products (enzymes, functional proteins, specialty ingredients) made under contract, not commodity dairy proteins ([[ch10-technology-fit]]).
- **Cultivated meat.** At USD 37 to 51 per kg of wet cells [@COST-47] {general|High}, cultivated meat costs roughly 7 to 15 times the retail price of lean pork or chicken breast in Vietnam (our calculation from [@COST-39; @COST-40]). With capex of about USD 48,000 to 96,000 per annual tonne, there is no near-term production case for Vietnam; the case is for research and regulatory readiness ([[ch26-plays]] play T8).

> **Correction.** In v0.6 this said labour was 17% and utilities 4 to 5% of cost in the regional precision-fermentation model, with depreciation the largest line; the source says labour 4%, utilities 17%, and feedstock (37%) the largest line.

## 9.6 What policy can change in the numbers

The regional study modelled incentives for representative plants and found that a 50% capital grant or non-dilutive funding raised company value the most (a reported NPV gain of USD 73 million), followed by a 10% cut in feedstock cost and a loan guarantee. Tax holidays ranked fourth of six, two to four times less effective than the best [@RGN-01] {general|High}. In Vietnam's case, that points to:
- **Capital:** shared or tolled tanks, capital grants and loan guarantees rather than more tax holidays ([[ch27-policy-options]]).
- **Feedstock:** stable access to glucose from cassava starch or domestic sugar at fermentation grade.
- **Tax neutrality:** allowing new feed ingredients to reclaim input VAT.
- **Time:** every month of feed or food approval is carried as capital cost ([[ch07-rules]]).

## 9.7 What this means

- **Investors:** model capital charges, not operating costs, for fermentation; for textured soy, ask for a delivered flour quote before a capex plan. Test any feed-protein pitch against USD 2,625 to 3,846 per tonne of fishmeal protein, against Chinese by-product protein, and against capex per annual tonne (verified benchmarks: USD 16,000 to 23,000). A claim below USD 6,000 needs evidence.
- **Startups:** sell function, not tonnage. Choose thermotolerant strains or design for hybrid cooling from day one. Start texturing in a ready-built factory at about USD 5 per m² a month.
- **Manufacturers:** feed mills can buy functional ingredients at a premium only with species-specific trial data. Food makers can produce textured protein in Vietnam at a small fraction of meat's retail price; demand and quality are the constraints, and a line beats duty-free Chinese imports only with food-grade flour below about USD 700 to 940 per t. Feed mills already pay about USD 1.1 per kg for imported inactive yeast; ask any new microbial supplier to beat that per unit of performance.
- **Policy makers:** the cheapest levers on cost are capital sharing (a public or tolled pilot line), input-VAT neutrality for new feed ingredients, and early signals on the capacity charge.
- **Research bodies:** two public goods are missing and cheap: an open Vietnamese fermentation cost model with local inputs, and a public series of domestic feed-ingredient prices.

**Related:** [[app-s12-costs]] (full input tables, both cost stacks, benchmarks), [[app-s6-feed-market]] (fishmeal, inclusion rates, trials), [[ch10-technology-fit]].

data.title: Technology fit: which platforms suit Vietnam
data.summary: We test ten technology families against seven Vietnamese conditions: feedstock, industrial base, science readiness, route to market, buyers, competition and capital intensity. Textured plant protein and functional microbial ingredients for aquafeed fit best today. Local legume and rice proteins, fungal foods and duckweed feed are worth proving. Precision fermentation fits only as high-value, low-dose products made under contract. Cultivated meat and seafood are research topics for this decade. Insects are a benchmark, not a recommendation.
data.body:
# 10. Technology fit: which platforms suit Vietnam

**In one paragraph.** No technology is a general answer for Vietnam. Each fits a specific combination of feedstock, buyer and rule. We score ten families against seven conditions drawn from the previous chapters. Two fit now: **textured plant protein**, because the rules are clear, the buyers exist and Vietnam imports what it would replace; and **functional microbial ingredients for shrimp and fish feed**, because Vietnam has the carbohydrate, the fermentation skills and a concentrated, motivated buyer base. Three are worth proving with pilots: **local legume and rice protein ingredients**, **fungal foods such as koji and mycoprotein**, and **duckweed grown on aquaculture effluent for feed**. **Precision fermentation** fits only for high-value, low-dose products made under contract, because public strains sit about 5 to 14 times below the titer the literature expects for bulk proteins and the product probably counts as a GMO product in Vietnam. **Cultivated meat and seafood** remain research topics: Vietnam has no food cell line and costs are 7 to 15 times the retail price of meat. **Insects** are an established feed incumbent and appear here only as a benchmark.

---

## 10.1 How we scored

Seven conditions, each rated **strong**, **moderate** or **weak** for Vietnam in 2026, on the evidence in chapters 2 to 9:

| Condition | Question | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| Feedstock | Does Vietnam have the raw material at a competitive price? | [[ch04-asset-map]] |
| Industrial base | Is there equipment, a co-packer or a host plant? | [[ch05-industrial-base]] |
| Science readiness | Is the technology proven at scale somewhere, and does Vietnam have the skills? | [[ch06-knowledge-talent]] |
| Route to market | Can the product be sold legally within 1 to 2 years? | [[ch07-rules]] |
| Buyers | Is there a named, reachable first customer? | [[ch02-alt-protein-today]] |
| Competition | Can it beat imports and incumbents on price or function? | [[ch03-regional]], [[ch09-economics]] |
| Capital intensity | Can the first plant be financed from Vietnamese and regional capital? | [[ch08-capital]] |

The ratings are our judgement {VN-direct|Medium}. The data behind each one are cited below and in the appendices.

## 10.2 The fit matrix

| Family | Feedstock | Industrial base | Science | Route | Buyers | Competition | Capital | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Textured plant protein (dry textured vegetable protein, TVP; gluten blends) | Moderate | Strong | Moderate | Strong | Strong | Moderate | Strong | **Build now** |
| Local legume and rice protein ingredients | Moderate | Moderate | Moderate | Strong | Moderate | Weak | Moderate | **Prove first** |
| Functional microbial feed ingredients (yeast, fungal, bacterial; 1 to 5% of diet) | Strong | Moderate | Moderate | Moderate | Strong | Moderate | Moderate | **Build with partners** |
| Bulk microbial protein for fishmeal replacement | Strong | Moderate | Moderate | Moderate | Moderate | Weak | Weak | **Marginal; test only with near-free carbon and tolling** |
| Fungal foods (koji, mycoprotein) | Moderate | Weak | Moderate | Moderate | Weak | Moderate | Moderate | **Prove first (koji); watch (mycoprotein)** |
| Duckweed and *Wolffia* | Strong | Weak | Moderate | Strong (feed); weak (food) | Moderate | Moderate | Strong | **Prove first (feed)** |
| Microalgae (spirulina, chlorella) | Moderate | Moderate | Strong | Strong | Weak | Weak | Moderate | **Niche; incumbents exist** |
| Precision fermentation | Strong | Weak | Weak | Weak | Weak | Weak | Weak | **Contract-made, high-value, low-dose only** |
| Gas fermentation (CO2, methane, off-gas) | Weak | Weak | Moderate | Moderate | Moderate | Weak | Weak | **Watch** |
| Cultivated meat and seafood | Weak | Weak | Weak | Weak | Weak | Weak | Weak | **Research and watch** |
| Insects (benchmark) | Strong | Strong | Strong | Strong | Strong | n/a | Moderate | **Incumbent; not a recommendation of this report** |

{{chart:chart-technology-fit-matrix}}

## 10.3 Plant protein

**Textured plant protein.** The technology is mature globally and cheap to install; the rules are ordinary food rules; and Vietnam imports what a domestic plant would replace.
