Every Vietnamese product with 10 g of protein or more per 100 g in our audit (10 of 10) ran on imported soy protein, textured soy or wheat gluten (two inferred from protein level); China is a major supplier and the largest for gluten [@FORM-01; @FORM-03; @FORM-05; @FORM-06; @FORM-07] {VN-direct|Medium}. We found no commercial textured-protein extrusion in Vietnam [@FORM-11; @FORM-12; @FORM-13] {VN-direct|Medium} and at most one Vietnamese extrusion study [@BIB-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. Buyers are named: frozen-food makers and vegetarian (*chay*) brands such as An Nhien, Au Lac, Xuan Hong, LC Foods, Cholimex, CJ Foods Vietnam, Vissan and Thoai An, plus co-packers [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. The weaknesses are feedstock (soy is about 98% imported [@FORM-09], and we found no food-grade line at the large Phu My crusher [@FORM-10] {VN-direct|Medium}) and competition from Chinese textured protein at USD 1.24 per kg FOB in 2025, about USD 1.29 to 1.38 landed duty-free (our calculation) [@TIC-12; @BUY-02; @FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}. High-moisture extrusion of whole-cut analogues is a second step once a dry line and a customer base exist.

**Local legume and rice proteins.** Mung bean is the main protein in mass-market *chay* fillings [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium}, and Vietnam imported USD 138 million of dried mung and black gram beans in 2023, 65% of it from Myanmar [@FORM-08] {VN-direct|Medium}. Protein quality is reasonable in pigs (DIAAS: soy isolate 97, mung bean 86, pea concentrate 70, brown rice concentrate 42) but human digestibility of mung bean measured in children was about 20% lower than the pig value [@SCI-40; @SCI-41; @SCI-42] {general|High}. Pea-rice blends can reach a PDCAAS of 1.0; we found no measured DIAAS for rice-legume blends [@SCI-43] {general|Medium}. Vinamilk's high-protein nut milks and plant yoghurts already use imported pea protein [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The plausible first market is replacing that imported pea protein, not replacing textured soy {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. Competition from Chinese pea and rice proteins is strong, so this needs a buyer specification and a pilot before a plant.

## 10.4 Microbial protein for feed

**The science supports partial, not full, replacement.** In whiteleg shrimp, gas-fermentation protein at 30% of a test diet gave growth no different from the control; halving fishmeal cut growth unless a bile acid was added. Methanotroph meal had lower digestibility in one Chinese screen [@SCI-23; @SCI-24] {general|High}. Black soldier fly meal did no better (growth fell at 30% replacement) [@SCI-27] {general|High}. A 2025 preprint reports mixed-culture protein grown on soybean-processing wastewater replacing 50% of fishmeal in shrimp consistently and up to 90% on some outcomes, directly relevant to Vietnam's tofu and soy-milk industry but not yet peer reviewed [@SCI-25] {VN-adjacent|Medium}.

**Function sells better than protein.** Many benefits reported for novel proteins in shrimp and catfish are functional: better survival after pathogen challenge, palatability, or winter survival with beta-glucan (78% to 95% in striped catfish) [@FM-20; @FM-26; @FM-31; @FM-45] {general|Medium}. [[ch09-economics]] shows why that matters: bulk fishmeal replacement is marginal on price, while an ingredient sold at 1 to 5% of the diet for survival or feed efficiency can command a large premium: a pangasius mill could pay about USD 1,000 to 4,250 per tonne in total, and a shrimp mill USD 1,280 to 4,800 per tonne above fishmeal parity.

**Fit in Vietnam.** Carbohydrate is abundant ([[ch04-asset-map]]); aerobic fermentation skills and tanks exist inside amino-acid producers ([[ch05-industrial-base]]); about six firms make most shrimp feed ([[ch05-industrial-base]]); and inactive yeasts are already on the livestock feed list, while bacterial single-cell protein and fungal biomass need a feed trial and the aquafeed list has a drafting gap ([[ch07-rules]]) [@REG-32; @REG-33; @REG2-01] {VN-direct|High}. Thermotolerant yeasts such as *Kluyveromyces marxianus*, isolated from Thai cassava pulp, grow at 40 °C on raw cassava starch [@SCI-44; @SCI-45] {VN-adjacent|High}, which cuts the cooling penalty. The weakness is competition: Chinese by-product bacterial biomass is already sold in Vietnam [@FM-12] {VN-direct|Low}.

**Gas fermentation** (hydrogen and CO2, methane, industrial off-gas) is commercial in China for feed [@RGN-57; @FM-13] {general|Medium}, but Vietnam has no measured supply of suitable gas and a carbon-heavy grid ([[ch09-economics]]). Watch.

## 10.5 Fungal foods

- **Koji and solid-state fermentation.** Vietnam has a *tương* (fermented soybean paste) tradition, research groups with gene tools for *Aspergillus oryzae* [@RD-33; @RD-34] {VN-direct|Medium}, and a clear route: koji on food substrates goes through ordinary self-declaration ([[ch07-rules]]). *A. oryzae* cannot make aflatoxin but can make cyclopiazonic acid and 3-nitropropionic acid; industrial strains carry a deletion that removes the risk, so a koji business needs a characterised strain, not a wild starter [@SCI-19] {general|High}.
- **Mycoprotein and yeast food protein.** Published costs are about USD 29.6 per kg of protein [@COST-43] {general|High}, and every fungal or yeast food protein carries an RNA-reduction step (about 10% to 2% of dry weight by a 68 °C heat step) [@SCI-20] {general|High}. Published yields need care: the widely repeated "118.5 g/L" *A. oryzae* biomass on vinasse is not a broth concentration; the plausible flask value is about 5.9 g/L (our inference: 118.5 × 5% vinasse) [@SCI-18] {general|Medium}. Chinese capacity sets the price: China added 11,000 t of yeast-protein capacity in 2025, and a 20,000 t mycoprotein plant is under construction ([[ch03-regional]]). There is no novel-food route for a new fungal species ([[ch07-rules]]).

## 10.6 Duckweed and microalgae

- **Duckweed (*bèo*).** Protein is 20 to 30% of dry weight in *Wolffia* grown in the laboratory, up to 44% in another *Wolffia* sample [@SCI-34; @SCI-35] {general|High}. We plan on 10 to 30 t of dry matter per hectare per year, at or below the roughly 30 t reported in reviews [@SCI-36; @SCI-37] {general|Medium}. Duckweed is already a permitted livestock feed material [@REG-32; @REG-33] {VN-direct|High}, and Vietnamese researchers hold more than 100 wild samples [@RD-44] {VN-direct|Medium}. For food, manganese is the gate: EFSA could not establish the safety of whole *Wolffia* powder in 2021 because of manganese intake, but judged a *Lemna* protein concentrate safe in 2023 [@SCI-28; @SCI-29; @SCI-30] {general|High}. A "PDCAAS 0.89" figure repeated in earlier drafts has no traceable source {general|Low}. Fit: feed on aquaculture effluent now (with heavy-metal testing), food as a protein concentrate later.
- **Microalgae.** Vietnam has small spirulina producers selling supplements, a salt-tolerant spirulina strain reaching 48.7% protein, and a research base at regional level [@ECO-52; @ECO-53; @RD-21] {VN-direct|Medium}. Algae are on the feed list and spirulina is an ordinary food. But production is small and costly, and one source claims most spirulina sold in Vietnam is imported [@ECO-53] {VN-direct|Low}. A niche with incumbents, not a bulk protein route.

## 10.7 Precision fermentation

- **Titers.** The leading review says bulk food proteins need titers "above 50 g/L", an expert assertion rather than a modelled threshold [@SCI-01; @SCI-02] {general|High}. The best published leghemoglobin titers are 3.5, 7.27 and 10.1 g/L [@SCI-03; @SCI-04; @SCI-05] {general|High}, about 5 to 14 times below the 50 g/L benchmark (our calculation) [@SCI-01; @SCI-03; @SCI-04; @SCI-05] {general|Medium}. Heme proteins are used at low inclusion in a product, so the benchmark binds less for them.
- **Strains.** OPENPichia offers a *Pichia* host under a liberal licence allowing royalty-free commercial manufacture; users still accept a licence, and product patents still apply [@SCI-08] {general|High}.
- **Rules.** Precision-fermented proteins probably count as "products of a GMO" under Decree 43/2026, and production with a GM strain needs a closed-production certificate whose timeline is unpublished ([[ch07-rules]]).
- **Infrastructure.** Vietnam has no food-grade contract fermentation and no open pilot fermenter ([[ch05-industrial-base]]); the nearest are in Singapore, Thailand and China ([[ch03-regional]]).

**Fit.** High-value, low-dose ingredients (enzymes, heme and sweet proteins, specialty functional proteins), developed by Vietnamese groups that already express proteins in yeast ([[ch06-knowledge-talent]]) and made under contract abroad until a domestic tolling option exists. Not commodity dairy or egg proteins.

## 10.8 Cultivated meat and seafood

- **No food cell line.** The striped catfish lines that exist (India, Taiwan) were built for virology and toxicology. The best documented, PHT, needs 20% fetal bovine serum and grows attached to surfaces [@SCI-10] {VN-adjacent|High}; the others are known only from their published descriptions [@SCI-11; @SCI-46; @SCI-47] {VN-adjacent|Medium}. The "shrimp" line PmLyO-Sf9 is a black tiger shrimp and insect hybrid [@SCI-12; @SCI-13] {general|High}. No true continuous shrimp cell line was found.
- **Cost.** Modelled cost is USD 37 to 51 per kg of wet cells [@COST-47] {general|High}, 7 to 15 times the retail price of lean pork or chicken breast in Vietnam ([[ch09-economics]]). The best documented animal-free culture, of chicken cells under continuous perfusion, reached up to 130 million cells per mL [@SCI-16] {general|Medium}.
- **Rules.** No route in Vietnam; the nearest approvals are in Singapore ([[ch03-regional]]).

> **Correction.** In v0.6 this said the best animal-free culture reached about 28 million cells per mL, below cost-model densities; the source reports up to 130 million cells per mL in animal-component-free medium.

**Fit.** Research, not production: serum-free adaptation of striped catfish cells, growth-factor expression (which Vietnamese groups already do), and regulatory preparation. Watch Singapore and Korea for signals.

## 10.9 Insects: the benchmark

Black soldier fly meal is the one alternative protein made at industrial scale in Vietnam, with an 11,000 t a year design capacity and a seafood exporter's offtake ([[ch02-alt-protein-today]], [[ch08-capital]]). It is on the livestock feed list. As agreed in scope, this report treats insects as the incumbent that every microbial or plant feed protein must match on price, digestibility and supply security, not as a play we recommend.

## 10.10 What this means

- **Investors:** the two "build now" families have modest capital needs and B2B buyers. Everything else needs a pilot, a partner or a rule change first.
- **Startups:** pick a family where the route to market is already clear (textured protein, listed feed materials, koji) and sell function or import substitution, not novelty.
- **Manufacturers:** textured-protein supply and functional feed additives are the two families where a Vietnamese supplier could reach you within two years.
- **Research bodies:** the most useful work sits in the "prove first" row: DIAAS for local proteins, duckweed manganese and heavy metals on Mekong water, soy-wastewater protein in shrimp, thermotolerant strains on cassava streams, and characterised *tương* strains.
- **Policy makers:** three families (fungal foods, precision fermentation, duckweed food) move from "weak" to "moderate" on route to market with one change: a proportionate new-food procedure ([[ch27-policy-options]]).

**Related:** [[app-s13-science]] (the evidence family by family), [[ch26-plays]] (plays built on this matrix).

data.title: What Vietnam eats and pays for protein
data.summary: Vietnamese adults already eat enough protein and far more meat than national guidance advises, and everyday protein such as eggs and chicken is cheap, while imported plant-based analogues cost 12 to 18 times as much per gram of protein. These facts set the price, protein and format targets for any new protein.
data.body:
# 11. What Vietnam eats and pays for protein

**In one paragraph.** Any new protein in Vietnam enters a diet that is already rich in meat and still moving towards more of it. The national nutrition survey measured meat intake of 136.4 g per person per day in 2020, against a recommendation of 50 to 80 g, and animal foods now supply 42% of protein, twice the 1990 share. Health guidance asks people to eat legumes daily and red meat in moderation, while the livestock strategy's 2030 meat target has already been reached. Adults eat enough protein on average, so "more protein" is not the pitch. Children are not a protein market either: stunting (18% in 2023, 32% among ethnic minority children) is set before age two, and school lunches, even in upland boarding schools, already carry meat, fish or egg with enough protein and zinc; the documented shortfalls are breakfast, calcium and vitamin A. Soy foods are already everyday food: 40% of adults ate tofu, soy milk or beans the day before in a 2021 national survey. Protein is cheap: eggs and chicken cost VND 34,000 to 45,000 per 100 g of protein, tofu and dry legumes less, and lean pork about VND 71,000. Imported plant-based analogues cost VND 542,000 to 622,000. Protein sits in Vietnamese meals as noodle toppings, fillings, rolls and braised side dishes. When pork prices jumped 70% after African swine fever, households switched to chicken and imports, not to tofu. Together these facts give the targets a new protein must meet on price, protein content and format, and they show where demand is growing: poultry and eating out.

> **How to read Part III.** Part III looks at demand as a design input for the supply side studied in Parts II and IV. It does not plan consumer marketing. Besides the evidence tag, every demand claim carries a demand evidence tag: {dx:stated} for what people say in surveys, {dx:revealed} for what people and firms actually do (sales, prices, trade, menus, consumption statistics), {dx:tested} for tastings, auctions, choice experiments and trials, and {dx:inferred} for our inference from indirect evidence. Stated evidence usually overstates behaviour. Method and limits: [[app-m3-demand-method]].

---

## 11.1 A high-meat diet that is still rising

**Intake.** The General Nutrition Survey 2019 to 2020 (22,400 households in 25 provinces) measured meat intake of 136.4 g per person per day in 2020, up from 84 g in 2010; urban residents ate 155.3 g. The national recommendation is 50 to 80 g [@DIE-01; @DIE-02; @DIE-03] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. We found no newer national intake survey: a September 2026 article on the National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) still used the 2020 figures [@APR-42] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-meat-intake-2020}}

**Supply.** FAO food balance sheets put meat supply at 60.5 kg per person in 2023 (carcass weight), up from 41.0 kg in 2010, and total protein supply at 102.2 g per person per day, of which 43.2 g (42%) came from animal foods. The animal share was 21% in 1990 and 28% in 2000 [@DIE-07; @DIE-08] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Rice still supplies 27.0 g of protein a day and soy foods only 4.9 g [@DIE-07] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-animal-protein-share}}

**Daily reach.** The grams understate how widely plant protein is eaten. The one national probability survey of what people ate, the Diet Quality Questionnaire (a Gallup telephone sample of 1,007 adults, 13 November to 12 December 2021), found that 40.0% of adults had eaten dried beans, soybeans, tofu, soy milk or bean flour on the previous day, with no urban and rural gap (40.5% and 39.2%). In the same survey 92.1% had eaten meat, poultry or fish and 76.1% unprocessed red meat [@APR-36; @BRD-01; @BRD-03] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Soy foods are an everyday side for two adults in five, eaten beside meat rather than instead of it (our inference) {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. Full indicators: `diet_quality_vietnam.csv` and [[app-d1-diet-chay-prices]].

**Direction.** The OECD-FAO outlook projects meat food use per person rising from 49.8 kg in 2025 to 62.2 kg in 2035 (retail weight), a rise of 25%. Poultry leads, from 17.0 to 25.8 kg; pork rises only from 28.6 to 31.5 kg [@DIE-11] {VN-direct|Medium} {fx:projection}. With population growth this adds about 1.57 Mt of meat a year by 2035 (our calculation) [@DIE-11; @DIE-36] {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate}. Population rises only about 5% over the same decade, so almost all of the growth is more meat per person [@DIE-36] {VN-direct|Medium} {fx:projection}. Official targets point the same way. The livestock strategy (Decision 1520/QĐ-TTg) aims for 58 to 62 kg of carcass meat per person by 2030, a level FAO supply had already reached in 2023, while the health ministry's guidance asks for red meat in moderation (section 11.6) [@APR-10; @DIE-07] {VN-direct|High} {fx:projection}. The balance model of Part IV uses the same outlook ([[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]). {{kn:kn-meat-growth-2035}}

**Who eats more.** At home, urban and rural households now use the same amount of meat (2.60 kg per person a month in 2024); urban meat growth has moved to eating out. The richest fifth uses 3.17 kg and the poorest 1.97 kg, but the poorest fifth's meat use nearly doubled from 2010 to 2024, so growth now comes from lower-income households catching up [@DIE-05] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Home meat use has been flat since 2022, the first pause since 2010. With eating out recovering and FAO supply still rising in 2023, this is not yet evidence of a plateau in total meat eaten [@DIE-05; @DIE-07] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

## 11.2 Enough protein for adults, and for school-age children

Average protein intake is about 73 to 80 g per person per day: 72.8 g measured in 929 adults in Hanoi and Hung Yen (former Thai Binh) in 2022 [@DIE-32] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}, and about 80 g derived from the national survey's energy and protein shares [@DIE-01] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. The 2026 recommendation is about 0.93 g per kg of body weight, with a 50 g reference for labels, and it asks for "high-quality protein from diverse animal and plant sources" rather than a set animal share [@DIE-04] {VN-direct|High}. So for the average adult, protein is sufficient and meat is in excess of guidance.

Children's nutrition problems are real, but for school-age children they are not a protein gap (our inference from the school evidence below; an earlier draft described "too little high-quality protein at very low cost in poor upland districts"). Stunting among under-fives fell from 29.3% (2010) to 19.6% (2020) and 18% (2023), and it is 32% among ethnic minority children [@APR-27; @DIE-01; @DIE-03] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Low serum zinc affected 53.3% of children aged 6 to 59 months in 2020 [@APR-42] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Stunting is set largely before age two, the first 1,000 days that UNICEF and the World Bank target [@APR-44] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}, so it runs through complementary feeding and home diets, not school meals (our inference) [@NQR-28; @NQR-29] {general|Medium} {dx:inferred}, and UNICEF's 2027 to 2031 programme for Viet Nam accordingly prioritises preventive nutrition through "school food and complementary food standards" and marketing restrictions [@APR-27] {VN-direct|High} {dx:stated}. What school plates carry:

- **Urban lunches.** One Hanoi primary school's published lunch sheets (25 days) carry about 31.8 g of protein (21.2 to 38.6 g), against a 2026 recommendation of 32 to 49 g for the whole day for boys aged 6 to 11 [@PMR-26; @NQR-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **Upland boarding schools.** In 13 ethnic-minority boarding schools in five upland provinces that publish their menus (22 school-weeks, 353 meals, 2026), 240 of 242 lunches and dinners carried a meat, fish or egg dish, and pork appeared in 102 of 124 lunches, 82% (our coding, `upland_school_weeks.csv`) [@UPL-01; @UPL-02; @UPL-03; @UPL-04; @UPL-05; @UPL-06; @UPL-07; @UPL-08; @UPL-09; @UPL-10; @UPL-11; @UPL-12; @UPL-13; @UPL-14; @UPL-15; @UPL-16; @UPL-17] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. The four kitchens that publish cost sheets bought about 110 to 270 g of raw pork per pupil a day, including a lunch paid for under the border-commune decree (Decree 339/2025) [@UPL-01; @UPL-04; @UPL-07; @UPL-09; @UPL-10] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Tofu appears beside or inside pork dishes, except in one egg-and-tofu lunch; no textured soy or mock meat appears in any of the 353 meals [@UPL-01; @UPL-02; @UPL-03; @UPL-04; @UPL-05; @UPL-06; @UPL-07; @UPL-08; @UPL-09; @UPL-10; @UPL-11; @UPL-12; @UPL-13; @UPL-14; @UPL-15; @UPL-16; @UPL-17] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}.
- **Weighed diets.** Kitchen-weighed boarding diets at two schools in Yen Bai (now Lao Cai) in 2019 met protein and zinc needs (zinc at 131 to 157%) but supplied only 36.5% of calcium and 41 to 45% of vitamin A [@UPL-18] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The thin meal is breakfast: 86% of boarding breakfasts carry little or no animal food [@UPL-01; @UPL-02; @UPL-03; @UPL-04; @UPL-05; @UPL-06; @UPL-07; @UPL-08; @UPL-09; @UPL-10; @UPL-11; @UPL-12; @UPL-13; @UPL-14; @UPL-15; @UPL-16] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Full data: `upland_school_weeks.csv`.

Two consequences follow for new protein. First, a plant dish that removes all the meat or fish from a lunch would need added zinc, because national school guidance doubles a child's zinc requirement (5.6 to 11.2 mg a day at age 6 to 7) when a diet has little animal protein [@APR-04] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}; every one of the 124 upland lunches coded carried meat, fish or egg [@UPL-01; @UPL-02; @UPL-03; @UPL-04; @UPL-05; @UPL-06; @UPL-07; @UPL-08; @UPL-09; @UPL-10; @UPL-11; @UPL-12; @UPL-13; @UPL-14; @UPL-15; @UPL-16; @UPL-17] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. A blend keeps protein quality: a minced dish with 20 to 30% of its protein from textured soy scores a DIAAS (a protein-quality score) of about 97 or more on the older-child pattern (our calculation, using pork at 113 to 137 and, as a proxy for textured soy, extruded soybean at 65 to 97 scored on the young-child pattern) [@NQR-05; @NQR-07] {general|Medium} {dx:inferred}. Second, the stunting agenda sits before school age. There a plant product must register as a food for children under 36 months [@NQR-04] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}, be scored against the stricter young-child protein-quality pattern [@PRA-02; @NQR-31] {general|Medium} {dx:inferred}, and compete with milk, meat and fortified cereal blends, which is where the trial evidence sits [@NQR-28; @NQR-29; @NQR-30; @NQR-31] {general|Medium} {dx:tested}. School routes are assessed in [[ch15-channels]].

Overweight is rising at the same time: among 5 to 19 year olds it rose from 8.5% to 19.0% between 2010 and 2020 (26.8% in cities), and adult diabetes from 5.3% to 10.9% (2010 to 2022, modelled) [@DIE-01; @DIE-28] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Vietnam's protein-related problems are too much meat in cities and poor feeding before age two in upland and ethnic minority communities; neither is a gap that a cheap school protein dish would fill (our inference) {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-stunting}}

## 11.3 The price ladder a new protein must climb

We priced common proteins at Bach Hoa Xanh, WinMart and Co.op online on 24 September 2026 and converted them to VND per 100 g of protein with values from the Vietnamese Food Composition Table [@DIE-12] (full inputs in `demand_protein_prices.csv`).

| Food | VND per 100 g of protein | USD | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dry soybeans | 14,500 | 0.56 | [@DIE-22; @DIE-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Tofu, household average paid (VHLSS) | 19,600 | 0.75 | [@DIE-05; @DIE-12] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:inferred} |
| Tofu, supermarket (composition-table protein) | 30,000 | 1.16 | [@DIE-23; @DIE-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Hen eggs | 34,300 (40,000 at regular price; 55 g egg assumed) | 1.32 | [@COST-41; @DIE-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Mung beans; peanuts | 36,900; 38,700 (peanut listing's ingredient line reads red beans) | 1.42; 1.49 | [@DIE-20; @DIE-21; @DIE-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Chicken thigh; chicken breast | 39,000; 44,800 | 1.50; 1.72 | [@COST-40; @DIE-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Lean pork | 70,900 | 2.73 | [@COST-39; @DIE-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Pangasius fillet | 74,100 | 2.85 | [@DIE-15; @DIE-13] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Fresh UHT milk | 89,200 | 3.43 | [@DIE-18; @DIE-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Beef | 119,000 to 143,000 | 4.6 to 5.5 | [@DIE-16; @DIE-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Shrimp | about 200,000 | 7.7 | [@DIE-15; @DIE-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Filled *chay* wrappers (audit median) | 369,000 | 14.2 | [@FORM-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Imported plant-based analogues (audit) | 542,000 to 622,000 | 21 to 24 | [@FORM-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |

{{chart:chart-protein-price-ladder}}

Three benchmarks follow {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}:

- **The plant floor** is tofu and dry legumes at about VND 15,000 to 40,000 per 100 g of protein.
- **The mass animal floor** is eggs and chicken at VND 34,000 to 45,000. This is the price a mass-market protein food competes with. {{kn:kn-protein-price-floor}}
- **The mainstream meat reference** is lean pork at about VND 71,000. Beef (about VND 119,000 to 143,000) and shrimp (about VND 200,000) are premium, and shrimp is the one mass protein where a seafood analogue has wide price headroom.

Imported analogues sit at 12 to 18 times the price of eggs and chicken breast per gram of protein, and about 8 to 9 times lean pork [@FORM-01; @COST-39; @COST-40; @COST-41; @DIE-12] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The premiums that coincided with stalling demand in the United States and Europe were 35 to 77% per kilogram ([[ch13-consumers]]; [@GLB-03; @GLB-09; @GLB-10]) {general|High} {dx:revealed}. Vietnam's gap is an order of magnitude larger. {{kn:kn-analogue-price-gap}}

## 11.4 Where protein sits in the dish

Meat took 26.7% of household food spending in 2024 (VND 349,800 per person a month), fish 8.4%, eggs 1.3% and tofu 0.7%. Meals eaten away from home took 22.5% of food spending: 29.6% in cities and 16.1% in rural areas, with the highest spending in the South East [@DIE-05] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Eating out has not recovered its 2018 peak share of 26.7% [@DIE-05] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}.

We found no measured portion weights for the protein part of *phở* (rice noodle soup), *bún* (rice vermicelli dishes), *cơm tấm* (broken rice with grilled pork) or *bánh mì* (filled baguette), and log this as a high-priority open question [[app-r1-open-questions]]. What the evidence does show:

- The carbohydrate bases carry little protein: flat rice noodles 3.2 g, rice vermicelli 1.7 g and bread 7.9 g per 100 g [@DIE-12] {VN-direct|High}. In noodle dishes the protein is almost all topping.
- In noodle dishes the protein is sliced or minced meat, meatballs or fish cake on top; in rice meals it is a side dish such as braised pork or fish, egg or tofu in tomato sauce; in *bánh mì* it is a filling of pork roll (*chả lụa*), pâté, grilled meat or egg (our description, not measured) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.
- The traditional *đồ chay* (traditional vegetarian food) industry already makes analogues of exactly these components: vegetarian pork roll, meatballs, fish cake and beef slices [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

The formats that fit Vietnamese dishes are toppings, fillings, rolls, balls and mince, not whole-muscle steaks or burgers.

## 11.5 Price shocks and what people switch to

Pork prices swing hard; chicken prices barely move. After African swine fever reached Vietnam in 2019, the pig producer price rose 70% from 2019 to 2020 (VND 46,076 to 78,138 per kg) while the chicken price stayed flat [@DIE-25] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. USDA records pork consumption down 12.6% in 2019, chicken up 26.2% and chicken imports up 107% [@DIE-10] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Home tofu use did not move (0.44 kg per person a month in 2018 and in 2020), while home egg and fish use rose [@DIE-05] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}.

This is the clearest revealed evidence of cross-protein substitution in Vietnam, and it ran to other animal proteins. It has two uses for frontier actors. First, it warns that a pork shock does not by itself send buyers to plant protein. Second, it sizes the cost motive processed-meat makers already have, which is steady rather than a hedge. Soy extension saves money at every hog price since 2019: replacing 20% of the lean in *chả lụa* saves about VND 9,100 to 16,600 per kg at 2019 and 2020 prices, so a pork shock changes the size of the saving, not its sign, and 20% extension trims only about a sixth of a recipe's exposure to the shock (our calculation) [@DIE-25; @HXE-01] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. The extender a new protein must beat is therefore hydrated soy, not pork ([[ch14-frontier-demand]], [[ch16-business-buyers]]). COVID-19 in 2020 confounds the home-use figures, and we found no published cross-price elasticities for Vietnam that we could read.

## 11.6 Health and food safety as demand drivers

Food-safety worry is near universal. More than 90% of respondents in a pork study in two provinces worried about contaminated pork [@DIE-30] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}, and pork shoppers in northern Vietnam feared chemical hazards more than microbes [@DIE-31] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. What people pay for safety is more modest than what they say. A hypothetical choice experiment in Hanoi and Hai Phong found premiums of 70% for pork from certified abattoirs and up to 102% for hormone- and drug-free pork [@DIE-29] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:tested}; an auction with real money found 20% [@DIE-30] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:tested}. Plan on the lower figure.

Rising overweight and diabetes [@DIE-01; @DIE-28] {VN-direct|Medium}, and official messaging that Vietnamese are "cutting rice and eating more meat" [@DIE-38] {VN-direct|Medium}, give a health reason to eat less meat, and current guidance says so. The Ministry of Health's Ten tips to 2030 (Decision 3594/QĐ-BYT, November 2024) ask people to combine animal and plant foods, to eat fish, poultry, and nuts and seeds daily and to eat red meat in moderation [@APR-17; @APR-18] {VN-direct|High} {dx:stated}. Its guidance under the new Law on Disease Prevention (Decision 1982/QĐ-BYT, 1 July 2026) tells people with diet-related chronic disease to use diverse animal and plant protein, prioritising fish, lean meat, eggs, milk and legumes [@APR-16; @APR-15] {VN-direct|High} {dx:stated}. Neither names an alternative or plant-based product; Decision 1982 names legumes and the Ten tips name nuts and seeds [@APR-16; @APR-17] {VN-direct|High} {dx:stated}. A sponsored article tied to a soy-products company already uses this health-policy hook [@APR-43] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Revealed behaviour does not yet follow the guidance: home meat use rose in every income group from 2010 to 2024 [@DIE-05] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. We found no nationally representative survey of why Vietnamese eat less meat, when they do.

## 11.7 Vietnam against its neighbours

Vietnam eats far more meat than its income predicts. At about USD 13,500 per person (PPP, 2023) its meat supply of 60.5 kg already exceeds Japan's long-run plateau of 45 to 50 kg (from FAO's historic series, not like-for-like with the new series) and is more than twice Thailand's 24.5 kg, and it is close to China's at the same income in 2013 (59 kg) [@DIE-07; @DIE-08; @DIE-09] {VN-adjacent|High} {dx:revealed}.

{{chart:chart-animal-protein-ladder}}

Three readings follow {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:inferred}:

1. **No single income level marks a meat plateau.** Plateaus run from about 25 kg (Thailand) to about 80 kg (Taiwan) and are set by food culture and fish supply more than by income. No neighbour has shown a sustained fall in meat per person as income grew.
2. **The animal share of protein levels off at 55 to 60%** in Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Malaysia. At 42%, Vietnam has room to rise; Thailand shows that a fish-rich diet can hold near 40%.
3. **The demand that novel protein could take a share of is growing in tonnes.** Each 1% of meat protein is about 9,200 t of protein a year on 2023 supply data, worth roughly VND 3,600 to 6,500 billion (USD 140 to 250 million) at today's chicken-to-pork prices per gram of protein (our calculation; supply overstates intake) [@DIE-07; @COST-39; @COST-40; @DIE-12] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

## 11.8 What this means for the frontier

- **Price.** Mass-market protein foods compete with eggs and chicken at VND 34,000 to 45,000 per 100 g of protein; a meat analogue in mainstream retail must aim at lean pork (about VND 71,000) or below. Above beef it is a premium or novelty item. A mass product priced above pork is not supported by any revealed evidence we found.
- **Protein.** Do not sell "more protein" to adults. Do sell meat-like protein density inside meat-replacing formats: 12 to 20 g per 100 g, against 19 g for lean pork and a 4.7 g median for today's *chay* foods ([[ch02-alt-protein-today]]). At 10 g per 100 g a food qualifies for a "high protein" claim ([[ch13-consumers]]).
- **Format.** Build for the dish: toppings, fillings, rolls, balls and mince for home cooking and street food.
- **Growth.** Poultry, not pork, carries most projected meat growth to 2035; poultry-style formats deserve as much attention as pork analogues. Urban growth is in eating out, which points to foodservice and B2B routes ([[ch15-channels]]).
- **Nutrition.** Do not pitch a new protein as the answer to child undernutrition. For school-age children, including upland boarders, published menus and weighed diets show protein and zinc met at lunch and dinner; the documented shortfalls are breakfast, calcium and vitamin A. A plant dish that removes all the meat needs added zinc and little sodium; a blend in minced dishes needs nothing extra. Stunting is set before age two, where a plant product must meet the young-child protein-quality pattern, register as a food for children under 36 months and beat fortified cereal and milk products {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

**For each reader.**
- **Startups:** set price targets per 100 g of protein against eggs, chicken and lean pork, and design formats for named dishes.
- **Investors:** demand is growing in tonnes, but the money is in low-price everyday protein; models that need consumer premiums above about 20% are not supported by revealed evidence.
- **Manufacturers:** a pork extender saves money at every pork price; as a hedge it removes only about a sixth of a recipe's exposure to a pork shock, so value it on the saving and test a new extender against your own soy recipe.
- **Research bodies:** measure protein per serving in common dishes and publish a current food composition table that includes dishes and *chay* foods; measure phytate, zinc and DIAAS (on both the young-child and older-child patterns) of tofu, textured soy and blended minced dishes, and add textured soy to the composition table that school menu software uses.
- **Policy makers:** the 2026 recommendations, the Ten tips and Decision 1982 already favour diverse protein including legumes, and school guidance (Decision 3958/QĐ-BYT) sets no animal share, although the menu software still prints an animal-protein standard of at least 48% ([[ch15-channels]]). State zinc and iron per lunch by absorption band and sodium per lunch in the menu software, and note that mandatory fortification (Decree 09/2016) reaches no soy protein food [@APR-04; @NQR-02; @APR-16; @APR-17] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **International organisations:** separate the urban "too much meat" problem from child undernutrition, and within child undernutrition separate school-age children (plates already carry protein and zinc; breakfast, calcium and vitamin A are the gaps) from children under two (complementary-food standards, where plant products face the young-child protein-quality pattern, registration and trial evidence favouring milk or fortified blends). An India roundtable is examining adding plant and fermented proteins to feeding schemes on cost and protein-quality grounds [@AFN-14] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:stated}; Vietnam's school plates point to micronutrients instead. A fortified plant item for boarding-school breakfasts or charity-funded lunches is a research option to test on calcium and vitamin A as well as zinc, not a product brief.

**Related:** [[app-d1-diet-chay-prices]], [[ch12-chay-baseline]], [[ch15-channels]], [[ch18-demand-sizing]].

data.title: The incumbent: chay, tofu and soy milk
data.summary: Chay, vegetarian eating on lunar days and festivals, is Vietnam's largest plant-protein occasion, served by tofu, soy milk, mushrooms and cheap mock meat, and we estimate that existing chay days already avoid about 25,000 t of meat protein a year. It is the cheapest place to launch a higher-protein ingredient, but the wrong place to count meat displacement.
data.body:
# 12. The incumbent: chay, tofu and soy milk

**In one paragraph.** In Vietnamese usage *chay* is three things at once: a practice (not eating animal flesh on set days of the lunar month and at festivals), a cuisine (*cơm chay*, *bún chay*) and a product category (the frozen *thực phẩm chay* aisle). It is Vietnam's largest plant-protein eating occasion, and it is served by tofu, soy milk, mushrooms and cheap industrial *đồ chay* (traditional vegetarian food), not by modern analogues. No survey asks about chay days, but national diet surveillance caps them: on an ordinary day in late 2021, 7.9% of adults ate no meat, poultry or fish. Revealed signals are strong and regular: specialist sellers report two to three times normal sales in the seventh lunar month, and mainstream retail 20 to 40% more. On a stated assumption that about 30% of people keep 2 to 3 chay days a month, chay days are about 2.5% of all person-days (about a third of that ceiling; about 5% is the practical upper bound) and already avoid about 25,000 t of meat protein a year, as much as the Part IV alternative-protein scenario assumes for 2030 to 2035. Chay foods are cheaper than meat per kilogram but protein-poor, so they are expensive per gram of protein. Their trust problems are borax, microbes and unlabelled goods rather than hidden meat, and the national vegetarian standard is voluntary and broader than Buddhist chay. For frontier actors chay is a ready shelf, cold chain and set of buyers for a higher-protein ingredient, and the wrong place to count meat displacement.

---

## 12.1 How many people eat chay: unmeasured, but capped

- **The religious base.** Pew Research Center's face-to-face probability survey (n = 2,255, June to September 2023) found that 38% of Vietnamese adults identify as Buddhist, 48% report no religion and 86% offered food or drink to ancestors in the past year. It asked nothing about diet [@CHY-06] {VN-direct|High} {dx:stated}. Official counts of Buddhists differ threefold: 4.6 million in the 2019 census against more than 14 million registered followers in the 2023 government White Paper [@CHY-08; @CHY-07] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}. Lay people who keep lunar chay days include many who say they have no religion.
- **The calendar.** The schedules described in academic and press sources are consistent: two days a month (the 1st and 15th of the lunar month, *mùng một* and *ngày rằm*), four days (adding the 14th and the last day), eight or ten days, and whole months, above all the 1st lunar month and the 7th, which holds the *Vu Lan* festival [@CHY-09; @CHY-10; @CHY-25; @CHY-26] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Every Vietnamese academic survey we found recruited at chay restaurants, pagodas or universities, so none gives a prevalence [@CHY-09; @CHY-10; @CHY-11] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}.
- **A ceiling from national diet data.** No probability survey asks about chay, but one asks about diet. The Diet Quality Questionnaire (Gallup, 1,007 adults by mobile telephone, 13 November to 12 December 2021, an ordinary month with two principal chay days) found that 92.1% of adults had eaten meat, poultry or fish on the previous day, so 7.9% (95% interval 5.3 to 11.0%) had a flesh-free day (our calculation from the published share) [@APR-36; @BRD-01; @BRD-03] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. A chay day is flesh-free, so this caps chay-day person-days. Vietnam sits mid-region on this measure, below Thailand (9.8%, surveyed in 2023) and China (14.9%) and above the Philippines (5.8%) and Cambodia (3.3%); food lists differ, so the comparison is indicative [@APR-36; @BRD-03] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Lunar chay days do not make Vietnam an outlier in meat-free days. {{kn:kn-flesh-free-days}}
- **Online panels overstate it.** Rakuten Insight's online panel (n = 4,018, November 2021) found 86% had eaten "plant-based alternatives", the highest of 13 markets, and 10% said they eat only plant-based food [@CHY-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Vietnamese respondents count tofu, soy milk and *đồ chay* as plant-based, so these numbers measure familiarity with the incumbent, not demand for new products.
- **Rejected.** The widely repeated "about 10% of Vietnamese are vegetarian" has no survey behind it and we do not use it [@CHY-15; @CHY-18] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}. National diet data contradict it: only 7.9% of adults (at most 11.0%) had a flesh-free day, and that share must hold chay keepers as well as any full-time vegetarians [@APR-36] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

The single cheapest piece of missing evidence in Part III is still a chay-day question in a probability survey ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]). A cheaper first step may exist: if Gallup holds the interview dates of the 2021 survey (not confirmed), the flesh-free share on recall days that fell on the lunar 1st or 15th can be compared with other days. About 65 recall days fall on the two principal chay days, so power is low: even a doubling would be only borderline detectable (our calculation) [@BRD-03] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

## 12.2 The lunar calendar in the till

Every figure below is a quote to the press, so each is Low on its own. Taken together, from 2024 to 2026, both main cities and several independent sellers, they support a Medium-confidence conclusion: chay demand roughly doubles in specialist channels in the 7th lunar month, rises 20 to 40% in mainstream retail, and moves the prices of supply-constrained items (fresh mushrooms) but not of tofu {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-vu-lan-uplift}}

| Signal | Size | Year and place | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chay shop sales in Vu Lan against previous months | About 2 times; one shop 3 times | 2024, Ho Chi Minh City | [@CHY-16] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| GO! hypermarkets, chay sales month on month | +20 to +40% | 2024 | [@CHY-16] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| Saigon Co.op chay stock; chay sales | +40%; +20% | 2024 | [@CHY-16; @CHY-17] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| One manufacturer's chay volume, year on year | 3.5 times | 2024 | [@CHY-17] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| One Hanoi chay shop, Vu Lan orders | Rise significantly from lunar day 10 to 15, most on days 14 and 15 (no multiplier given) | 2026 | [@CHY-20] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| One Ho Chi Minh City tofu maker | Output +15 to +20%, price unchanged | 2026 | [@CHY-19] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| Straw and king oyster mushrooms | About VND 150,000 to 160,000 per kg, against 80,000 to 100,000 normally | 2026 | [@CHY-22] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| One Hanoi restaurant, all offering trays (not chay only) | Buying power -20 to -30% on 2025 while input costs rose 15 to 20%; buyers shifting to chay or simple trays under VND 1 million | 2026 | [@CHY-21] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| Chinese textured protein (HS 2106.10) shipped to Vietnam, two months before the Vu Lan month | 1.33 times an average month (5 of 6 years); flat to the world and to Thailand | 2019 to 2024 | [@BRD-05; @BRD-07] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |

> **Correction.** In v0.6 this table said Hanoi chay sellers reported 2 to 3 times normal Vu Lan volume and that a Hai Phong caterer's chay tray orders fell 20 to 30%; the sources say the 2 to 3 times is a fruit seller's quote, the chay shop gives no multiplier, and the 20 to 30% fall is one Hanoi restaurant's buying power across all offering trays.

Two design lessons follow. One tofu maker flexed volume, not price, which suggests tofu stays the price anchor even at the peak. Fresh mushrooms cannot flex supply, so their prices roughly double, which is an opening for a shelf-stable protein that holds its price through the peak. One Hanoi restaurant's soft 2026 season suggests that offering-tray demand is price sensitive [@CHY-21; @CHY-19; @CHY-22] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}.

The calendar reaches the ingredient order book, but in a smaller swing. China-reported monthly trade data show a Vietnam-specific rise of about a third in textured protein shipments before the Vu Lan month, while the same code to other destinations stays flat, and shipments fall to 38% of an average month in the *Tết* (lunar new year) month, when every Vietnam-bound flow, feed included, dips [@BRD-05; @BRD-07] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Vietnam's own import records do not show the pre-Vu Lan rise [@BRD-06] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. This is revealed evidence that part of the imported textured protein goes into chay on the lunar calendar; it does not size that part (`trade_seasonal_summary.csv`).

## 12.3 The size of the incumbent

| Category | What we know | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Soybeans used for food (tofu, soy milk, sauces) | About 550,000 t of beans a year (2025/26), roughly 5 kg per person; FAO food balance sheets agree (533,000 t and 5.31 kg per person in 2023) | [@CHY-45; @DIE-07] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Tofu bought or made for home use | 0.43 kg per person a month (2024), flat since 2012 and down 14% from 2010; about 520,000 t a year (our calculation, home use only) | [@DIE-05] {VN-direct\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| Daily reach of soy foods and beans | 40.0% of adults ate dried beans, soybeans, tofu, soy milk or bean flour on the previous day (2021); urban 40.5%, rural 39.2% | [@APR-36; @BRD-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Branded soy milk | About VND 5,300 billion (USD 204 million) in 2025 (our derivation from Vinasoy revenue and its 90.6% share of branded soy milk in 2024, per Bao Viet Securities; the supply chapters use about 80% of all soy milk, an older and broader base) | [@CON-26; @CON-27; @CON-28] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:inferred} |
| Mushrooms | 250,000 to 270,000 t produced (press citing institutes; another source gives a tenth of this) | [@CHY-51; @NOV-78] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| Industrial *đồ chay* | No audited sales figure found; Vissan's 2026 plan gives no chay split, its 2026 shareholder meeting set no chay target, and its only 2026 chay news was two Vu Lan dumpling products | [@CHY-30; @AIB-14; @AIB-16] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Retailers' own-label chay | Co.op Select frozen chay dumplings, spring rolls and rice rolls made by GN Foods; Lotte Mart Choice L chay spring rolls and dumplings | [@CPC-15; @AIB-30; @FORM-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Chay restaurants | At least 3,275 listings on Foody in 23 former provinces (1,873 in Ho Chi Minh City, 401 in Hanoi, 201 in Da Nang), cumulative and including closed venues | [@CHY-31] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Chains | The largest we could count, Loving Hut, has 13 outlets; premium Chay Garden 2; Hum 3 (2018) | [@CHY-32; @CHY-34; @CHY-36] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Pagoda kitchens | 18,544 Buddhist places of worship; meals and purchasing unmeasured | [@CHY-07] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |

{{kn:kn-chay-listings}} {{kn:kn-soy-milk-market}}

Tofu is the country's plant-protein staple, but it is flat and northern. Households in the Red River Delta use 0.69 kg a month, 3.6 times the Mekong Delta's 0.19 kg [@DIE-05] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Soy milk is the one plant category that sells at national scale through modern brands, and it grew in 2025: Vinasoy sold 264 million litres (up 4%) and its revenue rose 14% for the year, with soy-milk revenue up 22% in the fourth quarter, alongside a 13-fold rise in parent QNS's promotion spend [@AIB-05; @AIB-06; @CON-28; @CON-29] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Why plant milk worked where plant meat did not is discussed in [[ch13-consumers]].

{{chart:chart-tofu-by-region}}

The published market sizes for Vietnamese vegetarian or vegan food (USD 103 to 112 million, "USD 1 billion", and "USD 500 million" for plant-based meat alone) have no visible method and we do not use them [@CHY-13; @CHY-18; @CHY-15; @CHY-16] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}.

## 12.4 What chay buyers value, tolerate and fear

**Imitation meat is mainstream and religiously tolerated.** Monks quoted in Buddhist media call *giả mặn* (chay food that imitates meat) a skilful means that reduces killing; a minority of Buddhist writers say it keeps the mind attached to meat; we found no binding Sangha ruling against it [@CHY-53; @CHY-54; @CHY-55] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. One Ho Chi Minh City chay shop named *chả chay* (mock pork roll) and mushrooms as its best sellers in Vu Lan 2024 [@CHY-26] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. The authors of a 2019 southern study observe that periodic eaters prefer processed foods in their chay meals while strict vegetarians mostly eat unprocessed plant foods [@CHY-09] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. That is the key split: the periodic majority buys mock meat; the strict minority buys whole foods [@CHY-09; @CHY-26] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Two Hanoi sellers reported in 2026 that buyers are moving from "industrial" chay to mushrooms, lotus, beans and vegetables [@CHY-20; @CHY-21] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}; we log this as a possible regional difference or trend ([[app-r2-disagreements]]).

**The allium rule binds a minority.** Strict Buddhist cooking avoids the five pungent plants (*ngũ vị tân*: onion or scallion, chives, garlic and two small alliums). The Sangha newspaper's advisory panel says this binds people who have taken the Bodhisattva precepts, not lay people keeping lunar days [@CHY-52] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Mainstream industrial chay ignores it: in our re-read of the retail audit, at least 36% of chay-named products with an ingredient list name onion, garlic, shallot or leek, and about 5% (3 of 64) name egg or dairy [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed} ([[app-d3-retail-demand-signals]]). Allium-free and egg-free variants are a requirement for pagoda kitchens, offerings and strict buyers, not for the mass market.

**Trust is the weakest point, and the problem is safety, not hidden meat.** Unlabelled mock meat at VND 60,000 to 250,000 per kg is sold openly in Ho Chi Minh City markets; inspectors seized a tonne of untraceable *chả chay* in 2025 and 500 kg of Chinese textured soy without Vietnamese labels, transported as "chay spare ribs", in 2022 [@CHY-23; @CHY-59; @CHY-60] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. The recurring cases are about safety: borax in *chả đòn chay* (chay pork roll; 6,573 kg seized in An Giang in 2022) and in tofu skin, a botulism case in 2020, and expert warnings about additives, dyes and reused oil in the main 2026 exposé [@TRU-16; @TRU-14; @TRU-04; @LBL-23; @CHY-23] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Meat in chay is a latent rumour, not a live scandal. A Can Tho University team built a DNA test for meat in vegetarian food, citing "many cases" of meat found in chay foods, but reported no prevalence data [@CHY-61] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. We found no press or official report confirming meat in a Vietnamese chay product from 2015 to 2026. The only official case is an April 2021 seizure of more than 3 t of *chả đòn chay* in An Giang on suspicion of meat and fish, with no published result; meat-in-chay stories circulate as a relayed 2015 Taiwanese scandal and as social-media videos [@TRU-18; @TRU-01; @TRU-30] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-meat-in-chay-cases}}

**Inspections check papers, not meat.** After the 2020 botulism case, Hanoi inspected 93 chay facilities and fined 14 a total of VND 55 million; the checks covered hygiene, origin papers and storage, and no meat content was reported. We found no official report of meat-DNA testing of chay [@LBL-23; @LBL-24] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. A test is close: in February 2025 the state testing centre QUATEST 3 announced a validated real-time PCR screen for vertebrate DNA (tested on 86 species, detection limit 0.001%), to be offered once its accreditation registration is approved [@TRU-24] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

> **Correction.** In v0.6 this said QUATEST 3 had sold a PCR screen for 86 animal species since February 2025; the source says the method was validated then and will be offered only once registration is approved, and the 86 species are its test panel.

**Certification is voluntary and broader than Buddhist chay.** The national standard TCVN 13625:2023 (equivalent to ISO 23662:2021) defines vegetarian and vegan claims, but its "vegetarian" allows egg, milk and honey and it has no allium rule, so its chay is broader than the chay that pagoda kitchens buy. V-Label is offered through SGS; we found no national or Buddhist chay certification in use [@LBL-15; @CHY-57; @CHY-58] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. A false chay claim is already unlawful, because labels must be truthful and names must not mislead about composition [@LBL-06; @LBL-09] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

## 12.5 Price: cheap per kilogram, dear per gram of protein

Street chay costs VND 15,000 (2026) to 30,000 (2024) a plate against VND 30,000 to 35,000 for a meat rice plate in Ho Chi Minh City in 2026 [@CHY-38; @CHY-42; @CHY-40] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. In modern retail, Vissan's frozen chay spring roll (*chả giò*) sold 38% below its meat version [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}; the other same-brand pairs we found are low confidence and range from 52% below to 19% above the meat version [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Premium chay dining costs VND 239,000 to 379,000 a head at a premium buffet (2026) and VND 350,000 to 400,000 a bill at a well-known restaurant (2022) [@CHY-33; @CHY-37] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

Per gram of protein the picture reverses. With a median of about 4.3 g of protein per 100 g, filled chay wrappers cost a median VND 369,000 per 100 g of protein and market mock meat roughly VND 120,000 to 200,000 (assuming 4.5 to 5 g of protein), against VND 66,000 for tofu on label values [@FORM-01; @CHY-20] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. The buyer does not see this, because chay is bought per kilogram and per plate. It defines the headroom for a better ingredient: at today's shelf price, a *chả* (sausage or loaf) with 12 g of protein per 100 g would deliver protein at roughly VND 50,000 to 75,000 per 100 g, in tofu's range (our calculation) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

## 12.6 A channel, but not a displacement route

**Where chay is a ready channel.** Signed frozen chay sections with several brands exist in the modern chains we audited, and markets carry fresh and loose chay [@FORM-01; @CHY-26; @CHY-20] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Buyers already pay for chay chicken, fish, shrimp, ham, sausages and spare ribs [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}, so a higher-protein analogue asks no one to accept a new idea. Retailers already commission own-label chay from Vietnamese makers, so a better ingredient can reach the shelf through a co-packer [@CPC-15; @AIB-30] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Demand is predictable, with fortnightly peaks and two big months a year. And the high-protein chay products already rely on imported Chinese textured soy or gluten ([[ch02-alt-protein-today]]), so a domestic replacement is a purchasing decision by manufacturers, not a behaviour change by consumers {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

**Where it resists.** Price ceilings are low, and in 2026 one Hanoi restaurant reported offering-tray buying power falling as costs rose [@CHY-21; @CHY-38] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Some sellers report a shift away from processed ("industrial") chay [@CHY-20; @CHY-21] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}. The strict segment wants whole plants [@CHY-09; @CHY-20; @CHY-21] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}. Offering trays are bought for presentation and ingredients (our reading: not protein) [@CHY-24] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}. Chay manufacturers and shop owners, in the interviews we found, talk about price, convenience, freshness, safety and natural ingredients; none asked for more protein.

**The displacement arithmetic.** On a stated assumption that 30% of people keep 2.5 chay days a month, chay days are about 2.5% of all person-days (our assumption and calculation; no survey measures either input) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. That uses about a third of the 7.9% flesh-free ceiling from national diet data. The illustrative range we gave earlier (20 to 50% keeping 2 to 4 days, 1.3 to 6.7%) overreaches at the top: 6.7% would need 85% of all flesh-free days to be chay days and exceeds the survey's lower confidence bound of 5.3%, so about 5% of person-days is the practical upper bound (our calculation) [@APR-36; @BRD-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. Multiplied by average meat protein per person-day, existing chay days avoid about 25,000 t of meat protein a year in 2025 (our calculation, [[app-d8-demand-model]]) {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate} {dx:inferred}. That is the same order as the Part IV S-ALT scenario, which assumes 1% of meat protein (about 11,800 t) replaced by plant-based and fermented foods in 2030 and 3% (about 39,000 t) in 2035 ([[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]). {{kn:kn-chay-days-share}}

Three consequences follow {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}:

1. Chay days are already in the meat baseline. A novel protein that wins chay-day protein replaces tofu, imported textured soy, gluten and mushrooms. It improves nutrition and substitutes imports; it displaces no meat. Retailer ratio methods that count protein-rich foods by weight, as WWF's 2025 method does, would score protein-poor chay foods at face value, so impact should be counted in protein, not kilograms [@AFN-34] {general|Medium} {dx:inferred}.
2. Meat displacement needs either more chay occasions (a third day a month, chay breakfasts, canteen chay days) or entry into ordinary meals. [[ch18-demand-sizing]] shows that added chay days are, on paper, the cheapest route to the S-ALT volumes. Organised promotion of plant-based eating is small: Humane World for Animals included Viet Nam in its 2025 plant-based menu training (370 or more chefs and 570 or more nutritionists across seven countries), and Dharma Voices for Animals runs a pagoda-based programme at Phap Van Pagoda in Hanoi [@AFN-23; @AFN-36] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
3. We found no evidence on compensation, that is, whether people who eat chay on the 1st and 15th eat more meat on other days.

## 12.7 What this means for the frontier

- **Sell an ingredient first.** The winning first product is a protein base (textured, fungal or blended) that existing chay makers and retailers' own-label co-packers put into *chả*, *giò*, *nem*, dumplings and spring rolls.
- **Design target.** Lift product protein from 4 to 5 g to 10 to 12 g per 100 g while keeping the shelf price inside today's range (supermarket about VND 56,000 to 190,000 per kg for filled wrappers; market VND 60,000 to 90,000 per kg for *giò* and *nem*) [@FORM-01; @CHY-20] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. At 10 g per 100 g a food meets the "high protein" (*cao đạm*) condition of the voluntary standard TCVN 14429:2025; of 43 audited plant-protein foods, the 7 that already meet it are all frozen analogues, and only 6 of 18 filled wrappers reach even the 5 g "source" level [@LBL-03; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed} ([[ch13-consumers]]).
- **Build for the calendar.** At retail, plan capacity and frozen stock for two to three times normal demand in the 1st and 7th lunar months [@CHY-16] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. An ingredient maker should plan for a smaller swing: China-reported shipments run about a third higher in the two months before the Vu Lan month and fall deeply in the *Tết* month, though Vietnam's own import records show no pre-Vu Lan rise [@BRD-05; @BRD-06; @BRD-07] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **Lead with safety and a full label.** A registered maker, a full label, few additives and a short ingredient list meet the category's live trust problems (borax, microbes, unlabelled goods). "Verified meat-free" is a secondary reassurance, which a PCR screen could supply once QUATEST 3 offers it. Avoid "lab", "future of meat" and environmental claims as the main message.
- **Offer allium-free and egg-free variants** for pagoda kitchens and strict buyers, clearly labelled.

**For each reader.**
- **Startups:** your first customers are chay makers and the co-packers of retailers' own-label chay; price per kilogram of finished product, not per gram of protein, is what their buyers see.
- **Investors:** underwrite on per-kilogram price parity with existing *đồ chay* and repeat orders from manufacturers; demand is seasonal and price sensitive.
- **Manufacturers:** a declared protein content would be new on the chay shelf. The claim conditions are set by TCVN 14429:2025 and need no registration; print the number ("10 g đạm/100 g"), because *giàu đạm* (rich in protein) is not a defined term. Test reformulations at the Vu Lan and first-month peaks, when trial is highest.
- **Research bodies:** publish a composition table for chay foods and develop allium-free flavour systems. Test borax, preservatives, microbes and protein first, and add animal DNA by asking QUATEST 3 about its new animal-DNA screen. Publish with the Vietnam Food Administration (VFA), publish the methods and do not name small makers: a 2016 consumer-association survey of fish sauce (101 of more than 150 samples flagged) led to delistings, a Ministry of Health rebuttal and a backlash against the testers [@TRU-24; @TRU-19] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **Policy makers:** TCVN 13625:2023 already defines vegetarian and vegan claims, and false chay claims are already unlawful. Ask VFA to state that an unqualified *chay* or *thuần chay* (vegan) claim means the vegan criteria, with egg or milk named in a qualifier and allium-free left as a voluntary claim. The new Food Safety Law, which the National Assembly takes first comments on in October 2026 and considers for passage in May 2027, and its decree are the window [@APR-07; @LBL-15] {VN-direct|Medium}. Target safety inspections (borax, microbes, labels) before the 1st and 7th lunar months.
- **International organisations and funders:** fund the cheapest chay evidence first (a lunar-date tabulation of the 2021 Diet Quality Questionnaire, then a chay-day question in a survey) and a chay safety and composition survey; count impact only for added chay occasions, not upgraded ones, and count it in protein, not kilograms. Match the route to the funder's rules: several diet-change funders exclude Vietnam or this kind of work ([[ch18-demand-sizing]], [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).

**Related:** [[ch02-alt-protein-today]], [[app-d1-diet-chay-prices]], [[app-d3-retail-demand-signals]].

data.title: Consumers and new proteins: what people say and what they buy
data.summary: Vietnamese survey respondents are open to plant-based meat, yet only 15% intend to eat less meat and only 3% eat it weekly, and imported analogues cost 12 to 18 times chicken or eggs per gram of protein. Plant milk is the one modern plant category at scale, and consumers want more protein choice in familiar dishes, not a meat replacement.
data.body:
# 13. Consumers and new proteins: what people say and what they buy

**In one paragraph.** Asked in an online survey, urban Vietnamese are aware of plant-based meat (90%), have often tried it (42%) and are the most willing in Southeast Asia to choose it at the same price as meat (74%). Yet only 15% intend to eat less meat, the lowest of six countries, and only 3% eat plant-based meat weekly, much of which is probably traditional mock meat. What people do tells a starker story. Imported analogues entered through bars, cafés and gourmet shops from 2019 and had left the shelves we audited by 2026; they cost 12 to 18 times chicken or eggs per gram of protein. The one modern plant category that sells at scale is plant milk, priced at or below dairy and made by local incumbents: online, the best-selling plant milk sells 60 to 79% of the litres of the best-selling dairy milk. Protein sells in that aisle only as a premium niche, and a protein claim on soy milk did not lift its sales. From 2027 a sugary-drink excise may fall on sweetened plant milks but not on dairy, so new plant milks should stay at or below 5 g of sugar per 100 ml. Twenty grams of protein from a chay wrapper costs more than a whole street meal. Abroad, plant-based meat peaked in 2020 to 2021, trial did not turn into habit, price parity on its own did not create growth and meat purchases did not fall; in the region, firms that launched branded analogues mostly went quiet or moved to private label. Vietnamese respondents ask for more variety, food they know how to cook, fewer additives and safer food, not a replacement for meat. That is a brief for ingredients inside familiar foods, with a numeric protein claim (10 g per 100 g for "high protein") where the food earns it.

---

## 13.1 The evidence is thin, and almost all of it is stated

We built a register of every consumer study with Vietnamese data on plant-based foods, meat reduction or new proteins (26 studies, [[app-d2-consumer-evidence]]). Only one large survey gives Vietnam numbers on plant-based meat: GFI APAC's "Decoding demand", run by The Good Growth Co. in 2023 on an online panel of 5,971 people in six countries, 1,049 of them in the Hanoi region and Ho Chi Minh City [@CON-01; @CON-02; @CON-03] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. The rest are two commercial online panels (Rakuten Insight 2021 and 2025), one academic urban survey (Delley et al., snowball sample, n = 616) and about ten small student or convenience samples [@CON-06; @CON-07; @CON-08] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. No Vietnamese study of new proteins reaches our top quality grade (a probability sample with a full method). The one national probability survey that touches the subject, the Diet Quality Questionnaire (Gallup, 2021), asks only whether people ate soy foods or meat the day before: 40% of adults had eaten beans, tofu or soy milk ([[ch11-protein-diet]], [[ch12-chay-baseline]]) [@APR-36; @BRD-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. We found no choice experiment, auction or in-store price test for plant-based meat or milk in Vietnam, and no household purchase panel data for these categories. Marketplace sales counters, which we read for this report, are the nearest thing to purchase data (section 13.5). Every consumer number below should be read with that in mind.

## 13.2 Aware, curious, rarely buying

| Measure (GFI, 2023, online panel) | Vietnam (n = 1,049) | Six-country average | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Have heard of plant-based meat | 90% | 91% | [@CON-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:stated} |
| Have ever tried it | 42% | 47% | [@CON-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:stated} |
| Eat it monthly or more | 20% | 20% | [@CON-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:stated} |
| Eat it weekly or more | 3% | 5% | [@CON-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:stated} |
| Intend to reduce meat | 15% (lowest of six) | 21% | [@CON-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:stated} |
| Would choose it at the same price as meat | 74% (highest of six) | 62% | [@CON-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:stated} |

{{chart:chart-pbm-funnel}}

{{kn:kn-pbm-weekly}} {{kn:kn-intend-cut-meat}}

Three cautions apply. First, modern analogues were almost absent from Vietnamese shops, so many respondents probably read "plant-based meat" as traditional mock meat; the Vietnamese questionnaire wording is not public (our inference) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Second, Vietnamese respondents report 43.3 meat-eating occasions a month, second only to Thailand, and an urban survey found only 4% flexitarians among meat eaters [@CON-02; @CON-08] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Demand is for more kinds of protein, not for less meat. Third, the much-quoted "5% to 63%" is a regional, hypothetical figure: 5% of all six-country respondents eat plant-based meat weekly, and 63% say they would eat it "always" or "often" if all their concerns were resolved. No Vietnam split is public [@CON-02; @ECO-24] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:stated}. It is not a forecast.

Rakuten's broader category ("plant-based alternatives", mostly plant milk) shows Vietnam with the highest trial rate of any Asian market (86% in 2021, 92% in 2025), but the share of Vietnamese triers who have tried meat alternatives stayed at 47 to 49% [@CON-06; @CON-07] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}.

## 13.3 What would make people eat more, and why they would

Asked what would make them eat more plant-based meat, Vietnamese respondents chose affordability less often than any other country (38% against an average of 47%) and chose availability (31%), variety (29%), fewer additives (27%, highest of six) and knowing how to cook it (22%, highest of six) more often. They were the least likely to want a product that "tasted more like meat" (23%) [@CON-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Rakuten's 2025 panel agrees: "difficult to find where I live" is the top Vietnamese barrier (33%) and cost is cited by only 21%, the lowest of the six Southeast Asian markets in the survey [@CON-07] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}.

Health is the first reason people give in every source (55% of Rakuten's Vietnamese panel say plant-based products are healthier) [@CON-07] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. A soy-milk maker already uses that motive: a sponsored soy-nutrition article cites the new Law on Disease Prevention and the Ministry of Health's Ten tips on nutrition [@APR-43] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Food safety is the motive specific to Vietnam: urban Vietnamese rate "a very high level of food safety" at 5.35 on a 6-point scale, against 4.59 in Switzerland, and worry about hormones and drug residues in meat [@CON-08; @CON-10] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Environmental concern is weak: it ranks sixth of seven Rakuten reasons and had a small negative effect in one Hanoi student sample [@CON-07; @CON-13] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}. Family influence is strong, and meat is "non-negotiable" at special meals [@CON-08; @CON-10] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}.

Lower stated price sensitivity should not be over-read. It sits next to a revealed price gap of an order of magnitude (section 13.4), and in a Hanoi study price had the largest effect of any factor on attitudes to new proteins [@NOV-02] {VN-direct|High} {dx:stated}.

## 13.4 Price: what people say, pay and face

**Stated.** GFI asked respondents to choose between plant-based meat and meat at a grocery shop as the relative price moved. At parity, 74% of Vietnamese respondents chose plant-based meat; at 20% dearer, 64%; at 50% dearer, 47%; at double, 26% [@CON-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. GFI itself says this shows relative interest, not willingness to pay. For design, it says: reach roughly price parity with the meat replaced, because stated interest falls by over a third at +50%. {{kn:kn-parity-choice}}

{{chart:chart-price-parity-choice}}

**Revealed.** The imported analogue on Vietnamese shelves in September 2026 cost VND 542,000 to 622,000 per 100 g of protein, 12 to 18 times eggs and chicken ([[ch11-protein-diet]]) [@FORM-01; @COST-40; @COST-41] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The clearest evidence that urban Vietnamese pay a premium for a plant product is café oat milk: in 2023 OatSide oat milk was used in nearly 100 cafés and outlets, and drinks made with nut milks such as OatSide were listed VND 10,000 to 15,000 dearer per cup than cow-milk drinks [@CON-35] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

**Tested.** None in Vietnam for plant-based meat, blends or plant milk. The nearest tested Vietnamese evidence is about safety and GMO labels: a real-money auction put the premium for safer pork at 20% [@DIE-30] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:tested}, and another found an 84% premium for soymilk labelled non-GM [@NOV-08] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:tested} ([[ch14-frontier-demand]]).

**What 20 g of protein costs.** Re-reading the retail audit for demand ([[app-d3-retail-demand-signals]]), the median cost of 20 g of protein, a meal's protein, is about VND 13,000 from tofu or dried textured soy, VND 56,000 from a frozen meat analogue, VND 74,000 from a filled chay wrapper and VND 91,000 from plant milk [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. From eggs or chicken it is VND 7,000 to 9,000 and from lean pork about VND 14,000 ([[ch11-protein-diet]]). A street rice plate with meat costs VND 30,000 to 35,000 in Ho Chi Minh City [@CHY-40] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. So the protein in most packaged alternatives costs more than a whole meal. The exception is bulk: dry soy-and-gluten pieces bought online in 1 kg bags give 20 g of protein for about VND 1,800 to 6,000, the cheapest protein in our retail data (on a borrowed label protein range; our calculation) [@MKT-03; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-protein-cost-serving}}

{{chart:chart-protein-cost-serving}}

## 13.5 What people actually buy

**Plant-based meat has not found a footing.** Mintel logged no plant-based meat launches in Vietnam from 2022 to the second quarter of 2023 [@ECO-23] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Beyond Meat (2019, a craft-beer bar), OmniFoods (gourmet retail 2022; Starbucks Vietnam's summer 2023 menu), Next Meats and Heura came through restaurants and gourmet shops [@ECO-15; @ECO-16; @ECO-20] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. None was on the shelves of the 11 stores we audited in September 2026, including the two gourmet chains that stocked them in 2022; the only extruded modern analogue was one Italian brand in one gourmet store [@FORM-01; @ECO-15] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. CP's Meat Zero chay range is listed on Kamereo, a platform supplying restaurants and cafés, but it was not orderable in September 2026 and its eight listings show 386 units (80 kg) sold in all; no Meat Zero, Beyond or Omni listing appeared on Lazada or Tiki [@AIS-25; @ECR-06; @MKT-03; @MKT-05] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. We found no trace of a local startup (VMEAT) after 2022, and no Vietnam launch by a Korean startup backed by a Vietnamese fund in 2024 [@ECO-19; @BRD-18; @ECO-65] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Meanwhile incumbents extend their chay lines: Vissan launched two chay products for Vu Lan 2026 [@CHY-29] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

**Plant milk is the category that sells.** Vinasoy's soy-milk revenue was about VND 4,800 billion in 2025 (our sum of nine-month and fourth-quarter segment revenue), implying a branded soy-milk market of about VND 5,300 billion (USD 204 million) (our derivation from Vinasoy's 90.6% share of branded soy milk in 2024, whose basis, value or volume, is not stated; the supply chapters' figure of about 80% refers to all soy milk on an older base) [@CON-26; @CON-27; @CON-28] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Vinasoy sold 264 million litres in 2025 (up 4%); its revenue rose 14%, with Veyo nut milks up 50%, premium Fami up 36% and e-commerce sales up 135% [@AIB-05; @AIB-06] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Plant milks were 51 of the 186 products in the retail audit, across 14 brands [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Vinamilk reported double-digit growth in nut milk in early 2026 [@ECO-44] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Vietnam imported USD 3.9 billion of tree nuts in 2025 (up 40%), which USDA attributes partly to plant-milk demand among younger consumers [@APR-34; @AIB-40] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

Household purchases online now show the scale. On Lazada and Tiki, read without logging in on 25 September 2026, the best-selling plant milk sells 60% and 79% of the litres of the best-selling dairy milk; domestic nut and soy milks lead, and imported oat is under 2% of the plant-milk litres read (cumulative counters on 96 listings; our calculation) [@MKT-03; @MKT-05] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Kitchens buy differently: on Kamereo, plant milks are about 4% of milk litres and 1.5 to 2.1% of milk protein, and the plant best seller is imported Oatside oat milk, marketed for coffee (our inference: bought for coffee, not protein) [@ECR-06] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed} (`kitchen_platform_counters.csv`). Inside Vietnam's largest dairy company plant milk is still small: plant-based products were 1.30% of Vinamilk's range in FAIRR's 2024 index, with no time-bound target [@AFN-21] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}, and Vinamilk's 2025 annual report positions plant milk as a nutrition product that is "no longer seen as a substitute for animal milk" [@AIB-01] {VN-direct|High} {dx:stated}.

**Search behaviour tells the same story.** From 2019 to 2026, Google search interest in *sữa hạt* (nut or seed milk) averaged about 17 to 19 times that in *thịt thực vật* (plant meat). *Sữa hạt* has roughly tripled since 2019; *thịt thực vật* peaked in 2021 to 2022, has fallen by about 60% since, and its top query is "what is plant meat?". *Thuần chay* (vegan) rose about tenfold from 2019 to 2024 [@CON-37] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-search-ratio}}

{{chart:chart-search-interest}}

**Why plant milk worked and plant meat did not (our inference).** {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}

| Factor | Plant milk | Plant-based meat |
|---|---|---|
| Price against the animal product | Mass soy milk about VND 22,900 per litre (2026, on promotion), below cow milk at about VND 33,000 to 45,000 per bottle of OatSide's size, 1 L (2023); about VND 25,200 in 2028 if the sugary-drink excise applies and is passed on [@FORM-01; @CON-35; @FTR-18] | Imported analogues (n = 2): 12 to 18 times chicken or eggs per gram of protein [@FORM-01; @COST-40; @COST-41] |
| Maker | Local incumbents with plants and national distribution | Imports and micro-startups |
| Familiarity | Soy milk long established, made at home too | Burger and sausage formats; the familiar version is cheap *đồ chay* |
| Role in the diet | A healthy addition, a children's drink, a coffee ingredient | Sold as a replacement to people who do not want to cut meat |
| Channel | Traditional and modern trade, cafés, e-commerce (mostly incumbents' official stores) | Restaurants and gourmet shops only |

**A tax that may fall on plant milk but not on dairy.** From 1 January 2027 drinks above 5 g of total sugar per 100 ml that count as *nước giải khát* (soft drinks) under the standard TCVN 12828:2019 pay an 8% excise, rising to 10% from 2028, and since 1 January 2026 they have lost the 2% VAT cut; milk and dairy products are exempt [@FTR-01; @FTR-02; @FTR-05; @FTR-09] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Cereal milks are named in the standard's scope. Whether soy and nut milks are in scope is unresolved, and we found no official letter or ruling on it [@FTR-05; @FTR-13] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
