Core Fami soy milks carry 6.5 to 9.3 g of sugar per 100 ml, above the line [@FTR-17; @FTR-18] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. If the tax applies and is passed on in full, mass soy milk would cost about VND 25,200 per litre in 2028, still 24 to 44% below the 2023 cow-milk price (our calculation from a 2026 promotional soy-milk price) [@FORM-01; @CON-35] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. The finding that plant milk sells at or below dairy prices survives; the design rule for new plant milks is to stay at or below 5 g of total sugar per 100 ml. Policy otherwise leaves plant milk out: the 2026 dairy strategy (Decision 309/QĐ-TTg) does not mention it and says school milk programmes use "only fresh milk" [@FTR-31; @APR-11] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-sugary-drink-excise}}

**Plant milk did not succeed on protein, and protein now sells in it only as a niche.** Most plant milks carry 0.7 to 2.5 g of protein per 100 ml [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Vinamilk's high-protein nut milk (5 g per 100 ml, mainly pea protein), and searches for it, were the first sign that protein content itself sells in this aisle [@BUY-16; @CON-37] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Purchases now confirm it, as a premium niche. At Vinamilk's Lazada store it shows about 16,100 cases sold (about 70,300 L and 3.5 t of protein): about 11% of the Vinamilk nut-milk litres read but 29% of their protein. It costs 24% more per litre and about 37% as much per gram of protein (cumulative counters; our calculation) [@MKT-03; @MKT-04] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. A protein claim alone does not lift sales. Vinamilk's GoldSoy soy milk, sold with "up to 3.2 g protein per 100 ml", sells less than unclaimed soy milks on Lazada (3,100 cases against 14,800 for a walnut soy milk at 2.0 g, although GoldSoy costs 39% less per litre) and on the Kamereo kitchen platform (2,609 units against 5,758 and 5,828 for two dearer unsweetened soy milks) [@MKT-03; @MKT-05; @ECR-06] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. The same company promotes its high-protein dairy milk as "more easily absorbed than plant-origin protein" [@AIB-03] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}.

## 13.6 Who buys first

The likely first buyers are urban 25 to 44 year olds who eat a lot of meat and want variety, and urban households anxious about health and food safety, not students. GFI's "Curious" segment (aware, not yet tried, leaning towards cutting red meat) is 43% of the Vietnamese sample, and about two-thirds of the region's most enthusiastic buyers are over 35 [@CON-02; @CON-03; @ECO-23] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Delley et al. place 65% of urban meat eaters in three segments (anxious, suggestible, proactive) that are open to change for health and safety reasons [@CON-08] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Students, the focus of most Vietnamese papers, have low incomes, and across the six markets 18 to 24 year olds are the least aware of plant-based meat [@CON-13; @CON-02] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}.

As a ceiling rather than an estimate: if the 3% weekly rate held for all 39.4 million urban residents, weekly eaters would number about 1.2 million (our calculation) [@MAC-19; @CON-02] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. The real number is smaller, because the panel is online adults in two cities, stated frequency overstates purchase and much of it is probably mock meat.

## 13.7 What happened abroad, and why it matters here

Vietnam can learn from markets that ran the modern plant-based experiment first. Most of this evidence is general or from comparable Asian markets ([[app-d7-global-benchmarks]]).

- **Peak and plateau.** US plant-based meat sales fell from USD 1.4 billion (2021) to USD 1.0 billion (2025) and units from 281 million to 173 million; the category's share of meat sales halved from 1.4% to about 0.7% [@GLB-01; @GLB-02] {general|High} {dx:revealed}. UK and Dutch volumes fell; Germany was flat [@GLB-08; @GLB-09; @GLB-10; @GLB-11] {general|High} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-us-pbm-decline}}
- **The ceiling.** In the most favourable markets, modern plant-based meat reached 3.1% (Germany) and 4.1% (Netherlands) of pre-packaged meat volume in 2024. Frequent buyers (12 or more times a year) were 8.6% of UK and 9.7% of German households in 2024 [@GLB-09; @GLB-10; @GLB-11] {general|High} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-west-ceiling}}
- **Trial without habit.** US household penetration fell from 19 to 20% to 11% while the repeat rate stayed above 60% [@GLB-01; @GLB-02]; in an earlier household panel (Neuhofer and Lusk, 2018 to 2020), 40% of buyers bought only once [@GLB-19] {general|High} {dx:revealed}.
- **Price matters, parity is not enough.** Demand is price elastic (about -0.8 to -1.6 in US scanner data), yet Dutch retailers' price-parity pledges left the plant share of protein sold flat at about 42 to 43% from 2023 to 2025 while plant-based meat volume fell [@GLB-16; @GLB-03; @GLB-12; @GLB-08; @GLB-10] {general|High} {dx:revealed}.
- **Little displacement.** Most US plant-based meat buyers keep buying meat, and household ground-meat purchases did not fall after a first plant-based purchase; plant milk, by contrast, displaces 0.43 to 0.93 units of dairy per unit bought [@GLB-19; @GLB-28; @GLB-22] {general|High} {dx:revealed}. An analysis of 1.2 million transactions in seven restaurants in the US, Canada and Australia (2026) found essentially no evidence that modern alternative proteins reduced meat purchases [@AFN-07] {general|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **Formats that hold up** are ingredient-like (strips, pieces, tofu); burgers lost share in the Netherlands [@GLB-09; @GLB-10; @GLB-11; @GLB-01] {general|High} {dx:revealed}.
- **Asia with a vegetarian tradition did not become an analogue market.** Thai meat alternatives were USD 21 million against USD 803 million of dairy alternatives (2020); Taiwan, with about 3 million vegetarians, had USD 36 million of modern plant-based retail sales (2021); Japanese soy milk is near record output while soy meat contracted [@GLB-52; @GLB-57; @GLB-55; @GLB-56] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Beyond Meat suspended its China operations in 2025 [@AIS-45] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Where a modern analogue did sell well, it was hidden inside a familiar dish at a low price: a Hong Kong-made pork substitute (OmniPork) in dumplings at a Taiwanese chain [@GLB-59] {VN-adjacent|Low} {dx:revealed}.
- **Regional firms moved away from their own consumer brands.** Of 24 alternative-protein startups and scale-ups that entered, tested or left Vietnam and Southeast Asia from 2019 to 2026, 7 are active, 4 pivoted, 2 exited and 11 show no activity (our register, `firm_outcomes.csv`). Every pivot moved towards private label, co-manufacturing, a retail blend or non-food uses: TiNDLE to private label from 2026, GOOD Meat to a 3% cultivated blend, Vow to co-manufacturing. Restaurant-launched brands such as Karana, Float Foods and Phuture went quiet [@AIS-28; @AIS-37; @NOV-10; @NOV-12; @BRD-08; @BRD-09; @BRD-10] {VN-adjacent|Low} {dx:revealed}. TiNDLE's co-founder and former chief executive, Andre Menezes, told AgFunderNews in 2025 that there is "no real underlying consumer demand to shift away from meat" [@AIS-29] {general|Medium} {dx:stated}. In Vietnam we found no sign of activity after 2022 for any of four meat-analogue startups, while all three makers of traditional or whole-food formats (mushroom floss, cashew cheese, tempeh) are trading [@AIS-39; @AIS-42; @AIS-43; @ECO-15; @ECO-17; @ECO-19; @BRD-18; @BRD-19] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed} (`firm_outcomes.csv`; [[ch15-channels]]).

{{chart:chart-us-pbm-trend}}

The lesson for Vietnam, where the price gap is ten times larger than in the markets that stalled, is not to copy the branded-analogue model (our inference) {general|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

## 13.8 Words on the pack

*Chay* is the incumbent word: it appears in 87 of 186 audited product names, and it carries Buddhist and traditional associations and a cheap, low-protein reputation (our inference) [@FORM-01; @CON-37] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. *Thuần chay* (vegan) is the modern word; its search interest rose to a 2024 peak and has eased since. *Thịt thực vật* (plant meat) and *đạm thực vật* (plant protein) were media words of 2021 to 2022 and have faded [@CON-37] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Incumbents use *thực vật* (plant) for modern dairy alternatives and as a protein claim ("100% protein từ thực vật" on one frozen dumpling) [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

**The protein claim is already defined.** A voluntary national standard taken from Codex, TCVN 14429:2025, sets "source of protein" at 5 g and "high protein" (*cao đạm*) at 10 g per 100 g of food, or 2.5 g and 5 g per 100 kcal [@LBL-03; @LBL-04] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. *Giàu đạm* (rich in protein), the phrase an earlier draft used, is not a defined term, so it is judged only against the rule that labels be truthful. The per 100 kcal route lets watery foods claim "high" at 4 to 5 g per 100 g, so a maker who wants the word to carry weight should print the number (for example "10 g đạm/100 g") on the front. The claim needs no registration and no advertising approval, but for function claims such as "builds muscle" we found no approval route for ordinary foods [@LBL-03; @LBL-05; @REG-02; @LBL-19] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Protein itself has had to appear on non-exempt pre-packaged labels since 1 January 2026 (Circular 29/2023, now Circular 30/2026); foods from small food businesses, which (our inference) cover most wet-market chay, are exempt [@LBL-01; @LBL-02] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-high-protein-claim}}

**The shelf already qualifies without claiming.** Of 43 audited plant-protein foods with a label value, 20 (47%) meet the "source" condition per 100 g and 7 (16%) meet "high", all seven of them frozen analogues; none carries a claim. Counting the per 100 kcal route, 27 of 38 and 13 of 38 would qualify (our calculation) [@FORM-01; @LBL-03] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The protein claim is an open position, not a regulatory problem.

**Fake chay does not undercut it today.** We found no confirmed case of meat in a Vietnamese chay product from 2015 to 2026; chay's live trust problems are borax, microbes and unlabelled goods ([[ch12-chay-baseline]]) [@TRU-18; @CHY-23] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. In our reading, a protein claim is credible when it rides on a registered maker, a full label and a short additive list; "verified meat-free", from a PCR screen once QUATEST 3 offers one, would be a secondary reassurance [@TRU-24; @TRU-04] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

No study has tested which words Vietnamese shoppers trust, and the one revealed test is discouraging: a protein claim on soy milk did not lift its sales (section 13.5). Our inference is that *chay* works for religious and periodic occasions, while a numeric protein claim with a food-safety signal is the more promising frame for meat eaters, provided the food is dense enough to make it (10 g per 100 g) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. The words around fermentation and cultivated meat are in [[ch14-frontier-demand]].

## 13.9 What this means for the frontier

- **Make products for the meals people already eat.** Vietnamese respondents asked for variety and cooking know-how more than any other country and for meat-like taste less than any other.
- **Price per serving against the meat replaced.** At parity or below for the mass market; stated interest falls by over a third at +50%.
- **Raise protein visibly** (10 g or more per 100 g for meat-like foods, the "high protein" level of TCVN 14429:2025; 5 g or more per 100 ml for drinks), print the number, keep ingredient lists short and signal food safety.
- **Plant milk is the proven category.** Barista milks for *cà phê sữa đá* (iced milk coffee), high-protein milks and local nut, seed and bean bases are the consumer openings with revealed demand. High-protein milks sell as a premium niche, not the volume line. A sugary-drink excise from 2027 may fall on sweetened plant milks but not on dairy, so design new plant milks at or below 5 g of total sugar per 100 ml.
- **Measure repeat, not launch.** Abroad, trial did not turn into habit; ignore launch spikes. Marketplace counters are cumulative, so read them twice, a month apart, to get a rate.

**For each reader.**
- **Startups:** do not launch premium imported-style analogues into gourmet channels expecting mass uptake; that route has been tried since 2019. In the region, brands placed on restaurant menus mostly went quiet or pivoted, while the Vietnamese survivors make familiar foods with little capital ([[ch15-channels]]).
- **Investors:** the revealed demand is in plant milk and in incumbents' chay lines; underwrite on repeat purchase and cost per gram of protein, not survey intent.
- **Manufacturers:** protein content, food safety and fewer additives are open positions on the shelf; about half of the audited plant-protein foods could already claim "source of protein". Check whether your sweetened plant milks are *nước giải khát* and plan recipes at or below 5 g of sugar per 100 ml.
- **Research bodies:** build tested-evidence capacity (sensory panels in Vietnamese dishes, choice experiments, label tests of numeric protein claims) instead of more small student surveys.
- **Policy makers:** food-safety and healthy-protein messages match consumer motives; meat-reduction messages do not, since only 15% intend to cut meat. A written ruling on whether soy, nut and cereal milks above 5 g of sugar are *nước giải khát*, before 1 January 2027, would remove an avoidable uncertainty ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).
- **International organisations and funders:** fund a Vietnamese choice experiment, an in-store price test and a label-trust test; each costs tens of thousands of USD ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).

**Related:** [[app-d2-consumer-evidence]], [[app-d7-global-benchmarks]], [[app-d3-retail-demand-signals]].

data.title: Fermentation, cultivated meat and blends: demand for the frontier categories
data.summary: Vietnam has no tested or revealed consumer evidence for cultivated meat or precision-fermented foods, only stated attitudes from young or online samples. Blending into foods people already buy is the most likely entry route, but a new fungal or fermented extender must beat hydrated soy, not lean meat, and avoid being framed as filler.
data.body:
# 14. Fermentation, cultivated meat and blends: demand for the frontier categories

**In one paragraph.** For the categories the frontier cares most about, Vietnamese demand evidence is thinnest. There is no tested or revealed consumer evidence on cultivated meat or precision-fermented foods in Vietnam, only stated attitudes from young or online samples, which place Vietnamese respondents among the more open in Asia. The Asian precedents temper that: after almost six years of legal sale in Singapore, cultivated meat has sold tens of thousands of servings, Singapore's government now cites weaker-than-expected acceptance, the products that reached customers were blends with 3 to 20% cultivated cells, and the two cultivated seafood firms in which Vietnamese exporters took positions have turned to pet food and skincare, with no food product on sale. Precision fermentation reaches Asian markets as a business-to-business ingredient for nutrition makers that already pay premiums, and Vietnamese formula makers already market one target ingredient, lactoferrin, while also advertising "non-GMO". A GMO label is costly in Vietnam (an 84% auction premium for non-GM soymilk), but the mandatory label applies only above 5% of ingredients, so low-dose ingredients such as lactoferrin escape it and the clash is with voluntary non-GMO claims and high-inclusion uses. "Fermented" (*lên men*) reads as positive. Vietnamese already buy blends without noticing: 31% of one large processor's meat formulations list soy protein. Blending into foods people already buy is still the most likely entry route for fungal, fermented and plant proteins, but soy extension already saves processors VND 9,100 to 16,600 per kg of *chả lụa* at every annual hog price from 2019 to 2024, so a new extender competes with hydrated soy, not with lean meat, and must win on sensory tolerance or on the label while avoiding *độn* (filler), a fraud word in Vietnam.

---

## 14.1 Cultivated meat and seafood

**Vietnamese evidence is stated only.** A five-country Asian survey (n = 3,005) places Vietnamese respondents, with Chinese, in the most open segment ("open-minded seekers"); we could read only the abstract, so the Vietnam split is an open question [@NOV-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. A survey of 393 young Vietnamese found about a quarter "optimists" about in-vitro meat [@NOV-03] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. No Vietnamese study has measured behaviour, used a representative sample, tested a name or measured willingness to pay a stated price. In Asian studies that tested rather than asked, acceptance was lower: Chinese consumers in a 2020 choice experiment would pay less for cultivated than for farm-raised meat [@NOV-29] {general|Medium} {dx:tested}, and in Japan the stated social acceptance of cultured meat was 40.9% against 70.2% for plant-based meat [@NOV-30] {general|Medium} {dx:stated}. Treat Vietnamese openness as a ceiling.

**Revealed demand in Asia is tiny.** GOOD Meat reported "more than 2,000 servings" sold in Singapore from December 2020 to May 2024 [@NOV-10] {VN-adjacent|Low} {dx:revealed}; Vow reported "more than 25,000 dishes" from April 2024 to August 2025 [@NOV-14] {VN-adjacent|Low} {dx:revealed}, then moved from its own food production to co-manufacturing in 2026 after layoffs in 2025 and May 2026 [@AIS-37] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Neither has published repeat purchase. In November 2025 Singapore's environment minister, Grace Fu, cited "weaker-than-expected consumer acceptance globally", and the Singapore Food Agency left cultivated meat out of its short-term food-security plan [@NOV-22] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. We found no approvals in Korea, Japan, China or Thailand, and no cultivated seafood approved for human food anywhere in Asia [@NOV-25; @NOV-13; @NOV-21] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-cultivated-sg-servings}}

**What reached customers were blends.** The only retail cultivated product in Asia, GOOD Meat 3, is 3% cultivated chicken, sold at S$7.20 per 120 g, about VND 405,000 per 100 g of protein (our calculation), close to the imported analogues on Vietnamese shelves [@NOV-10; @FORM-01] {VN-adjacent|Low} {dx:inferred}. Aleph Farms' steak, approved in Singapore in August 2026, is 10 to 20% cultivated beef in a plant-protein base [@NOV-18] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The commercial form of cultivated meat is, for now, a hybrid ingredient.

**Vietnamese seafood exporters bought options, and the options have faded.** Vinh Hoan took a stake in Avant Meats (2021) and co-invested in Shiok Meats; Minh Phu signed a research memorandum with Shiok (2022); we found no later news from either Vietnamese side [@NOV-74; @NOV-75; @NOV-76] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Both partners have since turned to non-food revenue. Avant's Singapore unit went into voluntary winding-up in January 2026, and its Hong Kong parent now sells a skincare ingredient made from cultivated fish cells while saying it is still seeking Singapore approval for its cultivated fish; Umami Bioworks, which merged with Shiok, sells cultivated seafood as pet food and signed a skincare and supplements partnership at the end of 2025 [@AIS-34; @AIS-35; @AIS-36] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The stakes were strategic interest by seafood incumbents. They are not evidence of buyer demand, and no food product has come of them yet; seafood exporters remain the natural hosts for cultivated seafood research ([[ch26-plays]], T8) (our inference).

> **Correction.** In v0.6 this said both partners had left human food; the sources say they have added pet food and skincare revenue, and Avant says it is still seeking Singapore approval for its cultivated fish.

## 14.2 Precision-fermented proteins

**A business-to-business market for premium function.** In Asia precision fermentation reaches the market as an ingredient sold to firms that already pay for function: lactoferrin for infant and medical nutrition (conventional lactoferrin about USD 800 per kg, one company's claim), whey protein for sports and clear drinks, sweet proteins for sugar reduction (a Singapore approval in May 2026; a 100 t a year line in China) [@NOV-45; @NOV-44; @NOV-47; @NOV-48] {VN-adjacent|Low} {dx:revealed}. The two Asian consumer launches we found (a precision-fermented ice cream and a precision-fermented milk in Singapore supermarkets, 2022) left no trace of sales [@NOV-43] {VN-adjacent|Low} {dx:revealed}.

**Vietnamese buyers exist and pay.** VitaDairy, Nutifood and Morinaga all market lactoferrin formulas in Vietnam in 2025 and 2026 [@NOV-59; @NOV-60; @NOV-61] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. In June 2026 Nutifood agreed with Military Hospital 175 to run two clinical studies of medical nutrition products, one of them plant-based [@BUY-19] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. We found no public statement of interest in precision-fermented proteins from any Vietnamese dairy or formula maker; our site searches of three national news sites for *lên men chính xác* (precision fermentation) returned no articles, which is a limited search, not proof of absence {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

**The GMO collision is narrower than it looks.** The same buyers sell GMO-free: VitaDairy lists "không biến đổi gen" (non-GMO) among its product's "10 NOs", beside hormones and antibiotic residues, and Vinasoy advertises non-GMO too [@NOV-62; @NOV-63] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. An experimental auction in Vietnam found an 84% willingness-to-pay premium for soymilk carrying non-GM information [@NOV-08] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:tested}, and Vietnamese consumers' implicit attitudes to genome-edited and GM foods are closely linked unless detailed information is given [@NOV-07] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:tested}. Purified precision-fermented proteins probably count as products of a GMO under Decree 43/2026 ([[ch07-rules]]), but the mandatory GMO label applies only when a GM ingredient is more than 5% of total ingredients, and not when neither the modified gene nor its product can be detected (Decree 15/2018 Art 10; Joint Circular 45/2015 Art 1) [@REG-18; @REG-02; @LBL-10] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. A Vietnamese lactoferrin formula contains 80 mg per 100 g, about 0.08% (our calculation), so a precision-fermented lactoferrin at that dose would need no GMO label [@LBL-25; @LBL-10] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. The clash is with the buyers' voluntary "non-GMO" claims, which may not stay truthful, and with high-inclusion uses such as a drink whose main protein is precision-fermented whey. Whether a recombinant protein identical to the native one is a "detectable product of the modified gene" is the one legal question left open {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. The regulatory answer is also a demand answer. {{kn:kn-gmo-premium}}

## 14.3 Biomass fermentation, fungi and the meaning of "fermented"

Vietnam's food culture is built on fermentation: *nước mắm* (fish sauce), *tương* (fermented soybean paste), *mắm* (fermented fish or shrimp) and *men* (starter cultures). *Lên men* (fermented) is a positive word in marketing and media: Vinasoy's Veyo is sold as a "naturally fermented nut milk" for digestion, and VnExpress opens a 2026 health piece by calling fermented foods delicious and good for gut health [@NOV-63; @NOV-64] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. In a Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City sample of young people, 46% said they would try an energy bar made with protein from brewing and distilling by-products (spent yeast and distillers' grains) [@RD-32] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Nobody has tested *lên men* against other words on a protein label. Our inference: "fermented" is the best available frame for yeast, koji and fungal biomass; it helps less for precision fermentation, where a high-inclusion product may have to say GMO {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. A fermented protein is already on offer to Vietnamese makers: since May 2025 the distributor ACC has marketed Angel Yeast's yeast protein (55 to 90% protein, company claim) for bakery, dairy, plant-based dairy and meat alternatives, with sampling and application support; no price or named user is public [@AIS-38; @CPC-21] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

Mycoprotein has not proved itself with Asian consumers. Quorn's Philippine owner saw its meat-alternative sales fall from about PHP 15.4 billion (2022) to PHP 13.6 billion (2024) (our calculation from its segment reports), 79% of them in the UK [@NOV-50] {general|High} {dx:revealed}; it halted a fifth fermentation plant and closed plants in 2024, calling it "a declining market", and Quorn revenue fell a further 2.9% at constant currency in 2025 [@AIS-44; @AIS-48] {general|Medium} {dx:revealed}. China approved its first mycoprotein in December 2025, as a business-to-business ingredient [@NOV-49] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Vietnam's mushroom habit is a real bridge (king oyster mushroom is a common meat-texture substitute), and one Vietnamese startup, Emmay, reports that its sales of mushroom and mycelium foods rose from 1.5 to about 2 t a month in 2023, with about 10% of revenue from exports (company report) [@AIS-39] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. But readers criticise mushroom mock meat for heavy seasoning and additives, and one startup markets itself on 3 to 5 additives against 15 to 23 in rivals [@NOV-65; @NOV-77] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. A clean label is a design requirement for any fungal product.

## 14.4 Blends: the most likely entry route

**The 93% figure measures interest in trying.** GFI APAC's press release says 93% of surveyed consumers were interested in at least trying blended meat. It comes from the same urban online survey in which 5% eat plant-based meat regularly; the full report is form-gated and the Vietnam result is not public [@NOV-35; @NOV-36] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:stated}. In Vietnam, 95% were at least slightly and 55% very interested in blends, against 49% very interested on average [@CON-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Read these as low resistance to the idea, not as demand.

**Tested evidence is more useful.** In a blind test of 20 blended products by Singapore's A*STAR food institute (November 2025, more than 100 tasters), a chicken mince with 30 to 50% plant protein beat 100% chicken, blends were 1.8 times more likely than plant-based meat to be liked, and purchase intent for blends was about 1.4 times that for plant-based meat, though still below meat. Most tasters preferred blends of about 75% animal meat [@NOV-37; @NOV-39; @NOV-40] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:tested}. In a US test, a 70% beef and 30% mushroom blend beat plant-based burgers when tasted blind but lost demand once people were told what was in it [@GLB-30] {general|Medium} {dx:tested}. Japan's 50:50 pork and plant sausage is sold business to business, to restaurants, hotels, school lunches, canteens and packaged-food makers; we found no retail launch [@NOV-41] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. In Singapore a soy-enhanced beef and chicken range co-developed by Temasek's Nurasa was due to go on sale through a meat importer's retail channels in September 2025 [@AIS-10] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}, and GFI APAC expects Asia's first large-scale foodservice rollouts of blended meat in 2026 [@AIS-06] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:stated}. {{kn:kn-blend-preference}}

**Vietnam already eats blends.** In an online label audit of 118 Vissan products, 22 of 67 unique meat formulations (33%) list soy protein and 25 (37%) list at least one added protein (soy, wheat, milk protein or egg white), mostly in value lines [@BUY-05] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Vissan's mainstream sausage is 58% lean pork plus soy protein, starch and fibre; its *giò lụa* lists soy and milk protein; TH true NUT walnut "nut milk" contains fresh cow's milk [@NOV-56; @NOV-57; @NOV-58] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Soy is not only a value-line filler: Vissan's DHA "nutrition" pork sausage lists soy and declares more lean than its plain counterpart (58% against 55%), while the cheapest *giò lụa* we priced (VND 124,200 per kg, below retail lean pork) cuts cost with chicken, pork fat, water and starch, not soy [@BUY-05; @COST-39] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. All seven commercial Vietnamese emulsion sausages tested in a 2018 study contained soy protein, and consumers liked the best of them as well as peanut-protein versions, though three scored lower [@HXE-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:tested}; Masan's Omachi noodle cup is sold "with a real meat stick" whose ingredients include soy protein and starch [@TRU-25] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. These proteins are functional binders at undisclosed inclusion rates, not declared replacements. Still, mixed-protein meat products from the country's largest processors sell at mass scale without a label penalty. {{kn:kn-vissan-soy-share}}

**No rule stands in the way.** No national standard sets a minimum meat content for heat-treated, non-heat-treated ready-to-eat or canned processed meat (TCVN 7049:2020, 7050:2020, 7048:2020), so a 20 to 30% extender keeps the meat product name [@LBL-11; @LBL-13; @LBL-12] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. If the name names a meat, its share must be printed, and Vissan already sells meat-named products at 27 to 65% named lean; a 55% lean sausage with 20 to 30% of its lean replaced would still declare 38.5 to 44% (our calculation) [@LBL-06; @BUY-05] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}.

**Soy extension already pays, so the benchmark is soy, not meat.** Hydrated to 18% protein, textured soy costs a processor about VND 10,000 to 15,000 per kg, against VND 83,000 to 141,000 for lean trimmings at 2019 to 2024 annual hog prices; a 50% protein textured soy would stop paying only above about USD 8.9 to 15.0 per kg dry, about 7 to 12 times China's 2025 export price for textured protein (HS 2106.10, free on board) (our calculation, pricing lean at 1.8 times the live hog price) [@DIE-25; @AIB-15; @TIC-12] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Replacing 20% of the lean in a *chả lụa* (steamed pork roll) saves VND 9,100 to 16,600 per kg, 14 to 16% of raw-material cost, at the 2019 and 2020 hog prices. The pork cycle changes the size of the saving, not its sign, and extension trims only about a sixth of a recipe's exposure to a pork price shock (our calculation) [@HXE-01; @DIE-25] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. A new fungal or fermented extender therefore has to beat hydrated soy, about USD 2.6 to 2.8 per kg of protein (about USD 0.7 to 1.2 per kg dry at 45% protein), and the chicken, skin, starch and water that value lines already use. To earn more, it must let the processor replace more meat unnoticed than soy does, or carry a label benefit {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Because extension pays everywhere but is not done everywhere, product identity, texture and trust set its reach, not cost. And because Chinese textured protein and isolates enter at 0% duty, blends will carry imported soy unless a domestic maker wins the business ([[ch16-business-buyers]]; [[ch18-demand-sizing]]) [@FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-hybrid-saving}}

**Formats set the ceiling.** Coarse products tolerate about 25% replacement: 25% hydrated soy concentrate improved beef patties [@HXE-05] {general|Medium} {dx:tested}, and 25% mycoprotein replacing lean pork was preferred in a Chinese red sausage [@HXE-06] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:tested}. Fine emulsions tolerate less: 6% added soy protein isolate lowered liking of Taiwanese emulsified pork meatballs, whole mushroom kept quality only at 10%, and a US study put practical lean replacement below 30% [@HXE-08; @HXE-07; @HXE-04] {general|Medium} {dx:tested}. In the one Vietnamese consumer test of *chả lụa* recipes, graininess and uneven texture cut liking, which rules out textured granules in *giò* and *chả* [@HXE-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:tested}. We found no sensory study supporting 50% replacement in a pork product; the working caps are 10 to 20% in fine emulsions and about 30% in coarse mince [@HXE-09; @HXE-12; @HXE-04] {general|Medium} {dx:tested}. Nutrition is not the obstacle: a 20 to 30% soy extender keeps a minced-pork dish at a DIAAS of about 97 or more on the older-child pattern, with 12 to 19% less zinc per gram of protein than all-pork (our calculation) [@NQR-05; @NQR-07] {general|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

**Why blending is still the likely route (our inference).** {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}
- It avoids the "fake meat" and "artificial" frames: the product is still meat, and the novel part is an ingredient. It does not avoid the older *độn* (filler) frame, which buyers apply to hidden or cost-cutting extension of *giò* and *chả*; that frame attaches to how extension is done and named, not to a listed ingredient (14.5).
- It matches revealed Asian practice: cultivated products are 3 to 20% cells, and blends go to canteens, processors and meat importers.
- It does not have to beat meat on price: any extender clears the lean-meat test, and a new one competes with soy on cost or on sensory tolerance.
- The cost motive is already there: the saving from extension, not a hedge against pork prices, is why processors do it.
- No standard sets a minimum meat content, and naming rules already make the named meat's share visible.
- Blends displace meat by construction, which matters for the supply-security and welfare cases ([[ch18-demand-sizing]]).

What blending does not guarantee is a buyer: we found no Vietnamese processor statement of interest in fungal or fermented extenders, and no tasting data from Vietnam on them [@BUY-04; @BUY-10] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. For Vissan, a 20% extension of the lean in 30 to 50% of its output would save between half and all of its 2025 pre-tax profit, yet its labels suggest it does not extend at that scale ([[ch16-business-buyers]]) [@BUY-04; @BUY-05; @DIE-25] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Premium lines sell on meat content (one sausage brand on "88% meat" in 2022) and artisan sellers compete on "no filler", so blends start in value and industrial lines [@BUY-13; @TRU-27] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}.

## 14.5 Words, trust and religion

- **"Artificial" and "fake" are loaded.** The Vietnamese press uses *thịt nhân tạo* (artificial meat) for cultivated meat, for Beyond-style plant-based meat and even for cultivated shrimp; one article used three names in the same text [@NOV-69; @NOV-74; @NOV-81] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. A leading financial outlet framed cultivated meat as a "nightmare" relaying a claim about cancer-causing cells, with no safety evidence [@NOV-71] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. In 2025 fake-egg rumours hurt egg producers, and in 2026 police broke a ring that had sold about 65 tonnes of fake and chemically soaked beef, including pork treated to pass as beef [@NOV-73; @NOV-72] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. The same outlet uses *thịt giả* (fake meat) for both kinds of story: 6 of Dan Tri's first 11 results for the term were about plant-based or cultivated meat and 4 about fraud, and a 2020 headline warned diners that soy pork in restaurants could be a *cú lừa* (a trick) [@TRU-22; @TRU-10] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. A product marketed as "just like real meat" invites that association.
- ***Độn* (padding, filler) is a fraud word.** Press advice columns (2015 and 2019) and a provincial disease-control page teach readers that *giò* without small air holes "has been mixed with starch"; when pork prices spiked in 2019, a Hanoi shopper called makers who added starch dishonest and one seller said customers fell by nearly half; sellers now advertise *không độn bột* (no starch filler) and, for Chinese-style sausage, *không độn đạm đậu nành* (no soy protein filler) [@TRU-02; @TRU-03; @TRU-27] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Declared soy in branded processed meat draws no observed penalty: Dan Tri searches surfaced no story treating it as fraud [@TRU-22] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. We found no Vietnamese brand that markets a declared meat and plant-protein blend, but products that name a culinary plant part (chicken and shiitake sausage; a sausage flavoured with lotus seed, Xuxifarm Be Khoe, which also lists soy protein but does not market it) are sold as healthy [@TRU-32; @TRU-26] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}.
- **2026 is a year of processed-meat distrust.** Dan Tri reported at least six prosecutions of *giò chả* makers for borax between February and August 2026, and pork from pigs with African swine fever reached school meals and a canning plant [@TRU-07; @TRU-20] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The scandals are about borax, disease and species substitution, not plant protein.
- **No Vietnamese name has been tested.** In Singapore "cultivated meat" was the preferred English name and "cell-based" the least liked; process-heavy descriptions may raise feelings of unnaturalness across countries [@NOV-32; @NOV-82; @NOV-80] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:stated}. The only state use of a novel-meat name we found is *thịt nhân tạo*, in a 2025 provincial biotechnology scheme [@LBL-20] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **Halal is workable for export.** Singapore's Islamic council (2024) and Malaysia's JAKIM (December 2025) accept cultivated meat as halal under conditions on donor cells and growth media [@NOV-52; @NOV-53] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **Chay status is unresolved.** We found no Vietnamese Buddhist position on cultivated meat or precision-fermented dairy. Products made from animal cells are very unlikely to be sold as *chay*; animal-free precision-fermented proteins are an open question (our inference) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

## 14.6 What this means for the frontier

**What to make, in order.**
1. **Ingredients for blends:** fungal, biomass-fermented or plant proteins that replace 10 to 20% of the lean in fine emulsions (industrial *xúc xích*, sausage, first; *giò lụa* and *chả lụa*, pork rolls, later, as a fine isolate, concentrate or paste, not granules) and up to 30% in coarse mince (*xíu mại* meatballs, dumpling and spring-roll fillings, nuggets). Price near hydrated soy for the extension job (about USD 2.6 to 2.8 per kg of protein) or against egg and milk protein for the binding job ([[ch16-business-buyers]]). The finished product keeps at least 10 g of protein per 100 g.
2. **Functional precision-fermented proteins for business buyers** (lactoferrin, specialty whey, sweet proteins), for export or specialty nutrition. Low-dose uses fall outside the mandatory GMO label; high-inclusion uses wait for the detectability question to be answered.
3. **Cultivated meat and seafood** as research, a seafood-exporter partnership or an export base; there is no domestic consumer demand to design for before the mid-2030s.

**Labels.** Avoid *nhân tạo* (artificial), anything that sounds like *giả* (fake), *độn* and "x% meat replaced" wording. Name the plant part as a culinary or health ingredient (*nấm hương*, shiitake; *đạm nấm*, mushroom protein; *hạt sen*, lotus seed), lead with *lên men* for fermentation, and state the meat share only as the label law requires. Test names before launch.

**For each reader.**
- **Startups:** aim first to supply processors and caterers with an ingredient, not a consumer brand; publish protein per 100 g and price per kilogram of protein against hydrated soy, not lean pork; keep the label short; and check the GMO status of any high-inclusion precision-fermented product before a Vietnamese consumer launch.
- **Investors:** discount stated acceptance; Asian revealed sales of cultivated meat are in the tens of thousands of servings, and the cultivated seafood partners of Vinh Hoan and Minh Phu have turned to pet food and skincare for revenue, with no food product on sale, so do not count the exporters as co-investors for a food product. For extenders, underwrite the saving against the processor's own soy recipe, not against meat, and look for offtake letters from processors or nutrition makers.
- **Manufacturers:** blending is not new to you, and soy at 20% already saves money at every pork price. Pilot a fungal extender only if it lets you replace more meat unnoticed than soy, or carries a label your buyers prefer; test it against your soy formula at equal saving, in a coarse format first.
- **Research bodies:** run a blind test in industrial *xúc xích* and one coarse format at equal processor saving against the processor's soy recipe (for example 25% fungal against 20% soy), with an informed arm that names the fungal ingredient on the front; add a randomised name and label test and a price choice experiment; the HUST group behind existing Vietnamese studies is an obvious partner.
- **Policy makers:** the new Food Safety Law (first comments in October 2026, passage considered in May 2027) should keep the permissive naming regime: we found no rule that reserves *thịt*, *sữa* or *phô mai*, and names need only not mislead and show the quantity of any ingredient they name [@APR-07; @LBL-06] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Aim vocabulary guidance at state and media use rather than at producers. Narrow the GMO question to whether an identical recombinant protein is a detectable product of the modified gene [@LBL-10] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Percentage labelling of blends is already law whenever the meat is named, since Decree 37/2026 carries the rule of Decree 43/2017 [@LBL-08; @LBL-09] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}; a voluntary industry code to state the meat share under generic names (*giò lụa*, *xúc xích*) is what remains, and its value is defence against a *độn* accusation.
- **International organisations:** support a representative national survey on new foods that includes rural and older consumers; all current Vietnamese data are urban and young.

**Related:** [[ch10-technology-fit]], [[ch21-frontier-technology]], [[app-d2-consumer-evidence]], [[ch16-business-buyers]].

data.title: Where protein is bought and eaten: retail, foodservice and institutions
data.summary: Traditional markets and small grocers still take 83% of food retail, so a chilled or frozen alternative sits in the frozen vegetarian aisle, in retailer private label or in kitchens. In factory canteens, a large, price-set protein channel, only an ingredient that beats tofu and dry soy-gluten pieces fits, and branded meat replacements are the wrong start in schools.
data.body:
# 15. Where protein is bought and eaten: retail, foodservice and institutions

**In one paragraph.** Channels decide what form a new protein can take. Traditional markets and small grocers still take 83% of Vietnam's USD 55.5 billion food retail and about 80% of fresh meat, so a chilled or frozen alternative cannot follow meat into the wet market; it can sit only where the frozen *chay* aisle already is, in modern stores and in retailer private label made by existing co-packers, or go through kitchens. Two chains, Bach Hoa Xanh and WinCommerce, now run about 8,750 stores between them. Foodservice is large (USD 26.6 billion) and fragmented; chains have trialled meat-free items for eight years without disclosing a success, and regional startups that put their own analogue on restaurant menus mostly went quiet. Factory canteens are a large, price-set protein channel: up to about 1.2 billion shift meals a year, mostly at VND 20,000 to 35,000, whose caterers lead with pork, fish and chicken and put tofu in 9% of protein dishes. Kitchens already buy tofu and domestic dry soy-gluten pieces at VND 4,000 to 9,500 per 20 g of protein, so only an ingredient that beats those fits, not a branded analogue. School lunches cost VND 35,000 to 40,000, and national guidance (Decision 3958/QĐ-BYT, 2025) already asks for plant protein twice a week, but menus use it on 15% of days and fill it with tofu beside meat, while the menu software prints an animal-protein floor of 48%. An ingredient sold into that slot replaces tofu, not meat; the only school route that removes meat is a labelled blend in the minced-meat and fish-cake dishes served on 28.5% of days. Upland boarding kitchens spend their new public meal money mostly on pork. Corporate commitments are not a volume lever, and Nha Trang's hotels are a showcase, not a volume channel.

---

## 15.1 Retail: a wet-market country moving to minimarts

| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Food retail sales, 2024 | USD 55.5 billion | [@CHN-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Traditional channels (small grocers and markets), 2024 | 83% of value | [@CHN-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Supermarkets, hypermarkets, convenience, 2024 | 9%, 3%, 1% | [@CHN-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Food e-commerce, 2024 | About 1%, growing 29% | [@CHN-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Grocery and food on Shopee, Lazada, Tiki and TikTok Shop, H1 2026 | VND 19.55 trillion (about USD 750 million), up 151%; 6.7% of marketplace sales | [@ECR-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Modern trade share of grocery, 2024 to 2025 (company view) | 12% to 14% in one year | [@CHN-15] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| Bach Hoa Xanh stores, end of August 2026 | 3,612 (1,000 or more opened in 2026) | [@CHN-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| WinCommerce stores, mid-2026 | 5,141 (about 550 opened in H1 2026; rural WinMart+ stores reporting nearly 60% growth) | [@CHN-15] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| WinCommerce store targets (2026 AGM) | About 6,100 by end 2026; 13,000 by 2030 | [@AIB-12; @AIB-13] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:stated} |
| Fresh meat sold through traditional channels | About 80% of the market (year not stated) | [@CHN-18] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| Pork retailers selling in wet markets | Over 95% | [@CHN-19] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |

{{kn:kn-food-retail-traditional}} {{kn:kn-two-chains-stores}}

Four things follow for a new protein {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}:

- **Two listings reach most of modern grocery.** A listing at Bach Hoa Xanh or WinCommerce reaches roughly 8,750 stores (3,612 plus 5,141, our sum) [@CHN-12; @CHN-15]. All foreign-owned hypermarkets and supermarkets together number fewer than 200 (our count): Central Retail runs 43 GO! hypermarkets, 9 Tops and 23 Lan Chi stores, Lotte Mart 17 stores, and AEON 9 malls with 30 planned by fiscal 2030 [@AIB-31; @AIB-33; @AIB-34] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The two big chains' growth is minimart-led and rural, so modern trade is no longer only an urban premium channel [@CHN-12; @CHN-15] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Tax and invoicing rules from 2025 that require traceable transactions are expected to favour modern trade further [@CHN-05] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.
- **The cold-chain slot already exists.** Large-format stores such as Lotte Mart Nha Trang have signed frozen chay sections of two or more door units, stocked by SG Food, Vissan, CJ Cau Tre, bibigo and private labels [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. We found no current figure for household freezer ownership; formats that need no cold chain (dry textured protein, retort pouches, cans) are the only way into the 650,000 traditional outlets [@CHN-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.
- **Private label reaches that slot without a consumer brand.** Saigon Co.op sells more than 2,500 private-label products from more than 100 Vietnamese makers at 15 to 30% below comparable brands, and one certified co-packer, GN Foods, makes all five Co.op Select frozen chay dishes; Lotte Mart sells its own Choice L chay [@AIB-28; @CPC-15; @FORM-01; @ORG-14] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Today's private-label chay is starch and vegetable led, sells at VND 107,800 to 141,500 per kg and carries no protein claim, and we found no chay house brand at WinCommerce (one store checked online) or AEON [@CPC-15; @CPC-19; @CPC-20; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. A higher-protein version of an existing SKU is a reformulation for the co-packer and a listing decision for the retailer, not a new brand (our inference; untested).
- **The integrated meat groups own the chilled meat route in modern trade.** Masan MEATLife sells chilled pork in WinCommerce stores and C.P. Vietnam runs more than 1,000 shops [@CHN-17] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. They are the natural makers of hybrid products, but their own diversification is into animal protein: Vissan is building a 32,000-head pig farm, Masan MEATLife is moving into marinated and processed branded meat, and Vinamilk's Vinabeef chilled-beef plant (10,000 t a year) is operating [@AIB-15; @AIB-12; @AIB-04] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}.

**E-commerce grows fast; it is an incumbents' channel for milk and a small makers' channel for dry chay.** Grocery and food on the four big marketplaces sold VND 19.55 trillion in the first half of 2026. That is about 2 to 3% of food retail value on the 2024 base, up from about 1% (our calculation, first-half sales doubled for a year; Metric does not publish its category definition) [@ECR-02; @CHN-01] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Shopee Mall (official) stores took 85% of liquid-milk sales on Shopee in early 2026 (Vinamilk 54%), and official or mall stores sold 93 to 100% of the milk units we read on Lazada [@ECR-01; @MKT-03] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Households buy plant milk online at a scale close to dairy: the best plant-milk SKU sells 60% of the litres of the best dairy SKU on Lazada and 79% on Tiki, against about 3% in the kitchen channel (our calculation on cumulative counters) [@MKT-03; @MKT-05; @ECR-06] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Dry chay pieces are different: nine listings of dry soy-and-gluten "ribs" show about 40,700 kg sold, 82% of it from one small shop without an official store, while frozen chay sells hundreds of kilograms per listing and no imported analogue appears [@MKT-03; @MKT-04] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. For a new protein, e-commerce is a place to test a milk or processed product through an incumbent's official store, and a real route for a small maker of dry chay ingredients; it is not a cheap launch route for a new consumer brand {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

## 15.2 Foodservice: large, fragmented, and silent about meat-free trials

Foodservice was worth USD 26.6 billion in 2024 across about 323,000 outlets: full-service restaurants 69% of sales, cafés and bars 18%, street stalls and kiosks 10% of sales from about 152,000 outlets, and fast food 3% from about 11,000 [@CHN-03] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. More than 50,000 operators closed in the first half of 2025 [@CHN-03] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Fast-food chains are few (about 1,000 outlets) but buy centrally and can list a product nationally overnight; hotpot and grill chains are protein-heavy and centrally supplied, an under-examined route for hybrid and *chay* protein [@CHN-06] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

| Year | Operator | What was offered | Price | Outcome | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2018 | KFC Vietnam | Chay chicken burger and floss rice for lunar July | VND 39,000 | Not published; no evidence it was repeated | [@CHN-22; @CHN-23] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| 2019 | BiaCraft (craft-beer bars) | Beyond Burger | not found | First Beyond Burger in Vietnam, per BiaCraft | [@ECO-16] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| 2023 | Starbucks Vietnam | OmniFoods sandwich and bake, summer menu | not found | Ended | [@ECO-20] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| 2025 | Lotteria Vietnam | "Burger Zero Meat" with a vegetable patty, seven cities incl. Nha Trang | VND 39,000 | Not published; current listing not verified | [@CHN-24; @CHN-25] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| 2025 | Pizza 4P's | Vegetarian menu in all restaurants (cheese, vegetable, mushroom) | not stated | No meat analogues | [@CHN-27] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| Not shown (cumulative counter) | CP Meat Zero on Kamereo (HoReCa platform) | Eight imported plant-based pork SKUs | VND 175,000 to 378,000 per kg | 386 units on the sold counter; none orderable on 25 September 2026 | [@AIS-25; @CPC-12] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |

The pattern: mass chains priced meat-free items at parity with core items (VND 39,000), timed them to the lunar calendar and used vegetables or chay ingredients rather than imported analogues; the imported premium analogues came through a craft bar, a café chain and a HoReCa (hotel, restaurant and catering) distributor and did not stay. No operator has disclosed volumes, repeat rates or why items ended {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. Read chain launches as supply signals, not as demand evidence, until outcomes are known.

**Startups that sold their own analogue through restaurants fared no better.** Of 24 regional and Vietnamese alternative-protein firms that entered, tested or left the market from 2019 to 2026, 7 are active, 4 pivoted, 2 exited and 11 show no activity after their last dated news; of the 12 that launched their own brand on restaurant or café menus, 7 are dormant (our register, `firm_outcomes.csv`) [@AIS-28; @BRD-08; @BRD-10] {VN-adjacent|Low} {dx:revealed}. We found no sign of activity after 2022 at any of the four Vietnamese meat-analogue startups in our register (`firm_outcomes.csv`) [@ECO-15; @ECO-19], while all three makers of familiar formats (mushroom floss, cashew cheese, tempeh) are trading [@AIS-39; @AIS-42; @AIS-43; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Three of the four pivots in our register moved towards private label, co-manufacturing or non-food ingredients and the fourth relaunched a retail blend under its own brand (`firm_outcomes.csv`); TiNDLE co-founder Andre Menezes said there is "no real underlying consumer demand to shift away from meat" [@AIS-28; @AIS-29] {general|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The regional exception, Indonesia's Green Rebel, grew through foodservice partners with regional dishes and raised USD 10.5 to 12.5 million in early 2026 [@AIS-30; @AIS-31] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. With 24 firms and "dormant" meaning only "no news found", this shows no advantage for menu placements of a branded analogue, not a proven disadvantage; no startup in the register has yet tried to sell an ingredient to Vietnamese incumbents (`firm_outcomes.csv`, `firm_base_rates.csv`) {VN-adjacent|Low} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-firm-outcomes}}

**Corporate commitments are not a volume lever in Vietnam.** One published commitment binds business units here: Accor's Good Food Policy asks all its hotels for 50% vegetarian or plant-based dishes by 2030 (Novotel 25% by 2026), and Accor ran 43 hotels in Vietnam in October 2024 [@AFN-40; @AFN-41; @AFN-18] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. The metric counts dishes, which tofu, vegetables and noodles can fill (our inference). Marriott's 2026 to 2030 goals contain no food goal; IHG, Hilton and Minor have cage-free egg pledges whose Asian delivery lags far behind (IHG East Asia and Pacific 4.1% of hotels aligned in 2024 against 70.3% globally; Hilton Asia Pacific managed hotels 42% in 2025; Minor Hotels Asia Pacific and Indian Ocean 13% of egg volume in 2025) [@CPC-01; @CPC-04; @CPC-05; @CPC-07] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Sodexo's Vietnamese operation is unconfirmed, and Lever Foundation, which turns pledges into procurement ratios in Asian hotels and caterers, extended its plant-based work to India and Thailand in July 2026, not Vietnam [@CPC-08; @CPC-10; @AFN-39] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. We found no Vietnamese protein buyer with a published diversification target ([[ch16-business-buyers]]; `corporate_commitments.csv`).

## 15.3 Institutions: a large, price-set protein channel

**Factory canteens.** About 4.15 million people worked in industrial parks and economic zones at the end of 2023 [@CHN-37] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The trade union's floor is VND 25,000 a meal when a caterer is hired and VND 20,000 when the firm cooks itself (regions I and II; VND 22,000 and 18,000 in regions III and IV), and each meal must include a protein food [@AIB-43] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Prices paid run from VND 17,000 to 40,000: Hai Phong's 2026 average is about VND 27,000 in the west and 31,000 in the east, with some firms at VND 17,000; foreign-invested factories there pay VND 22,000 to 35,000 and northern garment firms VND 17,000 to 25,000 [@UPL-34; @CHN-39; @CHN-38] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The contract catering market is about USD 2 billion a year; food is 60 to 80% of the meal price; suppliers report informal commissions of VND 500 to 1,000 per meal to clients' purchasing staff; and Haseca, which calls itself a leading caterer, reports more than 200,000 meals a day from more than 120 kitchens in five tiers of VND 18,000 to 45,000 (company claim) [@CHN-41; @AIB-36] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. At about 300 meal days a year, industrial-park canteens serve up to about 1.2 billion meals (our upper-bound calculation) [@CHN-37; @CHN-39] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-canteen-meals}}

**What canteens serve.** Five caterers' published sample menus (172 protein dishes, 2023 to 2025) lead with pork (33%), fish (26%) and chicken (13%), then egg (10%), tofu (9%, only 3% plant-only) and beef (6%); minced or processed meat makes up 17% of protein dishes [@UPL-27; @UPL-28; @UPL-29; @UPL-30; @UPL-32] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Haseca rotates "2 days pork, 2 days chicken or fish, 1 day tofu or egg" with a main dish of 90 to 120 g; one caterer serves *chay* dishes on two lunar days a month; none names textured soy or mock meat [@UPL-32; @UPL-33] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. These are marketing samples, four of the five from the south. Shift-meal nutrition guidance (Decision 1982/QĐ-BYT, chapter V) sets no plant slot and no protein norm, and an occupational-health institute expert quoted in the trade union's newspaper advises 30 to 50% of protein from animal sources [@APR-16; @UPL-36] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. A canteen ingredient therefore has two slots: the tofu slot, where it competes with tofu, and the minced-meat slot, where a blend displaces pork. Because chicken leads only 13% of protein dishes, a canteen meal switched to plant protein spares few animals; [[ch18-demand-sizing]] carries that arithmetic {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-canteen-dish-mix}}

{{chart:chart-canteen-dish-mix}}

**What a protein ingredient must hit in a canteen** (our calculation) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. With food at 60 to 80% of a VND 25,000 to 35,000 meal, the food budget is VND 15,000 to 28,000 [@CHN-41; @CHN-39]. If the protein dish takes about half, it has VND 7,500 to 14,000. Twenty grams of protein from eggs or chicken breast costs VND 6,900 to 9,000 at retail ([[ch11-protein-diet]]). From a branded retail textured or gluten analogue (VND 112,000 per 100 g of protein, [@FORM-01]) it costs VND 22,400, more than the whole protein budget. From textured plant protein at the supply study's indicative ex-factory cost (VND 3,700 to 10,700 per 100 g of protein, [[ch09-economics]]) it costs VND 740 to 2,140. {{kn:kn-canteen-protein-budget}}

The price that binds, though, is what kitchens already buy. On Kamereo, a platform that supplies more than 4,000 restaurants, cafés and hotels (company claim), 20 g of protein costs about VND 4,000 to 5,100 as domestic dry soy-gluten pieces (on a borrowed protein range), VND 7,200 to 9,500 as branded firm tofu, VND 8,800 as eggs, VND 9,600 as chicken breast and VND 13,900 as minced pork (our calculation) [@CPC-12; @AIS-26; @DIE-12] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Loose tofu shows 78,058 units on the platform's sold counter, while CP Meat Zero, listed at 1.5 to 2.1 times CP's own minced pork per kilogram for the minced and roast SKUs (about 3.3 times for the bologna), shows 386 units across eight SKUs and could not be ordered on 25 September 2026 [@CPC-12; @AIS-25] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. A new ingredient must beat dry soy-gluten pieces on cost per gram of protein or on function, and reach caterers through the chay-piece makers and HoReCa distributors that already supply them; a branded analogue at retail prices does not fit {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

**Schools: price, buyers and trust.** Lunch costs VND 35,000 in Ho Chi Minh City (2025 to 2026) and VND 40,000 in Hanoi for 2026 to 2027, of which the city pays VND 28,000 and parents VND 12,000 (Resolution 84/2026/NQ-HĐND) [@PMR-06; @PMR-32; @PMR-33] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. In 2025 to 2026 Hanoi subsidised lunch for about 768,000 primary pupils at VND 20,000 (VND 30,000 in mountain communes and on Red River sandbars), a VND 3,063 billion budget; 90% of its schools provide *bán trú* (school lunch and midday care) [@CHN-29] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. That budget buys roughly 100 to 150 million subsidised meals a year (our calculation from the budget and meal price) [@CHN-29] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. We found no national count of pupils eating at school. Menus are written by caterers, not by the state: in Hanoi a ward evaluation council assigns caterers and food, milk and water suppliers to each school, the caterer writes the menu with grams and calories and the principal co-signs, and one caterer wrote near-identical menus for three schools [@PMR-05; @PMR-06; @PMR-22; @PMR-23; @PMR-24] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. A Hai Phong school tender fixes the price at the regulated norm, scores caterers on capability and on the extra portion value they add, and asks for a food-safety certificate, revenue of at least VND 3 billion, three school or industrial-zone contracts and certified food suppliers [@PMR-07] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. In April 2026 about 300 tonnes of pork from pigs with African swine fever, relabelled as clean, reached 26 Hanoi public schools and private kindergartens through two caterers [@CHN-36] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The Prime Minister's Dispatch 64/CĐ-TTg of 13 September 2026 requires traceable suppliers and procurement "not based solely on lowest price" [@CHN-30] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}, and Directive 33/CT-TTg (14 August 2026) adds supplier listing, inspection and capacity evaluation and daily public disclosure of the caterer, ingredients, invoices, menus and photos of meal trays, without restricting any food type [@PMR-02; @AIB-42] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. In September 2026 Hanoi parents took school-meal samples to the national food-safety testing institute to check the meat in them [@TRU-21] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

**The rule asks for plant protein; menus fill it with tofu.** Our first reading took school meals to be guided by Decision 1340/QĐ-TTg (2016), a school-milk programme whose target of animal protein above 40% of total protein ran only to 2020 [@CHN-33] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. The rule now in force is MOH Decision 3958/QĐ-BYT (25 December 2025). It sets no animal share. It asks for protein at 13 to 20% of energy, animal protein on at least 4 to 5 days a week "alternating with plant protein (legumes, tofu) at least twice a week", fish 2 to 3 times a week and limits on processed meat and sausages; its 139-item food table lists tofu, soybeans and soy milk but no textured soy, gluten or analogue. It is guidance with no sanction, and it excludes preschools [@AIB-39; @APR-04] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. The menu software sheets that one Hanoi school (Nguyen Trai) publishes, from MOET, Ajinomoto Vietnam and NIN, still print a standard of "animal protein at least 48%" of each lunch's protein; 9 of that school's 25 published days fall below it [@PMR-26; @AFN-46] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-menu-software-floor}}

**What schools serve.** In 48 published school-weeks (239 lunch days) from 22 primary schools in Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi and Hai Phong, March to September 2026, 36 days (15.1%) had plant protein in a protein dish, almost always tofu; only 9 of 48 weeks met the twice-weekly rule; 1 day in 239 had no animal protein; and none of 333 protein dishes used textured soy, *chay* mock meat or a branded analogue [@PMR-10; @PMR-24; @PMR-31] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Tofu is served as a second dish beside a meat or fish main (27 of 36 plant days) or cooked into a meat dish (8 of 36). Minced or processed meat or fish dishes (meatballs, pork loaf, sausages, fish cakes) appear on 28.5% of days [@PMR-10; @PMR-31] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. At Nguyen Trai, lunches carry about 31.8 g of protein on the menu, 17.5 g of it animal (our calculation from 25 days of its software sheets) [@PMR-26] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. Day-level coding is in `school_menu_weeks.csv`. {{kn:kn-school-plant-days}}

**The school verdict.** Do not start in schools with a branded or meat-replacement product. A plant ingredient sold into the required plant slot replaces tofu, not meat, and competes with it on cost: tofu costs VND 4,900 to 7,500 per 25 g of protein and a textured-soy ingredient VND 925 to 2,675 before oil, sauce and labour (our calculation; textured-soy cost from [[ch09-economics]]) [@DIE-05; @DIE-23; @PMR-24; @DIE-12] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. The slot is small: at today's frequency it holds about 1,000 t of protein a year (660 to 1,580 t), and about 2,800 t if every school met the rule (our calculation from an assumed 0.5 to 1.2 billion school lunches a year) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. The only school route that removes meat is a named processor's labelled blend in minced-meat and fish-cake dishes: a 25% blend in every such dish would remove about 460 t of meat protein a year (our calculation) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. A 20 to 30% soy extender keeps the dish's protein quality at a DIAAS of about 97 or more (older-child pattern), with 12 to 19% less zinc per gram of protein than all-pork, so blends raise no nutrition objection; a dish that removes all meat would need added zinc [@NQR-05; @NQR-07; @APR-04] {general|Medium} {dx:inferred}. For school-age children protein is not the gap; the documented shortfalls are breakfast, calcium and vitamin A (below). Korea shows what a rule change can do: all 17 education offices recommend plant-based school meals once or twice a month, and Seoul's plant-based menus carried 26.7 g of protein against 29.9 g for regular ones in 2023 [@AFN-42] {VN-adjacent|High} {dx:revealed}.

**The rule window and the milk precedent.** Decision 973/QĐ-TTg (School Health Programme 2026 to 2035, 1 June 2026) orders a MOET circular on *bán trú* meal organisation in 2026 and MOET digital tools for balanced menus in 2027 to 2028 [@PMR-01; @APR-12] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Press coverage describes a model with 400 standard menus and a daily carton of fresh milk, which the decision's text does not name [@AFN-45] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. The dairy strategy (Decision 309/QĐ-TTg, 2026) says school milk programmes use "only fresh milk" [@FTR-31; @APR-11] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}, and Hanoi's 2018 school milk tender went to Vinamilk, whose milk is made entirely in Vietnam, with the state, the supplier and parents sharing the cost [@CHN-34] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Plant milk reaches schools only as a gift: Vinasoy has donated 13.8 million boxes of soy milk to 906,848 pupils since 2016, and plans to donate 1 million boxes to 30 schools in 2026 to 2027 [@AIB-06; @AIB-08] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The levers for plant protein in schools are the menu software's default and food list, the 2026 circular and the few caterers that each write one menu for many schools, not a nutrition target {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

**Upland boarding and border-commune meals.** Public money now buys meals for ethnic-minority boarders and lunch for border-commune pupils: VND 936,000 a month and 15 kg of rice per semi-boarder (Decree 66/2025), VND 1,170,000 and 15 kg per full boarder in the new boarding schools (Decree 188/2026), and VND 450,000 and 8 kg for about 418,000 pupils in land-border communes (Decree 339/2025; more than VND 2,000 billion and 30,000 t of rice a year at draft stage) [@UPL-20; @UPL-21; @APR-09; @UPL-22] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. School kitchens, not caterers, cook, and they spend the money on pork. In 13 boarding schools in five provinces that publish menus (22 school-weeks, 2026), 240 of 242 lunches and dinners carried a meat, fish or egg dish and pork appeared in 102 of 124 lunches (82%; our register `upland_school_weeks.csv`); at one border school pork took 97% of the Decree 339 lunch money (rice aside) on pork days, and pork and tofu together 91% on tofu days [@UPL-01; @UPL-02; @UPL-03; @UPL-04; @UPL-05; @UPL-06; @UPL-07; @UPL-08; @UPL-09; @UPL-10; @UPL-11; @UPL-12; @UPL-13; @UPL-14; @UPL-15; @UPL-16; @UPL-17] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Kitchens already stretch pork with tofu: on tofu days at Muong Nhe the lunch used 35% less pork, its protein items cost 27% less (the whole lunch 25% less), for about 8% less protein (our calculation) [@UPL-01] {VN-direct|High} {dx:inferred}. No textured soy or mock meat appears in 353 meals. The thin meal is breakfast (86% carry little or no animal food; our menu coding, `upland_school_weeks.csv`), and the only kitchen-weighed boarding diets we found met protein and zinc needs but supplied 36.5% of calcium and 41 to 45% of vitamin A [@UPL-01; @UPL-18] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Stunting (32% among ethnic minority children under five) [@APR-27] is a problem of children below school age, outside school kitchens {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. At one Quang Ngai school suppliers need a business registration and a food-safety certificate, and a former principal in Bac Ha, Lao Cai, was arrested in 2024 for diverting more than VND 765 million of boarding support after inspectors had found meals cut, so the plan is not always the plate [@UPL-26; @UPL-24] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The one plant product with an observed job here is a pork extender sold at the tofu price per gram of protein; nobody has asked these kitchens whether they would buy it {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-upland-meals-animal}}

**Hospitals and the military.** A 2025 request for quotations for patient meals at a public hospital in Ho Chi Minh City (about 81,800 rice and 20,500 porridge meals a year) requires at least 1,800 kcal a day for the rice diet (1,200 kcal for porridge) and, per meal, at least 60 g of lean meat, fish, chicken or seafood or at least 120 g of tofu as a full replacement, with a tofu version among three sample menus [@AIB-44] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The tofu swap gives about 13.1 g of protein against 11.4 g (our calculation) [@AIB-39]. It is the one public-meal specification we found that lets a plant food replace meat, and it names tofu. The army's basic food allowance is VND 72,000 per soldier a day under Circular 96/2025/TT-BQP [@AIB-45] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}; we found no ration composition or procurement rule. Workplace and hospital meal guidelines are not legally binding [@APR-26] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

> **Correction.** In v0.6 this said the hospital tender requires 60 g of protein a day; the source sets no daily protein figure, and 60 g is the minimum weight of meat or fish per meal.

{{chart:chart-institutional-meals}}

## 15.4 Tourism and the Nha Trang hypothesis

Vietnam received 21.2 million international visitors in 2025 (up 20%) and 15.9 million in the first eight months of 2026; China was flat and Korea down in 2026 while Russia and India grew fast [@CHN-43; @CHN-45] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Khanh Hoa (Nha Trang) received 5.5 million international visitors in 2025 and has 70,500 rooms, over 40% of them four and five star; its visitors come mainly from Korea, Russia and China [@CHN-47; @CHN-48; @CHN-49] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Direct flights from India, the one fast-growing market with structural vegetarian demand, land in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang, not Nha Trang [@CHN-52] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}.

**Verdict.** The project's hypothesis that Nha Trang's tourist-driven hotels and restaurants are a channel for plant-based products is not supported as a volume channel. Our rough calculation gives 1 to 2 million vegetarian or vegan meal occasions a year from international visitors to Khanh Hoa, against 100 to 150 million subsidised school lunches in Hanoi alone and up to 1.2 billion factory meals nationally [@CHN-47; @CHN-29; @CHN-37; @CHN-39] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. It is plausible as a small showcase for premium analogues and higher-protein chay dishes in four and five star hotels, and hotels now have one named reason to meet a supplier: Accor's target of 50% vegetarian or plant-based dishes by 2030 binds its 43 Vietnamese hotels, and it has signed a Mercure in Nha Trang [@AFN-40; @AFN-41] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. The target counts dishes, which vegetables and tofu can fill, and Accor's 2025 cage-free pledge was "not yet achieved in Asia" [@AFN-18] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. One Vietnamese tempeh maker names a Sheraton hotel among its customers [@AIS-43] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. The hypothesis is cheap to test: interview 20 hotel and restaurant food-and-beverage managers, Accor's first, and audit 30 menus. Domestic tourists who keep chay days may matter more there than foreign vegetarians (untested).

## 15.5 Channel economics: absent, not weak

We found no retrievable Vietnamese source on retailer listing fees, trade margins, payment terms, distributor margins or frozen distribution costs per kilogram. The numbers we have are from catering (food at 60 to 80% of meal value; commissions of 2 to 4% of a VND 25,000 meal) [@CHN-41] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}, the supply study's finding that dried soy analogues retail at 5 to 17 times the indicative ex-factory cost of their protein ([[app-s12-costs]]), Saigon Co.op's private label priced 15 to 30% below comparable brands, with a supplier portal that answers a product pitch within 10 working days but whose public pages list no document requirements [@AIB-28; @CPC-17; @CPC-18] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}, and the first public kitchen-delivered prices, on Kamereo (15.3) [@CPC-12] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Anyone modelling a consumer product should get three buyer quotes before setting a price.

## 15.6 Which channel carries which product first

Ranks are our judgement from the evidence above; size is documented, fit is mostly inferred, and there is no tested evidence in any Vietnamese channel {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

| Product | First route | Second route | Not first | What it must be |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Textured plant protein ingredient | Chay and processed-meat makers, who already import textured soy and gluten, including small makers of dry chay pieces that sell online and to kitchens | Contract caterers, reached through chay-piece makers and HoReCa distributors (Kamereo, MM Mega Market); later, school, hospital and upland school kitchens for the tofu slot | Own-brand retail; a "replaces meat" pitch to schools | Near the Chinese landed price; cheaper per gram of protein than dry soy-gluten pieces (about VND 4,000 to 5,100 per 20 g) and tofu; dry, tolerant of bulk cooking, traceable, with food-safety certificates |
| Higher-protein chay product | Incumbent chay brands in the modern frozen sections, and retailer private label made by an existing certified co-packer (Co.op Select through GN Foods; Lotte Mart Choice L) | Lunar-calendar foodservice: chain limited-time items, chay restaurants, canteen chay days | Wet markets, schools | At or below the meat version's price, 10 g or more protein per 100 g (the "high protein" condition of TCVN 14429:2025), familiar formats |
| Hybrid meat and plant product | Integrated meat groups (Masan, C.P., Vissan) and their stores, starting with industrial *xúc xích* (sausage) and coarse fillings | Factory canteens (minced dishes are 17% of protein dishes) | Schools, except later as a named processor's labelled blend in minced-meat and fish-cake dishes (28.5% of audited school days) | Cheaper or better tolerated than the processor's own soy recipe; plant part named as an ingredient; never sold as *độn* (filler) |
| Premium modern analogue | Premium restaurants and café chains in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi | Premium import-led retail and e-commerce; four and five star hotels as a showcase (Accor's dish target) | Mass retail, canteens, schools, and B2B foodservice distribution (CP Meat Zero was listed on Kamereo and is not orderable) | Chef-grade performance in named dishes; imported analogues at today's prices have not stuck |
| Cultivated or precision-fermented product | Business-to-business ingredient into hybrids through large manufacturers | Premium restaurant showcase | All mass and institutional channels until a new-food route exists | A regulatory route first ([[ch07-rules]]) |

## 15.7 What this means for the frontier

- **Sell ingredients to the firms that feed kitchens and factories before building a shelf brand.** Large, price-set protein demand is in canteens and in manufacturers that already buy imported textured soy and gluten; reach caterers through the chay-piece makers and HoReCa distributors that supply them, and beat tofu and dry soy-gluten pieces per gram of protein.
- **If you make a consumer chay product, design it for the frozen chay section** of the big chains (at or below the meat price, 10 g or more protein per 100 g, familiar formats), or take a protein upgrade of an existing private-label SKU to the retailer through its co-packer.
- **Do not start in schools with a branded or meat-replacement product.** Enter later as a caterer ingredient that beats tofu on cost, or as a named processor's labelled blend in minced dishes.
- **Price meat-free foodservice items at parity** and time launches to the lunar calendar.
- **Use e-commerce to test,** through an incumbent's official store or, for dry chay pieces, through specialist shops; do not build a business on tourists, and use hotels as a showcase only if you already supply the big cities.

**For each reader.**
- **Startups:** sell a familiar food with little capital, and aim first for ingredient, private-label or co-packing supply to incumbents (a chay maker, a caterer, a retailer's co-packer). A restaurant menu listing for your own analogue brand is not a business customer: in the region such firms mostly went quiet or pivoted. No founder has yet tested the ingredient route, so treat it as the hypothesis to test, not a proven path.
- **Investors:** channel access is concentrated (two grocery chains, a few meat groups, a few large caterers and one private-label co-packer for chay); back companies whose product a channel partner buys as an ingredient or under its own label, and price foodservice churn as risk. Corporate commitments add no volume here.
- **Manufacturers:** incumbent chay makers hold the frozen sections and convenience contracts; a co-packer can take a protein upgrade to a retailer's private label without a consumer brand; HoReCa distributors already sell tofu and dry soy-gluten pieces to kitchens in volume; integrated meat groups are best placed to launch hybrids.
