- **Research bodies:** work on bulk-cooking functionality (holding, reheating, broth absorption) and dry formats that travel without a cold chain; run a two-week plate-waste trial with one caterer that writes one menu for several schools, testing a textured-soy dish in the plant slot and a 20 to 30% blend in one minced dish, with the published daily menus as a free control series.
- **Policy makers:** national guidance already has no animal share. Ask MOET, NIN and Ajinomoto to replace the menu software's "animal protein at least 48%" default with protein-quality, zinc and iron targets and to add textured soy and legume products to its food list, and write both into the MOET *bán trú* circular due in 2026 and the digital menu tools due in 2027 to 2028 (Decision 973/QĐ-TTg). Supplier documents are now set by Directive 33/CT-TTg; transparent canteen procurement helps new entrants more than subsidies.
- **International organisations and funders:** match the trial to your unit. A canteen trial should log the dish species it replaces, because chicken leads only 13% of canteen protein dishes (our coding, `canteen_dishes.csv`) and pork dishes spare few animals; import substitution and protein upgrades on existing chay days spare none ([[ch18-demand-sizing]]). Humane World for Animals, which trained chefs and nutritionists in Viet Nam in 2025, is an implementer to partner with [@AFN-23] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}; Viet Nam is not listed as a School Meals Coalition member [@APR-38] {VN-adjacent|Low} {dx:revealed}. Corporate commitments are a weak lever: fund implementation measurement at Accor's Vietnamese hotels and a disclosure request to Vinamilk, not a new pledge campaign. Fund the missing channel data (margins, listing fees, frozen distribution costs, national *bán trú* coverage).

**Related:** [[app-d4-channels]], [[ch16-business-buyers]], [[ch18-demand-sizing]], [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]].

data.title: Business buyers: the market for protein ingredients
data.summary: The clearest revealed demand for new protein in Vietnam comes from firms: Vietnam imported about USD 285 million of protein ingredients in 2023, and domestic makers have no tariff shelter. A new ingredient must match Chinese landed cost on commodity grades, match hydrated soy as a meat extender, or be priced against egg and dairy proteins on function.
data.body:
# 16. Business buyers: the market for protein ingredients

**In one paragraph.** The clearest revealed demand for new protein in Vietnam comes from firms. Vietnam imported about USD 285 million of protein ingredients in 2023, including USD 87 million of plant proteins, and the plant proteins that China reports shipping to Vietnam nearly tripled in tonnage from 2019 to 2025, to about 54,000 t, at about USD 0.9 to 1.3 per kg. Most of that jump is a cheap HS 3504 flow with no lunar timing that Vietnamese customs mostly did not record as 3504, which fits feed better than food; textured protein, by contrast, rises a third before the Vu Lan *chay* season. Chinese, ASEAN and Korean protein ingredients enter at 0% duty, so a domestic maker has no tariff shelter against Chinese product landing at about USD 1.3 to 1.4 per kg. Industrial *đồ chay* (traditional vegetarian food) makers are the most import-dependent and most switchable buyers; meat processors already use soy, wheat, milk and egg proteins as binders, and 31% of one large processor's meat formulations list soy protein, though extension that would pay at every pork price is not done at scale; Vinamilk buys pea protein for a soy-free high-protein nut milk that sells as a niche; infant and medical nutrition makers pay dairy-protein prices of USD 8 to 14 per kg. We found no Vietnamese protein buyer that publishes an alternative-protein target, and no Vietnamese food company piloting mycoprotein, precision-fermented dairy protein or a novel-protein hybrid, though a Chinese yeast protein is now marketed to makers. The price ladder has two rungs, commodity plant proteins at about USD 2 per kg of protein and egg, dairy and premium plant proteins at USD 7 to 18 (mostly 7 to 11), and a new ingredient must choose its rung and its job.

---

## 16.1 What the trade data reveal

No customs code maps cleanly to one protein ingredient: soy isolate appears under both HS 3504 and HS 2106.10, 2106.10 also carries supplement premixes, and 3504 carries peptones and collagen peptides. Vietnam's own reported quantities for these lines are flagged as estimated, so values are the better Vietnam-side measure, and partner-reported exports give tonnages to 2025 [@BUY-01; @BUY-02] {VN-direct|High}.

| Ingredient (HS line) | 2019, USD million (Vietnam-reported) | 2023, USD million (Vietnam-reported) | 2025, USD million (partner-reported, FOB) | 2025 tonnes | Main origin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Other protein substances incl. soy isolate (3504) | 7.4 | 22.2 | 40.5 | 26,953 | China | [@BUY-01; @BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Protein concentrates, textured protein (2106.10) | 37.0 | 34.0 | 39.4 | 15,304 | USA by value, China by tonnage | [@BUY-01; @BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Wheat gluten (1109) | 15.2 | 31.1 | 28.8 | 21,991 | China | [@BUY-01; @BUY-02] {VN-direct\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| Whey (0404.10) | 47.2 | 65.7 | 78.7 | 64,003 | USA, Turkiye, Spain | [@BUY-01; @BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Whey protein concentrate 80% or more (3502.20) | 10.7 | 10.8 | 16.2 | 1,634 | USA, Germany | [@BUY-01; @BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Casein and caseinates (3501) | 17.8 | 33.6 | 12.4 | 1,410 | New Zealand, Germany | [@BUY-01; @BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| Egg white and egg powders (3502.11, 0408) | 9.7 | 15.9 | 16.9 | 2,536 | India | [@BUY-01; @BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Gelatin (3503) | 40.6 | 62.2 | 42.8 | 6,778 | China, France, Korea | [@BUY-01; @BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| **All lines (13 in 2019 and 2023; 12 in the 2025 partner data)** | **190.1** | **285.0** | **286.1** | **142,758** | | [@BUY-01; @BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |

{{kn:kn-protein-ingredient-imports}}

**Plant proteins are the fastest-growing tonnage.** China-reported shipments of HS 3504, 2106.10 and 1109 to Vietnam rose from 18,375 t (2019) to 28,323 t (2023), 51,130 t (2024) and 53,976 t (2025), worth USD 59.7 million in 2025 [@BUY-02] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Most of the 2024 jump came from HS 3504 at about USD 1 per kg (see below). Wheat gluten from all origins doubled, from 11,327 t (2019) to 21,991 t (2025) [@BUY-02] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. China-origin textured protein (2106.10) grew 54% from 2019 to 2025; it did not triple. In 2025 Vietnam imported 12,832 t of 2106.10 from its three low-cost origins, China, India and Serbia, which is the pool a domestic soy extrusion line could serve [@BUY-02; @TIC-12] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-china-plant-protein-tonnage}}

{{chart:chart-plant-protein-imports}}

**Monthly data separate chay food from the new 3504 flow.** China's monthly shipments of textured protein to Vietnam run 33% above an average month in the two months before the Vu Lan month, the peak of *chay* eating in the seventh lunar month, in five of six years (2019 to 2024), against 4% for the same code to the world and 2% to Thailand; that seasonal excess is about 5.5% of annual tonnage, some 550 t in 2024 (our calculation) [@BRD-05; @BRD-06] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The 2024 jump in HS 3504 has no such timing. It began in October 2023, was priced at USD 1.03 per kg against USD 2.46 for all China's 3504 exports, and was mostly not recorded as 3504 by Vietnamese customs (38% of China's reported value in October to December 2023, against full-year ratios of 84 to 101% in 2019 to 2022) [@BRD-05; @BRD-06; @BUY-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Price, timing and mirror records all support the reading that the jump is a feed, pet-food or technical protein, not a food isolate; the importers are still unidentified. If it is not food, the imported food pool is nearer 35 kt of product than the 40 kt the demand model uses ([[ch18-demand-sizing]]) (our calculation) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. For an ingredient supplier the seasonal swing is modest: about a third more demand before Vu Lan and a trough in the *Tết* (lunar new year) month, not the two to three times swing of retail chay sales (`trade_seasonal_summary.csv`).

**What the trade data cannot tell us.** The split between food and feed, and between buyer segments, is not visible at six-digit level. Treat plant-protein imports as an upper bound for food demand until a declaration-level dataset (eight-digit code, description, importer) is analysed; this is one of the cheapest public goods on the demand side ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).

## 16.2 The price ladder

| Ingredient, 2025 | USD per kg | USD per kg of protein (assumed grade) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wheat gluten, China | 1.31 | 1.75 (75%) | [@BUY-02] {VN-direct\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| Textured protein and soy concentrate, China | 1.24 | 1.91 (65%) | [@BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Soy protein isolate, China (seven sample shipments) | 1.76 to 2.20 | 1.96 to 2.44 (90%) | [@BUY-07] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| Pea protein, China (two shipments) | 2.00 to 3.00 | 2.50 to 3.75 (80%) | [@BUY-09] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| Pea protein, United States or France (two shipments) | 6.75 to 8.50 | 8.44 to 10.63 (80%) | [@BUY-09] {VN-direct\|Low} {dx:revealed} |
| Egg white powder, India | 5.90 | 7.38 (80%) | [@BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Casein, New Zealand | 7.59 | 8.63 (88%) | [@BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Whey protein concentrate 80, United States | 8.13 | 10.16 (80%) | [@BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Whey protein concentrate 80, Germany | 14.05 | 17.56 (80%) | [@BUY-02] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |

{{chart:chart-ingredient-price-ladder}}

The ladder has two rungs {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. Commodity plant proteins cost about USD 1.7 to 2.4 per kg of protein at the border; egg, dairy and premium plant proteins cost USD 7 to 11 and more [@BUY-02; @BUY-07; @BUY-09] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. The Chinese textured-protein price of USD 1.24 per kg is China's lowest to any of eight Asian and US partners (world average USD 1.95), and India (2,372 t at USD 0.98) and Serbia (259 t at USD 0.85) sold lower still, so a domestic line would meet the lowest-priced grade on the market [@TIC-14; @BUY-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-border-protein-price}}

**No tariff shelter.** Chinese, ASEAN and Korean product pays no duty: HS 2106.10, 3504 and 1109 are at 0% under ACFTA, AKFTA and RCEP in 2025 to 2027 and under ATIGA (0% in the latest schedule we read, to 2022) with a certificate of origin, and pea protein (3504) also enters at 0% from France under EVFTA and Canada under CPTPP [@FTR-32; @FTR-33] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The most-favoured-nation rates (5% for 2106.10, 3% for 3504, 10% for gluten) apply only to other origins, chiefly the United States [@REG2-20; @REG2-23; @FTR-32; @BUY-02] {VN-direct|Medium}. With freight, insurance and port costs, Chinese textured protein lands at about USD 1.29 to 1.38 per kg, or about USD 2.0 to 2.1 per kg of protein (our calculation, `t1_landed_competitor.csv`, assuming freight and insurance at 3 to 8% of FOB value, port and inland costs of USD 15 to 40 per t and 65% protein) [@TIC-12; @FTR-32] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Whether every importer claims the preference is not known; declaration data would show it. {{kn:kn-fta-duty-china}}

A new ingredient must decide which rung, and which job, it competes on (our calculation) [@BUY-02; @TIC-12] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}:
- **Commodity textured protein or isolate:** match Chinese landed cost.
- **Meat extender** (10 to 30% of the lean; hundreds of tonnes at a large processor): match hydrated soy, about USD 2.6 to 2.8 per kg of protein. For a fungal biomass at 45% protein that is about USD 0.7 to 1.2 per kg dry, unless it lets the processor replace more meat unnoticed than soy ([[ch14-frontier-demand]]).
- **Binder or functional protein** (1 to 3% of a recipe; tens of tonnes a buyer): price against egg and dairy proteins. Fungal biomass at 45% protein could reach about USD 3.3 per kg against egg white and USD 3.9 to 4.6 per kg against casein or whey concentrate if it delivers binding, texture, flavour or solubility. Here it meets a Chinese yeast protein already marketed in Vietnam (16.5).

Ingredient distributors list gluten as "contact for price", and retail prices of dried textured soy (VND 327,000 to 500,000 per kg) are about 10 to 16 times the Chinese border unit value of USD 1.24 per kg for HS 2106.10 (our calculation) [@BUY-36; @BUY-37; @FORM-01; @BUY-02] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. The first public business-to-business prices we found are for finished kitchen products: on Kamereo, a platform supplying restaurants and hotels, domestic dry soy-gluten chay pieces sell at VND 135,000 per kg (VND 118,692 by the carton), about VND 20,000 to 25,000 per 100 g of protein on a borrowed protein range, and firm branded tofu at about VND 36,000 to 48,000 per 100 g of protein (our calculation) [@CPC-12; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

## 16.3 Who the buyers are

**Chay makers: the most switchable.** Every protein-dense local chay product in our audit uses imported textured soy, soy concentrate, soy isolate or gluten ([[ch02-alt-protein-today]]). The makers are owner-managed firms that can trial a new ingredient in weeks but each buys small volumes: An Nhien (imported Serbian soy concentrate on its label), Au Lac (an exporter), Thoai An (35% gluten in its vegetarian pork roll), LC Foods (textured soy granules of 4 to 7 mm), SG Food and the chay lines of Vissan, CJ Cau Tre and Cholimex [@FORM-01; @FORM-28; @EXP-38] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. A Vietnamese plant-based startup founder said in 2021 that more than 90% of its raw materials were imported because domestic ones had "two problems, quality and price" [@BUY-38; @AIS-41] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}. Chay makers also reach shelves through retailer private label: one certified co-packer, GN Foods, makes all five Co.op Select frozen chay dishes, using wheat protein, soybean or no protein ingredient [@CPC-15; @ECO-35] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. And they sell dry pieces to households and kitchens: small online shops have sold about 40,700 kg of dry soy-and-gluten "ribs" on Lazada, and a domestic brand, Panko, sells similar pieces to kitchens through Kamereo; the makers behind the online shops are not named, so they are a buyer group still to trace [@MKT-03; @MKT-04; @CPC-12] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}.

**Meat processors: low-inclusion blends already.** In an online label audit of 118 Vissan products, 22 of 67 unique meat formulations (33%) list soy protein and 25 (37%) list at least one added protein, mostly in value lines such as canned meats, pâté, *giò lụa* (plain, and with head meat or skin) and nutrition sausages [@BUY-05] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. The pattern is functional: added proteins bind water and fat and cut meat cost. Vissan made 18,547 t of processed food in 2025 and plans 20,350 t in 2026 [@BUY-04] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Illustratively, if 30 to 50% of that output carried soy protein at 1 to 3%, Vissan would buy about 55 to 280 t a year (our calculation) [@BUY-04; @BUY-05] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}: as a binder buyer, a large processor is a customer of tens to hundreds of tonnes, not thousands. Extension is a larger prize that Vissan has not taken. A 20% extension of the lean in the same lines would need 224 to 434 t of textured soy (or 249 to 482 t of fungal biomass) and save VND 58 to 112 billion a year at median hog prices, against a 2025 pre-tax profit of VND 105.1 billion; its labels suggest it does not extend at that scale (our calculation, `hybrid_prize.csv`) [@BUY-04; @BUY-05; @TIC-12; @DIE-25] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Because soy extension pays at every pork price ([[ch14-frontier-demand]]), what limits it is product identity, texture and trust, not cost. Vissan's 2026 shareholder meeting set no chay target, and one of its two large projects is a 32,000-head pig farm (the other relocates its slaughter and processing plant) [@AIB-14; @AIB-15] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The business press describes Masan MEATLife as a "consumer protein platform" [@BUY-10], and Masan says it is moving into marinated and processed branded meat [@AIB-12] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. C.P. Vietnam, whose revenue was THB 101.3 billion in 2025 (food THB 8.2 billion), runs a USD 250 million processed-chicken complex and owns a caterer, Dzine Food Solutions; its parent's Meat Zero plant-based range, imported from Thailand, was listed on a Vietnamese HoReCa (hotel, restaurant and catering) platform and is no longer orderable [@BUY-31; @AIB-19; @AIS-25] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

**Dairy and plant milks: the clearest pull for a non-soy isolate.** Vinamilk's high-protein nut milk delivers 9 g of protein per 180 ml "mainly from pea" and is sold as soy-free, lactose-free, non-GMO, gluten-free and glyphosate-free, aimed at "people wary of soy"; its page sets 5 g per 100 ml as the threshold for a high-protein claim [@BUY-16] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. A press summary of Vinamilk's H1 2026 results (total revenue VND 35,034 billion) names its high-protein and plant milks among the contributors to domestic results [@BUY-15] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. This is the only large Vietnamese buyer we found using a non-soy protein isolate. Its pull is product-led, not commitment-led: FAIRR records Vinamilk's plant-based products at 1.30% of its range with no timebound diversification target, and Vinamilk promotes its high-protein dairy milk on milk protein being "more easily absorbed" than plant protein [@AFN-21; @AIB-03] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. The high-protein nut milk sells as a niche: about 70,300 L on Vinamilk's Lazada store, about one-eighth of its standard nut milk by litres (our calculation on cumulative counters) [@MKT-03; @MKT-04] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. The wider plant-milk business is growing: Vinasoy sold 264 million litres in 2025 with its Veyo nut milks up 50%, and Vietnam imported USD 3.9 billion of tree nuts in 2025, up 40%, partly for plant milk [@AIB-05; @AIB-40] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Two fiscal rules shape the category. Regional plant-milk imports are duty-free (2202.99 at 0% under ACFTA, ATIGA and AKFTA, though 12 to 18% under RCEP in 2025 to 2027; most-favoured-nation rates of 20 to 30% apply to non-FTA origins), so local makers' advantage is distribution, not tariffs [@FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. From 1 January 2027 drinks above 5 g of total sugar per 100 ml pay an 8% excise (10% from 2028); dairy is exempt, whether soy and nut milks count is unresolved, and the reference high-protein nut milk lists 6.5% added sugar, so an isolate buyer will want formulations at or below 5 g ([[ch13-consumers]]) [@FTR-01; @FTR-02; @FTR-05; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}.

**Infant and medical nutrition: demanding and slow.** These makers use whey protein concentrate (Vietnam imported 1,634 t in 2025), demineralised whey, casein and milk protein concentrates, market "non-GMO" and are moving towards clinical research (Nutifood signed a memorandum of understanding on research and clinical trials with Military Hospital 175 in June 2026) [@BUY-02; @BUY-19] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. They are the buyers for precision-fermented dairy proteins, but qualification is slow and regulatory status is the gate; low-dose ingredients such as lactoferrin fall below the 5% trigger of the mandatory GMO label ([[ch14-frontier-demand]]).

**Instant noodles: volume, not yet protein.** Vietnam ate 8,231 million servings in 2025, about 81 per person, fourth in the world [@BUY-03] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Acecook uses soy protein only in seasoning and garnish sachets, but already buys pea starch, a co-product of pulse protein fractionation, and calcium-fortifies its best-selling brand; we found no protein-fortified noodle [@BUY-22] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Its July 2025 strategy moves into convenient seasonings, ready-to-eat foods and meal-replacement snacks; the nutrition steps it lists for existing lines are calcium, vitamin B12 and real meat and vegetables in instant pho and bun, and it makes no protein claim [@AIB-18] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. A pulse-protein plant would have starch buyers waiting.

**Seasoning, bakery and sports nutrition.** Seasoning makers buy protein as flavour (for example bone-and-meat extract in Aji-ngon) [@BUY-26] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}; bakery protein demand is likely egg and dairy (our inference from egg-albumin and dairy-protein imports) [@BUY-02] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}; sports nutrition imports finished products, not ingredients [@BUY-08] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}.

## 16.4 What buyers specify

- **Meat pastes and sausages:** gel strength, water and fat binding, emulsion stability through retort sterilisation, bland flavour and light colour, used with starch, fibre, phosphates and carrageenan [@BUY-05] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Two isolates at the same price can perform differently in the same paste [@BUY-42] {general|Medium}. For extension rather than binding, fine emulsions take a fine isolate (or a similar fine ingredient) at 10 to 20% of the lean, not granules, and coarse mince up to about 30% [@HXE-09] {general|Medium} {dx:tested}. We found no published Vietnamese study of soy protein in *giò lụa*; the nearest are a 2017 study of emulsion sausages, which found soy protein in all seven commercial sausages tested, and a 2021 study showing that graininess and uneven texture cut liking of *chả lụa* [@HXE-02; @HXE-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:tested}. No national standard sets a minimum meat content, and a meat named in the product name must be quantified, so an extender keeps the product name [@LBL-11; @LBL-06] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}; buyers whose premium lines sell on "no filler" will not want one [@TRU-27] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.
- **Plant milks and nutrition drinks:** solubility, low viscosity, stability through UHT treatment, neutral flavour, a complete amino-acid profile, and documents for soy-free, non-GMO and glyphosate-free claims [@BUY-16] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Mung bean isolates of 85 to 88% protein have been made from Thai-grown beans (transfer assumption: similar beans and processes) [@BUY-47] {VN-adjacent|Medium}.
- **Chay analogues:** granule size (for example 4 to 7 mm) and slices, in 20 to 25 kg bags [@FORM-28; @FORM-11; @FORM-13] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}; we infer that buyers also check rehydration ratio and chewiness, and that exporters want non-GMO claims and halal certificates (one exporter, Au Lac, is halal-certified) [@EXP-38] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.
- **All buyers:** certificates of analysis and traceable origin. Food-safety crises in 2025 and 2026, including about 130 t of pork from pigs with African swine fever at a canned-meat maker whose H1 2026 revenue then fell 32%, and enforcement against a nut-milk maker whose product failed its own declared specification, have, we infer, raised the documentation bar for any new supplier [@BUY-20; @BUY-45; @MAC-31] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}. Vinamilk's 2025 annual report says traceability and label compliance are becoming "mandatory rather than a competitive advantage" and names price competitiveness and quality as supplier criteria [@AIB-01] {VN-direct|High} {dx:stated}.

Minimum order quantities, shelf-life requirements and qualification times were not published by any buyer we could read. Qualification time is the most important unknown for a founder ([[app-r1-open-questions]]).

## 16.5 How ingredients are bought

Large processors import major ingredients directly and buy minor ones through distributors, and in-person contact is expected [@MAC-31] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Plant proteins sit between: large buyers import containers (16 t pea protein shipments in 2025), while small firms buy 20 to 25 kg bags from distributors such as VMC Group, TDGIMEX and Brenntag [@BUY-09; @BUY-35; @BUY-36; @BUY-37; @FORM-11] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Food Ingredients Vietnam (May 2026) listed about 250 exhibitors, mostly Chinese, including pea protein and US dairy protein suppliers and two Chinese soy protein makers (Sinoglory and Yuxin), but none of the global soy isolate brands (ADM, IFF, Fuji Oil, Yuwang) [@BUY-33] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Distributors now also sell fermentation-derived protein: ACC (Asia Ingredients Group) has marketed Angel Yeast's yeast protein (55 to 90% protein and a PDCAAS of 1.0, company claims) to Vietnamese bakery, beverage, dairy, plant-based and meat-alternative makers since May 2025, with sampling and application support; no price or named user is public [@AIS-38; @CPC-21; @CPC-22] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Kitchens buy finished plant protein through HoReCa distributors: Kamereo lists 37 tofu SKUs and dry soy-gluten pieces, and MM Mega Market about 39 chay prepared foods and 31 tofu items, but neither lists dry textured soy, gluten or a Western analogue [@CPC-12; @CPC-13; @CPC-14] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

## 16.6 Novel protein: a clean negative, with two qualifications

We found no Vietnamese food company piloting mycoprotein, precision-fermented dairy protein or a hybrid meat product using a novel protein, and no Vietnamese protein buyer publishing an alternative-protein or protein-diversification target. The Asia Protein Buyers 100 (February 2026) covers five Vietnamese buyers, placing Vinamilk in Tier 3, Masan in Tier 4, Vinh Hoan in Tier 5 and Minh Phu and Nam Viet in Tier 6, and finds only 2 of 100 Asian buyers publishing alternative-protein sourcing targets [@AFN-18; @AFN-21] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. In the 2025 annual reports and 2026 shareholder meeting records we read for Vinamilk, Masan, Vissan and C.P.'s parent, we found no such target for Vietnam, and incumbents' protein diversification is into animal protein: Vinabeef chilled beef, a Vissan pig farm and Masan processed meat [@AIB-01; @AIB-12; @AIB-19; @BUY-04] {VN-direct|High} {dx:stated}. CP Foods sells Meat Zero with no quantified target.

Two qualifications. A small Vietnamese startup, Emmay, reported sales of 1.5 to about 2 t a month of mushroom and mycelium foods in 2023, including a shiitake mycoprotein made by fermentation, with exports about 10% of 2023 revenue (company report) [@AIS-39] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. And a Chinese yeast protein has been marketed to Vietnamese makers through ACC since May 2025, with no named user (16.5). The corporate moves on record remain the seafood exporters' cultivated-meat stakes, whose partners have since turned to non-food revenue, with no food product yet ([[ch14-frontier-demand]]). The one novel-ish ingredient with proven corporate uptake is a non-soy plant isolate in dairy (pea at Vinamilk); the one hybrid category with proven uptake is conventional (soy, wheat and milk proteins in meat pastes).

## 16.7 The buyer map and first customers

| Rank | Segment | Current protein-ingredient spend (1 to 5) | Likelihood of switching to a domestic or novel ingredient (1 to 5) | Price and specification to meet | Ease of first trial (1 to 5) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Industrial chay makers and frozen chay co-packers | 3 | 5 | At or below Chinese textured protein landed at 0% duty (about USD 1.29 to 1.38 per kg in 2025); granules and slices; non-GMO; halal | 5 |
| 2 | Plant milks and adult nutrition drinks | 3 | 4 | USD 2 to 7 per kg in bulk (the pea band; duty-free from China, and from France and Canada under EVFTA and CPTPP); soluble, UHT-stable, neutral, soy-free, non-GMO; drinks at or below 5 g sugar per 100 ml | 3 |
| 3 | Meat processors | 3 | 3 | Binder: soy isolate parity near USD 1.8 to 2.2 per kg; extender: hydrated soy parity (about USD 2.6 to 2.8 per kg of protein); gel, emulsion, retort stability | 3 |
| 4 | Seasoning and flavour | 3 | 3 | Priced as flavour; umami; clean label | 3 |
| 5 | Instant noodles | 2 | 2 | Textured garnish at Chinese parity; pulse starch co-products | 2 |
| 6 | Infant formula and medical nutrition | 4 | 2 | Whey concentrate parity USD 8 to 14 per kg; infant-grade dossiers; regulatory clarity | 1 |
| 7 | Bakery and snacks | 2 | 1 | Egg white parity near USD 5.9 per kg with whipping and binding; yeast protein already offered | 2 |
| 8 | Sports nutrition | 1 | 1 | Imports finished goods | 1 |

Scores are our judgement from the evidence above [@BUY-02; @BUY-05; @BUY-16; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

**Plausible first customers, by product** {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}:
- **Domestic textured soy or soy-gluten protein:** An Nhien, Au Lac, Thoai An, LC Foods and SG Food first (fast trials, import substitution); then the frozen chay lines of Cholimex, CJ Cau Tre and Vissan, retailer co-packers (GN Foods for Co.op Select), makers of dry chay pieces sold to kitchens and online, and contract caterers through HoReCa distributors; Acecook for noodle garnish. This matches play T1, which [[ch26-plays]] recasts as an import-substitution plant best owned by a chay maker, co-packer or distributor and financed with debt, not venture equity; the soy pool a line can serve is up to about 12,800 t a year of HS 2106.10 imports (2025; the code also covers concentrates and isolates, so the textured share is unknown) ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).
- **Rice or mung bean protein isolate:** Vinamilk (replacing or complementing imported pea), Vinasoy (nut milks), Nutifood (medical and diabetic nutrition), with starch co-products sold to noodle makers. It would compete with duty-free pea protein and with Angel Yeast's yeast protein, which ACC markets for plant-based dairy. This matches play T10. Vietnam imports most of its mung beans, so a "domestic" isolate may still rest on imported beans.
- **Fungal biomass, split by job:** as a binder (1 to 3% of a recipe, tens of tonnes a buyer), priced against egg and milk protein at about USD 3.3 to 4.6 per kg dry, for value lines at Vissan and Masan MEATLife, bakery egg replacement, and Ajinomoto Vietnam and Cholimex as a flavour-active ingredient for chay seasonings and dumplings; as an extender (10 to 30% of the lean, hundreds of tonnes a buyer), at hydrated-soy parity of about USD 0.7 to 1.2 per kg dry unless it allows more replacement than soy. This matches play T9.
- **Precision-fermented dairy protein:** Nutifood and Vinamilk specialty nutrition, for bioactive proteins rather than bulk whey, after the Food Safety Law (passage considered in May 2027) and the GMO detectability question are settled; low-dose uses already fall outside the mandatory label. This matches play T7.

## 16.8 What this means for the frontier

**For each reader.**
- **Startups:** if you build a textured protein line, you are building an import-substitution plant, not a venture: aim to be owned by or contracted to a chay maker, co-packer or distributor, and test two things first, the delivered price of food-grade defatted soy flour (above about USD 700 to 940 per t the margin fails for a 1 t/h line at 70% use) and whether three buyers will order 2,000 t a year ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]). For an isolate, design for the dairy buyer, keep drinks at or below 5 g of sugar per 100 ml and plan to sell the starch co-product. Pitch fungal biomass by job: against egg and dairy proteins as a binder, against hydrated soy as an extender. Expect trials to be won with certificates, not claims.
- **Investors:** plant-protein imports are worth about USD 87 to 109 million a year at the border (2023 to 2025), an unknown share of it feed, and prices are capped by Chinese supply that pays no duty; returns depend on volume, co-products and distribution, not premiums. A Chinese dry textured-protein line lists at USD 11,000 to 100,000 and installs for about USD 0.3 to 1.4 million, so the funding need is mostly working capital, suited to debt and trade finance. Dairy and nutrition buyers pay 3 to 5 times more per kilogram of protein but qualify suppliers slowly.
- **Manufacturers:** joint development with a local protein maker can secure soy-free and traceable supply, but not a tariff advantage, since pea protein from China, France and Canada is duty-free too. A co-packer can take a protein upgrade to a retailer's private label without a consumer brand. Meat processors already own the cheapest extender, soy: test any new one against your own soy recipe.
- **Research bodies:** publish functional tests of local proteins in Vietnamese formats (industrial *xúc xích*, *giò lụa*, UHT nut milk, noodle garnish) at equal cost to the ingredient they would replace, and offer pilot samples in 20 to 25 kg lots, which is how small buyers test.
- **Policy makers:** national eight-digit subheadings for soy isolate, pea protein and textured protein would make demand visible; a clear answer on whether an identical recombinant protein is a detectable GMO product matters because leading buyers market "non-GMO"; a written ruling before 1 January 2027 on whether soy, nut and cereal milks above 5 g of sugar per 100 ml are *nước giải khát* (soft drinks) would settle plant-milk formulation.
- **International organisations and funders:** fund a declaration-level customs analysis, a price sheet of delivered quotes for food-grade defatted soy flour and Chinese textured soy, and a standing panel of 10 to 15 research and development buyers; together they would answer the food-and-feed split, the T1 margin and the qualification-time question for every founder.

**Related:** [[app-d5-buyers]], [[ch26-plays]], [[app-s1-directory]], [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]].

data.title: Export demand: who abroad would buy Vietnamese alternative protein
data.summary: Vietnam exports almost no protein ingredients, but it exported USD 128.2 million of dumplings and other stuffed pasta in 2023, and its tariff edge abroad comes with conditions. Retail demand for finished plant-based meat is falling in the United States and flat in Europe, and for feed the clearest pull is at home.
data.body:
# 17. Export demand: who abroad would buy Vietnamese alternative protein

**In one paragraph.** Vietnam exports almost no protein ingredients today: USD 0.52 million of textured and concentrated protein in 2023, against about USD 34 million of imports under the same code and USD 380 million of Chinese exports in 2024. What it does export at scale is wrapped food: USD 128.2 million of dumplings, wontons and other stuffed pasta in 2023, about 250 times its textured-protein exports, and in 2025 it out-supplied China and Thailand in the UK, the US and Korea. That base, with protein substances sold mainly to Europe (probably mostly marine by-product peptides, on our reading), is what an export plant-protein product would join; plant-based brands are not. Abroad, retail demand for finished plant-based meat is falling in the United States and flat in Europe. European retailers' plant-protein targets are real but flat, and they are met with pulses, price cuts and hybrids made in Europe, not with Asian imports. Japanese and Korean buyers take textured protein from China and from their own plants. Vietnam's clearest structural advantage is tariffs: zero duty into the EU, the UK and Japan on lines where Thai and Chinese goods pay 6 to 13%, and a 17.4-point edge over China and Thailand on dumplings in Japan under CPTPP. The edge has conditions. EU-bound wrapped foods may contain at most 20% non-originating flour or starch by weight, Vietnam cannot ship meat-filled foods to the EU, the first buyers are importers and brand owners that ask for IFS or BRCGS certification, and CJ is moving part of its EU dumpling supply to Hungary. The United States now charges Vietnamese goods an extra 12.5%, EU rules restrict 32 meat names, and any novel ingredient needs its own approval abroad. On feed, seafood buyers' standards do not require microbial protein, and only BAP counts algae and other aquatic microorganism ingredients towards its marine-ingredient target; the revealed pull is at home, where Vietnam imports about 9,200 t of inactive yeast a year for food and feed, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg.

---

## 17.1 What Vietnam exports now

| Export line | Latest value | Main markets | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Textured protein and protein concentrates (2106.10) | USD 0.52 million (2023) | Japan, US, Korea | Direct alternative-protein export; untested | [@EXP-39] {VN-direct\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| Protein substances (3504) | USD 13.0 million (2023) | Spain, UK, Korea, Denmark | Mostly marine by-product protein (inferred) | [@EXP-39; @EXP-49] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Stuffed pasta: dumplings, wontons (1902.20) | USD 128.2 million, 30,013 t (2023) | US, Australia, UK, Korea, Canada, Japan, Netherlands | The existing export base for plant-protein wrapped foods; vegetarian share not separable at six digits | [@XBA-29] {VN-direct\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| Seafood (all) | USD 11.32 billion (2025) | China and Hong Kong, US, Japan, EU, Korea | Processing skills; feed-standard pull | [@EXP-16; @EXP-31] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Cashew (all forms) | USD 5.23 billion, 766,585 t (2025) | China, US, Netherlands | Cashew milk, cheese and cream bases | [@EXP-18] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Rice | 7.5 Mt, USD 3.83 billion (January to November 2025) | Philippines, Indonesia, China (2023) | Rice protein (no export found) | [@EXP-43; @EXP-39] {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Cassava starch | USD 1.06 billion, 2.15 Mt (2023) | China 93.5% | Fermentation feedstock, sold as starch | [@EXP-39] {VN-direct\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| Instant and other noodles and pasta (1902.30) | USD 268 million (2023) | US, Cambodia, Germany, Poland | Diaspora and Asian-grocer channel | [@EXP-39] {VN-direct\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| Glutamic acid and salts, mainly MSG | USD 106 million (2023) | Japan, US, Cambodia | Proof of export-scale industrial fermentation | [@EXP-39] {VN-direct\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| Inactive yeasts and dead single-cell organisms (2102.20) | USD 11.2 million (2023); 8,166 t at USD 1.39 per kg (2025, partner-reported) | Japan, US, Singapore, Finland | Closest code to single-cell protein; Vietnam also imports about 9,200 t a year for food and feed together (17.5) | [@EXP-39; @FBA-19; @FBA-17] {VN-direct\|High} {dx:revealed} |

{{kn:kn-textured-protein-exports}}

{{kn:kn-stuffed-pasta-exports}}

Four points stand out {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

- **Textured protein is untested as an export, and China sets its price** (USD 380 million of HS 2106.10 exports in 2024, a code that covers all protein concentrates as well as textured protein, at about USD 2.13 per kg on Comtrade-estimated weight) [@EXP-40] {general|High} {dx:revealed}. The tariff edge is unused here: EU27 imports of textured protein from Vietnam were USD 0.01 million (3 t) in 2025, against USD 42.6 million from China [@XBA-28] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}.
- **Vietnam already sells wrapped foods at scale.** In 2025, partner-reported imports of stuffed pasta from Vietnam were USD 48.1 million in the US, 32.4 million in the EU27, 15.5 million in Japan, 14.8 million in the UK, 13.3 million in Korea and 10.6 million in Australia. Vietnam out-supplied China and Thailand in the UK, the US and Korea and was second to China in the EU, Japan and Australia [@XBA-28] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Most of these foods are filled with meat or seafood. The Vietnam-made plant items we found on Western shelves are vegetable-led, at 3.6 to 6.2 g of protein per 100 g: a supermarket own-brand jackfruit fillet and a vegetable bun in the UK, vegetable spring rolls in North America and a vegetable gyoza in Australia [@XBA-26; @ORG-12] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}.
- **Seafood chains may already sell protein ingredients to Europe.** Vietnam exported USD 13.0 million of protein substances (HS 3504) in 2023, mainly to Spain, the UK, Korea and Denmark [@EXP-39] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Vinh Hoan, a pangasius exporter, sells collagen peptides and gelatin [@EXP-49], and Vietnam is the largest producer of ASC-certified pangasius [@EXP-32] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Our reading is that certified seafood chains such as Vinh Hoan's collagen line are the nearest template for a business-to-business novel protein export; we found no source on what European buyers require of these ingredients {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.
- **The firms that hold foreign buyers are food exporters, not plant-based brands.** Wrapped-food, cashew and seafood exporters already have the buyers, certifications and cold or dry export logistics. We found no Vietnamese exporter of cashew milk or cashew cheese with verifiable volumes, and no Vietnamese seafood exporter selling plant-based seafood abroad [@EXP-19; @EXP-49; @XBA-20] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. One small mushroom and mycelium food maker reports exports of about 10% of its revenue to the UK, Australia, India and the Netherlands [@AIS-39] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}.

> **Correction.** In v0.6 this said European ingredient buyers accept Vietnamese protein ingredients when they come from a certified, traceable seafood chain; the cited sources give only trade values and Vinh Hoan's collagen and gelatin line, so this is now marked as our inference.

## 17.2 What foreign markets are buying

| Market | Latest revealed signal | Direction | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| United States | Plant-based meat and seafood USD 1.0 billion in 2025 (value down 10%, units down 11%; value down 17% since 2023); 11% of households buy it, against 38% for plant milk | Falling | [@EXP-02; @EXP-44] {general\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| Six large European markets | Plant-based foods EUR 4.75 billion in 2025 (value up 3.3%, volume up 4.8%); plant-based meat volume fell in the UK, the Netherlands and Spain and grew only where prices fell (France and Italy) | Flat to growing, price-led | [@EXP-05] {general\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| Germany, plant-based seafood | EUR 14.1 million in 2025, down 22% in value | Falling | [@EXP-05] {general\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| European retailers | Six Dutch chains target 60% plant protein by 2030 and Rewe 60% by 2035, but shares are flat (Lidl Netherlands 42.7% to 43.1%, 2023 to 2024; Sainsbury's 14% to 13%, 2022/23 to 2025/26); Tesco, Sainsbury's and Carrefour set no split target; Lidl GB targets 25% by 2030 | Targets real, progress flat | [@XBA-02; @XBA-08; @XBA-12; @XBA-14; @XBA-05] {general\|High} {dx:revealed} |
| Japan | Plant-based meat about USD 18 million (2022), under 0.5% of meat products; Otsuka Foods discontinued several Zero Meat products in 2025. Plant-protein ingredient imports 35,059 t (USD 149 million, 2022), but protein concentrates and textured protein (HS 2106.10) from Vietnam only USD 0.14 to 0.25 million a year (2024 to 2025) against USD 11.5 to 12.8 million from China; Fuji Oil, Japan's leading soy protein maker, has added textured soy capacity at home | Small, shrinking finished market; ingredient demand served by China and domestic makers | [@EXP-07; @XBA-17; @XBA-18; @XBA-28] {general\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Korea | Alternative meat about KRW 21 to 25 billion (USD 17 to 19 million, 2022 to 2023); textured protein from Vietnam USD 0.27 to 0.32 million a year (2024 to 2025) against USD 29.9 million from China (2025) | Small, slow growth; ingredients from China | [@EXP-08; @EXP-09; @XBA-28] {general\|Medium} {dx:revealed} |
| Asia-Pacific | All plant-based retail USD 9.2 billion (2025), about 88% of it dairy alternatives (our derivation) | Plant milk dominated | [@EXP-01; @EXP-10] {general\|Medium} {dx:inferred} |

Growth in rich markets is in plain, cheap, versatile formats: tofu, tempeh and seitan grew by almost 30% in Germany and the Netherlands in 2025, US "chunks, shreds and strips" grew in units while the category fell, and private label drives European volume [@EXP-05; @EXP-01] {general|High} {dx:revealed}. Brands are moving the same way: Singapore's TiNDLE switched to private label only from 2026 and plans to sell its US business, its former chief executive and co-founder saying there is "no real underlying consumer demand to shift away from meat" [@AIS-28; @AIS-29] {general|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

Retailer protein targets do not change this. Where they bite, retailers meet them with what is cheapest and closest: pulses, price parity and hybrids made in Europe, such as Albert Heijn's 15 hybrid products with field bean protein and Lidl's 60/40 beef and pea mince [@XBA-01; @XBA-02] {general|High} {dx:revealed}. Their direct food suppliers are European: Lidl's list of about 750 food suppliers for 2025 deliveries has none in East, South or Southeast Asia, and Asian foods reach it through European importers and traders [@XBA-07] {general|High} {dx:revealed}. So the targets are not a pull for Asian-made analogues, and a Vietnamese co-packer reaches a European discounter through an importer or brand owner that holds the contract (our reading) {general|Medium} {dx:inferred}. That is the segment a low-cost, tariff-free Asian contract manufacturer could serve. We found no verified case of a Western plant-based brand manufacturing in Vietnam, and no revealed sales data for China, Singapore, Australia or the Gulf [[app-r1-open-questions]].

## 17.3 Access: Vietnam's tariff edge, and four barriers

**The tariff edge.** Vietnamese textured protein, food preparations, plant drinks, soy sauce, stuffed pasta and prepared nuts enter the EU at 0% under the EU and Vietnam free trade agreement, against EU most-favoured-nation rates of 12.8% on textured protein, 9% plus an agricultural component on food preparations, 9.6% on plant drinks (duty-free for Vietnam since 1 January 2025) and 7 to 10.2% on prepared nuts, which Thai and Chinese goods pay [@EXP-23] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. The UK gives the same preference [@EXP-24] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Japan admits Vietnamese textured vegetable protein free, against 10.6% for most countries and 6.6% for Chinese goods [@EXP-41] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The EU and Thailand are still negotiating; the EU and Indonesia agreement was finalised in September 2025 but is not in force [@EXP-47; @EXP-48] {general|High}. {{kn:kn-eu-tariff-edge}}

The edge is largest on wrapped foods, where Vietnam already sells. Vietnamese dumplings and other stuffed pasta enter the EU at 0% against 8.3% plus EUR 6.10 (cooked) or EUR 17.10 (uncooked) per 100 kg, and Canada free against 11%. Japan charges Vietnamese stuffed pasta 3.9% under CPTPP in fiscal 2026 against 21.3% for China and Thailand, which have no concession: a 17.4-point edge on a line where Vietnam sold USD 15.5 million in 2025 [@ORG-02; @ORG-05; @ORG-07; @XBA-28] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. The UK charges 0% under both its Vietnam agreement and CPTPP [@ORG-03] {VN-direct|High}.

{{chart:chart-tariff-edge}}

**Barrier 1: the United States.** Since 24 July 2026 the US has charged an extra 12.5% Section 301 tariff on Vietnamese goods, against 10% for Malaysia, Indonesia and India and 12.5% for Thailand; cashews and coconuts are exempt, prepared plant-based foods are not [@EXP-22] {VN-direct|High}. The US is also the largest buyer of Vietnamese stuffed pasta (USD 48.1 million in 2025, up 71% on 2024), and that growth is now exposed to the surcharge [@XBA-28] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. With US plant-based meat sales falling, this argues against US-first plant-based exports. {{kn:kn-us-301-tariff}}

**Barrier 2: labels.** Since 19 August 2026 the EU restricts 32 meat terms on plant-based foods, including "meat", "chicken", "pork", "beef", "bacon" and "steak"; "burger", "sausage" and "nuggets" remain allowed for now, with a committee vote due in December 2026 [@EXP-25] {general|Medium}. Dairy names such as "milk" and "cheese" are reserved for milk products, and a 2017 court ruling confirmed that this applies to plant-based foods [@EXP-26] {general|Medium}. Export packs need descriptive names ("soy protein strips", "shiitake dumplings").

**Barrier 3: novel-food approvals abroad.** A Vietnamese product made from soy, gluten, cashew, coconut, rice, mushrooms or jackfruit needs no pre-market approval in the EU or Singapore; a new fungal strain, a precision-fermented protein or cultivated meat does [@EXP-46; @EXP-34] {general|High}. Because Vietnam has no new-food route of its own ([[ch07-rules]]), a Vietnamese novel-protein exporter would file its first dossier abroad. The US proposed tighter oversight of substances claimed to be GRAS on 10 August 2026 [@EXP-45] {general|High}.

**Barrier 4: rules of origin.** The zero rate depends on the recipe. We read the origin protocol of the EU agreement; its rules match the UK and Vietnam text on the chapter 19 rule and the tolerance article [@ORG-01; @XBA-30] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. For dumplings, buns and other chapter 19 foods the binding item is the wrapper: non-originating flour, starch or rice may make up at most 20% of product weight, the general tolerance cannot lift that cap, and flour milled in Vietnam from imported wheat is non-originating. Vietnamese rice flour and cassava starch are originating. Imported textured soy is not limited in dumplings. In *chay* (vegetarian) food preparations under heading 2106 it may make up 10% of product weight or, on our reading of the text, 10% of the ex-works price; soy isolate and wheat gluten are not limited [@ORG-01] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. CPTPP asks only for a change of chapter for stuffed pasta, so for the UK, Japan and Canada the recipe does not bind; RCEP sets the same rule for Japan [@XBA-30; @ORG-06] {VN-direct|High}. Meat is the other limit: Vietnam is not on the EU list of countries allowed to ship meat products (as adopted in 2021), and meat-filled stuffed pasta is not yet duty-free (EUR 6.787 per 100 kg in 2026, against EUR 54.30). EU-bound Vietnamese wrapped foods are therefore seafood-filled or plant-filled, and a plant-protein filling is the practical EU substitute for pork [@ORG-10; @ORG-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. The rules give domestic textured soy no export customer: a dumpling keeps its origin whatever soy it uses, and a *chay* preparation can meet the 2106 rule with isolate or gluten (our reading) {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

The EU deforestation regulation applies to soy from 30 December 2026 for large and medium operators; our reading is that Vietnamese plant-based foods made from imported soy protein fall outside it unless exported as soybeans, soy flour, oil or cake, which should be confirmed [@EXP-27; @EXP-28] {general|Low} {dx:inferred}. Fish and crustaceans are not covered commodities, so the regulation does not reach Vietnamese shrimp and pangasius exports through their feed; it reaches them only through retailer and certification rules (our reading) [@EXP-27] {general|Low} {dx:inferred}.

## 17.4 The diaspora channel: real, small, *chay*

About 2.3 million people of Vietnamese origin lived in the US in 2023, and 326,630 Vietnam-born people in Australia in 2025 [@EXP-35; @EXP-36] {general|High}. On 24 September 2026 a US Asian online grocer listed Vietnam-made vegetarian net spring rolls, vegan lemongrass "chicken" jerky, vegetarian soups, bao buns, oyster sauce, noodles, fermented tofu and pho broth bases at USD 3.50 to 13 a pack; none was marketed on protein, and US diaspora firms also make chay bases locally [@EXP-37] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Protein-rich chay already travels through Asian grocers: dry soy pieces at 48 to 61 g of protein per 100 g, made from imported soy isolate, and analogues at 40 to 42 g are recorded under Vietnamese brands in France, Germany, Spain, Norway and Colombia [@XBA-26; @XBA-27] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. Noodle and pasta exports (HS 1902.30) going to the US, Germany and Poland are consistent with a diaspora channel [@EXP-39] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. This channel could take protein-upgraded chay products at similar prices with frozen logistics in place; the gap is protein in frozen formats, not in dry pieces. It will not justify a novel-protein plant on its own {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

## 17.5 The pull that matters most for the frontier: feed

The most frontier-relevant export demand is indirect, through what seafood buyers require of feed. Read in full, the standards are neutral for microbial protein; the revealed pull is domestic.

- **Standards.** The Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) Feed Standard v1.2 has been mandatory since 2 February 2026. Certified mills must commit to deforestation- and conversion-free soy and palm (cutoff no later than 31 December 2020), buy eligible soy and palm at least equal to the volume in the ASC feed they sell (medium-risk ingredients may count as non-eligible until 2 February 2029), improve marine-ingredient sourcing over time, and report greenhouse gas emissions per tonne of feed, with no target [@FBA-01; @EXP-30] {general|High}. Feed stuffs need due diligence only on the ingredient maker, and any ingredient under 1% of a mill's yearly aquafeed intake counts as eligible automatically, without credit. BAP's feed mill standard credits ingredients from "algae and other aquatic microorganisms" towards its marine target; GLOBALG.A.P. says nothing about novel ingredients [@FBA-05; @FBA-06] {general|Medium}. On 25 September 2026 the ASC register listed 15 certified Vietnamese feed mills, the most of any country (15 of 114), and 6 more in initial audit [@FBA-04] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. From 1 May 2028 all ASC farm audits require compound feed from an ASC-certified mill [@FBA-02; @FBA-03] {general|Medium}. Vietnam is the largest producer of ASC-certified pangasius and third for ASC-certified shrimp [@EXP-32] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **Retailers.** UK supermarkets including Tesco, Sainsbury's, Aldi and Lidl, and seafood firms, committed to deforestation- and conversion-free soy, including soy embedded in products, by the end of 2025 [@EXP-33] {general|High} {dx:revealed}.
- **Revealed buying.** Vietnamese mills already buy microbial feed ingredients, though trade codes do not separate feed from food. Partner countries recorded 9,193 t of inactive yeast and other dead single-cell organisms (HS 2102.20) shipped to Vietnam in 2025, 2.4 times the 2019 tonnage, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg and mainly from China and Brazil; Vietnam also exported 8,166 t at USD 1.39 per kg [@FBA-17; @FBA-19] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. One export-facing pangasius group contracted at least 15,000 t of insect protein for feed over 2025 to 2027, which we cite as an incumbent benchmark [@EXP-50] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. We found no published purchase of bacterial, fungal or other microbial protein by a named Vietnamese mill, and Nutreco, a global aquafeed leader, reached 0.6% novel ingredients by volume in 2025 against a target of 5 to 10% [@FBA-13; @FBA-07] {VN-adjacent|High} {dx:revealed}.
- **The limit.** None of the buyer rules we found requires or rewards yeast, fungal or bacterial biomass (BAP's credit is for algae and other aquatic microorganisms), and we found no buyer that pays a documented premium for seafood raised on novel feed [@FBA-01; @FBA-05] {general|Medium} {dx:revealed}. And the buyer mix is shifting: in January to August 2026, seafood exports to China and Hong Kong rose 33% while those to the EU fell 1.6% [@EXP-31] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}, so the standards-driven pull is concentrated in a shrinking share of sales.

{{kn:kn-feed-yeast-imports}}

This changes how Part III reads the feed plays of the supply study (T2, T3; [[ch26-plays]]). The export standards are a compliance hurdle that any feed ingredient must clear, not a pull for microbial protein; the deadline that will bite is the ASC farm transition of May 2028, after which certified mills will ask every ingredient maker for due-diligence data. T2's demand is domestic and priced low: a Vietnamese microbial ingredient must match imported bulk yeast at about USD 1.1 per kg, or show in head-to-head trials a gain worth about 1.2 to 1.8% of shrimp-feed cost (our calculation) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]] carries the kill test.

## 17.6 Competitors and what would make Vietnam a preferred supplier

China dominates exports of protein concentrates and textured protein (HS 2106.10) and approved its first mycoprotein in 2025; Thailand has private-label plant-based exporters and a future-food roadmap but no EU agreement in force; Malaysia has a halal system and a lower US tariff [@EXP-40; @EXP-12; @EXP-13; @EXP-11; @EXP-52; @EXP-22; @EXP-47] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {dx:revealed}. In Japan, Fuji Oil supplies textured soy from its own plant in Japan [@XBA-18] {general|High} {dx:revealed}. CJ, a foreign owner of Vietnamese wrapped-food export capacity, opened its Kizuna dumpling plant in Tay Ninh (former Long An) in 2022 to supply Japan, the EU and Australia, and in 2024 planned to make its dumplings for Europe in Hungary from the second half of 2026 [@XBA-20; @XBA-23] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. Our synthesis of what would make Vietnam a preferred supplier {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}:

- **For EU and UK buyers, through importers and brand owners:** zero tariffs (6 to 13 points over Thailand and China), origin-compliant wrappers, seafood-grade food safety with IFS Food or BRCGS certification, frozen logistics already used by seafood exporters, and a plant-protein version of a wrapped food these buyers already take from Vietnam. The first buyers are European importers of Asian frozen foods and brand owners already making wrapped foods in Vietnam, not the retailers themselves [@EXP-23; @EXP-24; @XBA-04; @XBA-11; @XBA-07; @XBA-20; @XBA-25] {general|Medium} {dx:inferred}.
- **For Japanese buyers of wrapped foods:** the 17.4-point CPTPP edge on dumplings, with no recipe condition beyond a change of chapter. Who in Japan buys Vietnamese dumplings, and whether they would take a plant-protein version, is not known.
- **For Japanese and Korean ingredient buyers (weakly evidenced):** despite a 6.6-point edge over China in Japan, textured protein from Vietnam sold under USD 0.35 million a year in each market in 2024 to 2025, the leading Japanese maker is expanding at home and a leading finished brand discontinued several products in 2025 [@XBA-28; @XBA-18; @XBA-17; @EXP-41] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Keep this route only for a specified fungal or fermented protein with a named buyer; drop plain textured soy.
- **For seafood buyers and their feed mills:** a domestic microbial ingredient priced against commodity yeast, with the traceability data ASC mills will ask every supplier for from 2028.
- **Against:** the US tariff, no domestic protein-ingredient base, no novel-food approvals abroad, reliance on imported soy and gluten for every high-protein local product, European tier 1 supplier lists, and CJ's move of EU supply to Hungary.

## 17.7 What this means for the frontier

**For each reader.**
- **Startups:** the best-evidenced first export product is a vegetable or plant-protein version of a dumpling, bun or rice-paper roll that a buyer already takes from Vietnam, sold through European importers of Asian foods or brand owners that already make wrapped foods in Vietnam, and named without restricted meat or dairy terms. Protein-upgraded chay for the diaspora is second; the gap there is protein in frozen formats. Functional plant or fungal protein for Japanese and Korean manufacturers is weakly evidenced and needs a named buyer and specification first. Plant-based seafood for export remains the weakest bet on current evidence.
- **Investors:** export demand justifies co-packing capacity with IFS Food or BRCGS certification more than a greenfield brand. Price the US tariff and CJ's near-shoring to Hungary explicitly, prefer buyers without EU plants, and budget for foreign approvals for any novel ingredient. Export origin rules give a domestic textured-soy plant (T1) no customer.
- **Manufacturers:** IFS Food or BRCGS is the entry ticket: Lidl requires IFS or BRC with annual audits, and 74.8% of Carrefour's supplier sites in France were certified to IFS, BRC or FSSC 22000 in 2025. FSSC 22000 alone is not what Lidl names [@XBA-04; @XBA-11] {general|High} {dx:revealed}. For EU-bound wrapped foods, check the flour share of the wrapper and use Vietnamese rice flour or cassava starch where needed; ship to the UK, Japan and Canada under CPTPP. Cashew and seafood processors already own the buyers and cold chain an export plant-based or hybrid line needs. Feed mills supplying ASC farms will need certified status by May 2028 and should ask any microbial ingredient supplier for head-to-head trials against the yeast they already buy, priced per unit of performance.
- **Research bodies:** for feed, the export-relevant test is a head-to-head trial against commodity yeast plus the traceability and per-tonne carbon data ASC mills must report, not growth performance alone. For wrapped foods, cost a compliant rice-flour or cassava-starch wrapper against wheat.
- **Policy makers:** protect and use the EU, UK and Japanese preferences (6 to 13 points on plant-based lines and 17.4 points on dumplings in Japan). Publish an origin note for wrapped-food exporters on the EU 20% flour and starch cap and on the 10% tolerance by weight or value; imported soy protein is not the main constraint. Build a new-food route that mirrors EU and Singapore evidence requirements so that one dossier serves several markets, and support ASC-ready feed traceability before the 2028 farm deadline.
- **International organisations and funders:** replace a buyer survey with quote requests: one vegetable and one plant-protein wrapped SKU priced by three EU importers of Asian frozen foods and two brand owners already sourcing wrapped foods from Vietnam, with their certification and origin requirements. Retailer targets need no survey: they are published. Fund a first EU or Singapore dossier for a Vietnamese fungal or single-cell protein, and a feed carbon benchmark for Vietnamese shrimp and pangasius feed.

**Related:** [[app-d6-export]], [[ch03-regional]], [[app-s6-feed-market]], [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]].

data.title: How much demand? Seven routes to 2050
data.summary: Instead of a market-size number, we size seven routes by which domestic or novel protein could reach buyers, in three labelled scenarios. On a benchmark path they create demand for about 19,000 t of protein a year by 2035, mostly by replacing imported ingredients, but displace only about 2,350 t of meat protein (0.2%).
data.body:
# 18. How much demand? Seven routes to 2050

**In one paragraph.** We do not give a market-size number for Vietnamese alternative protein. Published figures have no traceable method, and global forecasts made in 2019 to 2021 overshot by one to two orders of magnitude. Instead, a small reproducible model (`tools/demand_model.py`) sizes seven routes by which domestic or novel protein could reach Vietnamese plates and foreign buyers, in three labelled scenarios, and separates the protein a route delivers from the meat protein it displaces. On a benchmark path anchored on what has happened elsewhere, the routes create demand for about 19,000 t of protein a year by 2035, mostly by replacing imported textured soy and gluten in foods Vietnam already makes. Only part of it would be made in Vietnam: about 11,000 to 17,000 t, depending on how large the import pool really is and how much of the hybrid, canteen and plant-milk protein a domestic maker wins. For soy extrusion, that supports about one line of 1 t per hour by 2035. The routes displace only about 2,350 t of meat protein, 0.2% of the total. In the units funders count, that spares about 2.4 to 2.7 million animals a year, 93 to 94% of them chickens and ducks, and avoids about 0.14 Mt CO2e; import substitution, the largest route, spares none. A stretch path, which assumes conditions not yet seen anywhere, displaces 0.7% by 2035 and 1.5% by 2050, against the 3% and 10% the Part IV S-ALT scenario assumes. Reaching S-ALT's modest 2030 level through hybrids alone would take three-quarters of all processed meat; through consumer analogues, more regular buyers than Vietnam has people. Existing chay days already avoid about 25,000 t of meat protein a year. The food side of S-ALT is exploratory; the demand that exists is for ingredients.

> **Scenarios, not forecasts.** Every value after 2025 in this chapter is our estimate from stated assumptions {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate} {dx:inferred}. Most assumptions have no Vietnamese measurement behind them (how many people keep chay days, how much meat goes into processed products, how much protein a canteen meal holds); each is listed with its basis in `demand_assumptions.csv` and [[app-d8-demand-model]]. The model uses the population and meat demand of the Part IV S-BASE scenario, so its numbers sit on the same basis as [[ch22-protein-balance-2050]].

---

## 18.1 Why not a market-size number

- **Vietnamese market sizes are untraceable.** "VND 1,000 billion", "USD 500 million" and "USD 103 to 112 million" for plant-based or vegetarian food carry no visible method and conflict with shelf and launch evidence; the supply study and every Part III stream rejected them [@ECO-17; @ECO-18; @CHY-13; @CHY-18] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}.
- **Global forecasts overshot.** Kearney forecast in 2019 that novel plant-based meat would be 10% of a USD 1,200 billion meat market in 2025; global retail sales were about USD 6.6 billion in 2025, about 0.55% (our comparison). Barclays' USD 140 billion by 2029 would need about 115% growth a year from 2025. BCG and Blue Horizon's plant-based price parity "by 2023" was not met at category level [@GLB-45; @GLB-44; @GLB-42; @GLB-05] {general|Medium} {dx:inferred}. Forecasts made at the 2019 to 2021 peak extrapolated launch-year growth, and several came from parties with an interest ([[app-d7-global-benchmarks]]). {{kn:kn-forecast-overshoot}}

{{chart:chart-forecast-vs-actual}}

So we size routes, not markets, and we label every result.

## 18.2 Seven routes and three scenarios

| Route | What it is | How it is sized | Displaces meat? |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 Ingredient import substitution | Domestic or novel protein replacing imported textured soy, soy concentrate and gluten bought by chay makers, meat processors and other food makers | Food share of 2025 plant-protein imports (about 40,000 t of product, about 26,000 t of protein; monthly trade points nearer 35,000 t), growing 4 to 8% a year; domestic share by scenario | No: replaces imports |
| R2 Chay occasions | Upgraded protein on existing chay days, plus any added chay days | 30% of people keeping 2.5 chay days a month (assumption); 20 g of protein per upgraded chay day; added days only in two scenarios | Only added days, net of 30% compensation |
| R3 Hybrid processed meat | Plant or fungal protein replacing part of the meat in *giò* and *chả* (pork rolls and loaves), sausages and fillings | 5% of meat eaten as processed products (assumption); adoption and replacement share by scenario; plant protein of any origin | Yes, 0.9 per unit replaced |
| R4 Institutional meals | Plant or novel protein in factory canteens and school lunches | 1.0 billion canteen and 0.8 billion school meals a year; 20 g of protein per protein dish (assumptions); adoption by scenario | Yes, 0.8 per unit (meal level); school protein sold into the plant slot would replace tofu, not meat |
| R5 Household modern analogues | Analogues bought by urban households | Regular (monthly) buyers as a share of urban residents; 3 kg a year each at 15% protein | Little: 0.2 per unit |
| R6 High-protein plant milks | Protein isolates added to plant milks | Plant milk volume (about 300 million litres in 2025) times high-protein share times 30 g per litre | No (dairy, if anything) |
| R7 Exports | Products or ingredients made in Vietnam and sold abroad | Tonnes by scenario at 25% protein (no revealed base for the ingredient part) | No (not in Vietnam) |

Displacement factors follow the evidence of [[ch13-consumers]] and [[app-d7-global-benchmarks]]: blends and canteen swaps remove meat by construction, while consumer analogues have not measurably displaced meat anywhere [@GLB-19; @GLB-17; @GLB-35; @GLB-39] {general|Medium} {dx:inferred}. A 2026 analysis of 1.2 million restaurant transactions in the US, Canada and Australia found "essentially no evidence" that modern alternative proteins reduced meat purchases [@AFN-07] {general|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

**What the route bases rest on.** We tested the bases of four routes against revealed evidence ([[app-m4-actor-check-waves]]). No model value changed; the readings below qualify them.

- **R2 chay days.** No probability survey asks about *chay* (vegetarian eating on lunar days), but the national Diet Quality Questionnaire asks about diet: in late 2021, 7.9% (5.3 to 11.0%) of adults ate no meat, poultry or fish on the previous day. That caps chay-day person-days. The central assumption (2.5% of person-days) uses about a third of the ceiling; the top of the range in [[ch12-chay-baseline]] would need nearly every flesh-free day to be a chay day [@APR-36; @BRD-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **R3 hybrids.** Cost does not limit this route: extending pork products with soy saves 14 to 16% of raw-material cost at 20% replacement, at every annual hog price from 2019 to 2024 (our calculation) [@DIE-25; @TIC-12; @BUY-05] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Adoption is limited by product identity, sensory ceilings (about 10 to 20% of the meat in fine emulsions, 30% in coarse mince) and trust. No Vietnamese brand sells a declared meat and plant-protein blend, buyers read hidden extension (*độn*, filler) as cheating, and 2026 is a processed-meat trust crisis [@HXE-04; @HXE-09; @TRU-22; @TRU-07] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. So the benchmark's 6% of processed meat by 2035 fits extension inside industrial *xúc xích* (sausages) and fillings under ingredient names, while the stretch path's 15% needs a positive frame for declared blends, not price parity. National diet surveillance cannot test the 5% processed share: its processed-meat item, eaten by 18.1% of adults on a given day, leaves out *giò* and *chả* [@APR-36; @BRD-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **R4 canteens and schools.** Five caterers' published menus lead with pork (33% of protein dishes), fish (26%) and chicken (13%); tofu appears in 9% (plant-only 3%), and none names textured soy [@UPL-27; @UPL-28; @UPL-29; @UPL-30; @UPL-32] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. School caterers' portions support the 20 g of protein per dish [@PMR-24; @PMR-26] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. For schools, the old basis (Decision 1340's animal-protein target, which ended in 2020) no longer holds [@CHN-33] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. MOH Decision 3958/QĐ-BYT (December 2025) sets no animal share and asks for plant protein (legumes, tofu) at least twice a week; audited menus meet that rule in only 9 of 48 school-weeks and fill the plant slot with tofu beside meat (our audit of [@PMR-10] to [@PMR-31], `school_menu_weeks.csv`) [@AIB-39; @PMR-10; @PMR-26] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. A plant ingredient sold into that slot replaces tofu; only a labelled blend in minced-meat and fish-cake dishes, served on 28.5% of audited days, removes meat. And D-BENCH's canteen share implies 36.6 million canteen meal-equivalents a year by 2035, about 37 times the meals Sinergia Animal's partner institutions expected to replace in three countries in 2023 and 16 times Humane World's 2025 commitments outside the US (2.3 million meals a year in seven countries) [@AFN-26; @AFN-23]; only caterers' own commercial use could reach it ([[app-d7-global-benchmarks]]) {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate} {dx:inferred}.
- **R7 exports.** The 25% protein share assumes that about 60% of exports are ingredients. Vietnam's textured-protein exports to the EU, the UK, Japan, Korea and Australia were 0 to 73 t each in 2024 to 2025, and the Vietnam-made wrapped plant foods found abroad carry 3.6 to 6.2 g of protein per 100 g [@XBA-28; @XBA-26; @ORG-12] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. At 5 to 12% protein, R7 would deliver 0.5 to 1.2 kt in 2035, not 2.5 kt (our calculation) {fx:estimate}. The export evidence is in [[ch17-export-demand]].

**The three scenarios** {fx:estimate}:
- **D-DRIFT, incumbent drift.** Novel protein stays a small import-substitution business; no hybrids to speak of; analogues remain a niche.
- **D-BENCH, benchmark path.** Each route grows to levels anchored on analogues observed elsewhere, scaled to Vietnam's channels and price gap: for example 25% of the ingredient pool supplied domestically by 2035, 6% of processed meat sold as hybrids, 3% of canteen protein, 2% of urban residents buying analogues monthly (against a Western ceiling of about 9 to 10% of households).
- **D-STRETCH, stretch.** Conditions not yet observed anywhere: per-serving price parity in local formats, hybrids in 15% of processed meat by 2035 and 35% by 2050 (which needs openly declared blends to be accepted, since extension already pays), canteen protein defaults, and chay keepers adding half a day a month by 2035 and one day by 2050.

## 18.3 What the routes deliver

| kt of protein a year | 2030 | 2035 | 2050 |
|---|---|---|---|
| D-DRIFT, delivered | 1.3 | 3.2 | 10.7 |
| D-BENCH, delivered | 5.9 | 19.1 | 66.7 |
| D-STRETCH, delivered | 14.1 | 45.6 | 171.5 |
| of which R1 import substitution (D-BENCH) | 3.5 | 11.6 | 44.6 |
| of which R7 exports (D-BENCH) | 0.8 | 2.5 | 7.5 |
| For comparison: Part IV S-ALT, food protein replacing meat | 11.8 | 39.3 | 144.6 |
| For comparison: Part IV S-ALT, microbial protein in feed | 55.8 | 160.2 | 514.1 |

All rows are our estimates on the S-BASE population (UN WPP [@GT-12]) and meat demand of Part IV, which follows the OECD-FAO outlook to 2035 [@QNT-01] {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate} {dx:inferred}.

{{chart:chart-demand-routes}}

Three readings follow {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate} {dx:inferred}:

1. **Ingredient import substitution is most of the demand.** In D-BENCH, R1 is about 60% of delivered protein in 2035 and two-thirds in 2050. The pool it draws on, food-grade plant-protein ingredients now imported mostly from China, is revealed demand today ([[ch16-business-buyers]]). Monthly trade suggests the food part of that pool is nearer 35,000 t of product than 40,000 t, because much of the post-2023 jump in HS 3504 imports is priced like feed protein and shows no *chay* season; at 35,000 t, R1 in 2035 is about 10,200 t of protein, not 11,600 t (our calculation) [@BRD-05; @BRD-06; @BUY-02] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.
2. **The food volumes are real but modest, and only part of them is textured soy.** At about USD 3 per kg of protein, D-BENCH is an ingredient business of roughly USD 57 million a year by 2035 and USD 200 million by 2050. The model converts all R1 to R4 ingredient output into textured-line equivalents (about 3.5 lines of 1 t per hour by 2035, 12 by 2050), but most of the R1 pool is gluten and isolates, which need wet-milling or isolate plants. For soy extrusion, 25% of a textured-type import pool of about 23,000 t in 2035 is about 5,700 t: one 1 t per hour line or two 0.5 t per hour lines, not three to four (our calculation) [@BUY-02; @TIC-12]. That supports a few specialised ingredient plants, as in play T1 ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]), not a consumer-led boom.
3. **Feed is the bigger protein market.** Part IV's S-ALT scenario puts microbial protein in feed at about four times its food volumes ([[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]). Nothing in the demand evidence changes the supply study's conclusion that feed leads food; Vietnam already imports about 9,200 t of inactive yeast a year for food and feed together ([[ch17-export-demand]]).

### How much of it is made in Vietnam

The 19,000 t headline counts protein the routes deliver, not protein made in Vietnam. Only R1 applies an explicit domestic share (25% of the pool by 2035 on D-BENCH). R2 to R6 count all plant or novel protein used in those routes, and much of it would be imported soy or pea unless a domestic maker wins the business: Chinese, ASEAN and Korean textured protein, isolates and gluten enter Vietnam duty-free [@FTR-32] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Hybrids are the clearest case, because processors would extend with soy they already import: at R1's 25% domestic share, the domestic part of R3 in 2035 is about 0.20 of 0.79 kt. R7 counts protein exported, not eaten in Vietnam.

| D-BENCH, 2035, kt of protein | Model reading | Strict reading |
|---|---|---|
| R1 import substitution | 11.6 (pool of 40,000 t of product) | 10.2 (pool of 35,000 t) |
| R2 to R6 (chay, hybrids, meals, analogues, plant milks) | 4.9 (protein of any origin) | 1.2 (25% domestic, as in R1) |
| Made in Vietnam for the home market | 16.55 | about 11.4 |
| R7 exports (made in Vietnam, sold abroad) | 2.5 (25% protein) | 0.5 to 1.2 (5 to 12% protein) |

So the benchmark path creates demand for about 19,000 t of protein a year by 2035, of which about 11,000 to 17,000 t would be made in Vietnam for the home market (our calculation) {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate} {dx:inferred}. The model's outputs are unchanged; this is a reading of them, and [[app-d8-demand-model]] (D8.3) shows the arithmetic.

## 18.4 What the routes displace, against S-ALT

| Meat protein displaced | 2030 | 2035 | 2050 |
|---|---|---|---|
| D-DRIFT | 0.1 kt (0.01%) | 0.2 kt (0.01%) | 0.5 kt (0.04%) |
| D-BENCH | 0.4 kt (0.04%) | 2.4 kt (0.18%) | 6.0 kt (0.41%) |
| D-STRETCH | 3.1 kt (0.27%) | 9.2 kt (0.71%) | 21.9 kt (1.52%) |
| Part IV S-ALT assumption | 11.8 kt (1%) | 39.3 kt (3%) | 144.6 kt (10%) |
| Existing chay days (already in the baseline) | about 29 kt (2.5%) | about 32 kt (2.5%) | about 36 kt (2.5%) |

All rows are our estimates {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-demand-bench-2035}}

{{chart:chart-displacement-vs-salt}}

In D-BENCH, the displacing routes are, in 2035, added chay days (about 0.9 kt), hybrids (0.7 kt) and canteens and schools (0.6 kt); consumer analogues contribute about 0.1 kt. The institutional figure includes about 0.06 kt from schools. School protein sold into the plant slot would replace tofu, not meat; counting it at zero lowers D-BENCH displacement in 2035 from 2.35 kt to about 2.29 kt, so "about 0.2%" stands (our calculation). Even in D-STRETCH the food routes reach about a quarter of S-ALT's 2035 assumption and about 15% of its 2050 assumption {fx:estimate}.

### The same routes in funder units

Welfare, climate and market-shaping funders do not count tonnes of meat protein. We converted the displaced protein into animals spared (carcass weight per animal from FAOSTAT for Vietnam), net CO2e avoided (life-cycle intensities for East and Southeast Asia, minus the footprint of the replacing protein) and meal-equivalents (one 20 g protein dish supplied by plant or novel protein instead of meat) [@FUF-03; @FUF-04; @FUF-05; @FUF-07] {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate} {dx:inferred}. Method and factors are in [[app-d8-demand-model]] (D8.7).

| Displacing routes R2 to R5 | 2030 | 2035 | 2050 |
|---|---|---|---|
| D-BENCH, animals spared (million a year) | 0.34 to 0.39 | 2.4 to 2.7 | 6.0 to 6.8 |
