| **Asia's fermentation market** | Several countries build capacity, trade openly and rely on each other's approvals | Chinese scale and costs set the regional price of every fermentation product; others shrink to niches | [@HSC-11; @HSC-13; @HSC-14; @FTB-42; @ECF-29] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |

{{chart:chart-scenarios-2050}}

## 23.2 The four worlds

### A. Regional workshop (benign imports, open market)

- **Picture in 2050.** Imported soy and maize stay cheap on average. Several Asian countries run fermentation plants and trade under shared or mutually recognised approvals. Vietnam, with a working new-food route and open pilot plants, hosts contract fermentation for regional brands, sells functional feed ingredients for shrimp and pangasius and makes textured and fungal food ingredients. High-value precision-fermentation ingredients arrive after first-generation patents lapse in the mid-2030s [@FTB-21] {general|Low}. Bulk microbial feed protein stays small because soybean meal is cheap.
- **Protein balance.** Soybean-meal need of about 7.0 to 10.4 Mt, depending almost entirely on the efficiency programme; microbial protein about 1 to 2% of high-protein feed protein, mostly as functional ingredients {fx:estimate}.
- **Active hubs.** Ho Chi Minh City with Dong Nai; Tay Ninh (former Tay Ninh and Long An) sugar hub; the Mekong river belt ([[app-f5-targets-hubs]]).
- **Grows from:** 2035 Scenario 3, regulated regional hub ([[ch19-outlook-2035]]).
- **Signposts.** An ASEAN reliance or mutual-recognition mechanism for novel foods; Thai, Indian or Korean plants exporting across the region; fishmeal below USD 1,800 per t for a year; China's soybean imports below 100 Mt a year.

### B. Comfortable price-taker (benign imports, Chinese price dominance)

- **Picture in 2050.** Imported protein stays cheap and Chinese scale sets the price of every fermentation product. Vietnam imports soybean meal and Chinese yeast, bacterial and textured proteins. Domestic alternative protein stays at *chay* processing, tofu and a few feed-additive lines. Feed mills gain from cheap inputs, but the country stays exposed to any later shock.
- **Protein balance.** Soybean-meal need of about 10.4 to 11.7 Mt (trend to high-income demand); microbial protein 1% or less of high-protein feed protein, largely imported {fx:estimate}.
- **Active hubs.** Ho Chi Minh City with Dong Nai, at small scale.
- **Grows from:** 2035 Scenario 1, import price-taker.
- **Signposts.** Imports of yeasts and protein preparations from China growing above 20% a year for three years; three or more Chinese single-cell or mycoprotein plants above 20 kt a year by 2030; non-Chinese Asian pilot plants underused or closing.

### C. Security build-out (chronic stress, open market)

- **Picture in 2050.** Repeated fishmeal shortages, more frequent crop losses in exporting countries and shipping scares make imported protein dear and unreliable. Asian governments co-operate on approvals and invest in domestic protein. Vietnam builds residue-based feed protein on cassava, rice straw and brewery side streams, becomes a regional source of aquafeed functional ingredients and demonstrates protein from renewable power on the Mekong shrimp coast (Ca Mau and Vinh Long) from the early 2030s, scaling it after about 2040.
- **Protein balance.** Soybean-meal need of about 7.0 to 8.8 Mt, with efficiency and alternative protein adding up; microbial protein 4 to 8% of high-protein feed protein, a stretch above any analogue today ([[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]) {fx:estimate}.
- **Active hubs.** All six candidate hubs, including the Mekong shrimp coast.
- **Grows from:** 2035 Scenario 2, feed-first domestic build-out, then Scenario 3.
- **Signposts.** Fishmeal above USD 2,500 per t for 12 months; two extreme El Niño events within a decade; joint maize or soybean losses above 10% in two major exporters in one year; war-risk insurance suspended on a main shipping lane.

### D. Squeezed importer (chronic stress, Chinese price dominance)

- **Picture in 2050.** Imported protein is dear and unreliable, and Chinese producers, with scale and state backing, capture most of the regional market for microbial and fermented protein. Vietnam depends on China for both soy-competing and fishmeal-competing protein. Domestic production survives where local feedstock, freshness or species-specific function give an edge, or where the state treats capacity as strategic.
- **Protein balance.** Soybean-meal need of about 7.0 to 10.4 Mt, with efficiency carrying most of the reduction; domestic microbial protein 1 to 3% of high-protein feed protein, more imported {fx:estimate}.
- **Active hubs.** The Mekong river belt; Tay Ninh selling sugar; Ho Chi Minh City with Dong Nai at small scale.
- **Grows from:** 2035 Scenario 1 under stress, or Scenario 2 with state support.
- **Signposts.** The chronic-stress signposts of Scenario C together with the Chinese-dominance signposts of Scenario B; an export-dumping episode for microbial protein.

Full descriptions: `scenarios_2050.csv`. All 16 signposts, with thresholds, where to watch and their September 2026 status: `signposts_2050.csv` and [[app-f2-drivers-signals]].

## 23.3 Where the signposts point in September 2026

The evidence points both ways on both axes, which is why we assign no probabilities.
- **Import stress: short-term stress, long-term baseline benign.** The 2026 anchoveta season landed about a quarter of a quota that was already the lowest in a decade, and world fishmeal output fell 26% year on year in January to April 2026 [@HSC-29; @HSC-30] {general|Medium} {fx:signal}. NOAA gives over 90% odds of a very strong El Niño in winter 2026 to 2027 [@HSC-28] {general|High} {fx:projection} (published probability). The fishmeal-to-soy price ratio reached 6.2 in August 2026 [@GT-15] {general|High}. Yet the OECD-FAO baseline to 2035 expects ample soy [@GEO-37] {general|Medium} {fx:projection}.

{{kn:kn-anchoveta-2026}}

- **Fermentation market: Chinese scale growing, but not alone.** China added 11,000 t of yeast-protein capacity in 2025, and a 20,000 t mycoprotein plant is under construction [@HSC-13; @HSC-14] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {fx:signal}, while its flagship gas-fermentation plant halted [@FTG-06] {VN-adjacent|Medium}. Thailand, India and Korea now fund public pilot plants and food-tech plans [@FTB-42; @FTB-43; @FTB-17; @VIS-14] {VN-adjacent|Medium} {fx:signal}. US clearances went to Chinese and non-Chinese precision-fermentation firms alike in 2025 [@FTB-18; @FTB-19] {general|Medium}.

## 23.4 Wildcards that jump between worlds

Some wildcards would move Vietnam from one world to another within a year ([[app-f2-drivers-signals]], `wildcards.csv`).

| Wildcard | Moves towards | Horizon |
|---|---|---|
| Multi-year anchoveta collapse holding fishmeal above USD 2,500 per t {fx:wildcard} | C or D | 2027, recurring to 2050 |
| A closure of the South China Sea or Malacca Strait lasting months {fx:wildcard} | C or D | 2030 to 2050 |
| Chinese export dumping of microbial protein {fx:wildcard} | B or D | 2028 to 2035 |
| A sustained soy glut as China cuts soybean-meal use {fx:wildcard} | A or B | 2030 to 2040 |
| ASEAN mutual recognition of novel-food approvals {fx:wildcard} | A or C | 2030 to 2035 |
| A serious novel-food safety scandal in Asia {fx:wildcard} | B (food); feed less affected | any year |

Sources: [@HSC-28; @GEO-40; @HSC-13; @GEO-10; @REG-63] {general|Low}.

## 23.5 Stress-testing the ten plays and six public goods

We scored each play from [[ch26-plays]] in each world: 2 where it thrives, 1 where it holds with conditions, 0 where it struggles. The scores are our judgement from the evidence in chapters 20 to 22 {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate}.

| Play | A. Regional workshop | B. Comfortable price-taker | C. Security build-out | D. Squeezed importer | Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 Domestic textured plant protein | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | Robust |
| T2 Functional microbial feed ingredients | 2 | 1 | 2 | 1 | Robust |
| T3 Bulk microbial protein for fishmeal replacement | 0 | 0 | 2 | 1 | Bet |
| T4 Cassava starch to fermentation sugar hub | 2 | 1 | 2 | 1 | Robust |
| T5 Shared pilot and tolling fermentation | 2 | 1 | 2 | 1 | Robust |
| T6 Duckweed on aquaculture effluent | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | Robust |
| T7 High-value precision-fermentation ingredients | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0 | Bet |
| T8 Cultivated seafood research | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | Option |
| T9 Koji and fungal foods on side streams | 2 | 1 | 2 | 1 | Robust |
| T10 Mung bean and rice protein for drinks | 1 | 1 | 2 | 1 | Robust |
| P1 Proportionate new-food procedure | 2 | 1 | 2 | 1 | Robust |
| P2 Aquafeed raw-material clarity | 2 | 1 | 2 | 2 | Robust |
| P3 Public feed-trial capacity | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | No-regret |
| P4 Protein-quality laboratory | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | No-regret |
| P5 By-product atlas | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | Robust |
| P6 Open cost model and price series | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | No-regret |

Classes: no-regret (strong in all four); robust (at least viable in all four); bet (weak in at least one world but strong in another: needs signposts before scaling); option (weak in at least one world and strong in none: cheap to hold as research). Reasons for each score: `play_robustness.csv`.

{{chart:chart-play-robustness}}

{{kn:kn-no-regret-plays}}

**Readings.**
- **Public infrastructure is the safest investment.** Feed-trial capacity, a protein-quality laboratory and an open cost and price series pay off in every world, because they serve imports and domestic products alike and carry the efficiency lever that chapter 22 found strongest.
- **Most business plays are robust but not strong everywhere.** Seven of the ten hold in every world with conditions; none thrives in the Comfortable price-taker world.
- **Two plays are bets on one axis each.** Bulk fishmeal replacement (T3) needs chronic import stress; high-value precision fermentation (T7) needs an open regional market. Each should scale only when its signposts trip ([[ch28-robust-moves]]).
- **The Security build-out world is the only one where everything works.** Readiness matters more than prediction: plants, sites and finance prepared in the late 2020s can scale quickly if that world arrives, and cost little if it does not.


## 23.6 What this means

- **Investors:** underwrite plays that hold in all four worlds and thrive in two (T2, T4, T5, T6, T9). Hold bets on T3 and T7 as options with named triggers: for T3, fishmeal above USD 2,500 per t for 12 months and a pilot cost within 1.2 times fishmeal-protein parity; for T7, a new-food route, an ASEAN reliance mechanism or regional capacity outside China, and an anchor customer ([[ch28-robust-moves]]).
- **Policy makers:** the no-regret plays are all public goods and all cheap. Inside the same external world, a new-food route and open pilot capacity decide whether Vietnam gets World A's outcomes or ends up a price-taker, as in World B.
- **Startups:** species-specific function, local feedstocks and freshness are the edges that survive Chinese price dominance.
- **Manufacturers:** worlds C and D are the ones that hurt feed mills. Formulation flexibility, multi-origin sourcing and qualified alternative ingredients are the hedges.
- **Research and international bodies:** tracking the 16 signposts yearly, and publishing them, is a low-cost service to every actor.

**Related:** [[ch19-outlook-2035]] (2035 scenarios), [[ch20-drivers-2050]], [[ch28-robust-moves]], [[app-f2-drivers-signals]].

data.title: Vietnam 2050: a vision for a measured, efficient and diversified protein supply
data.summary: A normative vision, not a forecast, in which by 2050 Vietnam needs about 7 to 9 Mt of imported soybean meal rather than 10.4 Mt on trend, makes 4 to 8% of its high-protein feed protein from microbes, and holds a regional role in contract fermentation and aquafeed ingredients. Milestones are tied to the five-year plans from 2026 to 2050.
data.body:
# 24. Vietnam 2050: a vision for a measured, efficient and diversified protein supply

**In one paragraph.** Chapters 20 to 23 explore what might happen. This chapter says what could be aimed for. It sets out one normative vision for Vietnam's protein supply in 2050 and works backwards to milestones in each five-year plan. The vision is deliberately led by feed security and industry, the framing that has proved most durable abroad, rather than by diet change, which is outside this study's scope. It asks for five things: measure the protein balance; economise on imported protein through feed efficiency and formulation; diversify sources with microbial protein and non-marine omega-3; specialise in the regional niches where Vietnam has an edge; and decarbonise and climate-proof the new capacity. Every number is a range drawn from Vietnam's own 2050 plans, from the balance model and from what other countries have achieved. No country we checked has a protein plan that reaches 2050; this one would be unusually long-range, and it should be reviewed at each five-year plan.

> **Vision, not forecast.** Everything in this chapter tagged *vision* is a goal that AltProtein Vietnam puts forward for discussion, not a prediction and not an official target. The benchmark evidence behind each goal is cited and tagged as usual. The ranges come from [[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]; their fit with each 2050 world is tested in section 24.7.

---

## 24.1 Why a vision, and why this framing

- **Nobody has a protein plan to 2050.** Protein horizons abroad mostly stop at 2030 to 2035: the EU, Canada and Singapore at 2035, Japan's basic plan at FY2030, and China, Israel and the Netherlands at 2030. Japan's MIDORI strategy (2050) and Denmark's land deal (2045) reach further but carry no protein indicator [@VIS-15; @VIS-08; @VIS-25; @VIS-13; @GEO-10; @VIS-23; @VIS-05; @VIS-49; @VIS-03] {general|Medium}. The one exception we found is a Japanese food-tech investment roadmap to 2040, reported only in the press, with about JPY 1 trillion for novel foods [@VIS-14] {VN-adjacent|Low}.
- **Vietnam's official 2050 plans cover inputs, not protein.** Non-hydro renewables at 74 to 75% of power, 10 to 20 Mt of clean hydrogen a year, an agricultural emissions cap of 56 MtCO2e and net zero are all official 2050 numbers; no official meat, feed or protein number goes beyond 2030 [@GT-11; @NTS-25; @NTS-24; @CLM-01; @NTS-07] {VN-direct|High} {fx:projection} (official targets). A protein vision can anchor on those inputs.
- **Security and industry framing lead, with climate as a co-benefit.** The EU's July 2026 plan is titled for resilience and strategic autonomy; Japan and Korea state targets as food security; Singapore left alternative protein out of its food-security targets for cost and acceptance reasons [@VIS-15; @VIS-13; @VIS-29; @VIS-25] {general|Medium} {fx:signal}.
- **Plans without a statistic cannot be judged.** The Dutch protein strategy published no quantitative targets, we found no published progress report for Canada's roadmap and Denmark's action plan has no indicators; Japan, the EU and China are tracked even when they miss [@VIS-05; @VIS-08; @VIS-10; @VIS-01; @VIS-11; @VIS-12; @VIS-13; @VIS-15; @GEO-11] {general|Medium}.
- **Backcasting works only when embedded.** Reviews name follow-up and monitoring as the weak link; a Dutch novel-protein backcast in the 1990s seeded a research programme, yet the country's 2020 strategy still published no quantified targets for its solution tracks [@VIS-37; @VIS-38; @VIS-41; @VIS-05] {general|Medium}.

{{kn:kn-protein-plan-horizons}}

## 24.2 The vision

> **Vision, not forecast.** By 2050 Vietnam feeds a larger and richer population, and supplies the world's shrimp and pangasius buyers, from a protein system that is **measured, efficient, diversified, specialised and low-carbon**. It publishes its protein and feed balance every year. It needs 7.0 to 8.8 Mt (about 7 to 9 Mt) of imported soybean meal instead of the 10.4 Mt that trend growth implies. It makes 4 to 8% of its high-protein feed protein from microbes, grown on Vietnamese carbohydrate and residues and, increasingly, on clean power. It sources 15 to 50% of its aquafeed omega-3 from algal and oilseed oils. It is a recognised regional supplier of contract fermentation and aquafeed functional ingredients. And it has the statistics, rules and pilot capacity to change course as the world changes. {fx:vision}

## 24.3 Five pillars

| Pillar | What it means by 2050 | Headline indicator (2050) | Why it is credible | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Measure** | A yearly national protein and feed balance with soybean-meal inclusion and feed conversion by species; a domestic-origin share of feed protein tracked against a 2028 baseline {fx:vision} | Domestic-origin share 11 to 22 points above the 2028 baseline | 0.5 to 1 point a year from 2028, close to the EU's target pace of about 0.9; Japan's flat record as the downside | [@VIS-15; @VIS-12] {general\|Medium} |
| **Economise** | Feed efficiency and formulation hold imported protein near today's level per unit of output {fx:vision} | Soybean-meal need 7.0 to 8.8 Mt, against 10.4 on trend (balance model, [[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]) | China cut soybean-meal share 0.14 to 0.45 points a year (2017 to 2025, our calculation from official and USDA series); Norway cut marine share of salmon feed 2.6 points a year (1990 to 2013) | [@GEO-10; @GEO-11; @VIS-19] {general\|Medium} |
| **Diversify** | Microbial protein and non-marine omega-3 become normal feed ingredients {fx:vision} | Microbial feed protein 4 to 8% of high-protein feed protein; non-marine omega-3 15 to 50% of aquafeed EPA plus DHA | Norwegian salmon feed reached 0.4% novel ingredients by mass in 2020; the upper end is a stretch above any analogue; algal and oilseed oils are commercial | [@VIS-18; @VIS-20; @AQF-19; @AQF-23; @AQF-24] {general\|Medium} |
| **Specialise** | Regional niches where Vietnam has an edge: cassava fermentation sugar; aquafeed functional ingredients for shrimp and pangasius; tolling on existing tanks; cultivated seafood cells from Vietnamese species in the 2040s {fx:vision} | Named regional products and hubs | Existing MSG, lysine and yeast tanks; large shrimp and pangasius feed markets in one delta (Ca Mau, including former Bac Lieu, farmed about 595,000 t of shrimp in 2025) | [@IND-01; @HUB-15; @HUB-13; @IND-66] {VN-direct\|Low} |
| **Decarbonise and adapt** | New capacity built increasingly on residue carbon and clean power, on climate-proof sites; agriculture within its emissions cap {fx:vision} | Agriculture at or below 56 MtCO2e; every new alternative-protein plant shown lower-carbon than the protein it replaces, on a published method | Official 2050 cap and power plan; our carbon test in chapter 21 | [@CLM-01; @GT-11; @CLM-13] {VN-direct\|Medium} |

## 24.4 Vision indicators

| Indicator | 2030 | 2035 | 2040 | 2050 | Trend (for comparison) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Soybean-meal import need, Mt | 7.8 to 8.3 | 8.1 to 9.0 | 7.8 to 9.2 | 7.0 to 8.8 | 8.5 / 9.5 / 10.0 / 10.4 |
| Microbial (non-insect) feed protein, share of high-protein feed protein | about 1% (about 50 kt of protein) | 1 to 3% | 2 to 4% | 4 to 8% | near 0 |
| Domestic-origin share of feed protein, points above the 2028 baseline | baseline published | +3.5 to +7 | +6 to +12 | +11 to +22 | flat |
| Non-marine share of aquafeed omega-3 | first qualified oils in shrimp and marine-fish feeds | rising | rising | 15 to 50% | near 0 |
| Public protein and feed-innovation line, USD a year | 5 to 15 M | same or higher | review | review | about 6 M (feed scheme) |
| Open food-grade pilot fermentation capacity | 10,000 to 30,000 L | expand on demand | review | review | none |

Vision values: {fx:vision}; the trend column is our model estimate {fx:estimate}. Values are drawn from the balance model and the benchmarks in `protein_strategies_benchmark.csv` [@QNT-01; @VIS-15; @VIS-18; @VIS-01; @VIS-04; @NTS-23] {VN-direct|Low}. The 2050 microbial share at the top of its range matches the balance model's S-ALT scenario, which sits above every real-world analogue; it is a stretch, not a target to be judged on alone.

{{kn:kn-vision-sbm-2050}} {{kn:kn-vision-microbial-share-2050}} {{kn:kn-vision-omega3-2050}}

## 24.5 Working backwards: milestones by five-year plan

The milestones are tied to Vietnam's planning cycle, so that each socio-economic plan can adopt, adjust or drop them. Full list: `vision_milestones.csv` (22 milestones).

| Plan period | Milestones {fx:vision} | Benchmarks that make them plausible |
|---|---|---|
| **2026 to 2030** | First national protein and feed balance by 2028, then yearly. New-food procedure with statutory timelines and reliance on reference regulators; aquafeed entries for microbial biomass and algal oils (2027 to 2028). Fermentation and feed-protein sites named in the MAE biotechnology-cluster plan (due December 2026). A dedicated USD 5 to 15 M a year protein line. One open food-grade pilot plant of 10,000 to 30,000 L by 2030. Soybean-meal need at or below about 8.3 Mt and microbial feed protein about 1% in 2030. | EU balance-sheet guidance; Korea's published review time of about nine to 12 months ([[ch03-regional]]); Denmark, Germany and Canada budgets; ScaleUp Bio and EECi pilot plants; the December 2026 deadline for MAE's biotechnology clusters [@VIS-15; @VIS-01; @VIS-24; @VIS-06; @RGN-13; @RGN-36; @HUB-09; @NTS-37] {general\|Medium} |
| **2031 to 2035** | Successor livestock and fisheries strategies carry protein-balance targets for 2035 to 2040. Soybean-meal need 8.1 to 9.0 Mt against 9.5 on trend. Microbial feed protein 1 to 3%. Domestic-origin share 3.5 to 7 points above baseline. First full review of the vision against the scenario signposts (2035). | EU 2035 feed-protein target; JRC stress-test logic [@VIS-15; @VIS-35] {general\|Medium} |
| **2036 to 2040** | Soybean-meal need 7.8 to 9.2 Mt; microbial feed protein 2 to 4%. Residue carbon and clean power supply a growing share of new fermentation capacity: most of it only if cellulosic or one-carbon sugar works [@NGF-11] (without that, residues cover about 10 to 15% of the S-ALT sugar need in 2040). | Balance model ([[ch22-protein-balance-2050]], [[app-f4-balance-model]]); the chapter 21 windows {VN-direct\|Low} |
| **2041 to 2045** | Aligned with the official 2045 goals, which are official targets rather than part of our vision {fx:projection}: biotechnology at 10 to 15% of GDP (Resolution 36) and developed, high-income status (Resolution 109/NQ-CP). Cellulosic or one-carbon sugar at modest scale if an Asian plant has proved the technology. If the five conditions of chapter 21 align, the first commercial protein-from-power plant on the Mekong shrimp coast. | Official 2045 goals; the chapter 21 windows and conditions [@NTS-01; @NTS-28; @NGF-11; @FTG-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| **2046 to 2050** | Soybean-meal need 7.0 to 8.8 Mt against 10.4 on trend; microbial feed protein 4 to 8%; non-marine oils supply 15 to 50% of aquafeed omega-3; domestic-origin share 11 to 22 points above baseline; agriculture within its 56 MtCO2e cap. | Balance model ([[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]); China and Norway analogues; official cap [@GEO-10; @GEO-11; @VIS-19; @CLM-01] {VN-direct\|Low} |

{{chart:chart-vision-backcast}}

## 24.6 The map in 2050

The vision has a geography. Six candidate hubs open at different times ([[app-f5-targets-hubs]], `candidate_hubs.csv`) {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate}:
- **Ho Chi Minh City with Dong Nai:** pilot plants, tolling and food-grade fermentation, now to 2035; in our assessment the only hub where most assets already operate, including Vedan's and Ajinomoto's fermentation plants in Dong Nai and Saigon Hi-Tech Park [@IND-01; @IND-04; @IND-08; @IND-57] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **The Mekong river belt (Dong Thap, Can Tho, An Giang):** feed ingredients and side streams from pangasius and rice, 2027 to 2035 [@HUB-13; @HUB-14; @HUB-28] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Tay Ninh (former Long An and Tay Ninh):** fermentation sugar from cassava, 2028 to 2040, with the lowest industrial-park occupancy in the south (60.9% in the second quarter of 2026) and a large land bank, but not enough roots to carry a national sugar route alone [@FS-03; @COST-21] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **The Mekong shrimp coast (Ca Mau, Vinh Long):** aquafeed plus hydrogen, demonstration 2032 to 2035 and scale 2040 to 2045, on raised sites that use surface water [@HUB-15; @HUB-05; @CLM-14] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **The north (Hanoi Biotechnology High-Tech Zone, Bac Tu Liem):** research now; industry in the 2040s (our judgement) [@HUB-19; @HUB-20] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **The south-central coast (Khanh Hoa and Lam Dong, including former Ninh Thuan and Binh Thuan):** the best long-run solar and shrimp-hatchery niches, 2035 to 2050 [@HUB-02; @HUB-23] {VN-direct|Low}.

## 24.7 How the vision fares in each world

| Pillar | A. Regional workshop | B. Comfortable price-taker | C. Security build-out | D. Squeezed importer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Measure | Achievable | Achievable | Achievable | Achievable |
| Economise | Achievable | Achievable | Achievable, and urgent | Achievable, and carries most of the load |
| Diversify | Lower half of the range | Bottom of the range, mostly imported | Upper half of the range | Lower half, partly imported |
| Specialise | Strongest | Weak | Strong | Narrow (local niches) |
| Decarbonise and adapt | Achievable | Achievable | Achievable if clean power is delivered | Achievable, at higher cost |

Our judgement from [[ch23-scenarios-2050]] {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate}. Three of the five pillars are achievable in every world. The diversification and specialisation pillars depend on the world, which is why their milestones are ranges and why the vision needs a review cycle.

## 24.8 What would make us revise it

- **Upwards:** fishmeal above USD 2,500 per t for 12 months; an ASEAN reliance mechanism for novel foods; delivered green hydrogen below USD 2 per kg in southern Vietnam; a working cellulosic sugar plant in Asia.
- **Downwards:** a sustained soy glut; Chinese export dumping of microbial protein; a serious novel-food safety scandal in Asia; no feed-protein balance published by 2030.
- **Review cycle:** at each five-year plan (2030, 2035, 2040, 2045), using the 16 signposts in `signposts_2050.csv` and the method in [[app-m2-futures-method]]. Vietnam's own foresight studies advise small, high-quality scenario workshops because statistics are thin [@VIS-45] {VN-direct|Low}. *Vietnam 2035*, written jointly by the World Bank and the planning ministry, is the precedent for a jointly authored national vision [@VIS-46] {VN-direct|Medium}.

## 24.9 What this means

- **Policy makers:** the 2026 to 2030 milestones are small, cheap and mostly administrative: a statistic, a route, a named site, a budget line and a pilot plant. The successor livestock and fisheries strategies (before 2030) are the natural home for protein-balance targets.
- **International bodies:** the balance sheet and the review cycle are where technical assistance adds most; the EU's new balance-sheet method is a ready template.
- **Investors:** the vision implies microbial feed-protein capacity of about nine times Entobel's current Vietnamese insect-meal capacity (11 kt a year of product) by 2030, comparing protein with protein (our calculation), and a regional contract-fermentation niche; the protein-from-power opportunity is a 2040s option.
- **Manufacturers:** the vision's largest single lever is yours: feed efficiency and formulation. Sharing anonymised inclusion and conversion data is the first step.
- **Startups and researchers:** the vision rewards process know-how on Vietnamese feedstocks, strains and species, not generic platforms.

**Related:** [[ch28-robust-moves]] (the moves that deliver the 2026 to 2030 milestones), [[ch27-policy-options]] (the policy options), [[app-f5-targets-hubs]].

data.title: What demand asks of the frontier: product targets, plays and public goods
data.summary: Demand in Vietnam pulls new protein as an ingredient inside foods people already eat, sold to the firms and kitchens that make them, and soy, not meat, is the price an extender must beat. We turn this into eleven target product profiles, a demand check of the ten plays and twenty-one cheap moves, each with a funder or budget.
data.body:
# 25. What demand asks of the frontier: product targets, plays and public goods

**In one paragraph.** Part III's answer to "what demand exists for new protein in Vietnam?" is clear, even where the evidence is thin. Demand pulls new protein as an ingredient inside foods Vietnamese already eat, sold to the firms and kitchens that make them: chay makers replacing imported textured soy, meat processors extending pork, plant-milk makers adding protein, canteens feeding workers on about VND 25,000 to 31,000 a meal, and exporters of dumplings and other wrapped foods. It does not pull branded replacements for meat. We tested this against 80 named actors and 16 further lines of research ([[ch29-actor-check]]). The core answer holds, but the route to each buyer is narrower and more concrete than our first reading suggested. The rules on school menus, protein claims, blend labels, tariffs and sugary drinks are already written; soy, not meat, is the price an extender must beat; and domestic textured soy is an import-substitution plant best owned by a chay maker, co-packer or distributor and financed with debt, not a venture bet. This chapter turns that into eleven target product profiles, a demand check of the ten plays of [[ch26-plays]] and twenty-one cheap moves, each with the funder or budget that would pay for it.

> **Method note.** How the actor check was run, which questions Part III answered and what each new line of research changed are in [[ch29-actor-check]] and [[app-m4-actor-check-waves]]. This chapter carries the results into the product profiles, the play check and the moves.

---

## 25.1 Demand findings that change what to make

**Ten findings from Part III.**

1. **The price to beat is eggs and chicken,** at VND 34,000 to 45,000 per 100 g of protein; lean pork (about VND 71,000) is the ceiling for a mass meat analogue. Imported analogues sit at 12 to 18 times eggs and chicken ([[ch11-protein-diet]]) {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-protein-price-floor}}
2. **Adults do not need more protein; dishes need denser protein.** Protein sits in toppings, fillings and rolls; chay foods have a median of 4.7 g per 100 g against 19 g for lean pork ([[ch11-protein-diet]]). For school-age children protein is not the gap either: published Hanoi primary-school lunches carry about 31.8 g (our calculation), and upland boarding lunches and dinners carried meat, fish or egg in 240 of 242 meals; the documented shortfalls are breakfast, calcium and vitamin A [@PMR-26; @UPL-01; @UPL-02; @UPL-03; @UPL-05; @UPL-06; @UPL-07; @UPL-08; @UPL-09; @UPL-10; @UPL-11; @UPL-12; @UPL-13; @UPL-14; @UPL-15; @UPL-16; @UPL-17] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Stunting (18% of children under five in 2023, 32% among ethnic minority children) is a problem of the youngest children, where plant products face the young-child protein-quality pattern and registration as foods for children under 36 months [@APR-27; @NQR-01; @REG-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
3. **Few want to eat less meat** (15% of urban online respondents, [[ch13-consumers]]), and meat per person is projected to rise 25% by 2035 ([[ch11-protein-diet]]) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}.
4. **What people ask for is variety, cooking fit, fewer additives and safety,** not a closer copy of meat ([[ch13-consumers]]) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:stated}.
5. **The modern plant category that sells is plant milk,** with soy milk priced at or below dairy, and nut milk at premium-dairy prices, by local incumbents. The best plant-milk SKUs sell 60 to 79% of the litres of the best dairy SKUs on Lazada and Tiki, and Vinamilk's high-protein nut milk sells as a premium niche of about 70,300 L at its Lazada store [@MKT-03] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
6. **Chay is the ready channel and the wrong impact count:** a shelf, a cold chain, a calendar and makers already buying imported protein, but chay days are already in the meat baseline ([[ch12-chay-baseline]]) [@CHY-23]. Fake chay is a latent rumour, not a live scandal: we found no confirmed case of meat in a Vietnamese chay product from 2015 to 2026 [@TRU-22], and a laboratory PCR test for animal DNA in chay food has been developed [@TRU-24]; chay's live trust issues are borax, microbes and unlabelled goods [@TRU-14; @TRU-16; @TRU-18; @CHY-23] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
7. **Blends are the entry route, and soy already holds it.** One large processor lists soy protein in 31% of its meat formulations [@BUY-05], and seven commercial Vietnamese sausages in one study contained soy; in that test, sausages made with soy or peanut protein were liked equally [@HXE-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
8. **Words carry risk:** *nhân tạo* (artificial) and *giả* (fake) are loaded, and *độn* (padding, filler) means hidden cost-cutting; *lên men* (fermented) helps. A declared soy ingredient in branded sausages draws no observed penalty [@NOV-69; @NOV-81; @TRU-02; @TRU-03; @NOV-63; @TRU-22] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
9. **Kitchens and factories come before shelves, and they already buy cheap plant protein.** Only an ingredient fits a canteen's protein budget of VND 7,500 to 14,000 a meal, and domestic dry soy-gluten pieces already reach kitchens at about VND 4,000 to 5,100 per 20 g of protein, against VND 7,200 to 9,500 for firm branded tofu and VND 8,800 for eggs (our calculation from [@CPC-12; @CHN-41; @CHN-39]) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-canteen-protein-budget}}
10. **The volumes that exist are business-to-business.** On the benchmark path the routes create demand for about 19,000 t of protein a year by 2035, of which about 11,000 to 17,000 t made in Vietnam for the home market, mostly as import substitution, and displace about 0.2% of meat protein ([[ch18-demand-sizing]]) {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-demand-bench-2035}}

**Six findings from the actor check that change the picture.**

- **Schools buy tofu beside meat, and the rule that mattered has expired.** Decision 1340's animal-protein target ended in 2020 [@CHN-33]. The current guidance, Decision 3958/QĐ-BYT (December 2025), sets no animal share and asks for plant protein (legumes, tofu) at least twice a week. Published menus in our audit (`school_menu_weeks.csv`) meet that in only 9 of 48 school-weeks, plant protein appears on 15.1% of 239 lunch days, almost always as tofu beside a meat dish, and the menu software that caterers use prints a standard of "animal protein at least 48%". A plant ingredient in the plant slot competes with tofu and replaces tofu, not meat; the only school route that removes meat is a labelled blend in the minced-meat and fish-cake dishes served on 28.5% of days [@AIB-39; @PMR-10; @PMR-26] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. The rule window is Decision 973/QĐ-TTg: a MOET *bán trú* (school lunch and midday care) circular due in 2026 and digital menu tools due in 2027 to 2028 [@PMR-01] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}.
- **A sugary-drink excise will shape plant milk.** From 1 January 2027 drinks above 5 g of total sugar per 100 ml pay 8% (10% from 2028); dairy is exempt and whether sweetened soy, nut and cereal milks are in scope is unresolved. Core Fami soy milks carry 6.5 to 9.3 g, and the reference high-protein nut milk is also above 5 g [@FTR-01; @FTR-02; @FTR-05; @FTR-17; @FTR-18] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}.
- **There is no tariff shelter.** Textured protein, soy isolate, pea protein and gluten enter from China, ASEAN and Korea at 0% under ACFTA and RCEP; the 5%, 3% and 10% duties apply only to other origins, and Chinese, French and Canadian pea protein also enter duty-free [@FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **Retailer private label is a working route for chay.** All five Co.op Select frozen chay dishes are made by one certified co-packer, GN Foods, and Lotte Mart sells its own chay label; the products are starch and vegetable led and carry no protein claim [@CPC-15; @AIB-28; @ECO-35; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- **Most label rules are already in force.** A high-protein claim needs 10 g per 100 g (TCVN 14429:2025, voluntary), and 20 of 43 audited foods already meet the source-of-protein condition per 100 g without claiming it; TCVN 13625:2023 already defines vegetarian and vegan claims; any ingredient named in a product name must be quantified; no standard sets a minimum meat content; and the GMO label applies only above 5% of ingredients [@LBL-03; @LBL-15; @LBL-06; @LBL-11; @LBL-12; @LBL-13; @LBL-10] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}.
- **Soy is the extender benchmark, not meat.** Replacing 20% of the lean in *chả lụa* (steamed pork roll) with hydrated soy saves VND 9,100 to 16,600 per kg at every annual hog price from 2019 to 2024 (our calculation), so a new extender must beat hydrated soy at about USD 2.6 to 2.8 per kg of protein, and win on sensory tolerance or the label, not on price against pork [@HXE-01; @DIE-25; @HXE-10; @TIC-12] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

## 25.2 Target product profiles

A target product profile states what a product must be for the demand that exists. The full profiles, with sources, are in `target_product_profiles.csv` {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. TPP-11 is a feed profile for play T2. A zinc-fortified soy dish base for upland school kitchens was proposed and withdrawn: the kitchens it named already serve meat almost every day, so it stays only as a research option for fortified breakfast items [@UPL-04] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.

| Profile | First buyers | Price target | Protein target | Must have | First test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TPP-01 Domestic textured soy or soy-gluten protein | Chay makers and dry chay-piece makers; co-packers incl. GN Foods; distributors (Brenntag, VMC, TDGIMEX) | At or below Chinese landed textured soy (USD 1.29 to 1.38 per kg); delivered soy flour below about USD 700 to 940 per t | 50 to 70% as sold | Made from soy flour or meal; several shapes; non-GMO where asked; debt-financed owner | Five delivered soy-flour quotes; conditional orders of 2,000 t a year from three buyers |
| TPP-02 Higher-protein chay foods | Incumbent chay brands; Co.op Select (GN Foods) and Lotte Choice L private label | Today's chay shelf (VND 56,000 to 173,000 per kg) | 10 to 12 g per 100 g | "10 g đạm/100 g" on the front; short label; stock for lunar peaks | Pitch a 10 g version of a Co.op Select SKU; minimart repeat test |
| TPP-03 Hybrid extender for processed meat | Vissan, Masan MEATLife, C.P., CJ, SG Food | At or below hydrated soy (about USD 2.6 to 2.8 per kg of protein) | Finished product 10 g or more per 100 g | 10 to 20% in fine emulsions, up to 30% in coarse mince; plant part named as an ingredient | Blind test at equal saving against the processor's soy formula, in *xúc xích* (sausage) |
| TPP-04 Canteen protein ingredient | Caterers via chay-piece makers and HoReCa distributors; later school, hospital and upland kitchens | Beat dry soy-gluten pieces (VND 4,000 to 5,100 per 20 g of protein) | About 20 g per adult dish; 10 to 15 g per child | Bulk-cook tolerant; caterer documents; no children's claims | Caterer trial with extender and school arms |
| TPP-05 Rice or mung bean isolate for plant milks | Vinamilk, Vinasoy, Nutifood, TH | Between Chinese and Western pea protein (about USD 2 to 7 per kg in bulk), unprotected by tariff | 80 to 88% isolate; drinks at 5 g or more per 100 ml | UHT-stable, neutral, soy-free; host drink at or below 5 g sugar per 100 ml | Samples to two dairy research teams |
| TPP-06 Fungal biomass functional ingredient | Bakery, seasoning makers, processors | Against egg white, dairy proteins and yeast protein, not soy | About 45% dry basis | Clean label; binding and umami | Trials benchmarked against yeast protein and egg white |
| TPP-07 Precision-fermented specialty protein | Formula and medical nutrition makers; export | Against conventional lactoferrin and whey concentrate | Infant and medical grade | GMO question settled for high-inclusion uses | Legal opinion on the one open GMO question |
| TPP-08 Export plant-based wrapped foods | EU and UK importers and brand owners of Asian wrapped foods; CJ's Kizuna plant | Near European private-label prices | Protein claims where true | IFS or BRCGS; EU wrappers within the 20% flour cap | Quotes from three importers and two brand owners |
| TPP-09 Diaspora protein-upgraded chay | Asian grocers abroad | USD 3.50 to 10 a pack | 10 g or more per 100 g | Frozen logistics; tariff risk priced | Listing test with one importer |
| TPP-10 Cultivated meat or seafood | None domestic before the mid-2030s | Not applicable | Not applicable | Hybrid format; not sold as chay | Research partnerships only |
| TPP-11 Functional microbial feed ingredient (T2) | 15 ASC-certified feed mills; importers of feed yeast | At or below imported bulk yeast (about USD 1.1 per kg) unless trials show a gain | Priced on performance | Head-to-head data; listed raw material; ASC data | 1 to 2% tank trial against the mill's current yeast |

## 25.3 The ten plays, checked against demand

The market-pull scores of [[ch26-plays]] were set from supply-side evidence of buyers. Part III's evidence suggests two changes and no reductions, and the actor check keeps both while replacing the evidence behind T1 and T2 {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}:

| Play | Market pull, supply view | Demand view | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 Domestic textured plant protein | 4 | **5** | Several named buyers already buy the imported equivalent: HS 2106.10 imports from China, India and Serbia were 12,832 t in 2025; export origin rules add no customer [@BUY-02; @TIC-12; @ORG-01] |
| T2 Functional microbial feed ingredients | 4 | 4 | Vietnam already imports about 9,200 t of inactive yeast a year for food and feed, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg; export standards do not require microbial ingredients, and BAP counts algae and other aquatic microorganism ingredients toward its marine-ingredient target [@FBA-17; @FBA-01; @FBA-05] |
| T3 Bulk microbial protein for fishmeal | 3 | 3 | Same pull as T2; price-led (our judgement; the ASC feed standard neither requires nor rewards microbial protein [@EXP-29]) |
| T4 Cassava sugar hub | 2 | 2 | Export demand is for starch; no new protein demand [@EXP-39] |
| T5 Shared pilot and tolling | 2 | 2 | An enabler; adds a need for application and sensory trials |
| T6 Duckweed feed | 2 | 2 | Not examined by the demand streams |
| T7 High-value precision-fermentation ingredients | 2 | 2, conditional | Buyers of the target ingredient exist and sell non-GMO; the GMO label bites only above 5% of ingredients [@NOV-59; @NOV-62; @NOV-63; @LBL-10] |
| T8 Cultivated seafood research | 1 | 1 | Revealed Asian sales are tiny; the regional cultivated-seafood firms have turned to pet food and skincare for revenue, with no food product on sale [@NOV-10; @AIS-34; @AIS-35] |
| T9 Koji and fungal foods | 2 | 2 (3 if a processor pilots a fungal extender above soy parity) | Fermented reads well; the route is blends and chay ingredients, but soy already fills the extender role [@NOV-63; @NOV-56; @NOV-57] |
| T10 Mung bean and rice protein for plant drinks | 3 | **4** | Vinamilk buys pea protein for a soy-free high-protein milk that sells as a niche; the sugary-drink excise and duty-free pea protein narrow the room [@BUY-16; @MKT-03; @FTR-02; @FTR-32] |

**T1: the market pull stands, the thesis changes.** T1 keeps a market pull of 5 because named chay makers already buy the imported product. But the pool a soy extrusion line can serve is at most about 12,800 t of HS 2106.10 imports from three low-cost origins, not the whole estimated food-use pool of 40,000 t of imported plant-protein ingredients: the near tripling of plant-protein imports is mostly HS 3504 protein at about USD 1 per kg, which needs other plants [@BUY-02; @TIC-12; @TIC-14] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Capital is not the barrier. Shandong makers list complete lines of 0.2 to 1.5 t an hour, with dryer, at USD 11,000 to 100,000 (list prices) [@TIC-02; @TIC-03; @TIC-07]; by our calculation a whole plant installs for about USD 0.3 to 1.4 million, and working capital of USD 0.6 to 3.5 million is the larger need {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-tvp-line-capex}} There is no tariff shelter: Chinese product lands at USD 1.29 to 1.38 per kg, and India-origin textured soy lands lower still. The delivered price of food-grade defatted soy flour, 63 to 85% of cost and imported from the same countries that export the finished product, sets the sign of the margin (our calculation) [@TIC-12; @TIC-13; @BUY-02; @FTR-32] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-t1-flour-breakeven}} The benchmark path supports about one 1 t/h line, or two 0.5 t/h lines, by 2035. T1 is therefore an import-substitution plant best owned by a large chay maker, a group of chay makers, a co-packer or an ingredient distributor and financed with debt and trade finance, not venture equity: its return is a commodity spread that Chinese exporters can compress, it holds no intellectual property and its exit is a trade sale {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

**T2: the same score on revealed evidence.** Our first reading took T2's pull from export feed standards. Those standards are largely neutral: ASC v1.2, BAP and GLOBALG.A.P. do not require a microbial ingredient, although BAP counts algae and other aquatic microorganism ingredients toward its marine-ingredient target; from 1 May 2028 ASC farm audits will need feed from an ASC-certified mill, and 15 Vietnamese mills are certified [@FBA-01; @FBA-02; @FBA-03; @FBA-04; @FBA-05; @FBA-06] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. The revealed pull is that Vietnam already imports about 9,200 t of inactive yeast a year (HS 2102.20, food and feed together), 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg, and Vietnam already exports a product in the same HS code [@FBA-17; @FBA-19] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Nutreco, a global leader in animal nutrition and aquafeed, reached 0.6% novel ingredients group-wide in 2025 (1.5% in its aquafeed arm, Skretting) against a 5 to 10% target [@FBA-07] {VN-adjacent|High} {dx:revealed}.

**What changes in the ranking.** With the two market-pull changes and the published weights, domestic textured plant protein (T1) leads the balanced preset at 3.95, against 3.9 for the cassava sugar hub (T4), and plant-drink proteins (T10) move up to third place for startups, joint third for manufacturers and fourth for investors. The lead is 0.05: a one-point fall in T1's market pull or defensibility returns first place to T4. T1 leads under the balanced, investor, startup and manufacturer presets; T4 stays first or second under every preset and leads under the policy, research and international presets, where the shared pilot and tolling play (T5) stays second. The frontier bets (T7, T8) stay where they were (our calculation from `plays.csv`, `play_weight_presets.csv` and `play_demand_check.csv`) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

**Proposed supply-score changes, not applied.** We have not changed `plays.csv`. The actor-check evidence suggests three supply-score changes, recorded in the `note_v0_4` column of `play_demand_check.csv` for readers to apply with the interactive ranking in [[ch26-plays]]: T1 capital efficiency from 4 to 5 and Vietnam advantage from 3 to 2, which nets to zero on the balanced score (T1 stays first at 3.95 and first under the investor, startup and manufacturer presets); and T2 defensibility from 3 to 2, on weak evidence, which would leave T5 sole third under the balanced preset (our calculation) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.

**Demand-side kill tests** to add to the plays (`play_demand_check.csv`):

- **T1** fails if delivered food-grade defatted soy flour costs more than about USD 700 to 940 per t for a 1 t/h line at 70% utilisation (USD 590 to 900 for a 0.5 t/h line), if fewer than three buyers sign conditional orders totalling at least 2,000 t a year, or if India-origin textured soy (USD 0.98 per kg FOB) becomes the reference price (our calculation) [@TIC-12; @TIC-13; @BUY-02] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.
- **T2** fails if two head-to-head trials at 1 to 2% inclusion against the commodity yeast mills already buy show no gain worth the price gap (about 1.2 to 1.8% of shrimp-feed cost), or if the delivered price stays above about USD 1.1 per kg without such a gain [@FBA-17] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.
- **T7** is confined to export and business-to-business uses if purified precision-fermented proteins must carry a GMO declaration at the doses buyers use.
- **T9** fails if, at the replacement level that gives the same saving as soy, a fungal blend in industrial *xúc xích* or a coarse filling scores below the processor's own soy-extended formula in a blind test, or if no processor will pay above hydrated-soy parity (about USD 1.2 per kg dry, the 2025 unit value of HS 2106.10 imports from China, at an assumed 45% protein) [@TIC-12; @HXE-10] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.
- **T10** fails if an isolate cannot reach the band between Chinese and Western pea protein with UHT stability, or if host drinks cannot be made at or below 5 g of total sugar per 100 ml once plant milks are ruled inside the sugary-drink excise [@FTR-02] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

## 25.4 Twenty-one cheap moves, and who would pay

Most of the demand gaps in Part III can be closed for tens of thousands of USD. The full list, with who, when and who would pay, is in `demand_moves.csv`; the underlying questions are in [[app-r1-open-questions]]. Every move now names a payer, or says why none was found. Only four of the original nineteen moves have a funder whose stated scope fits and that accepts Vietnam: two consumer-acceptance studies fit the Bezos Centre for Sustainable Protein at NUS, and two naming and GMO rules fit Nova Vista's market-shaping programme. Diet-change and culture-change work is excluded by Nova Vista and now by ACE Movement Grants, and ReRoot Asia has no Vietnam track [@AFN-05; @AFN-15; @AFN-29; @FUF-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. {{kn:kn-funder-fit}} The rest belong to industry, to trade bodies or to national budgets.

**Measure.**

- **Chay days (DMV-01).** First ask the Global Diet Quality Project or Gallup to tabulate the 2021 flesh-free share (7.9% of adults) by the lunar date of the recall day, then add a chay-day question to a probability survey [@APR-36; @BRD-03]. *Who would pay:* no philanthropic payer; national survey budgets (NSO, NIN) or GAIN's Diet Quality Questionnaire.
- **Customs declarations (DMV-02)** for HS 3504, 2106.10, 1109 and 2102.20.10 (yeast for animal feeding), to split food from feed and name the buyers of T1 and T2 products. *Who would pay:* partly Nova Vista or World Bank and ADB technical assistance; otherwise a would-be T1 or T2 owner.
- **Sensory and choice tests (DMV-03) and a randomised label and name test (DMV-04).** *Who would pay:* the Bezos Centre at NUS, with a Vietnamese institute.
- **One canteen and school trial with three arms (DMV-05):** an extender or canteen ingredient in minced dishes; a chay-day menu; and a school arm in which one caterer that writes one menu for several schools serves a textured-soy or blended dish in the plant slot and in one minced dish, with daily published menus as controls. Log the dish species replaced, because animals spared per meal differ about 34-fold between a pork and a chicken dish (our calculation) and chicken leads only 13% of canteen protein dishes [@UPL-27; @UPL-28; @UPL-29; @UPL-30; @UPL-32; @FUF-03]. *Who would pay:* the extender arm partly fits Nova Vista's procurement lever and the Bezos Centre; Humane World Viet Nam fits the chay-day arm as implementer, but no current funder both covers Vietnam and funds diet change; the school arm has no external payer.
- **A minimart repeat test (DMV-06), the share of meat eaten as processed products (DMV-09) and a Nha Trang hotel and menu audit (DMV-10).** *Who would pay:* industry and AltProtein Vietnam; Humane World fits the hotel audit as implementer.
- **Quote requests to wrapped-food buyers (DMV-11):** one vegetable and one plant-protein SKU from three EU importers of Asian frozen foods and two brand owners already sourcing from Vietnam [@XBA-20], with their certification and origin requirements. Retailer protein targets need no survey; they are published [@XBA-02; @XBA-14]. *Who would pay:* industry and trade bodies.
- **A soy-flour price sheet (DMV-21):** five delivered quotes for food-grade defatted soy flour and three for Chinese plain textured soy, with the T1 breakeven. It costs tens of hours and decides the T1 kill test [@TIC-12; @TIC-13]. *Who would pay:* the would-be owner or its lender.

**Build public goods.**

- **A chay safety and composition survey (DMV-07)** that tests borax, preservatives, microbes and protein first, with animal DNA as a PCR screen (the QUATEST 3 method awaits accreditation); publish with VFA, publish methods and do not name small makers [@TRU-24]. *Who would pay:* partly the Bezos Centre, UNICEF Viet Nam or ACIAR; otherwise food-safety budgets.
- **A standing panel of research and procurement buyers (DMV-08)** to publish specifications, minimum orders and qualification times. *Who would pay:* an industry association.
- **A feed carbon-footprint benchmark (DMV-12)** that helps ASC-certified mills meet GHG reporting; it will not by itself create demand for microbial ingredients [@FBA-01]. *Who would pay:* partly ADB Ventures, IFC or ACIAR; otherwise the mills.

**Set rules (policy makers).** These add a demand-side reason to the policy options of [[ch27-policy-options]]. The Food Safety Law takes first comments at the National Assembly's October 2026 session and is considered for passage at the May 2027 session, so a new-food clause needs to be in the draft revised between the two sessions, in practice by early 2027 [@APR-07] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Two of the four label moves are largely law already and need enforcement and testing, not new rules; one should defend a permissive regime; one shrinks to a single question [@LBL-06; @LBL-10; @LBL-15] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. Decree 37/2026 has replaced Decree 43/2017 for goods labels, and Circular 30/2026/TT-BYT has replaced Circular 29/2023 for nutrition labels.

- **Chay claims (DMV-13).** TCVN 13625:2023 already defines vegetarian and vegan claims, but its vegetarian class allows egg, milk and honey and it says nothing on alliums. Ask VFA to state that an unqualified *chay* or *thuần chay* (strict vegetarian) claim means the vegan criteria, with egg or milk named in a qualifier, and enforce the existing rules alongside DMV-07.
- **Blend labels (DMV-14).** Any meat named in a product name must already be quantified. Narrow the move to a voluntary industry code for generic names such as *giò lụa* (steamed pork roll) and *xúc xích* that states the meat share when a plant or fungal protein replaces 10% or more of the meat; its value is defensive, as proof against a *độn* accusation [@LBL-06; @TRU-03]. *Who would pay:* the processors.
- **Names (DMV-15).** We found no rule that reserves *thịt* (meat), *sữa* (milk) or *phô mai* (cheese); names must only not mislead, and practice already qualifies meat words. Defend this permissive regime in the new Food Safety Law decree and aim vocabulary guidance at state and media use.
- **GMO status (DMV-16).** The GMO label applies only above 5% of ingredients, so lactoferrin-type uses (about 0.08%) are not caught. Ask MAE and VFA one question: is a recombinant protein identical to the native protein a detectable product of the modified gene, and may a product containing one below 5% still claim non-GMO? *Who would pay for DMV-15 and DMV-16:* Nova Vista, or for a small Vietnamese organisation ACE Movement Grants (policy work only, deadline 18 October 2026).
- **School menus (DMV-17).** National guidance already has no animal share. Ask MOET, NIN and Ajinomoto to replace the menu software's 48% animal-protein default with protein-quality, zinc, iron and sodium targets per lunch, and to add textured soy and legume products to the software's food list, inside the MOET circular due in 2026 and the digital tools due in 2027 to 2028 [@PMR-26; @PMR-01]. A second version is a procurement standard for innovative protein in public and state-enterprise canteens. *Who would pay:* UNICEF Viet Nam's 2027 to 2031 programme for the school version; Nova Vista's procurement lever for the canteen version.
- **Customs subheadings (DMV-18)** for soy isolate, pea protein and textured protein. *Who would pay:* MOF's own budget, partly World Bank or ADB.
- **An origin note for exporters (DMV-19)** on the EU cap of 20% non-originating flour and starch in wrapped foods and the 10% tolerance for imported textured soy in 2106 foods, and on claiming CPTPP for the UK; imported soy protein is not the main constraint [@ORG-01]. *Who would pay:* industry and trade bodies.
- **A written sugary-drink ruling (DMV-20):** the Ministry of Finance to state, before 1 January 2027, whether soy milk (TCVN 12443:2018), nut and cereal milks above 5 g of total sugar per 100 ml are *nước giải khát* (soft drinks) [@FTR-01; @FTR-13]. *Who would pay:* the plant-milk makers.

## 25.5 What not to do

- Do not size a business on stated survey intent or on the published Vietnamese market sizes; neither has a revealed basis.
- Do not launch premium imported-style analogues into gourmet channels expecting mass uptake, and do not enter foodservice with an imported branded analogue through business-to-business distributors: CP Meat Zero minced was listed on Kamereo at 1.5 to 2.1 times CP's own minced pork per kg, and none of its eight SKUs was orderable in September 2026 [@AIS-25; @CPC-12] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}.
- Do not price a mass product above pork, a chay product above today's chay shelf, or an extender above hydrated soy without proof that it allows more undetected replacement.
- Do not lead with "meat replacement", "the future of meat", "lab" or environmental claims, and do not use *độn* or "x% meat replaced" wording; lead with taste in familiar dishes, protein, safety and origin, and name the plant part as an ingredient.
- Do not name products *thịt nhân tạo* (artificial meat) or market cultivated or precision-fermented products to chay buyers.
- Do not start in schools with a branded or meat-replacement product. The school plant slot is small (about 1,000 t of protein a year, our calculation from an estimated 0.8 billion school lunches a year in `demand_assumptions.csv`), filled by tofu and under-used; enter later as a caterer ingredient that beats tofu on cost, or as a labelled blend in minced dishes [@PMR-10; @AIB-39; @CHN-29; @CHN-31] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Do not start in wet markets or tourist hotels either.
- Do not pitch a fortified soy dish to upland boarding or border-commune kitchens as filling a meatless lunch: their published lunches carry meat almost every day, and a Decree 339 lunch spent 79 to 98% of its non-rice money on pork (91 to 98% on pork and tofu together). Pitch cost per gram of protein against pork, which these kitchens already stretch with tofu [@UPL-01; @UPL-04] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}.
- Do not present import substitution, or protein upgrades on existing chay days, to welfare or climate funders as meat displaced, animals spared or CO2e avoided: they deliver none (our reasoning), and ACE Movement Grants will not fund diet-change work in any region [@FUF-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.
- Do not count sales into existing chay days as meat displaced.

## 25.6 What would change our view

- A tested Vietnamese study (choice experiment or in-store trial) showing repeat purchase of a modern analogue or blend at 20% or more above the meat it replaces.
- Retail or e-commerce panel data showing sustained growth of modern plant-based meat since 2024.
- A probability survey, or a lunar-date tabulation of the 2021 diet survey, showing that chay keeping is rising among young urban people, which would make added chay days a real displacement route.
- A large processor launching a declared blend with a novel protein, or a formula maker sourcing a precision-fermented protein.
- A new Food Safety Law, now expected to be considered for passage in May 2027, with a working new-food route and a clear treatment of purified fermentation proteins.
- Delivered soy-flour quotes below about USD 700 per t, which would make a domestic textured-soy line pay even at the high-cost end.
- A food-safety shock in meat followed by a measurable switch to plant proteins, which the 2019 to 2020 pork shock did not produce.

**For each reader.**

- **Startups:** sell a familiar food with little capital, and aim first for ingredient, private-label or co-packing supply to incumbents. A restaurant menu listing for your own analogue brand is not a business customer: in the region such firms mostly went quiet or pivoted. Of 24 regional and Vietnamese firms since 2019 in our firm register (`firm_outcomes.csv`, counted in `firm_base_rates.csv`, our calculation), 7 are active, 4 pivoted, 2 exited and 11 are dormant; we found no sign of activity after 2022 at any of the 4 Vietnamese meat-analogue startups, while all 3 makers of traditional formats are trading. TiNDLE (pivoted to private label), Emmay (trading) and Karana (dormant in our register) are examples [@AIS-28; @AIS-39; @BRD-08]. No founder has yet tested the ingredient route, so treat it as the hypothesis to test, not a proven path {VN-direct|Low} {dx:revealed}.
- **Investors:** T1 is a debt-financed import-substitution plant for a chay maker, co-packer or distributor, not a venture thesis; underwrite the delivered soy-flour price, conditional orders and cost per gram of protein. Investors now say they fund offtake, contracted revenue and unit economics, which T1 and T10 can show and consumer analogues cannot [@AIS-01; @AIS-15] {general|Medium} {dx:stated}.
- **Manufacturers:** a domestic textured soy, a non-soy isolate for drinks at or below 5 g of sugar per 100 ml, and a fungal ingredient that beats your own soy-extended formula are the three new ingredients your products can use. Test blends first in industrial *xúc xích* and coarse fillings, not *giò lụa*, blind and at equal saving against your soy recipe; keep 10 to 20% replacement in fine emulsions and 30% in coarse mince; and consider private-label chay through an existing co-packer [@HXE-01; @HXE-04; @HXE-09; @CPC-15] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}.
- **Research bodies:** the tested-evidence gap (sensory, choice and label tests in Vietnamese formats) is the most useful thing you can close for the whole sector, and the Bezos Centre at NUS is the one funder whose scope fits it.
- **Policy makers:** most label rules already exist; enforce them, defend permissive naming, answer the single GMO question, rule on plant milks and the sugary-drink excise before 2027, and put protein quality, zinc and cost into the school menu software.
- **International organisations and funders:** match the route to your unit and your rules. Welfare funders: a canteen trial with Humane World Viet Nam, focused on chicken dishes, which lead only one protein dish in eight in our coding of caterers' menus [@UPL-27; @UPL-28; @UPL-29; @UPL-30; @UPL-32]. Market-shaping funders: canteen procurement and the naming and GMO rules; Nova Vista's programme funds procurement, advance market commitments and retailer ratio targets, excludes whole-food, culture-change and diet-change work, and wants more policy staff especially in Japan and Korea. R&D funders: isolate and fungal functionality and Vietnamese blind tests. Nutrition agencies: protein quality and zinc in school food standards. On the benchmark path the displacing routes spare about 2.4 to 2.7 million animals a year by 2035, 93 to 94% of them chickens and ducks, and avoid about 0.14 Mt CO2e (our calculation, [[ch18-demand-sizing]]), so climate is a co-benefit, not the case; corporate pledges are a weak lever, since Accor's dish target is the only one we found that binds Vietnamese units [@AFN-05; @AFN-23; @FUF-03; @FUF-04; @AFN-40] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. The chay-day survey item belongs in national surveys.

**Related:** [[ch26-plays]], [[ch27-policy-options]], [[ch18-demand-sizing]], [[ch29-actor-check]], [[app-m4-actor-check-waves]], [[app-r1-open-questions]].

data.title: Ten plays and six public goods
data.summary: We describe ten concrete plays, each with the tests that would kill it, and score them on seven criteria with weights readers can change. Domestic textured plant protein, functional microbial feed ingredients and a cassava-to-fermentation-sugar hub lead under almost every weighting, and six public goods would lower the cost of every play.
data.body:
# 26. Ten plays and six public goods

**In one paragraph.** A "play" here is a specific business or programme that someone could start in Vietnam, with a named product, buyer and partner. We describe ten, from a textured-protein line that could sell within two years to cultivated-seafood research that will not reach a plate this decade. Each play states what must be true for it to work and the tests that would kill it, so that readers can check it rather than take it on trust. We score the plays on seven criteria and publish the weights, so each audience can re-rank them. Three plays lead under almost any weighting: **domestic textured plant protein (T1)**, **functional microbial feed ingredients for shrimp and pangasius (T2)** and a **cassava-starch-to-fermentation-sugar hub (T4)**. **Shared pilot and tolling fermentation (T5)** is what most fermentation plays need first. The textured-protein line is cheap to equip but earns its margin only if food-grade soy flour can be bought below about USD 700 to 940 per t, so it suits an incumbent with buyers and bank credit better than a venture-backed startup. Six public goods, mainly rules, trial capacity and data, would lower the cost of all of them.

> **Read with care.** [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]] checks these plays against demand evidence. The demand evidence suggests raising market pull for domestic textured plant protein (T1, from 4 to 5) and mung bean and rice protein for plant drinks (T10, from 3 to 4), and leaves the other plays unchanged; with those two scores T1 leads the balanced ranking. The scores on this page remain the supply-side scores; `play_demand_check.csv` holds the demand view and demand-side kill tests.
>
> **New evidence on T1.** New cost and buyer evidence changes the T1 thesis: a domestic textured-protein line is an import-substitution plant best owned by a chay maker, co-packer or ingredient distributor and financed with debt and trade finance, not venture equity; Chinese product enters duty-free and the delivered price of food-grade soy flour decides the margin. T2's market pull now rests on revealed buying: Vietnam already imports about 9,200 t of inactive yeast a year for food and feed, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg. Proposed score changes are recorded as text in [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]] and `play_demand_check.csv`: T1 capital efficiency 4 to 5 and Vietnam advantage 3 to 2 (no change to its balanced score; T1 still leads the demand-view balanced ranking at 3.95), and T2 defensibility 3 to 2 (weak evidence; it would leave T5 alone in third place under the balanced preset). The scores in 11.2 are unchanged.

> **How to use this chapter.** The scores are our judgement, based on the evidence in chapters 2 to 10. They are a starting point for discussion, not an investment rating. The data file `plays.csv` holds every field shown here, and `play_weight_presets.csv` holds the weights, so the website can let readers change them.

---

## 26.1 How the plays are scored

| Criterion | What a 5 means | What a 1 means |
|---|---|---|
| Market pull | Several named buyers already buy the imported or incumbent equivalent | No identifiable buyer or need |
| Vietnam advantage | A clear, hard-to-copy Vietnamese edge | Any neighbour does it as well or better |
| Technical readiness | Commercial elsewhere, skills present in Vietnam | Laboratory stage with major unknowns |
| Route to market | Ordinary food or listed feed rules apply | No legal route exists |
| Capital efficiency | First revenue for under a few USD millions, or via tolling | Tens to hundreds of USD millions before revenue |
| Defensibility | Function, logistics or IP that imports cannot easily match | Commodity with cheaper imports |
| Public value | Large contribution to protein security or national capability | Little wider benefit |

**Weight presets** (percent; each row sums to 100):

| Preset | Market | Advantage | Readiness | Route | Capital | Defensibility | Public value |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Balanced | 15 | 15 | 15 | 15 | 15 | 10 | 15 |
| Investors | 25 | 10 | 15 | 10 | 20 | 15 | 5 |
| Policy makers | 10 | 20 | 10 | 5 | 10 | 10 | 35 |
| Startups | 20 | 10 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 5 | 5 |
| Manufacturers | 30 | 10 | 25 | 15 | 10 | 5 | 5 |
| Research bodies | 10 | 25 | 10 | 10 | 5 | 5 | 35 |
| International bodies and DFIs | 10 | 20 | 15 | 10 | 10 | 5 | 30 |

## 26.2 The scores

| Play | Market | Advantage | Readiness | Route | Capital | Defensibility | Public value | Balanced score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 Domestic textured plant protein | 4 | 3 | 5 | 5 | 4 | 2 | 3 | 3.80 |
| T2 Functional microbial feed ingredients | 4 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3.45 |
| T3 Bulk microbial protein for fishmeal replacement | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 1 | 1 | 4 | 2.65 |
| T4 Cassava starch to fermentation sugar hub | 2 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3.90 |
| T5 Shared pilot and tolling fermentation | 2 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 3.45 |
| T6 Duckweed on aquaculture effluent for feed | 2 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 3.30 |
| T7 High-value, low-dose precision fermentation | 2 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 2.10 |
| T8 Cultivated seafood research | 1 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 1.55 |
| T9 Koji and fungal foods on side streams | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 3.00 |
| T10 Mung bean and rice protein for plant drinks | 3 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3.05 |

Source: AltProtein Vietnam scoring ([[ch10-technology-fit]] and the evidence cited in each play) {VN-direct\|Medium}.

{{chart:chart-plays-scoring}}

**Top three under each preset.**

| Preset | First | Second | Third |
|---|---|---|---|
| Balanced | T4 (3.90) | T1 (3.80) | T2 and T5 (3.45) |
| Investors | T1 (3.80) | T4 (3.50) | T2 (3.40) |
| Policy makers | T4 (3.95) | T5 (3.85) | T2 (3.65) |
| Startups | T1 (4.15) | T4 (3.85) | T2 (3.35) |
| Manufacturers | T1 (4.15) | T4 (3.75) | T2 (3.45) |
| Research bodies | T4 (4.15) | T5 (4.00) | T2 (3.70) |
| International bodies and DFIs | T4 (4.10) | T5 (3.85) | T1 (3.65) |

**Reading.** T1, T2 and T4 are robust: they stay in the top three or four under every preset. T4 scores highly because it carries little technical or legal risk and uses Vietnam's clearest advantage, but its weak point is market pull: no fermenter has yet committed to buy the sugar. T5 rises when public value is weighted, which is the case for public or development money. T7 and T8 stay at the bottom under every preset; that does not mean they are worthless, only that they are not near-term plays for Vietnam.

## 26.3 The plays

### T1. Domestic textured plant protein

- **What.** Dry textured soy protein and soy-gluten granules and slices, made in Vietnam for *chay* brands, frozen-food makers and co-packers. High-moisture whole cuts come later.
- **Why Vietnam.** Every audited Vietnamese product with 10 g of protein or more per 100 g runs on imported textured soy, soy protein or gluten, much of it from China; we found no commercial extrusion in Vietnam; ordinary food rules apply [@FORM-01; @FORM-02; @FORM-05; @FORM-11] {VN-direct|Medium}. There is no tariff shelter: Chinese, ASEAN and Korean textured protein enters at 0% under ACFTA, ATIGA, AKFTA and RCEP [@FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}. The pool a soy line can serve is up to about 12,800 t a year of HS 2106.10 imports (2025; the code also covers concentrates and isolates, so the textured share is unknown) [@BUY-02; @TIC-12] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Must be true.** Ex-factory cost at or below landed Chinese textured protein (USD 1.24 per kg FOB in 2025; USD 1.29 to 1.38 per kg landed, our calculation) [@TIC-12; @BUY-02] {VN-direct|Medium}; a supply of food-grade, low-temperature defatted soy flour below the breakeven price (about USD 700 to 940 per t delivered for a 1 t/h line at 70% utilisation; our calculation); buyers value freshness, customisation and local supply.
- **Kill tests.** Delivered flour costs more than about USD 700 to 940 per t; fewer than three buyers sign conditional orders totalling at least 2,000 t a year; Chinese landed price stays below Vietnamese full cost at 2,800 t a year (0.5 t/h at 70%) or 5,600 t (1 t/h at 70%), on 8,000 operating hours a year; Indian textured soy (USD 0.98 per kg FOB in 2025) becomes the reference price.
- **First customers.** An Nhien, Au Lac, Xuan Hong, LC Foods, Cholimex, CJ Foods Vietnam, Vissan, Thoai An, GN Foods (maker of at least one Co.op Select chay product) and other co-packers [@FORM-01; @CPC-15] {VN-direct|Medium}; the long tail of small chay makers through ingredient distributors such as Brenntag, VMC and TDGIMEX [@TIC-18; @BUY-36; @BUY-37] {VN-direct|Medium}. A 1 t/h line at 90% needs 26 to 131 buyers the size of Vissan's soy-protein use (our calculation).
- **Partners.** Extrusion-line suppliers; a soy crusher for a food-grade flake stream [@FORM-10]; FIRI for pilot trials; a bank or trade-finance provider for flour and receivables.
- **Horizon and capital.** 0 to 2 years. Chinese lines for textured vegetable protein (TVP) of 0.2 to 1.5 t/h with dryer are listed at USD 11,000 to 100,000 [@TIC-02; @TIC-03; @TIC-07] {general|Low}; installed in Vietnam, USD 0.28 to 1.38 million; working capital of USD 0.6 to 3.5 million is the larger need (our calculation; [[ch09-economics]], [[app-s12-costs]]). A European-grade line is unverified (USD 2.0 to 5.6 million installed on the earlier equipment assumption).

> **New evidence on T1.** The T1 thesis changes. T1 is an import-substitution ingredient plant, best owned by a large chay maker, a group of chay makers or co-packers, an ingredient distributor or a soy processor, and financed with bank debt and trade finance rather than venture equity. It has no intellectual property, its margin is a flour-to-texturate spread that Chinese exporters can narrow, and it displaces almost no meat. On the benchmark demand path it supports about one 1 t/h line, or two 0.5 t/h lines, by 2035, not three or four. Market pull stays at 5 in the demand view because named buyers already buy the imported equivalent. See [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]] for the demand check and the proposed score changes; the scores above are unchanged.

### T2. Functional microbial feed ingredients for shrimp and pangasius

- **What.** Yeast, fungal or bacterial biomass used at 1 to 5% of shrimp or fish diets and sold on survival, feed efficiency or palatability, made on Vietnamese carbohydrate.
- **Why Vietnam.** Abundant carbon; aerobic fermentation skills in amino-acid plants; a concentrated shrimp-feed industry ([[ch04-asset-map]], [[ch05-industrial-base]]); inactive yeasts already on the livestock feed list [@REG-32; @REG-33] {VN-direct|High}; trial evidence of functional benefits [@FM-20; @FM-31] {general|Medium}.
- **Must be true.** Repeatable species-specific trials show at least a 3 to 5% gain in survival or feed conversion at 1 to 5% inclusion; a legal route for aquafeed use; cost below the functional willingness to pay (about USD 1,000 to 4,250 per tonne in total for pangasius; USD 1,280 to 4,800 per tonne above fishmeal parity for shrimp; [[ch09-economics]]), and against the revealed price of the bulk inactive yeast mills already import, about USD 1,100 per tonne in 2025 [@FBA-17] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Kill tests.** Two independent tank or pond trials show no gain at 5% inclusion or less; two head-to-head trials at 1 to 2% inclusion show no gain worth the price gap over the commodity yeast mills already buy; Chinese by-product biomass [@FM-12], which enters duty-free [@FTR-32], delivers the same function for less.
- **Revealed demand.** Vietnam imported about 9,200 t of inactive yeast and dead single-cell organisms (HS 2102.20) in 2025, 2.4 times the 2019 tonnage [@FBA-17] {VN-direct|Medium}. Export feed standards (ASC Feed Standard v1.2, BAP, GLOBALG.A.P.) do not require microbial protein, although BAP counts algae and other aquatic microorganism ingredients toward its marine-ingredient target; from 1 May 2028 ASC farm audits need feed from ASC-certified mills, and 15 Vietnamese mills were certified in September 2026 [@FBA-01; @FBA-02; @FBA-03; @FBA-04; @FBA-05] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **First customers.** Sheng Long, CP Vietnam, Uni-President Vietnam, Tongwei, Grobest, Gromax, Skretting, De Heus, BioMar Viet Uc; integrated pangasius groups such as Vinh Hoan [@FM-04; @ECO-05; @FBA-04; @VCO-28; @VCO-09; @FBA-10] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Partners.** Amino-acid producers for tolling or co-product streams; shrimp trial laboratories; large feed groups for distribution.
- **Horizon and capital.** 1 to 3 years; low if tolled, otherwise in the fermentation capex range.

### T3. Bulk microbial protein for fishmeal replacement

- **What.** Fungal or bacterial protein at 10,000 t a year or more, replacing 25 to 50% of fishmeal in shrimp feed.
- **Why Vietnam.** The displaceable fishmeal pool is about 120 to 245 kt a year on central assumptions (our calculation, section S6.7 in [[app-s6-feed-market]]), of which about 25 to 90 kt is realistically contestable [@FM-04; @FM-05; @FM-08] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Must be true.** Capex below about USD 6,000 per annual tonne; near-free carbon; fishmeal near its 2026 high; a price below Chinese by-product and gas-fermentation imports.
- **Kill tests.** After a pilot, measured cost stays above 1.2 times fishmeal-protein parity at 2025 prices; no mill signs an offtake at 70 to 90% of fishmeal-protein parity.
- **First customers.** As T2.
- **Horizon and capital.** 3 to 6 years; tens of USD millions; a candidate for development-finance first-loss capital, as in the Entobel template ([[ch08-capital]]).

> **Correction.** Earlier drafts sized the displaceable fishmeal market at 350 to 450 kt a year. That range needs unsourced inclusion rates for snakehead and marine fish. The central estimate is 120 to 245 kt (our calculation), and the part novel proteins can realistically take in total, already contested by insect meal (Entobel) and Chinese microbial protein [@ECO-01; @FM-12; @ECO-69], is 25 to 90 kt (our calculation) [@FM-04; @FM-08] {VN-direct|Low}.

### T4. Cassava starch to fermentation sugar hub

- **What.** Turn part of the cassava starch Vietnam exports into fermentation-grade glucose next to starch factories, and co-locate fermenters there.
- **Why Vietnam.** Vietnam shipped 2.15 Mt of cassava starch in 2023, 93.5% to China, while China imported only USD 0.16 million of glucose syrup from Vietnam in 2024 [@RGN-53; @RGN-55] {VN-direct|High}. Starch factories cluster in Tay Ninh and the Central Highlands ([[ch04-asset-map]]).
- **Must be true.** Cassava prices stabilise after the 2025 to 2026 spike and the E10 fuel-ethanol roadmap [@FS-08; @FS-11; @FS-12] {VN-direct|Medium}; at least one fermenter commits to co-locate; wastewater and biogas infrastructure can serve fermentation.
