- **Kill tests.** No fermenter commits within two years; cassava volatility rules out long-term sugar contracts.
- **First customers.** Domestic fermenters; foreign biomass or precision-fermentation firms looking for a lower-cost ASEAN site ([[ch03-regional]]).
- **Horizon and capital.** 1 to 3 years; capital not estimated (standard starch-industry equipment; Vedan already built about 140,000 t a year of glucose capacity [@VCO-03] {VN-direct|Medium}).

### T5. Shared pilot and tolling fermentation

- **What.** A food-grade pilot line (hundreds of litres to a few cubic metres) plus negotiated tolling on existing industrial tanks, open to startups and researchers.
- **Why Vietnam.** Aerobic tanks exist inside Vedan, Ajinomoto and Daesang [@VCO-05; @IND-08; @IND-11], but we found no published tolling offer and no open pilot fermenter ([[ch05-industrial-base]]) [@INF-02; @INF-05] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Must be true.** An anchor host and an operator; enough users; public or development co-funding.
- **Kill tests.** No host accepts tolling terms; use below about a third of capacity in the first two years.
- **First customers.** Teams working on T2, T7 and T9; research groups; foreign firms testing Vietnamese feedstocks.
- **Partners.** Saigon Hi-Tech Park [@INF-06], FIRI, the amino-acid producers, and an access arrangement with Thailand's EECi pilot plant [@RGN-36].
- **Horizon and capital.** 2 to 4 years; pilot-scale capital, not estimated.

### T6. Duckweed on aquaculture effluent for feed

- **What.** Duckweed grown on pond or processing effluent and used in fish, poultry or pig feed; a food protein concentrate later.
- **Why Vietnam.** Duckweed is a permitted livestock feed material [@REG-32; @REG-33] {VN-direct|High}; there is a Vietnamese collection of more than 100 wild strains [@RD-44] {VN-direct|Medium}; the climate suits year-round growth.
- **Must be true.** Yields of 10 to 30 t of dry matter per hectare per year on Vietnamese sites (our planning range) [@SCI-36; @SCI-37]; heavy metals and manganese within limits [@SCI-28; @SCI-34]; cheap harvesting and drying.
- **Kill tests.** Field yields below 10 t per hectare per year; contaminants above feed limits on typical effluent.
- **First customers.** Integrated pangasius and tilapia farms; small feed mills; livestock farms.
- **Horizon and capital.** 1 to 3 years; low.

### T7. High-value, low-dose precision-fermentation ingredients

- **What.** Enzymes, heme or sweet proteins and specialty functional proteins developed by Vietnamese teams and made under contract abroad until a domestic option exists.
- **Why Vietnam.** Vietnamese groups already express proteins in yeast ([[ch06-knowledge-talent]]); low-dose products escape the bulk-protein titer benchmark (our inference) [@SCI-01; @SCI-05] {general|High}.
- **Must be true.** A product that is economic at 1 to 10 g/L (our assumption); freedom to operate [@SCI-08]; a foreign approval or an ingredient use outside novel-food rules; a clear GMO pathway ([[ch07-rules]]).
- **Kill tests.** No customer letter of intent after a sample programme; contract-manufacturing cost above target price at pilot scale.
- **Partners.** ScaleUp Bio, EECi or Chinese CDMOs [@RGN-10; @RGN-36; @RGN-24] {general|Medium}.
- **Horizon and capital.** 2 to 5 years; asset-light at first.

### T8. Cultivated seafood research

- **What.** Serum-free adaptation of striped catfish and shrimp cells, growth-factor expression and regulatory preparation, with foreign partners.
- **Why Vietnam.** Vietnam exports about USD 2.2 billion of pangasius a year ([[ch01-why-vietnam]]) [@MAC-01]; Vietnamese groups express growth factors and culture stem cells ([[ch06-knowledge-talent]]); Vinh Hoan has invested in regional cultivated-seafood firms [@CAP-16] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Must be true.** A food-suitable cell line (none known [@SCI-10; @SCI-12] {general|High}); five or more years of research funding; a scale-up partner.
- **Kill tests.** No serum-free, suspension-capable line after three years.
- **Horizon and capital.** 5 to 10 years or more; research grants.

### T9. Koji and fungal foods on food-grade side streams

- **What.** Solid-state fermented foods and ingredients using characterised *Aspergillus oryzae* or other food moulds on okara, broken rice or brewer's spent grain.
- **Why Vietnam.** A *tương* tradition; local gene tools for *A. oryzae* [@RD-33; @RD-34] {VN-direct|Medium}; koji on food substrates goes through ordinary self-declaration ([[ch07-rules]]).
- **Must be true.** A characterised strain without cyclopiazonic acid or 3-nitropropionic acid risk [@SCI-19] {general|High}; a food-grade substrate supply; acceptance in *chay* and mainstream dishes.
- **Kill tests.** Strain safety data cannot be obtained; sensory trials fail with target buyers.
- **Horizon and capital.** 1 to 3 years; low.

### T10. Mung bean and rice protein for plant drinks

- **What.** Concentrates or isolates from mung bean and rice, replacing imported pea protein in high-protein plant drinks and yoghurts.
- **Why Vietnam.** A large plant-milk industry; Vinamilk's high-protein line uses pea protein, for which no Vietnamese producer was found [@FORM-01] {VN-direct|Low}; ordinary food rules.
- **Must be true.** Functional and sensory parity; cost near imported pea protein; a buyer specification; reliable mung bean supply (65% of imports from Myanmar [@FORM-08]); honest protein-quality claims (human mung bean digestibility is about 20% below pig values [@SCI-42] {general|High}).
- **Kill tests.** Buyer rejects on taste or stability; cost exceeds imported pea protein by more than buyers will pay for local sourcing.
- **First customers.** Vinamilk, TH and other plant-milk makers.
- **Horizon and capital.** 2 to 4 years; moderate, not estimated.

{{chart:chart-plays-horizon}}

## 26.4 Six public goods

These are not businesses. They lower the cost and risk of every play above, and most are cheap. [[ch27-policy-options]] sets out who would do each.

| ID | Public good | What it unlocks | Policy options |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Proportionate new-food procedure | T7, T9, and food uses of T6 and fungal biomass | PO-015, PO-019 |
| P2 | Aquafeed raw-material clarity and generic microbial-biomass entries | T2, T3, T6 | PO-017, PO-018 |
| P3 | Public feed-trial capacity with standard protocols | T2, T3, T6 | PO-006, PO-021 |
| P4 | Protein-quality laboratory (amino acids, DIAAS) | T1, T9, T10, and any novel-food dossier | ([[ch27-policy-options]]) |
| P5 | Yearly by-product atlas (volume, location, price, composition) | T3, T4, T6, T9 | ([[ch27-policy-options]]) |
| P6 | Open cost model and public feed-ingredient price series | All fermentation plays; investor screening | ([[ch27-policy-options]]) |

## 26.5 Sequencing: a portfolio view

- **Now to 2028.** T1 (as an incumbent's or SME's debt-financed plant) and T2 as businesses; T4 if a fermenter commits; T9 and T6 as small pilots; P1 and P2 through the Food Safety Law and the next feed-list updates; T5 designed and funded.
- **2028 to 2031.** T5 in operation; T10 if a drinks buyer writes a specification; T7 through contract manufacturing; T3 only if T2 and T5 have proved the process and fishmeal stays high.
- **2031 onward.** T8 if a food-suitable cell line exists and a regional approval route is working.

## 26.6 What we do not recommend, and why

- **Replacing soybean meal in pig and poultry feed with fermentation protein.** The price gap is 4.6 to 5.1 times at the low end of our cost range ([[ch09-economics]]).
- **Premium imported-style consumer analogues as a first business.** They sell at an order of magnitude above chicken and egg protein and appear only in a few premium stores ([[ch02-alt-protein-today]], [[ch09-economics]]).
- **Commodity precision-fermented dairy or egg proteins made in Vietnam.** Titers, rules and missing infrastructure all point the other way ([[ch10-technology-fit]]).
- **Cultivated-meat production.** No cell line, no route, and costs 7 to 15 times retail meat ([[ch10-technology-fit]]).
- **Insect protein.** Out of this report's scope as a play; an established incumbent and benchmark ([[ch02-alt-protein-today]]).

## 26.7 What this means

- **Investors:** T2 is an investable near-term thesis; T1 is near-term too, but as bank debt and trade finance for an incumbent or SME plant, not a venture thesis; T3 and T4 need a strategic partner and development capital. Use the kill tests as diligence questions, starting with a delivered flour quote for T1.
- **Startups:** T1, T2, T6 and T9 can reach revenue on today's rules. Build the trial data (T2) or the buyer specification (T1, T10) before the plant; for T1, bring in a chay maker or distributor as co-owner or anchor buyer and start with flour quotes and conditional orders.
- **Manufacturers:** you are the natural owner of T1 and the first customer for T2 and T10. Pooled offtake from two or three chay makers behind one line, a letter of intent or a joint trial is the cheapest way to start one of them.
- **Policy makers:** P1 and P2 cost little and unlock several plays; T4 and T5 are where provincial and national investment promotion can act.
- **Research bodies:** T6, T8, T9 and the public goods P3 to P6 are research-led.
- **International bodies:** T3, T4 and T5 fit development finance and technical assistance.

**Related:** `plays.csv` (all fields), [[ch27-policy-options]], [[brief-investors]], [[brief-startups]], [[brief-manufacturers]].

data.title: Policy options
data.summary: Most of what would move alternative protein forward in Vietnam is cheap: a one-line clause in the Food Safety Law before passage is considered in May 2027, a joint note on precision-fermented proteins and two feed-list fixes. We rank 24 current options by impact, effort and timing, and the expensive ones are shared pilot fermentation and testing capacity.
data.body:
# 27. Policy options

**In one paragraph.** Vietnam does not need a new law or a new agency to give alternative protein a workable path. The most valuable step is also one of the cheapest and most time-bound: a short clause in the new Food Safety Law (first comments at the October 2026 National Assembly session and passage considered at the May 2027 session; the clause needs to be in the draft revised between the two, in practice by early 2027) that lets the Government regulate "new foods and new food ingredients", so that the detail can sit in a decree. Three other low-effort steps follow closely: a joint note from the agriculture and health ministries on the status of precision-fermented proteins under the new GMO decree, a raw-material section in the aquafeed list, and generic entries for microbial biomass in the livestock feed list. The costly options are about shared infrastructure: a pilot fermentation line, public feed trials and a protein-quality laboratory. This chapter sets out 33 options, ranks the 24 current ones (the other nine are earlier versions superseded by more specific options), and names, for each, the owning agency, the instrument to amend and a precedent. It is policy analysis, not legal advice.

> **Demand-side reasons.** Part III adds demand-side reasons for several of these options and seven cheap labelling, naming, procurement and statistics rules (DMV-13 to DMV-19 in [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]), which can ride on the same Food Safety Law window.

> **Timing and labels.** The law's timing is now settled: first comments in October 2026 and a vote considered in May 2027 [@APR-07] {VN-direct|Medium}. The label research narrows three options. The GMO label applies only above 5% of ingredients, so option 2's labelling half shrinks to one question on detectability; no rule reserves meat or milk words, so option 16 keeps the allergen list and recasts naming as guidance; and Chinese and ASEAN protein ingredients already enter duty-free, so option 24 touches only other origins [@LBL-10; @LBL-06; @FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}.

> **Neutrality note.** AltProtein Vietnam presents these as options with their evidence, costs and trade-offs. They are framed around food and feed security, industrial value and trade. Choosing among them is for Vietnamese policy makers.

---

## 27.1 Principles behind the ranking

1. **Proportionate, not permissive or prohibitive.** Most new proteins are ordinary foods or feeds with a new source. Rules should gate what is new, not everything that is different ([[ch07-rules]]).
2. **Rely on others' work.** Vietnam already fast-tracks GMOs approved in five developed OECD or G20 countries under Decree 43/2026; the same logic can apply to novel foods and feeds [@REG-18; @REG-23] {VN-direct|Medium}.
3. **Publish timelines and fees.** The regional study's most specific recommendation for Vietnam is to publish procedures and statutory timelines [@RGN-01] {VN-direct|High}. Korea's published fee and review period, even before any approval, gave applicants something to plan around [@RGN-34] {VN-adjacent|Medium}.
4. **Share capital, not only tax.** Capital charges and maintenance are most of the cost of fermentation protein ([[ch09-economics]]), and the regional study ranks capital grants and loan guarantees above tax holidays [@RGN-01] {general|High}.
5. **Use windows while they are open.** The Food Safety Law revision is a one-off opportunity; the next revision may be years away [@REG2-04; @REG2-05] {VN-direct|Medium}.

## 27.2 The ranked options

Ranked by impact on investability, feasibility and time-criticality. Effort: **Low** = a letter, guidance or list update; **Medium** = a circular or decree amendment; **High** = a new chapter of law, a new regime or major spending. The full table, with sources and notes, is `policy_options.csv`.

### Tier 1: cheap and time-critical (2026 to 2027)

| Rank | Option | Owner | Instrument | Precedent | Effort | Timeline |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (PO-015) | A short delegation clause in the new Food Safety Law: "The Government shall regulate the management of new foods and new food ingredients", with a definition based on history of use | MOH (Vietnam Food Administration) as drafter; National Assembly Committee on Science, Technology and Environment | Draft Law on Food Safety (amended) | Singapore FSSA 2025; Thailand Notification 376 | Low | October 2026 session (first comments) to May 2027 session (vote considered) |
| 2 (PO-016) | Joint MAE and MOH note: a purified protein made by a GM microorganism in contained use, with no viable GMO or recombinant DNA in the product, needs no GMO food-use certificate; and whether a recombinant protein identical to the native one is a "detectable product of the modified gene", which decides whether the GM label applies above 5% of ingredients | MAE (biodiversity and science departments); MOH | Official letter now; later a definitions amendment | Decree 43/2026 already separates organisms from products | Low | 3 to 6 months |
| 3 (PO-017) | Add a raw-material section to the aquafeed list, or state that livestock-list raw materials are allowed in aquafeed; add insect meal, inactivated yeast, microalgae, duckweed and fermented soybean meal | MAE Department of Fisheries | Circular amending Circular 16/2026 Appendix II | Circular 31/2022 added yeasts to the livestock list | Low | Next list update (2027) |
| 4 (PO-018) | Generic livestock-list entries for inactivated microbial biomass from safe strains (bacterial, fungal, microalgal), relying on foreign feed authorisations | MAE Department of Livestock Production and Animal Health | Circular amending Circular 21/2019 Appendix VI | Circular 31/2022 | Low | Next annual update (2027) |
| 5 (PO-019) | Novel-food procedure in the decree implementing the new law: a "not novel" determination on request; a traditional-food lane with a fixed objection window; a reliance lane for foods approved by two or more reference regulators; full assessment by recognised assessment units with a public positive list | MOH; Government | Decree replacing Decree 15/2018 | Thai assessment units; EU traditional-food notification; Decree 43/2026 fast-track | Medium | Drafting from 2026; in force 2027 to 2028 (after the law is voted, May 2027 session) |

Sources: [@REG2-01; @REG2-04; @REG2-05; @REG2-11; @REG-18; @REG-23; @REG-32; @REG-33; @REG2-26; @APR-07; @LBL-10] {VN-direct\|Medium}.

**Why these first.** Option 1 only works while the law is being drafted and debated: first comments at the October 2026 session, revision between readings and a vote considered at the May 2027 session [@APR-07] {VN-direct|Medium}. The clause needs to be in the revised draft by early 2027. Options 3 and 4 fix ambiguities that became costly once Decree 211/2026 introduced fines of VND 10 to 20 million per unlisted material, plus one to three months' suspension ([[ch07-rules]]). Option 2 removes the biggest legal unknown for precision fermentation at the cost of a letter.

### Tier 2: moderate effort, high value (2027 to 2028)

| Rank | Option | Owner | Instrument | Effort | Timeline |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 (PO-020) | One supervised novel-food pilot in the Hanoi sandbox, with MOH in the appraisal; in parallel a decree naming MOH as approving agency for food tests under the Law on Science, Technology and Innovation | Hanoi People's Committee; MOST; MOH | Hanoi decision; Government decree | Medium | 6 to 12 months (Hanoi); 12 to 24 months (national) |
| 7 (PO-021) | Publicly funded feed trials of microbial protein in whiteleg shrimp, pangasius, broilers and pigs, run as state science tasks so results qualify for the state-research exemption from separate trials | MAE; MOST | S&T task; Law on Animal Husbandry Art 37(2) | Medium | 12 to 24 months |
| 8 (PO-022) | Publish the timeline, fee and issuing level of the closed-production GMO certificate, with a model form for industrial fermentation strains | MAE | Guidance note | Low | 3 months |
| 9 (PO-023) | Tax guidance confirming that precision-fermentation and biomass-fermentation plants qualify as high-technology projects, and clarifying the agricultural raw-material test for fermentation on cassava or sugar | MOF (Tax Department); MOST | Guidance letter | Low | 3 to 6 months |
| 10 (PO-026) | Shared food-grade pilot fermentation line plus a tolling programme on existing industrial tanks | MOST; MAE; Ho Chi Minh City; Saigon Hi-Tech Park or FIRI | S&T programme or city investment | High | 24 to 36 months |
| 11 (PO-031) | Shift biomanufacturing support towards capital grants, loan guarantees and feedstock-cost support | MOF; MOST | Investment-support decrees | Medium | 12 to 24 months |
| 12 (PO-030) | Name alternative protein and biomanufacturing as priorities in the national, Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi venture funds, with a first-loss window for pilot plants | MOF; MOST; city People's Committees | Fund charters under Decree 264/2025 | Low | 6 to 12 months |

Sources: [@REG2-11; @REG2-12; @REG2-13; @REG2-14; @REG-47; @RGN-01; @CAP-29; @CAP-32; @CAP-34; @INF-02; @INF-06] {VN-direct\|Medium}.

### Tier 3: supporting options

| Rank | Option | Owner | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| 13 (PO-027) | Accredit amino-acid and protein-digestibility (DIAAS or PDCAAS) testing at a national reference laboratory, with phytate, zinc and iron analysis (phytate-to-mineral molar ratios), because plant zinc and iron are poorly absorbed and school guidance rates diets by them | MOH (NIFC); MAE (FIRI NACEFA) | Medium |
| 14 (PO-028) | Yearly national by-product atlas | MAE; National Statistics Office | Low |
| 15 (PO-029) | Input-VAT neutrality for new feed ingredients | MOF | Medium |
| 16 (PO-024) | Codex priority allergens on labels; on names, keep the permissive regime (no rule reserves meat or milk words) and issue guidance on neutral state vocabulary for new foods, not a naming rule | MOST with MOH | Low |
| 17 (PO-009) | Name alternative and novel protein ingredients in biotechnology programmes | MOST; MAE; MOH | Low |
| 18 (PO-007) | Provincial one-stop desks and published target timelines for feed procedures now decentralised to provinces | Provincial People's Committees | Low |
| 19 (PO-013) | Transition rules in the new Food Safety Law that protect existing self-declared products | MOH | Low |
| 20 (PO-032) | Publish grid emission factors for 2024 and 2025; signal capacity-charge levels early | MAE; MOIT | Low |
| 21 (PO-011) | Simplified access and benefit-sharing procedure and model contracts for public microbial collections | MAE; VAST; VNU; FIRI | Low |
| 22 (PO-033) | Pilot-plant access and regulatory cooperation with Thailand and Singapore | MOST; MOH; Ministry of Foreign Affairs | Low |
| 23 (PO-014) | Co-lead ASEAN work on common principles and reliance for novel foods | MOH; MOST | High |
| 24 (PO-025) | Review MFN import duties on food protein inputs not made in Vietnam at scale (wheat gluten 10%, protein concentrates 5%); these fall only on non-FTA origins, chiefly the United States, since Chinese and ASEAN product enters at 0% | MOF | Low |

Sources: `policy_options.csv`; for the changes to options 13, 16 and 24 [@NQR-16; @NQR-20; @LBL-06; @LBL-09; @FTR-32] {VN-direct\|Medium}. The remaining wave-1 options (PO-001 to PO-006, PO-008, PO-010, PO-012) are kept in the data file and superseded by the more specific options above.

{{chart:chart-policy-effort-impact}}

## 27.3 Trade-offs to weigh

- **Speed against caution.** A reliance lane (option 5) speeds access for foods approved elsewhere but imports other regulators' judgements. Limiting it to two or more reference regulators and keeping a veto for Vietnamese-specific concerns (diet patterns, allergens) is a common middle path.
- **Gate against open door.** Today, new protein foods enter through self-declaration with legal uncertainty ([[ch07-rules]]). A new procedure adds a gate for genuinely new ingredients. If it lacks timelines and assessor capacity, it could slow products that are legal today. Transition rules (PO-013) and a "not novel" determination reduce that risk.
- **Tariffs.** The trade-off is smaller than it looked. Chinese, ASEAN and Korean textured protein, isolates and gluten already enter at 0% under ACFTA, ATIGA, AKFTA and RCEP, and Chinese and ASEAN yeast and single-cell protein too, so the MFN duties protect a domestic textured-protein play (T1) or local yeast producers only against the United States and other non-FTA origins [@FTR-32; @FTR-33] {VN-direct|Medium}. Cutting them would change little for most buyers; raising them would not reach Chinese product.
- **Fermentation GMO status.** A light-touch reading for purified proteins (option 2) follows the product-based logic Decree 43/2026 already applies, but some consumers and trading partners may expect GM labelling. The mandatory label already applies only above 5% of ingredients and not where the gene and its product cannot be detected, so low-dose uses such as lactoferrin (about 0.08% of a formula) are outside it; the open question is high-inclusion uses [@LBL-10; @LBL-25] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Public money.** A pilot line (PO-026) is the one large public outlay. The case rests on use by several firms and research groups; without an anchor host and operator it risks becoming an idle asset, as has happened elsewhere.

## 27.4 Who does what

| Agency | Top actions |
|---|---|
| Ministry of Health (Vietnam Food Administration; NIFC) | Delegation clause and novel-food decree (1, 5); joint PF note (2); transition rules; protein-quality laboratory |
| Ministry of Agriculture and Environment (livestock and fisheries departments; biodiversity) | Aquafeed and livestock list fixes (3, 4); public feed trials (7); closed-production certificate guidance (8); by-product atlas; emission factors |
| Ministry of Science and Technology | Sandbox decree (6); high-tech criteria; pilot-line programme; allergen list and naming guidance; regional cooperation |
| Ministry of Finance | Tax guidance (9); incentive design (11); fund priorities (12); VAT neutrality; tariff review |
| Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi and cassava provinces (Tay Ninh and the Central Highlands) | City venture funds; sandbox; pilot-line host; co-location of fermentation with starch |
| National Assembly | Delegation clause between first comments (October 2026 session) and the vote considered at the May 2027 session |

After the 2025 mergers, one ministry (MAE) holds feed, aquafeed, GMO biosafety and genetic resources, and one (MOST) holds standards, the sandbox, high-tech status and IP, which makes coordination simpler than before ([[ch07-rules]], [[app-s10-admin-map]]).

## 27.5 What this means

- **Policy makers:** options 1 to 4 cost little, need no new agency and should be acted on in 2026 and 2027. Option 1 closes once the law is passed; the vote is considered at the May 2027 session, so the clause must be in the draft revised between readings, by early 2027.
- **International bodies:** the most useful support is technical: drafting help for the novel-food decree (through regulator-to-regulator agreements), funding for public feed trials and the protein-quality laboratory, and co-funding of a pilot line.
- **Research bodies:** options 7, 13 and 14 are research-led public goods; proposals ready before the next funding round will move faster.
- **Investors and companies:** track options 1 to 5 as signposts ([[ch19-outlook-2035]]). A written ministry opinion on your specific ingredient is still the cheapest risk reduction available today.

**Related:** [[app-s9-regulation]] (full legal register and route-by-route tables), [[ch07-rules]], [[brief-policy]], [[brief-international]].

data.title: Robust moves: what to do now that pays off in any 2050
data.summary: Testing 21 candidate moves against four possible worlds in 2050 gives nine no-regret moves that pay off in all of them, such as a national protein and feed balance, a feed-efficiency programme and shared pilot capacity. Most are public and cheap and can start in 2026 to 2028, while four bets should wait for named signposts.
data.body:
# 28. Robust moves: what to do now that pays off in any 2050

**In one paragraph.** A scenario set is useful only if it changes what people do today. We tested 21 candidate moves, drawn from the policy options and plays and from the futures research, against the four worlds of [[ch23-scenarios-2050]]. Nine are no-regret: they pay off whichever world arrives, most are public goods, and most can start in 2026 to 2028 at modest cost. Six are options: cheap to hold now, valuable in some worlds. Four are bets that should wait for named signposts, because they pay off in one world and lose money in others. Two are hedges that limit the damage of the bad worlds. The single strongest lever in the evidence, feed efficiency and formulation, is not an alternative-protein technology at all; it is the base on which every alternative protein will be sold.

> **Method note.** A move is **no-regret** if it pays off in all four worlds; an **option** if it is cheap to hold and pays off strongly in at least one; a **bet** if it needs a large commitment and pays off in only one or two; a **hedge** if its main value is limiting losses in the stressed worlds. This follows the EU Joint Research Centre's stress test, which found 8 of 29 policy challenges common to all four of its scenarios; we treat such items as no-regret [@VIS-35] {general|High}. Each classification is our judgement {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate}. Full table: `robust_moves.csv`.

---

## 28.1 Nine no-regret moves

| Move | What it involves | Lead actors | Start by | Why it pays off everywhere |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RM-01 Publish a national protein and feed balance** | Yearly balance of feed protein by source and origin, with soybean-meal inclusion and feed conversion by species | MAE; NSO; feed association | 2028 | The two largest levers in the balance model are unmeasured; every tracked foreign target has a statistic [@VIS-15; @VIS-13] {general\|Medium} |
| **RM-02 Feed-efficiency and formulation programme** | Amino acids, low-protein diets, precision feeding, by-product meals, feed-conversion benchmarks; soybean-meal inclusion falling 1 to 2% a year (relative) | MAE; integrators; feed mills; universities | 2027 | At 1% a year, with faster feed-conversion gains, cuts 2050 soybean-meal need by about 3.4 Mt in our balance model (QNT-model); China's relative decline since 2017 was about 1 to 3% a year, depending on the data series (our calculation) [@GEO-10; @GEO-11] {general\|Medium} {fx:estimate} |
| **RM-03 New-food and new-feed-ingredient routes with deadlines** | A new-food procedure with statutory timelines and reliance on reference regulators; aquafeed entries for microbial biomass and algal oils | MOH; MAE | 2027 to 2028 | Needed to import approved ingredients as well as to make them; the Food Safety Law window is open now [@REG-12; @REG2-01] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| **RM-04 Shared pilot and feed-trial capacity** | 10,000 to 30,000 L of open, food-grade pilot fermentation; public tank and pond trials | MOST; Ho Chi Minh City; universities; DFIs | 2030 | Rivals site pilot capacity in designated zones (Thailand's EECi has two 15,000 L fermenters); we found none open in Vietnam [@RGN-36; @FTB-42; @INF-02; @INF-05] {VN-adjacent\|Medium} |
| **RM-05 Protein-quality laboratory and open price series** | Accredited testing for protein quality, authenticity and contaminants; a public price and cost series | MOST; MAE; a university | 2028 | Imports and domestic products need the same checks; adulteration is a listed wildcard ([[app-f2-drivers-signals]]); none of the Vietnamese laboratory pages we read lists amino-acid digestibility tests [@INF-03; @INF-10; @INF-11; @INF-13; @INF-14] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| **RM-06 Residue-carbon rules and a by-product atlas** | Mapped volumes of cassava pulp, straw, stillage and brewery streams; collection contracts; feed-safety rules for side streams that match export-market rules | MAE; provinces; industry | 2028 | Straw must be fully collected on 1 million ha by 2030; EU feed law bans some waste streams [@NTS-32; @NGF-14] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| **RM-07 Omega-3 sourcing plan for aquafeed** | Qualify algal and oilseed omega-3 oils in shrimp and marine-fish feeds; track EPA plus DHA needs | Feed mills; MAE; research institutes | 2028 | Omega-3 is a tighter constraint than protein (our judgement), and the alternatives are commercial [@AQF-16; @AQF-19; @AQF-23] {general\|Medium} |
| **RM-08 Climate-proof siting** | Raised sites and surface water in the Mekong; process designs for cooling water at 40 °C | Provinces; MAE; investors | 2027 | Subsidence of about 1.1 cm a year; plants built after 2035 in coastal Ca Mau or Vinh Long face flood risk in their lifetime (our inference, as is the 40 °C design value) [@CLM-13; @CLM-14; @CLM-16] {VN-direct\|Medium} {fx:projection} |
| **RM-09 Process-engineering skills** | Fermentation operators and senior process engineers; industry placements | MOET; MOST; universities; industry | 2027 | Senior biotechnology talent is the named bottleneck; graduate targets already exist [@ECF-39; @ECF-41] {VN-direct\|Medium} |

{{kn:kn-no-regret-moves}}

**The public-good plays fold in.** Of the public-good plays P1 to P6 ([[ch26-plays]]), P1 and P2 become RM-03; P3 sits in RM-02 and RM-04; P4 and P6 become RM-05; P5 becomes RM-06. All six were already scored no-regret or robust in [[ch23-scenarios-2050]]; the related policy options are in [[ch27-policy-options]].

## 28.2 Six options: cheap to hold

| Move | What it involves | Pays off most in | Start by | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RM-10 Reserve hub sites** | Name fermentation and feed-protein sites in the MAE biotechnology-cluster plan (due December 2026) and in provincial hi-tech agriculture zones | A, C (D partly) | 2026 to 2027 | The bioeconomy map is still blank; provinces can now create hi-tech agriculture zones themselves [@HUB-09; @HUB-26; @NTS-37] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| **RM-11 Small permanent protein-innovation fund** | USD 5 to 15 M a year, reviewed each five-year plan | A, C; useful in all | 2027 | Denmark about USD 12 M, Germany about EUR 6 M (its protein-crop strategy) and Canada about USD 22 M (a plant-protein supercluster) a year; Denmark and Canada annualised by us from multi-year totals [@VIS-01; @VIS-24; @VIS-06] {general\|Medium} |
| **RM-12 Concessional finance window** | DFI co-finance and guarantees with a feed-mill offtake, ready to open when a signpost trips | C, D | 2028 (ready) | Cutting the capital charge from 12% to 9% does as much as the cost learning expected by 2030 (our calculation) {VN-direct\|Low} {fx:estimate} |
| **RM-13 Join regional approval and statistics networks** | Take part in any ASEAN reliance work and in the EU-style balance-sheet method | A, C | 2027 | Reliance is how smaller regulators keep pace (our judgement) {general\|Low}; the EU is developing harmonised feed and food protein balance sheets [@VIS-15] {general\|Medium} |
| **RM-14 Seed research on cultivated seafood cells and gas fermentation** | Small programmes with foreign partners on Vietnamese species and gas-fermentation strains | A, C | 2028 | Vietnam has 2 of 494 gas-fermentation papers (OpenAlex, September 2026) [@FTG-14] {VN-direct\|High} |
| **RM-15 Clear rules for second-hand fermentation equipment** | Customs and tax treatment; a register of available used tanks, 2027 to 2030 | C (A and D partly) | 2027 | Meati's assets sold for USD 75,000 against an estimated USD 15 to 20 M original spend [@FTB-38] {general\|Medium} |

{{kn:kn-capital-charge-lever}}

## 28.3 Four bets, each with a trigger

| Bet | Pays off in | Trigger before scaling | Why wait |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RM-16 Bulk microbial feed-protein capacity beyond about 1% of feed protein** | C (D partly) | Fishmeal above USD 2,500 per t for 12 months, and pilot cost within 1.2 times fishmeal-protein parity | The highest share we found is 0.4% novel ingredients in Norwegian salmon feed (2020) [@VIS-18] {general\|Medium} |
| **RM-17 Protein-from-power demonstration on the Mekong shrimp coast** | C (A partly) | Delivered green hydrogen below USD 2 per kg and firm renewable power below USD 45 per MWh | The five conditions of [[ch21-frontier-technology]]; the flagship hydrogen plant had only a fence, gate and part of its roads in May 2026 [@HUB-05] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| **RM-18 Contract precision-fermentation plant for export** | A (C partly) | A new-food route, an ASEAN reliance mechanism or regional capacity outside China, and an anchor customer | Works today only for high-value proteins [@FTB-41] {general\|Medium} |
| **RM-19 Cellulosic sugar from rice straw** | C (A partly) | An Asian straw plant above 80% of design capacity for a full year (our threshold) | Every US and European commercial plant has shut (Brazil's Raizen plant still runs); India's reached 62% [@NGF-11; @NGF-33] {general\|Medium} |

Triggers map to the signposts in `signposts_2050.csv`. A bet placed before its trigger trips is a speculative investment, not a policy.

## 28.4 Two hedges

- **RM-20 Diversified feed-protein sourcing and working stocks.** Multi-origin contracts, formulation flexibility and stocks of soybean meal and fishmeal sized to recent shocks. The 2026 Middle East conflict helped raise Vietnamese feed prices 10 to 14% between January and April 2026 (poultry association estimate) [@MAC-24; @COST-33] {VN-direct|Medium}. Protects against worlds C and D; costs little in A and B.
- **RM-21 Import monitoring and equal standards for protein imports.** Track volumes and unit values of microbial and fermented protein imports, and apply the same feed-safety and quality rules to imports and domestic products. No baseline series exists today {VN-direct|Low}. Limits the damage of a dumping episode in worlds B and D without closing the market.

{{chart:chart-robust-moves}}

## 28.5 Sequencing: the first three years

> **For policy makers.** Between September 2026 and the end of 2028, eight of the nine no-regret moves can start with existing institutions and modest budgets, alongside one cheap option. In order of urgency: (1) a new-food route in the Food Safety Law and its decree (RM-03, 2026 to 2027); (2) named sites in the MAE biotechnology-cluster plan (RM-10, an option, December 2026); (3) a feed-efficiency and formulation programme under the existing feed scheme (RM-02, 2027); (4) climate-proof siting rules for new plants (RM-08, 2027); (5) a skills programme linked to Decision 1002 (RM-09, 2027); (6) a first protein and feed balance (RM-01, 2028); (7) a by-product atlas and residue rules (RM-06, 2028); (8) a protein-quality laboratory and open price series (RM-05, 2028); (9) an omega-3 sourcing plan (RM-07, 2028). Shared pilot capacity (RM-04) follows by 2030.

## 28.6 By actor: the first move

| Actor | First move | Why first |
|---|---|---|
| MAE | Commission the protein and feed balance; add microbial biomass and algal oils to the aquafeed lists | The statistic enables every target; the lists are the cheapest route opening |
| MOH | A new-food procedure with timelines and reliance | The one window that closes (2026 to 2027) |
| MOST and Ho Chi Minh City | An open food-grade pilot plant | Rivals already have one |
| MOF and DFIs | A ready-to-open concessional window | Cheaper capital does as much as the learning expected by 2030 |
| Provinces (Tay Ninh, Ca Mau, Vinh Long, Dong Thap, Can Tho) | Raised, surface-water sites and residue-collection contracts | Land and water decide 25-year plant economics |
| Feed mills and integrators | Share anonymised inclusion and conversion data; qualify one non-marine omega-3 oil | The largest lever is theirs |
| Investors | Underwrite robust plays; hold bets as options with named triggers | Returns depend on which world arrives |
| Startups | Species-specific functional feed ingredients on local carbon | Holds in every world |
| Research bodies | Measurement of feed conversion and inclusion; process know-how on local strains | Fills the two largest gaps in the evidence |
| International bodies | Technical help on the balance sheet and the review cycle | A public good others can use |

## 28.7 What we could not resolve

The futures round leaves open questions that decide which world is unfolding and how large the moves should be. The most important: the current status of Thai Duong Feed's yeast-protein line; Vietnamese time series of feed conversion and soybean-meal inclusion; the purity and volume of CO2 at named sites; whether full-scale fermentation plants qualify for hi-tech agriculture zone incentives; and whether NDC 3.0 will add agriculture or livestock caps for 2035. All are logged in [[app-r1-open-questions]] with the futures prefix, and disagreements between sources in [[app-r2-disagreements]].

**Related:** [[ch23-scenarios-2050]], [[ch24-vision-2050]], [[ch27-policy-options]], [[ch26-plays]].

data.title: What frontier actors asked, and what the answers changed
data.summary: We checked the demand chapters against 80 named actors, from funders to food makers and regulators, and follow-up research changed how to act: schools fill plant-protein days with tofu, and only four of the original nineteen demand moves have a funder that fits and accepts Vietnam. The core conclusion stands: demand pulls new protein as an ingredient sold to incumbents.
data.body:
# 29. What frontier actors asked, and what the answers changed

**In one paragraph.** Part III was written for the people who could move alternative protein in Vietnam, so we asked whether it answers their questions. We named 80 real actors in four groups, read what each says it funds, buys, builds or regulates, turned that into 118 decision questions and checked each against Part III. It answered one in full and 71 in part; for most, the evidence behind the answer was weak or missing. The gaps were of a kind: Part III sized channels and prices well but did not map who decides, which rules already exist, who would pay, who already competes, or what a deal would look like. We then ran sixteen research lines in three waves, each asking a different kind of question, and stopped when the next candidates would add citations without changing a decision. The core conclusion survives: demand pulls new protein as an ingredient inside familiar foods, sold to incumbents. What changed is how to act on it: schools already reserve plant-protein days that tofu fills; a domestic textured-protein line is a debt-financed import-substitution project with no tariff shelter; soy is the price a new extender must beat; most of the label rules Part III proposed are already law; a sugar tax may reach sweetened plant milks from 2027; and only four of the original nineteen demand moves have a funder whose rules fit and that accepts Vietnam.

The method, the yield of each line and the reasons for stopping are in [[app-m4-actor-check-waves]]. The corrections are folded into chapters 11 to 18 and 25, the briefs and the executive summaries.

## 29.1 Who we asked about

We identified 20 actors in each of four groups (listed in `actor_register.csv`) from their own documents: requests for proposals, strategy pages, annual reports and meeting documents, mostly from 2024 to 2026, and laws and programme documents, including older ones still in force [@AFN-05; @AIB-01; @APR-01] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:stated}. For each actor we wrote the demand questions it would need answered before acting in Vietnam, and checked Part III for an answer.

| Group | Examples | Questions | Answered | Partly | Not answered | Out of scope | High-value questions |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Funders and field-builders | Coefficient Giving, Nova Vista, GFI and GFI APAC, Bezos Centre at NUS, ARE, FAIRR, Humane World, Lever, ACE | 30 | 0 | 19 | 10 | 1 | 12 |
| Investors and startups | Temasek and Nurasa, AgFunder, Better Bite, VinaCapital, Mekong Capital, IFC, ADB Ventures, TiNDLE, Green Rebel, Vietnamese founders | 25 | 1 | 19 | 3 | 2 | 13 |
| Incumbents and first buyers | Vinamilk, QNS and Vinasoy, Masan, Vissan, CJ, C.P., Acecook, Ajinomoto, Saigon Co.op, WinCommerce, industrial caterers | 30 | 0 | 16 | 14 | 0 | 10 |
| Policy, research and international bodies | Ministry of Health, National Institute of Nutrition, Ministry of Education, MAE, UNICEF, FAO, WHO, World Bank, ADB, CGIAR | 33 | 0 | 17 | 15 | 1 | 11 |
| **All** | **80 actors** | **118** | **1** | **71** | **42** | **4** | **46** |

Source: `actor_register.csv`, `actor_questions.csv`; our assessment {VN-direct\|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

{{kn:kn-actor-check}}

{{chart:chart-actor-coverage}}

Across all 118 questions the evidence was moderate for 27, weak for 49 and absent for 42; none was strong. Of the 72 answered in full or in part, 26 had moderate evidence, 41 weak and 5 none (our assessment) {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:inferred}.

## 29.2 What Part III missed

The misses share a pattern. Each is a different kind of question from the ones Part III asked, not a harder version of them.

- **Decisions, not attitudes.** One market-shaping funder, Nova Vista, counts "an identifiable decision-maker, a reason they might move, and a window" [@AFN-05] {general|High} {dx:stated}. Part III sized canteens and schools but did not say who writes the menus, which rules govern them or when those rules change.
- **Rules already on the books.** Several moves Part III proposed (school guidance without an animal share, percentage labels on blends, chay definitions) turned out to exist already, and a new tax it did not see (the sugary-drink excise) bears on its one proven modern category.
- **Transactions, not pools.** Investors now favour "strong offtake agreements" and "contracted revenue" [@AIS-01] and "clearer unit economics" [@AIS-15] {general|Medium} {dx:stated}. Part III named likely first buyers from labels and trade data but had no price, cost, margin or order.
- **Who pays.** Part III told funders to fund measurement, without checking whose rules allow it.
- **Who competes.** Part III framed competition as Chinese commodity protein; regional suppliers and cheap domestic dry soy pieces already sit inside the channels it recommends.
- **Units.** Welfare and climate funders count animals and CO2e; Part III counted tonnes of protein.

## 29.3 What the answers changed

Sixteen lines followed (listed in `expansion_lines.csv`). These are the findings that change what an actor should do.

**Schools already have plant-protein days, and tofu fills them.** Part III said school meals follow an old target to raise the animal share of children's protein. That target (Decision 1340, 2016) ended in 2020 [@CHN-33] {VN-direct|High}. The Ministry of Health's school-meal guidance of December 2025 sets no animal share and asks for legumes or tofu at least twice a week [@APR-04; @AIB-39] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. In 48 published school-weeks from Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi and Hai Phong, plant protein appeared on 15.1% of days, 9 weeks met the rule (our audit, `school_menu_weeks.csv`), tofu was served beside meat, and no dish used textured soy or mock meat [@PMR-10; @PMR-31] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. The menu software schools use still prints an "animal protein at least 48%" standard [@PMR-26] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. So a plant ingredient in the plant slot competes with tofu and replaces tofu, not meat; the only school route that removes meat is a labelled blend in minced-meat and fish-cake dishes (our reading of the menu audit, `school_menu_weeks.csv`) [@PMR-10; @PMR-31]; and the rule window is the School Health Programme 2026 to 2035 and the menu tools that follow it [@APR-12; @AFN-44] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. {{kn:kn-school-plant-days}} ([[ch15-channels]])

**The Food Safety Law window runs into 2027.** The National Assembly takes first comments in October 2026 and considers passage in May 2027 [@APR-07] {VN-direct|Medium}. Every supply-side and demand-side recommendation tied to "the October to November 2026 session" now has until early 2027 ([[ch07-rules]], [[ch27-policy-options]]).

**A domestic textured-protein line is an import-substitution project, not a venture thesis.** Chinese, ASEAN and Korean textured protein, isolates and gluten enter duty-free under ACFTA, ATIGA, AKFTA and RCEP [@FTR-32; @FTR-33] {VN-direct|Medium}. Chinese textured-soy lines are listed at USD 11,000 to 100,000 [@TIC-02; @TIC-03; @TIC-07] {general|Low}; installed in Vietnam a line costs about USD 0.3 to 1.4 million, and working capital is the larger need (our calculation, `t1_margin_payback.csv`) {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. Whether it pays turns on the delivered price of food-grade soy flour, which we could not verify [@TIC-12; @TIC-13] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. The benchmark path supports about one line by 2035. The natural owner is a chay maker, co-packer or distributor with buyers, financed by bank debt and trade finance. {{kn:kn-fta-duty-china}} ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]])

**Soy, not meat, is the price a new extender must beat.** Replacing a fifth of the lean in *chả lụa* (Vietnamese pork roll) with hydrated textured soy saved money at every annual hog price from 2019 to 2024 (our calculation from FAOSTAT hog prices and the Comtrade unit value of textured protein), so processors already own the cheapest extender [@DIE-25; @TIC-12] {VN-direct|Low} {dx:inferred}. A fungal or novel extender must replace more meat unnoticed than soy, or carry a label buyers prefer. No national standard sets a minimum meat content, and a named meat must already be quantified on the label under Decree 43/2017, a rule Decree 37/2026 probably carries over [@LBL-11; @LBL-12; @LBL-13; @LBL-06; @LBL-07; @LBL-08] {VN-direct|High}. What buyers punish is hidden cost-cutting, called *độn* (filler), not a declared ingredient [@TRU-02; @TRU-03; @TRU-22] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed} ([[ch14-frontier-demand]]).

**Most of the label moves are already law.** A high-protein claim needs 10 g per 100 g, or 5 g per 100 kcal, under a voluntary Codex-based standard [@LBL-03] {VN-direct|High}; the national vegetarian standard allows egg, milk and honey [@LBL-15] {VN-direct|High}; no rule reserves the words for meat or milk [@LBL-06]; and the GMO label applies only above 5% of ingredients, so lactoferrin-type uses are not caught [@LBL-10] {VN-direct|Medium}. The remaining asks are enforcement, one definition (unqualified chay should mean vegan) and one agency ruling on recombinant proteins ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).

**A sugar tax may reach plant milks.** From 2027 drinks above 5 g sugar per 100 ml pay an 8% excise (10% from 2028) and dairy is exempt [@FTR-01; @FTR-05] {VN-direct|High}. Whether soy and nut milks are in scope is unresolved. New plant milks and the isolates that go into them should be designed at or below 5 g ([[ch13-consumers]]).

**Retailers' own labels are a route to shelf; corporate pledges are not a volume lever.** Saigon Co.op's Co.op Select chay line is made by a named co-packer, so a protein upgrade can reach shelf without a consumer brand [@CPC-15; @AIB-28] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Only one published corporate commitment binds Vietnamese units (Accor's 50% vegetarian or plant-based dishes by 2030, which counts dishes, not protein), and we found no Vietnamese protein buyer with a published target [@AFN-40; @AFN-18; @AFN-21] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed} ([[ch15-channels]], [[ch16-business-buyers]]).

**Feed demand is revealed but priced low.** Vietnam imported about 9,200 t of inactive yeast (food and feed together) in 2025, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg, while the ASC feed standard neither requires nor rewards microbial protein and the BAP feed-mill standard only lets aquatic-microorganism meal count towards its marine-ingredient target [@FBA-17; @FBA-01; @FBA-05] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. A Vietnamese microbial feed ingredient must win head to head against the yeast mills already buy ([[ch17-export-demand]]).

**The export base is wrapped foods.** Vietnam exported USD 128 million of dumplings and other stuffed pasta in 2023, against almost no textured protein [@XBA-29; @XBA-28] {VN-direct|High} {dx:revealed}. European retailers' protein targets are flat and met with European products; the buyers are importers and brand owners who require IFS or BRCGS certification. For dumplings (Chapter 19), rules of origin bind on imported flour in the wrapper, not on the soy in the filling, so they give domestic textured soy no export customer [@ORG-01] {VN-direct|High} ([[ch17-export-demand]]).

**For school-age children protein is not the gap.** Stunting among children under five is 18% (2023) and 32% among ethnic minority children [@APR-27] {VN-direct|High}, but it is a problem of the youngest children. In 13 upland boarding schools, lunches and dinners carried meat, fish or egg in 240 of 242 published meals, while 95 of 111 breakfasts had little or no animal food (our menu audit, `upland_school_weeks.csv`) [@UPL-01; @UPL-02; @UPL-03; @UPL-05; @UPL-06; @UPL-07; @UPL-08; @UPL-09; @UPL-10; @UPL-11; @UPL-12; @UPL-13; @UPL-14; @UPL-15; @UPL-16; @UPL-17] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. Weighed boarding diets met protein and zinc but fell short on calcium and vitamin A [@UPL-18] {VN-direct|Medium} {dx:revealed}. A plant product is not the answer to a school protein gap that does not exist ([[ch11-protein-diet]]).

**Only four of the original nineteen demand moves have a payer.** A new USD 10 million market-shaping request for proposals excludes whole-food plant-based work, culture change and individual diet change, and wants more policy staff especially in high-innovation Asian economies such as Japan and Korea [@AFN-05] {general|High} {dx:stated}; the 2026 regional diet-change fund published no Vietnam application guide [@AFN-29] {VN-direct|Medium}; the leading animal charity evaluator's grants now exclude diet change [@FUF-01] {general|Medium}. In funder units, the benchmark path spares about 2.4 to 2.7 million animals a year by 2035, nearly all chickens and ducks, and avoids about 0.14 Mt CO2e; import substitution spares none (our estimate) {VN-direct|Low} {fx:estimate} {dx:inferred}. {{kn:kn-funder-fit}} {{kn:kn-animals-spared-2035}} ([[ch18-demand-sizing]])

**The regional firm record favours familiar foods sold to others.** Of 24 alternative-protein firms in Vietnam and the region since 2019 in our register (`firm_outcomes.csv`, our calculation), 7 are active, 4 pivoted (three of them towards private label, co-manufacturing or non-food), 2 exited and 11 are dormant (no news found, not proof of closure); none of the 4 Vietnam-based meat-analogue makers is active, while all 3 Vietnam-founded makers of traditional formats are {VN-adjacent|Low} {dx:revealed}. One dormant firm has an unknown first channel, so the channel rows in [[app-d4-channels]] sum to 23 firms and 10 dormant. TiNDLE's move to private label [@AIS-28] and Karana's regional expansion [@BRD-08] are examples, not the source of the counts. No founder has yet tried selling an ingredient to incumbents, so that route is the hypothesis to test.

> **Correction.** In v0.6 this paragraph said all four pivots moved towards private label, co-manufacturing or non-food, and cited two news items for the firm counts; the counts come from our register, where three of the four pivots moved that way (Eat Just relaunched a retail product under its own brand).

## 29.4 What each actor should take away

- **Funders and field-builders:** fund what fits your unit and your rules. Welfare funders: canteen menus with Humane World, which trained chefs and nutritionists in Viet Nam in 2025 [@AFN-23] {VN-direct|Medium}. Market-shaping funders: procurement of a canteen protein ingredient and the naming and GMO rules. R&D funders: ingredient function and Vietnamese sensory tests. National survey budgets, not philanthropy, should carry the chay-day survey question. See [[brief-international]].
- **Investors:** treat domestic textured protein as debt-financed import substitution with a flour-price kill test, and price blends against soy. Pitch import substitution to development finance on the import bill, not on climate. See [[brief-investors]].
- **Startups:** sell a familiar food with little capital, aim first for ingredient, private-label or co-packing supply, and bring a chay maker or distributor in as co-owner or anchor buyer. See [[brief-startups]].
- **Manufacturers and retailers:** you already own the cheapest extender and the private-label route; test a protein upgrade through a co-packer, and design plant milks at or below 5 g sugar. See [[brief-manufacturers]].
- **Policy makers:** use the School Health Programme to put protein quality, zinc and iron (not an animal share) into the menu software; enforce the label rules that exist; rule on plant milks and the excise before 2027. See [[brief-policy]].
- **Research bodies:** measure protein quality and zinc in tofu, textured soy and blends; run an equal-saving blind test of a fungal extender against soy. See [[brief-research]].

## 29.5 What the desk could not answer

The questions that now decide most need a call, a quote, a trial or purchased data, not more reading. The full list is in [[app-r1-open-questions]] (OQ-270 onwards) and [[app-m4-actor-check-waves]].

| Question | Why it matters | Who can answer |
|---|---|---|
| The delivered price of food-grade defatted soy flour | Decides whether a domestic textured-protein line pays | Five flour suppliers, through a partner buyer |
| Would three chay makers sign conditional orders at Chinese parity? | Turns the T1 market pull into offtake | Chay makers and ingredient distributors |
| Is the menu software's 48% animal-protein standard a default or a hard check, and does its food list include textured soy? | Decides whether a plant ingredient can be written into school menus | MOET, Ajinomoto, National Institute of Nutrition |
| Are sweetened soy and nut milks *nước giải khát* under the excise? | Sets plant-milk prices from 2027 | Ministry of Finance, Tax Policy Department |
| Would Saigon Co.op list a 10 g per 100 g version of a private-label chay dish? | Tests the cheapest route to shelf | Co.op private-label team with its co-packer |
| Does a fungal extender beat the processor's own soy recipe at equal saving? | Decides whether novel extenders have a job | Two processors and a sensory laboratory |
| Who would fund a Vietnamese canteen trial? | The welfare route has no payer today | Humane World Viet Nam, Coefficient Giving, the Navigation Fund |
| Which mills import feed yeast, and would they trial a Vietnamese product against it? | Names T2's buyers | Customs declaration data; mill nutritionists |

## 29.6 Where we stopped

Wave 7 ran six lines and all six changed something. Wave 8 ran six and five did. Wave 9 ran four: none changed a conclusion in Part III, one corrected a wave 8 proposal, one added a constraint and two were clean negatives. Every remaining candidate was either a deeper version of a question already answered or needed a method other than desk research. The signal came, as in earlier rounds, from asking different kinds of question rather than the same question harder. Details are in [[app-m4-actor-check-waves]].

data.title: What we do not know, and who can tell us
data.summary: Desk research has reached diminishing returns. The twenty unknowns that matter most can mostly be closed by a letter to a ministry, a phone call to a feed mill or a query to customs. We list them in priority order, with the play each one unblocks and who to ask. The full register holds 446 open questions and 352 recorded disagreements between sources.
data.body:
# 30. What we do not know, and who can tell us

**In one paragraph.** This report was built from public sources over ten research rounds, and by the end each new search added little. The remaining gaps are of a different kind: they sit in ministry files, company plants and customs records, not on the open web. Most can be closed cheaply, by a written question to a ministry, a call to a feed mill's technical manager or a customs data request. We list the twenty that matter most, ranked by how much they would change a decision in this report, with the play they unblock ([[ch26-plays]]) and who to ask. The full register holds 446 open questions (`open_questions.csv`) and 352 disagreements between sources, each with the position we took (`disagreements.csv`).

> **Demand questions.** Part III adds 114 demand-side open questions (OQ-156 to OQ-269, [[app-r1-open-questions]]). The ones that most change the demand picture are how many people keep chay days, how much meat is eaten as processed products, protein per canteen meal, the food and feed split of plant-protein imports, and any tested Vietnamese evidence on willingness to pay and names ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).

---

## 30.1 The twenty unknowns that matter most

| # | Unknown | Unblocks | Who to ask, or the cheapest way to close it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Does the draft Food Safety Law (August 2026 version) define "new food" or "new food ingredient", or delegate that to the Government? | P1 and all food plays | Draft portal of the National Assembly; the WTO notification attachment; the Vietnam Food Administration's legal division |
| 2 | Do purified precision-fermented proteins need a GMO food-use certificate beyond labelling, and what is the closed-production certificate's timeline and fee? | T7 | Written question to the MAE Department of Nature Conservation and Biodiversity and to the Vietnam Food Administration |
| 3 | Is a livestock-listed raw material (yeast, duckweed, insect meal) legal in aquafeed without a trial, given the aquafeed list has no raw-material section? | T2, T3, T6 | Written opinion from the MAE Department of Fisheries (aquafeed division) |
| 4 | Will Vedan, Ajinomoto or Daesang toll-ferment for third parties, and how much tank time is idle? | T2, T3, T5 | Direct inquiry to their R&D and corporate planning teams |
| 5 | What fishmeal share do Vietnamese shrimp and pangasius feeds actually use? | T2, T3 | One call each to technical managers at Uni-President Vietnam, Sheng Long and Grobest, or the Research Institute for Aquaculture No. 2 |
| 6 | How much Chinese microbial protein enters Vietnamese feed, and at what price? | T2, T3 | Customs lines HS 2309.90 and 2102.20; a quote from the importer (V-Group / CK Vietnam) |
| 7 | Is any textured soy protein extruded in Vietnam, and by whom? | T1 | Ask *chay* makers where their textured protein comes from; ask ingredient distributors which brands they sell |
| 8 | Import volumes of textured protein, soy isolate and gluten at 8-digit level, 2024 to 2025 | T1 | Vietnam Customs statistics or a trade-data service |
| 9 | Gate price of cassava pulp, and how it is used (wet sale, drying, biogas, dumping) | T3, T4 | Calls to three to five Tay Ninh starch factories; the Vietnam Cassava Association |
| 10 | Current prices of cassava starch, glucose syrup and molasses in Vietnam | T4 | Vietnam Cassava Association; Vietnam Sugarcane and Sugar Association; starch factories |
| 11 | Official aquafeed output by species (industry 3.9 to 4.8 Mt against USDA 6.5 Mt) | Market sizing for T2, T3 | The MAE Department of Fisheries annual review (feed chapter) |
| 12 | Does the 2030 target of 30 to 32 Mt of industrial feed cover aquafeed? (Answered at Medium confidence: livestock feed only; [[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]) | Market sizing; policy | MAE Department of Livestock Production and Animal Health |
| 13 | Which Vietnamese laboratories hold amino-acid and digestibility methods in their accreditation scope? | P4, T1, T10 | NACEFA, NIFC, Eurofins Sac Ky Hai Dang, CASE; the national accreditation body's search |
| 14 | How much chiller energy does a Vietnamese aerobic fermentation plant use per m³ of broth? | All fermentation plays | Vedan, Ajinomoto or AB Mauri plant engineers |
| 15 | Can a product made in Vietnam be sold in Singapore under an SFA novel-food approval? | T7; Scenario 3 | Singapore Food Agency import and overseas-establishment rules |
| 16 | ScaleUp Bio's 2026 capacity, pricing and willingness to take Vietnamese clients | T5, T7 | ScaleUp Bio business development |
| 17 | Whether Thailand's EECi pilot plant is food-grade, its fees and foreign-client terms | T5, T7 | EECi pilot plant contacts |
| 18 | Where Vietnam's high-protein plant drinks source their pea protein | T10 | Vinamilk procurement or investor relations; customs consignee data |
| 19 | Does a new feed ingredient such as single-cell protein automatically count as "animal feed" (not subject to VAT)? | T2, T3 | General Department of Taxation |
| 20 | Are fermentation-derived ingredients made in Vietnam accepted as halal by Malaysian and Indonesian certifiers? | Export plays | HALCERT (under MOST); a Malaysian certifier |

Source: `open_questions.csv` (fields `priority_rank`, `unblocks`, `cheapest_way_to_close`, `owner_org_to_ask`) {VN-direct\|Medium}.

**Reading.** Items 1 to 3 are regulatory and time-sensitive: each could be settled by a single written reply, and together they decide whether most plays have a clear route. Items 4 to 10 decide the economics of T1 to T4 and need industry calls rather than more desk research. Items 11 and 12 affect how large the future feed-protein market looks.

## 30.2 Where sources disagree

We recorded 352 disagreements between sources and stated the position we took for each ([[app-r2-disagreements]]). The ones that most affect this report's conclusions:

| Topic | The disagreement | Position taken |
|---|---|---|
| Aquafeed volume | Industry 3.9 to 4.8 Mt (2025) against USDA 6.5 Mt | Unresolved; both shown, never averaged ([[ch01-why-vietnam]]) |
| Displaceable fishmeal pool | Earlier drafts 350 to 450 kt against 120 to 245 kt central | 120 to 245 kt; the higher range needs unsourced inclusion rates ([[ch26-plays]]) |
| Entobel financing | "About USD 36 million" against USD 32.5 million documented | USD 32.5 million ([[ch08-capital]]) |
| E10 start date | 1 January 2026 against 1 June 2026 | 1 June 2026; January was the circular's effective date ([[ch19-outlook-2035]]) |
| Fishmeal price | USD 1,600 per t (a trade quote) against USD 1,794 per t (World Bank, same month) | World Bank series as benchmark; the quote is probably a lower grade |
| Precision-fermentation titer benchmark | "Above 50 g/L" presented as a calculated threshold | An expert assertion, not a modelled figure ([[ch10-technology-fit]]) |
| Protein-ingredient import tonnage | Vietnam-reported against China-reported mirror data | China's mirror data for tonnage; Vietnam's weights are estimated ([[ch03-regional]]) |
| Hawkwood cost structure | Earlier drafts read model feedstock as 10 to 18% of cost against 30 to 65% in cited studies | No conflict: model feedstock is 37 to 56%, within the cited ranges, and 10 to 18% is depreciation; labour and power are a minor share ([[ch03-regional]]) |

## 30.3 Limits of this report

- **Tools.** The general web-search budget ran out part-way through the first wave. After that, research used direct reads of known pages, legal databases, scholarly indexes (Scite and OpenAIRE) and trade data (WITS). Some sources could not be reached; each is logged ([[app-m1-method]]).
- **Language.** Vietnamese-language legal texts and press were read directly. Vietnamese-language journals are only partly indexed, so Vietnamese research output is undercounted ([[ch06-knowledge-talent]]).
- **Field data.** The retail audit is a convenience sample of 186 products in 11 stores in two cities in September 2026 ([[app-s2-retail-audit]]).
- **Cost stacks.** Indicative, not feasibility studies ([[ch09-economics]]).
- **No interviews.** This draft relies on documents. The unknowns above are the agenda for a round of interviews.

## 30.4 How to help close the gaps

Readers who hold any of these answers (ministries, feed mills, starch factories, laboratories, investors) can help. AltProtein Vietnam will record corrections in `open_questions.csv` and `disagreements.csv` and date each change, so the website can show what has been closed since publication.

**Related:** [[app-r1-open-questions]] (all 446), [[app-r2-disagreements]] (all 352), [[app-m1-method]].

data.title: Brief for investors
data.summary: For venture capital, impact investors, private equity and development finance. The near-term theses are B2B and mostly not venture-shaped. Domestic textured plant protein is an import-substitution plant for a chay maker, co-packer or distributor, financed with debt, with no tariff shelter and a margin set by the soy-flour price. Functional microbial feed ingredients must beat the yeast that mills already import. Deal history is one insect-meal plant. Underwrite capital intensity, input prices and rule risk, price against Chinese imports, and plan for trade-sale exits.
data.body:
# Brief for investors

**The short version.** Vietnam has a real supply-side case for alternative protein (it runs a huge animal-protein economy on imported plant protein) but almost no deal history: one insect-meal plant has raised more than USD 5 million. The near-term theses that survive our tests are business-to-business, and neither is a classic venture deal. Domestic textured plant protein (T1) is an import-substitution plant best owned by a chay maker, co-packer or distributor and financed with debt; it has no tariff shelter, and the delivered price of soy flour decides its margin. Functional microbial feed ingredients for shrimp and pangasius (T2) must beat the inactive yeast that mills already import. Everything that relies on fermentation at scale is decided by capital cost, not by Vietnam's cheap labour and power, and must be priced against Chinese imports. Exits are trade sales.

## What you need to know

1. **One precedent.** Entobel's USD 32.5 million insect-meal plant was financed by Mekong Capital, Dragon Capital and a USD 2.5 million IFC ticket, with Vinh Hoan (a seafood exporter) as anchor buyer. B2B feed product, local private-equity lead, development finance alongside, a named offtake: that is the template ([[ch08-capital]]).
2. **Thin venture market for this sector.** Vietnam's venture capital was about USD 509 million in 2025, of which agriculture took about USD 1 million. No technology IPOs in five years; realistic exits are trade sales to strategics or private-equity buyouts ([[ch08-capital]]).
3. **Capital decides fermentation economics.** On our indicative stack, capital charges and maintenance are 54 to 67% of the cost of fungal feed protein, which lands at USD 4,050 to 14,700 per tonne of protein against USD 2,625 to 3,846 for fishmeal protein ([[ch09-economics]]).
4. **The competitor is Chinese by-product protein.** Bacterial biomass from Chinese amino-acid fermentation is already sold into Vietnamese feed [@FM-12], and Chinese microbial protein enters duty-free [@FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}; a Chinese yeast-protein plant runs at 11,000 t a year and a 20,000 t mycoprotein plant is under construction ([[ch03-regional]]).
5. **Rules: feed is open, food is uncertain.** Yeasts, duckweed, algae and insects are listed feed materials; bacterial and fungal biomass need trials; the aquafeed list has a drafting gap. For food, there is no route to positive clearance of a new ingredient, and precision-fermented proteins probably count as GMO products ([[ch07-rules]]).
6. **Watch October 2026 to May 2027.** The Food Safety Law revision is the event that most changes food-side risk. The National Assembly takes first comments at its October 2026 session and considers passage at the May 2027 session, so a new-food clause needs to be in the draft revised between the two sessions, in practice by early 2027 [@APR-07] {VN-direct|Medium} ([[ch19-outlook-2035]]).

## Theses and how to test them

| Play | Thesis | Diligence question (kill test) |
|---|---|---|
| T1 Domestic textured plant protein | An import-substitution ingredient plant replacing Chinese textured soy for *chay* and frozen-food makers, best owned by a chay maker, co-packer or distributor and financed with bank debt and trade finance, not venture equity. Installed capex about USD 0.3 to 1.4 million; working capital USD 0.6 to 3.5 million (our calculations); no intellectual property; it displaces almost no meat | Is food-grade defatted soy flour delivered below about USD 700 to 940 per t (1 t/h line at 70% utilisation)? Have at least three buyers placed conditional orders totalling 2,000 t a year? Does ex-factory cost beat Chinese textured protein (HS 2106.10), which left China at USD 1.24 per kg FOB in 2025 and lands at about USD 1.29 to 1.38 per kg with freight, port and inland costs (our calculation; duty 0% under ACFTA)? [@TIC-02; @TIC-12; @FTR-32] {VN-direct\|Low} |
| T2 Functional microbial feed ingredients | Sell survival and feed-efficiency gains at 1 to 5% inclusion to about six shrimp-feed makers and integrated pangasius groups | Do two independent tank or pond trials show a gain at 5% inclusion or less? Is there a written ministry opinion on aquafeed use? Is the delivered price at or below imported bulk yeast (about USD 1.1 per kg in 2025), or do head-to-head trials show a gain worth the difference (about 1.2 to 1.8% of shrimp-feed cost at 2% inclusion in the low-cost case)? Is there a named anchor buyer, as Vinh Hoan was for insect meal? [@FBA-17; @EXP-50] {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| T4 Cassava-starch-to-sugar hub | Keep the starch-to-glucose step in Vietnam and co-locate fermentation | Has a fermenter committed? Can sugar be contracted despite cassava volatility? |
| T3 Bulk fishmeal replacement | Only with near-free carbon, tolling or brownfield capex, and sustained high fishmeal prices | Is capex below about USD 6,000 per annual tonne? Will a mill sign at 70 to 90% of fishmeal-protein parity? |
| T7 Precision fermentation (niche) | High-value, low-dose ingredients made under contract abroad | Is the product economic at 1 to 10 g/L titers? Is freedom to operate clear? |

Full cards, scores and weights: [[ch26-plays]]. Use the "Investors" preset.

{{chart:chart-plays-scoring}}

## Who else is here

Local private equity (Mekong Capital, Dragon Capital), VinaCapital Ventures, the IFC, ADB Ventures (no Vietnamese agrifood deal yet), regional seed specialists (Better Bite Ventures, Big Idea Ventures, ProVeg Incubator), and new state venture funds in Ho Chi Minh City (VND 500 billion) and Hanoi (VND 230 billion). Strategic acquirers by fit include feed, dairy, seafood and amino-acid groups ([[ch08-capital]], [[app-s11-capital]], [[app-s1-directory]]).

## What would make this more investable

- A new-food procedure with timelines in the Food Safety Law and its decree ([[ch27-policy-options]], options 1 and 5).
- Aquafeed and livestock feed-list fixes (options 3 and 4).
- Tolling access to existing fermentation tanks or a shared pilot line (T5).
- A development-finance first-loss tranche for a first fermentation-feed plant, made on the feed case (T2) or, for T1, on the import and jobs case, not on a climate label.
- For T1: a delivered soy-flour price sheet and conditional orders from chay makers, which cost tens of hours and decide the kill test ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).

## The demand side

- **The revealed demand is business-to-business, and a soy line can serve only part of it.** Plant proteins shipped from China to Vietnam nearly tripled from 2019 to 2025, to about 54,000 t, but the rise is mostly HS 3504 protein substances at about USD 1 per kg, priced like feed or technical protein rather than food isolate. Textured-type imports, the pool a soy extrusion line can serve, were at most about 12,800 t in 2025 [@BUY-02; @TIC-12] {VN-direct|Medium}. Chay makers are the most switchable buyers ([[ch16-business-buyers]]).
- **Size on the import-substitution pool, not on consumer forecasts.** On the benchmark path the routes create demand for about 19,000 t of protein a year by 2035, of which about 11,000 to 17,000 t made in Vietnam for the home market. For soy extrusion that is about one 1 t/h line or two 0.5 t/h lines, not three to four; the rest is gluten and isolates, which need other plants (our calculation) {VN-direct|Low}. Published Vietnamese market sizes have no traceable method, and global forecasts from 2019 to 2021 overshot by 10 to 100 times ([[ch18-demand-sizing]]).
- **T1 has no tariff shelter, cheap equipment and one decisive input.** Chinese, ASEAN and Korean textured protein, isolates and gluten enter duty-free. Chinese extrusion lines are listed at USD 11,000 to 100,000, working capital is the larger need, and the delivered price of food-grade soy flour (63 to 85% of cost, our calculation, [[ch09-economics]]) sets the sign of the margin. Export origin rules give domestic textured soy no customer: a dumpling made with Chinese textured soy keeps its origin [@FTR-32; @TIC-02; @TIC-13; @ORG-01] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Feed demand is revealed but priced low.** Vietnam imported about 9,200 t of inactive yeast for food and feed in 2025, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg, and the leading aquafeed maker Skretting reached 1.5% novel ingredients in 2025, against a 5 to 10% target for its parent Nutreco, which reached 0.6% group-wide. Export feed standards do not require microbial protein and reward only algae and aquatic microorganisms (BAP) ([[ch17-export-demand]]) [@FBA-17; @FBA-07; @FBA-01; @FBA-05] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Price blends and plant milks against what incumbents already use.** Soy extension already pays at every annual hog price from 2019 to 2024, so a new extender must beat hydrated soy (about USD 2.6 to 2.8 per kg of protein, our calculation), not pork [@HXE-01; @DIE-25; @TIC-12] {VN-direct|Low}. From 2027 drinks above 5 g sugar per 100 ml pay an 8% excise (10% from 2028) if plant milks count; the upper bound for the Vinasoy soy-milk business is about VND 384 to 480 billion a year, a strong reason for incumbents to reformulate (our calculation) [@FTR-01; @CON-26; @AIB-05] {VN-direct|Low}. Pea protein enters duty-free from China, France and Canada, so a domestic isolate has no tariff shelter either [@FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Impact screens.** T1 spares about no animals and avoids about no CO2e (soy replaces soy), so it will not count towards climate-screened targets such as ADB Ventures' 80% strong climate impact [@AIS-22] {VN-adjacent|Medium}. Pitch it to development finance on the import bill (about USD 16 to 23 million of imports replaced a year by 2035 on the benchmark path, gross; our model, [[ch18-demand-sizing]]), jobs and value added. Per tonne of protein delivered, a hybrid extender avoids about 57 t CO2e and spares about 540 animals; a canteen ingredient about 45 t and 750 to 1,100 animals (our calculation) [@FUF-03; @FUF-04] {general|Low}. Climate or welfare money fits blends and canteen ingredients, not T1.
- **Look for offtake, not surveys.** Lenders and investors increasingly weigh offtake agreements and operating economics [@AIS-01; @AIS-15] {general|Medium}, which T1 and plant-drink proteins (T10) can show and consumer analogues cannot (our assessment). 74% of urban online respondents say they would buy plant-based meat at parity, but only 15% intend to eat less meat ([[ch13-consumers]]).

What the actor check changed, and the questions only a quote or an order can answer, are in [[ch29-actor-check]].

{{kn:kn-fta-duty-china}} {{kn:kn-tvp-line-capex}} {{kn:kn-t1-flour-breakeven}} {{kn:kn-feed-yeast-imports}} {{kn:kn-china-plant-protein-tonnage}} {{kn:kn-demand-bench-2035}}

## Looking to 2050

- **Price two external questions:** whether imported feed protein comes under chronic stress, and whether Asia's fermentation market stays open or falls under Chinese price dominance. Plays T2 (functional feed ingredients), T4 (cassava sugar hub), T5 (shared pilot fermentation), T6 (duckweed feed) and T9 (koji and fungal foods) hold in all four 2050 worlds and thrive in two; T3 (bulk fishmeal replacement) and T7 (high-value precision fermentation) are bets that should scale only when their signposts trip ([[ch23-scenarios-2050]]).
- **Cost curves are engineering estimates, not observed trends.** Fermentation industries have cut costs 13 to 20% per doubling of output. Price feed-protein deals against fishmeal: on our estimates soybean-meal parity is out of reach to 2050 ([[ch21-frontier-technology]]).
- **Cheaper capital is a first-order lever.** Cutting the capital charge from 12% to 9% does as much for fungal feed protein as the cost learning expected by 2030 (our calculation). Concessional debt and guarantees matter more than grants ([[ch28-robust-moves]]).
- **Mind the scale.** Our alternative-protein scenario implies microbial feed-protein capacity of about nine times Entobel's current Vietnamese capacity (11 kt a year) on a protein basis by 2030 (about 4.5 times by tonnage; our calculation) and about 78 times by 2050; the highest national feed-sector share we found is 0.4% novel ingredients (Norwegian salmon feed, 2020) ([[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]).
- **Timing.** Second-hand fermentation tanks are a 2027 to 2030 window; protein from renewable power is a 2040s option on the Mekong shrimp coast, and only if five conditions align.

{{kn:kn-capital-charge-lever}} {{kn:kn-salt-plants-2050}}

**Read next:** [[front-exec-summary]] · [[ch08-capital]] · [[ch09-economics]] · [[ch26-plays]] · [[app-s11-capital]] · [[app-s12-costs]] · [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]] · [[ch29-actor-check]]. Codes such as T1 or PO-017 are decoded in [[front-how-to-read]].

data.title: Brief for policy makers
data.summary: For ministries, the National Assembly and provinces, the case is protein supply security and industrial value, and the cheapest high-value step is a new-food clause in the Food Safety Law before passage is considered in May 2027.
