Most label rules already exist and need enforcing, and the largest gap public money can fill is shared pilot and testing capacity.
data.body:
# Brief for policy makers

**The short version.** Vietnam produces animal protein at scale on imported plant protein: about 99% of the soy protein (our calculation from USDA supply data) and three-quarters of the maize in its feed [@MAC-04; @MAC-08; @MAC-01], roughly USD 10 billion of feed-ingredient imports in 2025 (our calculation) [@MAC-07; @MAC-08; @MAC-09; @MAC-10]. The 2030 livestock strategy targets 30 to 32 Mt of industrial feed, 8.5 to 10.5 Mt more in 2030 than in 2024 [@REG-54; @MAC-28]. Domestic alternative proteins can reduce that exposure where they meet a price or function. Vietnam has the carbohydrate, the fermentation skills and the buyers, but ranks joint last in the region (with Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines) on regulatory readiness [@RGN-01]. Most of the fix is cheap, and the most valuable step must be taken while the Food Safety Law is being revised: the National Assembly takes first comments at its October 2026 session and considers passage at its May 2027 session, so a new-food clause needs to be in the draft revised between the two sessions, in practice by early 2027 [@APR-07] {VN-direct|Medium}.

## What you need to know

1. **The strongest case is supply security, industrial value and trade** ([[ch01-why-vietnam]]). Environment and animal welfare are narrower motivations.
2. **Food rules: an open door but no gate.** New protein foods enter through self-declaration, yet "new-technology food not yet permitted for circulation" is recallable and no procedure grants permission. Firms face enforcement-discretion risk, not a ban ([[ch07-rules]]).
3. **Precision-fermented proteins probably count as GMO products** under Decree 43/2026; production with a GM strain needs a closed-production certificate with no published timeline or fee ([[ch07-rules]]).
4. **Feed rules are more open but have two gaps.** The aquafeed list has no raw-material section, and the livestock list has no entry for bacterial single-cell protein or filamentous fungal biomass. Since Decree 211/2026, unlisted use draws fines of VND 10 to 20 million per material and one to three months' suspension ([[ch07-rules]]).
5. **The region is moving.** Singapore has approved 18 novel foods; Thailand has a novel-food route with recognised assessment units and a 2026 to 2035 biotechnology framework that cites the same regional study that scores Vietnam 0 on rules; Korea amended an existing rule in about nine months ([[ch03-regional]]).
6. **Tax holidays are the weakest incentive for this industry.** Capital is most of the cost; a regional incentive study ranks capital grants and loan guarantees far above tax holidays ([[ch09-economics]]).

## Options, ranked

| Rank | Option | Owner | Effort | When |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Delegation clause in the Food Safety Law: "The Government shall regulate the management of new foods and new food ingredients" | MOH; National Assembly committee | Low | First comments October 2026; passage considered May 2027 [@APR-07] |
| 2 | Joint MAE and MOH note: purified precision-fermented proteins labelled GM above 5%, no GMO food-use certificate if no viable GMO or recombinant DNA remains | MAE; MOH | Low | 3 to 6 months |
| 3 | Raw-material section in the aquafeed list, or cross-reference to the livestock list | MAE | Low | 2027 update |
| 4 | Generic livestock-list entries for inactivated microbial biomass from safe strains | MAE | Low | 2027 update |
| 5 | Novel-food decree: "not novel" determination, traditional-food lane, reliance lane, recognised assessment units, public positive list | MOH; Government | Medium | Drafting Q4 2026 |
| 6 to 12 | Hanoi sandbox pilot; public feed trials; closed-production certificate guidance; high-tech tax guidance; shared pilot fermentation line; capital grants over tax holidays; fund priorities | MOST, MAE, MOF, cities | Low to High | 2027 to 2028 |

All 33 options, with instruments and precedents: [[ch27-policy-options]].

{{chart:chart-policy-effort-impact}}

## Alignment with national strategy

The options serve Resolution 36-NQ/TW on biotechnology (biotech 7% of GDP by 2030; replace imported biotech products), Resolution 57 on science and innovation (R&D 2% of GDP), and the livestock strategy (Decision 1520: feed and by-product use). None of these names alternative protein; naming it in biotechnology programmes and state venture-fund priorities is low-cost ([[ch07-rules]], [[ch08-capital]]).

## Trade-offs to weigh

Speed against caution in a reliance lane; the risk that a new gate slows products that are legal today (hence transition rules); tariffs that help food makers but weaken domestic ingredient makers; public spending on a pilot line that needs an anchor host to avoid becoming idle ([[ch27-policy-options]]).

## For provinces

Tay Ninh and the Central Highlands hold the cassava-starch industry that could host fermentation-sugar hubs (play T4). Ho Chi Minh City, Dong Nai and Hanoi hold the industrial parks, research institutes, city venture funds and the sandbox. Mekong Delta provinces hold the aquafeed buyers. The provincial map changed on 1 July 2025 ([[app-s10-admin-map]]).

## The demand side

- **Most label rules already exist; enforce them and settle two questions.** TCVN 13625:2023 already defines vegetarian and vegan claims, but its vegetarian class allows egg, milk and honey, so ask the Vietnam Food Administration to state that an unqualified *chay* or *thuần chay* (strict vegetarian) claim means the vegan criteria. Any meat named in a product name must already be quantified (Decree 37/2026 carries the rule of Decree 43/2017), so blends need only a voluntary industry code for generic names such as *giò lụa* and *xúc xích*. We found no rule that reserves *thịt* (meat), *sữa* (milk) or *phô mai* (cheese); defend that permissive regime in the new law. The GMO label applies only above 5% of ingredients, so one question remains for MAE and VFA: is a recombinant protein identical to the native one a detectable product of the modified gene? [@LBL-15; @LBL-06; @LBL-07; @LBL-10; @LBL-16] {VN-direct|High} ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]])
- **School meals: the animal-share target has expired, but the menu software still prints one.** Decision 1340 (2016) set targets that ended in 2020 [@CHN-33]. The Ministry of Health's Decision 3958/QĐ-BYT (December 2025) sets no animal share and asks for plant protein (legumes, tofu) at least twice a week. Our audit of published menus (`school_menu_weeks.csv`) finds that only 9 of 48 school-weeks meet that; menus serve tofu beside meat, and the MOET, Ajinomoto and NIN menu software prints a standard of "animal protein at least 48%" [@APR-04; @PMR-10; @PMR-26] {VN-direct|High}. Use the School Health Programme 2026 to 2035 (Decision 973/QĐ-TTg), the MOET *bán trú* (school lunch and midday care) circular due in 2026 and the digital menu tools due in 2027 to 2028 to replace that default with protein-quality, zinc, iron and sodium targets per lunch, and to add textured soy and legume products to the software's food list [@PMR-01] {VN-direct|High} ([[ch15-channels]]).
- **Children's nutrition: aim at the gaps that exist.** Stunting affects 18% of children under five (2023) and 32% of ethnic minority children, so it is a problem of the youngest children [@APR-27] {VN-direct|Medium}. For school-age children protein is not the gap: published Hanoi primary-school lunches carry about 31.8 g (our calculation), upland boarding lunches and dinners carried meat, fish or egg in 240 of 242 published meals (our menu coding), and weighed boarding diets met protein and zinc; the documented shortfalls are calcium and vitamin A, and our menu coding shows breakfast as the thin meal [@PMR-26; @UPL-01; @UPL-04; @UPL-09; @UPL-18] {VN-direct|Medium}. A plant dish that removes all meat needs added zinc; blends keep protein quality high ([[ch11-protein-diet]]).
- **Canteens and procurement.** Factory canteens serve up to 1.2 billion meals a year (our calculation from about 4.15 million industrial-park workers) [@CHN-37] and are a large, price-set protein channel. A procurement standard for innovative protein in public and state-enterprise canteens is the form of this move a market-shaping funder can back. Corporate pledges are a weak lever here: Accor's target of 50% vegetarian or plant-based dishes by 2030 is the only one we found that binds Vietnamese units, and we found no Vietnamese protein buyer with a published target [@AFN-05; @AFN-40; @AFN-18] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Rule on plant milks before the sugary-drink excise starts.** From 1 January 2027 drinks above 5 g of total sugar per 100 ml pay 8% (10% from 2028); dairy is exempt, and whether sweetened soy, nut and cereal milks count as *nước giải khát* (soft drinks) is unresolved. A written Ministry of Finance ruling before the tax starts would let makers plan recipes [@FTR-01; @FTR-02; @FTR-05] {VN-direct|High} ([[ch13-consumers]]).
- **Trade: tariffs give no shelter; origin rules and data matter more.** Chinese, ASEAN and Korean protein ingredients enter duty-free under ACFTA, ATIGA, AKFTA and RCEP, so changing most-favoured-nation rates cannot protect a domestic maker [@FTR-32; @FTR-33] {VN-direct|Medium}. Protect the EU, UK, Japanese and CPTPP preferences on wrapped foods (Japan's edge on Vietnamese dumplings is 17.4 points), publish an origin note on the EU cap of 20% non-originating flour and starch in wrappers, and create eight-digit customs subheadings for protein ingredients so that demand is visible [@ORG-01; @ORG-05] {VN-direct|High} ([[ch17-export-demand]]).
- **Measure before targeting.** No probability survey asks how many people keep chay days, although existing chay days probably avoid as much meat protein as the Part IV alternative-protein scenario assumes for 2030 to 2035 ([[ch12-chay-baseline]]). National survey budgets, not philanthropy, should carry that question, starting with a lunar-date tabulation of the 2021 diet survey, in which 7.9% of adults ate no meat, poultry or fish on the previous day [@APR-36] {VN-direct|Medium}. Do not set national targets from consultancy forecasts ([[ch18-demand-sizing]]).

What the actor check changed for regulators and public buyers is in [[ch29-actor-check]].

{{kn:kn-school-plant-days}} {{kn:kn-sugary-drink-excise}} {{kn:kn-fta-duty-china}} {{kn:kn-chay-days-share}} {{kn:kn-canteen-meals}}

## Looking to 2050

- **Vietnam's 2050 plans cover inputs, not protein.** Power, hydrogen and emission caps have 2050 numbers; meat, feed and aquaculture targets stop at 2030. The successor livestock and fisheries strategies and the national biotechnology strategy are the natural homes for protein targets ([[ch20-drivers-2050]], [[app-f5-targets-hubs]]).
- **The 2030 feed target appears to cover livestock feed only** (Decision 1625/QD-TTg) and looks out of reach on our model: 26.4 Mt against 30 to 32 Mt.
- **Feed efficiency does about twice the work of alternative protein** in cutting 2050 soybean-meal imports; the two act through different channels, and the combined case is not modelled ([[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]).
- **Nine no-regret moves pay off in all four 2050 worlds.** Eight can start by 2028 with existing institutions: a new-food route with deadlines, a feed-efficiency programme, climate-proof siting rules, a skills programme, a national protein and feed balance, residue-carbon rules, a protein-quality laboratory with an open price series, and an omega-3 sourcing plan. One cheap option belongs alongside them: naming fermentation and feed-protein sites in the MAE biotechnology-cluster plan (December 2026) ([[ch28-robust-moves]]).
- **A vision to debate, not a forecast:** 7 to 9 Mt of imported soybean meal in 2050 instead of 10.4 Mt, 4 to 8% microbial feed protein and 15 to 50% non-marine aquafeed omega-3, reviewed at every five-year plan ([[ch24-vision-2050]]).

{{kn:kn-feed-target-livestock-2030}} {{kn:kn-no-regret-moves}}

**Read next:** [[front-exec-summary]] · [[ch07-rules]] · [[ch27-policy-options]] · [[ch19-outlook-2035]] · [[app-s9-regulation]] · [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]] · [[ch29-actor-check]]. Codes such as T1 or PO-017 are decoded in [[front-how-to-read]].

data.title: Brief for startups and founders
data.summary: Founders should start where the legal route is already clear, with familiar plant foods, listed feed materials or koji, and aim first to supply incumbents rather than launch their own analogue brand. Domestic textured protein is a debt-financed plant to build with a vegetarian food maker or distributor, not alone on venture money.
data.body:
# Brief for startups and founders

**The short version.** Vietnam offers cheap operating inputs, abundant carbohydrate, co-packers and concentrated feed buyers, but no novel-food route, no open pilot fermenter and very little venture capital. The founders most likely to reach revenue in two years are those who pick a familiar product with a clear route today, need little capital, aim first to supply incumbents (as an ingredient, a private label or a co-packed line) rather than launch their own analogue brand, and borrow capacity rather than build it. No founder here has yet tested the ingredient route, so treat it as the hypothesis to test ([[ch29-actor-check]]).

## Pick a product with a route that exists today

| Product | Route | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Plant-based food from known ingredients (textured protein, *chay*) | Self-declaration | Immediate |
| Koji and traditional mould fermentation on food substrates | Self-declaration; keep strain and mycotoxin data | Immediate |
| Insect, duckweed, algae or yeast meal for livestock feed | Listed: factory certificate and conformity declaration | About 35 working days for the factory |
| The same materials in aquafeed | Unclear: ask the Department of Fisheries in writing | Trial may be required |
| Bacterial single-cell protein or new fungal biomass in feed | Trial, recognition, annual list update | About 40 working days plus the trial; our estimate is 6 to 18 months in total |
| Fungal biomass or mycoprotein food | Self-declaration, but no way to get pre-clearance | Immediate, with legal risk |
| Precision-fermented protein made in Vietnam | Closed-production GMO certificate, then a food route | Not published |
| Cultivated meat or seafood | No national route; Hanoi sandbox is the nearest option | Not published |

Source: [[ch07-rules]]. Unlisted feed materials are now fined (VND 10 to 20 million each, plus suspension), so run the trial first.

{{chart:chart-route-to-market}}

## Plays that suit founders

- **T1. Textured plant protein.** Buyers are *chay* brands, frozen-food makers and co-packers who now import Chinese textured soy and gluten. Full cost is about VND 3,800 to 7,900 per 100 g of protein (USD 0.76 to 1.57 per kg), against Chinese product landing duty-free at USD 1.29 to 1.38 per kg (2025) and Indian at about USD 1.08 to 1.15 (our calculations, `t1_cost_per_kg.csv` and `t1_landed_competitor.csv`, from Comtrade prices and the 0% ACFTA rate). Equipment is cheap: Chinese lines are listed at USD 11,000 to 100,000 and install for about USD 0.3 to 1.4 million (our calculation, `t1_margin_payback.csv`). Food-grade soy flour and working capital are the real needs. Do not raise venture money to build a line alone: bring in a chay maker or distributor as co-owner or anchor buyer, and start with delivered flour quotes and conditional orders [@TIC-02; @TIC-12; @TIC-13; @BUY-02; @FTR-32] {VN-direct|Low} ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).
- **T2. Functional microbial feed ingredients.** Sell survival and feed-efficiency gains at 1 to 5% of shrimp or pangasius diets. Get species-specific trial data first; most shrimp feed is made by about six firms ([[ch26-plays]]). Vietnam already imports about 9,200 t of inactive yeast a year for food and feed, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg, so plan head-to-head trials against the yeast they use [@FBA-17] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **T9. Koji and fungal foods.** Use a characterised *Aspergillus oryzae* strain (no cyclopiazonic acid or 3-nitropropionic acid risk) on food-grade side streams ([[ch10-technology-fit]]).
- **T6. Duckweed feed.** Low capital, listed for livestock; test heavy metals and manganese on your water ([[ch10-technology-fit]]).
- **T7. Precision fermentation.** Only high-value, low-dose products, made under contract abroad ([[ch26-plays]]).

{{kn:kn-tvp-cost}} {{kn:kn-tvp-line-capex}}

## Where to locate

- **Cassava and starch residues:** Tay Ninh (65 to 68 starch factories) and the Central Highlands. Cassava roots rose about 50 to 90% in price, depending on province, in the year to April 2026; build on residues, not roots ([[ch04-asset-map]], [[app-s4-feedstocks]]).
- **Industry, co-packers, parks and labs:** Ho Chi Minh City (including former Binh Duong and Ba Ria-Vung Tau) and Dong Nai. Industrial land about USD 186 per m² for the lease term; ready-built factories about USD 5 per m² a month ([[ch09-economics]], [[app-s5-facilities]]).
- **Aquafeed buyers and trials:** the Mekong Delta and Ho Chi Minh City.
- **Sandbox, research institutes, the Hanoi venture fund:** Hanoi ([[ch07-rules]], [[ch08-capital]]).

## Borrow capacity

- **Co-packers:** frozen-food processors already run vegetarian lines next to meat ([[ch05-industrial-base]]).
- **Feed mills:** about 269 mills at roughly half their capacity can host trials ([[ch05-industrial-base]]).
- **Fermentation:** Vedan, Ajinomoto and Daesang own the aerobic tanks; we found no published tolling offer, so ask ([[ch30-unknowns]]). For scale-up, ScaleUp Bio (Singapore, food-licensed, up to 10,000 L), EECi (Thailand, two 15,000 L tanks, food status to confirm) or Chinese CDMOs (largest and cheapest, more exposure of know-how) ([[ch03-regional]]).
- **Testing:** FIRI's NACEFA and NIFC for proximate analysis, contaminants and microbiology. Amino-acid and digestibility testing may need to go abroad ([[app-s8-labs-talent]]).

## Design for Vietnam

- **Cooling.** Cooling-tower water in the south arrives at about 31 to 33 °C (our engineering assumption). Chilled water adds roughly USD 70 to 180 per tonne of biomass; thermotolerant strains that grow at 40 to 45 °C avoid most of it ([[ch09-economics]]).
- **Power.** About 1,952 VND per kWh blended at 22 kV for a 24/7 plant, but the grid emits about 0.66 kg CO2 per kWh; a low-carbon claim needs renewable supply ([[ch09-economics]]).
- **VAT.** Feed is not subject to VAT, so a feed-ingredient maker cannot reclaim input VAT; budget 5 to 10% more on taxed inputs ([[ch09-economics]]).
- **Names and addresses.** Use the post-July 2025 province names in licences and investor documents ([[app-s10-admin-map]]).

## Money

Angels and family offices; regional seed specialists (USD 0.1 to 0.3 million: Better Bite Ventures, Big Idea Ventures, ProVeg Incubator); ADB Ventures (up to USD 4 million, climate lens); the Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi venture funds from late 2026; episodic international grants. A Singapore holding company, as Entobel used, can ease foreign investment ([[ch08-capital]], [[app-s11-capital]]).

## The demand side

- **Sell a familiar food with little capital, and supply incumbents first.** Aim for ingredient, private-label or co-packing supply to chay makers, meat processors, retailers and caterers. A restaurant menu listing for your own analogue brand is not a business customer: of 12 regional firms in our register (`firm_outcomes.csv`) that launched through restaurants, 7 are dormant and 3 pivoted. No founder has yet tested the ingredient route, so treat it as the hypothesis to test, not a proven path [@AIS-28; @BRD-08] {VN-adjacent|Low}.
- **Know the base rates.** Of 24 regional and Vietnamese alternative-protein firms since 2019 in our register (`firm_outcomes.csv`), 7 are active, 4 pivoted, 2 exited and 11 are dormant. Every pivot moved towards private label, co-manufacturing, a retail blend or non-food. None of the 4 Vietnamese meat-analogue startups is active; all 3 Vietnamese makers of traditional formats (mushroom floss, cashew cheese, tempeh) are [@AIS-28; @AIS-39; @BRD-08] {VN-adjacent|Low} ([[ch15-channels]]).
- **Price per gram of protein is the first gate, and kitchens already buy cheap plant protein.** Eggs and chicken sell protein at VND 34,000 to 45,000 per 100 g and lean pork at about VND 71,000 at retail [@COST-39; @COST-40; @COST-41; @DIE-12]; 20 g of protein from a packaged chay wrapper costs more than a whole street meal. Domestic dry soy-gluten pieces already reach kitchens at about VND 4,000 to 5,100 per 20 g of protein (protein assumed from similar labels), against VND 7,200 to 9,500 for tofu (our calculation) [@CPC-12; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|Low} ([[ch11-protein-diet]], [[ch13-consumers]]).
- **Private label is an open door.** Saigon Co.op's Co.op Select chay dishes are all made by one co-packer, GN Foods, and carry no protein claim. A version at 10 g of protein per 100 g [@DIE-04] qualifies for a high-protein claim and can reach the shelf without a consumer brand; Co.op's supplier portal answers a pitch within 10 working days [@CPC-15; @CPC-18; @LBL-03] {VN-direct|Medium} ([[ch16-business-buyers]]).
- **Build for the dish and the calendar.** Protein sits in Vietnamese meals as toppings, fillings, rolls and mince. Chay sales in specialist shops roughly double in the seventh lunar month, and one shop reported three times [@CHY-16]; for an ingredient maker the swing is smaller: China-reported textured-protein shipments to Vietnam run about a third above normal in the two months before *Vu Lan* (the seventh lunar month) and fall to about 40% of normal in the *Tết* (lunar new year) month, while Vietnam's own import records show no pre-Vu Lan rise [@BRD-05; @BRD-06] {VN-direct|Medium} ([[ch12-chay-baseline]]).
- **Words matter.** Our recommendation: lead with taste in familiar dishes, protein, safety and origin; avoid *nhân tạo* (artificial), "lab" and "future of meat", since the press uses *thịt nhân tạo* loosely [@NOV-69; @NOV-74]; *lên men* (fermented) reads well [@NOV-63; @NOV-64]. In a blend, name the plant part as an ingredient and avoid "x% meat replaced" wording (our recommendation) and *độn* (filler), which buyers read as cheating in *giò chả* [@TRU-02; @TRU-03] {VN-direct|Medium} ([[ch14-frontier-demand]]).

What the actor check changed for founders, with the firm register behind these numbers, is in [[ch29-actor-check]].

{{kn:kn-firm-outcomes}} {{kn:kn-protein-price-floor}} {{kn:kn-protein-cost-serving}}

## Looking to 2050

- **Windows open in sequence.** Functional feed ingredients, AI-assisted enzymes and tolling on existing tanks now; cheap second-hand tanks in 2027 to 2030; contract precision fermentation and food mycoprotein in 2030 to 2035 once a new-food route exists; residue sugar and protein from power in the 2040s ([[ch21-frontier-technology]]).
- **Edges that survive Chinese price dominance** are species-specific function, local feedstocks and freshness ([[ch23-scenarios-2050]]).
- **Design for the 2050 climate.** Use strains that grow at 40 °C or more, raised Mekong sites with surface water, and residue carbon if you want a climate claim: cassava-based microbial protein is not low-carbon by default.
- **Omega-3 may be the sharper opportunity than protein.** Vietnamese aquafeed needs about 11 kt of EPA plus DHA today and about 21 kt by 2050 (our estimate), and Vietnam's own fish oil is not an omega-3 source ([[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]).

{{kn:kn-omega3-need-2050}}

**Read next:** [[front-exec-summary]] · [[ch07-rules]] · [[ch10-technology-fit]] · [[ch26-plays]] · [[app-s4-feedstocks]] · [[app-s5-facilities]] · [[app-s8-labs-talent]] · [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]] · [[ch29-actor-check]]. Codes such as T1 or PO-017 are decoded in [[front-how-to-read]].

data.title: Brief for food and feed manufacturers
data.summary: Food, beverage and feed companies run on mostly imported protein and are the natural owners of a domestic textured-protein line and the first customer every play needs. Near-term options are to pool orders behind such a line, test new ingredients against the soy and yeast already in use, and design plant milks at or below 5 g sugar.
data.body:
# Brief for food and feed manufacturers

**The short version.** Vietnam's non-animal protein market is yours already: soy milk, tofu and industrial *đồ chay* made on the same lines as meat. But the protein in those products is imported, and so is the protein in your feed. Fishmeal at its highest price since at least 2020 and a feed-output target of 30 to 32 Mt by 2030 make protein supply a strategic question. The alternatives most likely to reach you within two years are domestic textured protein, which you are better placed to own or anchor than any startup, and functional microbial feed ingredients, which must beat the yeast you already buy. Both need you as a buyer or partner.

## Food and beverage

1. **Your shelf is low in protein and high in imported inputs.** Across the 43 audited foods with a label value, median protein was 4.7 g per 100 g. Every locally made product with 10 g or more per 100 g ran on imported textured soy, soy protein or gluten, much of it from China. About 77% of products relied on an imported protein ingredient, and 11% partly ([[ch02-alt-protein-today]], [[app-s2-retail-audit]]).
2. **Chay is often cheaper than meat per pack, not per gram of protein.** Filled wrappers hold 3 to 5 g of protein per 100 g. Chicken and eggs set the retail protein floor at about 34,000 to 45,000 VND per 100 g of protein ([[ch09-economics]]).
3. **Domestic textured protein is the nearest new supply (T1), and you are its natural owner.** Chinese textured soy enters duty-free under ACFTA; it left China at USD 1.24 per kg FOB in 2025 and lands at about USD 1.29 to 1.38 per kg with freight, port and inland costs. A Chinese-equipped 0.5 t/h line costs about USD 0.28 to 1.0 million installed and needs 2,000 to 3,600 t a year of orders, 16 to 28% of the 12,800 t of HS 2106.10 imports from China, India and Serbia in 2025 (an upper bound for textured protein, since the code also covers concentrates and isolates). At Chinese parity it clears a 15% margin only if food-grade soy flour is delivered below about USD 590 to 900 per t at 70% utilisation (USD 700 to 940 for a 1 t/h line). Freshness, shapes for local dishes and supply security are the other arguments (our calculation) [@TIC-02; @TIC-12; @TIC-13; @BUY-02; @FTR-32] {VN-direct|Low} ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).
4. **High-protein plant drinks use imported pea protein (T10).** Mung bean and rice proteins could replace it, with care on protein-quality claims: human digestibility of mung bean is about 20% below the pig values often quoted ([[ch10-technology-fit]]). Pea protein from China, France and Canada enters duty-free, so a domestic isolate competes on price and function, not on tariff [@FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}.
5. **Rules to watch.** The Food Safety Law revision takes first comments at the October 2026 National Assembly session and is considered for passage at the May 2027 session [@APR-07] {VN-direct|Medium}. Watch its allergen rules; no current rule reserves *thịt* (meat), *sữa* (milk) or *phô mai* (cheese) for animal products. From 1 January 2027 a sugary-drink excise may reach sweetened plant milks ([[ch07-rules]], [[ch27-policy-options]]).

{{chart:chart-retail-protein-archetypes}}

## Feed

1. **Fishmeal reached USD 2,500 a tonne in August 2026**, about 6 times the price of soybean meal. At 15% inclusion, fishmeal adds about USD 375 per tonne of shrimp feed at that price [@FM-01] ([[ch09-economics]]). Vietnamese mills paid less than that benchmark but the gap is closing: imported fishmeal averaged about USD 1,610 per t FOB in January to July 2026, up about 38% on 2025 (our calculation; partner-reported, and 2025 lacks Peru and Ecuador) [@FBA-20] {VN-direct|Low}.
2. **Novel proteins replace part of fishmeal, not all of it.** Most trials support about 25 to 60% replacement per ingredient without growth loss (for the best-studied microbial protein in shrimp, growth matched the control at 30% of a test diet); early life stages need their own trials ([[ch10-technology-fit]], [[app-s6-feed-market]]).
3. **Function is worth more than protein.** Survival after disease challenge, palatability and winter survival are where microbial ingredients earn a premium at 1 to 5% inclusion (T2) ([[ch26-plays]]).
4. **Check the legal route before using a new material.** Aquafeed's permitted list has no raw-material section, and unlisted use now draws fines ([[ch07-rules]]).
5. **Chinese microbial protein is already on the market**, as a by-product of amino-acid fermentation. Compare any new supplier against it, not only against fishmeal ([[ch02-alt-protein-today]]).
6. **You already buy microbial ingredients.** Vietnam imported about 9,200 t of inactive yeast for food and feed in 2025, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg. Ask any new supplier for head-to-head trials against the yeast you use, priced per unit of performance [@FBA-17] {VN-direct|Medium}.
7. **Certification will tighten, but it does not reward microbial protein.** From 1 May 2028, ASC farm audits require feed from ASC-certified mills; 15 Vietnamese mills are certified. The ASC feed standard sets no requirement and gives no credit for microbial ingredients; BAP credits only algae and aquatic microorganisms [@FBA-02; @FBA-03; @FBA-04; @FBA-01; @FBA-05] {VN-direct|Medium}.

{{chart:chart-price-to-beat}}

## What you could do in the next 12 months

- Pool offtake from two or three chay makers or co-packers, with a distributor, behind one textured-protein line; or give a startup a specification, a trial order and a volume commitment. Start with five delivered quotes for food-grade soy flour (T1).
- Host a head-to-head trial of a Vietnamese functional microbial ingredient against the yeast product you already buy, at 1 to 2% inclusion, and state the price per unit of performance you would pay (T2).
- Write a pea-protein replacement specification for plant drinks at or below 5 g of sugar per 100 ml (T10). Ask the Ministry of Finance for a written ruling on whether your sweetened plant milks are *nước giải khát* (soft drinks), and plan recipes below 5 g.
- Blind-test any fungal extender at equal saving against your own soy recipe, in industrial *xúc xích* (sausage) or a coarse filling (T9).
- Pitch a 10 g of protein per 100 g version of a private-label chay dish through your co-packer.
- Share by-product data (okara, spent grain, broken rice, processing residues) for the national by-product atlas.
- If you own fermentation tanks, consider tolling for third parties; it is the single biggest missing piece in the ecosystem (T5).

## Export angles

A Singapore approval is the regional credential for novel foods; Malaysia has ruled that cultivated meat can be halal; halal acceptance of Vietnamese fermentation-derived ingredients is an open question ([[ch03-regional]], [[ch30-unknowns]]).

Rules of origin shape wrapped-food recipes. For EU buyers, check the flour share of wrappers: non-originating flour or starch may be at most 20% of product weight, and flour milled in Vietnam from imported wheat counts as non-originating. Use Vietnamese rice flour or cassava starch where needed, and ship to the UK, Japan and Canada under CPTPP, which accepts imported flour and textured soy. Switching to domestic textured soy does not change origin for dumplings [@ORG-01; @ORG-04; @ORG-05; @ORG-07] {VN-direct|High} ([[ch17-export-demand]]).

## The demand side

- **Your shelves already hold the demand, and a protein claim is open.** Chay sales in specialist shops roughly double in the seventh lunar month (one shop reported three times), and Vissan's chay line sells 38% below its meat version ([[ch12-chay-baseline]]). A high-protein claim needs 10 g per 100 g (TCVN 14429:2025 with the 50 g NRV of TCVN 7088:2025, voluntary); 20 of 43 audited foods meet the per-100 g source condition, and none makes the claim [@LBL-03; @LBL-04; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|High}. Chay's live trust issues are borax, microbes and unlabelled goods; we found no confirmed case of meat in a Vietnamese chay product in our news searches (2015 to 2026) [@TRU-14; @TRU-16; @LBL-23; @TRU-18; @TRU-22] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Private label and co-packing are working routes.** All five Co.op Select frozen chay dishes are made by one co-packer, GN Foods, and Thai Corp Inter.VN and Vi Nguyen make its tofu; Lotte Mart sells its own Choice L chay. These products are starch and vegetable led and carry no protein claim, so a co-packer can take a protein upgrade to the retailer without a consumer brand. HoReCa (hotel, restaurant and catering) distributors already sell tofu to kitchens in volume and list domestic dry soy-gluten pieces, and the imported analogue that tried this route is no longer orderable [@CPC-15; @CPC-12; @AIS-25; @FORM-01] {VN-direct|Medium} ([[ch15-channels]]).
- **Blends are already yours, and soy is the benchmark.** You already own the cheapest extender: soy at 20% saves about VND 9,100 to 16,600 per kg of *chả lụa* (steamed pork roll), or USD 350 to 640 per tonne at VND 26,000 per USD, at 2019 to 2020 hog prices, and extension has paid at every annual hog price from 2019 to 2024. Pilot a fungal extender only if it lets you replace more meat unnoticed than soy, or carries a label your buyers prefer, and test it against your soy recipe, not against all-meat. Keep replacement to 10 to 20% in fine emulsions and 30% in coarse mince, name the plant part as an ingredient, and avoid *độn* (filler) and "x% meat replaced" wording (our calculation) [@HXE-01; @DIE-25; @TIC-12; @AIB-15; @HXE-04; @HXE-09; @TRU-02] {VN-direct|Low} ([[ch14-frontier-demand]]).
- **Plant milk: design at or below 5 g of sugar.** Plant milk is still the modern plant category that sells: the best plant-milk SKUs sell 60 to 79% of the litres of the best dairy SKUs on Lazada and Tiki [@MKT-03] {VN-direct|Medium}. Check whether your sweetened plant milks are *nước giải khát* under TCVN 12828:2019. From 2027 those above 5 g of total sugar per 100 ml would pay an 8% excise (10% from 2028), and since January 2026 they have lost the 2% VAT cut; dairy is exempt [@FTR-01; @FTR-05; @FTR-09] {VN-direct|High} ([[ch13-consumers]]).
- **Export: wrapped foods, not textured protein.** Vietnam exported USD 128.2 million of dumplings and other stuffed pasta in 2023, against almost no textured protein. The European route runs through importers and brand owners of Asian wrapped foods supplying retailers that require IFS or BRCGS certification; European retailers meet their protein targets with European products. Under CPTPP, Japan gives Vietnamese dumplings, except those with mainly shrimp fillings, a 17.4-point tariff edge over China and Thailand [@XBA-29; @XBA-04; @XBA-07; @ORG-05] {VN-direct|High} ([[ch17-export-demand]]).

What the actor check changed for food makers, retailers and caterers is in [[ch29-actor-check]].

{{kn:kn-hybrid-saving}} {{kn:kn-sugary-drink-excise}} {{kn:kn-stuffed-pasta-exports}} {{kn:kn-feed-yeast-imports}} {{kn:kn-vissan-soy-share}} {{kn:kn-chay-days-share}}

## Looking to 2050

- **On trend, soybean-meal need rises from 7.2 Mt (2025) to about 10.4 Mt (2050).** The two largest levers, soybean-meal inclusion and feed conversion, are in your hands, and nobody publishes them. Sharing anonymised data would make a national protein balance possible ([[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]).
- **Plan for recurring shocks.** In the stressed 2050 worlds, fishmeal shortages, joint crop failures in exporting countries and shipping scares recur; the 2026 Middle East conflict helped raise Vietnamese feed prices 10 to 14% between January and April 2026. Formulation flexibility, multi-origin sourcing and working stocks are the proven hedges ([[ch23-scenarios-2050]], [[ch28-robust-moves]]).
- **Qualify one non-marine omega-3 oil** for shrimp and marine-fish feeds; alternatives could supply 15 to 50% of aquafeed omega-3 by 2050.
- **Watch trash-fish replacement and offshore cages:** they turn marine-fish growth into formulated, protein- and fishmeal-dense feed demand.

{{kn:kn-efficiency-vs-alt}} {{kn:kn-maize-joint-loss-4c}}

Codes such as T1 or PO-017 are decoded in [[front-how-to-read]].

data.title: Brief for universities and research institutes
data.summary: Vietnam's research strengths, in aquafeed trials, yeast protein expression, stem-cell culture, koji genetics and microalgae, sit next to alternative protein rather than inside it. The most useful work pairs a Vietnamese raw material or species with a missing study, and the binding constraint is shared pilot fermentation, food extrusion and protein-quality testing.
data.body:
# Brief for universities and research institutes

**The short version.** Vietnam's novel-food research intensity is about a quarter to a third of Thailand's, but it is at the regional level in aquafeed protein replacement and microalgae, and has real skills in yeast protein expression, stem-cell culture and koji genetics. Vietnam has almost no published work on texturisation, mycoprotein, precision-fermented food proteins or food cell lines. The most useful research combines a Vietnamese raw material or species with a missing study, and the most useful infrastructure is shared.

## Where Vietnam stands

{{chart:chart-research-benchmark}}

- **Strengths:** fish and shrimp feeding trials; protein expression in yeast (including growth factors); serum-free stem-cell culture; gene tools for *Aspergillus oryzae* and *Cordyceps*; microalgae cultivation, including a salt-tolerant spirulina at 48.7% protein ([[ch06-knowledge-talent]]).
- **Gaps:** extrusion and texturisation (at most one study), mycoprotein, precision-fermented food proteins, fish or shrimp food cell lines, and any Vietnamese DIAAS or PDCAAS study ([[ch06-knowledge-talent]]).
- **Infrastructure:** no open pilot fermenter, no food extruder at any university or institute we found, and no laboratory page listing accredited amino-acid profiles or protein-digestibility testing ([[ch06-knowledge-talent]], [[app-s8-labs-talent]]).

## Research questions Vietnam is well placed to answer

1. A DIAAS or PDCAAS reference dataset for Vietnamese proteins: mung bean, rice, spirulina, catfish side-stream isolates, spent yeast, and the plant proteins children already eat (tofu, textured soy and blended minced dishes), scored on both the young-child and the older-child patterns with phytate and zinc measured. Human mung bean digestibility, measured in children, is about 20% below pig values [@SCI-42] ([[ch10-technology-fit]]). A fortified soy item for upland boarding schools is a research option, not a product profile: test it at breakfast, and on calcium and vitamin A as well as zinc [@NQR-05; @UPL-18] {VN-direct|Medium}.
2. Bacterial single-cell protein and fungal meal in pangasius and whiteleg shrimp diets, including early life stages and functional endpoints (survival, disease challenge).
3. Mixed-culture protein from tofu and soy-milk wastewater in shrimp (a 2025 preprint reports 50% fishmeal replacement consistently and up to 90% on some outcomes).
4. Thermotolerant yeasts (40 to 45 °C) on raw cassava starch and pulp, with measured cooling savings in a tropical plant.
5. Fungal biomass from cassava pulp and peel with a food-grade safety package (cyanide, mycotoxins, RNA, digestibility).
6. Characterised Vietnamese *tương* (*A. oryzae*) strains with cyclopiazonic acid and 3-nitropropionic acid data.
7. Duckweed: yields, manganese and heavy metals on Mekong water; protein concentrates.
8. Texturisation of rice distillers'-grain and broken-rice protein; extrusion of local legume blends.
9. Serum-free, suspension adaptation of striped catfish cells; *Pichia*-made growth factors tested on fish cells.
10. Bacterial protein from pig-farm and cassava-starch biogas.

Source: [[ch06-knowledge-talent]] section 6.3 and [[app-s7-research]].

## Public goods research bodies could lead

- **Protein-quality laboratory** (amino acids, DIAAS, and phytate, zinc and iron with phytate-to-mineral molar ratios) at a national reference laboratory (policy option PO-027) [@NQR-16; @NQR-20] {general|Medium}.
- **Public feed trials** of microbial protein as state science tasks, whose results then qualify for the legal exemption from separate trials (PO-021).
- **Yearly by-product atlas** of volume, location, price and composition (PO-028).
- **Open cost model** for fermentation with Vietnamese inputs, and a public series of domestic feed-ingredient prices ([[ch26-plays]], P6).

## Funding and partners

- **Domestic:** NAFOSTED (most acknowledged), VINIF (mainly scholarships and fellowships), state science tasks under the new science law, which allows acceptance of research risk ([[ch06-knowledge-talent]]).
- **International:** ACIAR funds 23 Vietnamese projects, none on alternative protein; alternative-protein grant windows (for example Coefficient Giving's USD 30 million request) are episodic and need a ready proposal and often an international co-applicant ([[ch08-capital]]).
- **Partners:** Thai groups (cassava-pulp thermotolerant yeasts; EECi pilot plant), Chinese groups (cassava-to-protein and gas-to-protein feed), Indian fish cell repositories, and Singapore's pilot and regulatory ecosystem ([[ch03-regional]]).

## Talent

Can Tho University alone has a 2026 quota of 860 places in food technology, biotechnology and aquaculture. The gap is specialist: extrusion, food-grade downstream processing, sensory and structure work on analogues, protein-quality scoring, and cell culture for food ([[ch06-knowledge-talent]]).

## The demand side

- **The biggest gap is still tested evidence.** Vietnam has one large online consumer survey, no choice experiment or in-store price test for plant-based products, no name or label test and no probability survey of chay practice ([[ch13-consumers]], [[app-m3-demand-method]]).
- **Test new extenders against soy, not against all-meat.** Processors already extend pork with soy: one large processor lists soy protein in 31% of its meat formulations [@BUY-05]. This saved money at every annual hog price from 2019 to 2024 (our calculation from hog prices, `hybrid_savings.csv`) [@DIE-25]. The study that decides whether a fungal or novel extender has a job is a blind test at equal saving against the processor's own soy recipe, in industrial *xúc xích* (sausage) or a coarse filling rather than *giò lụa* (steamed pork roll), at 10 to 20% replacement in fine emulsions and up to 30% in coarse mince [@HXE-01; @HXE-09] {VN-direct|Low} ([[ch14-frontier-demand]]).
- **Other studies that would change decisions:** a blind and repeat test of a chay food at 10 g of protein per 100 g; a price choice experiment; a randomised label test (*chay*, *giàu đạm* (high protein), *thịt nuôi cấy* (cultivated meat), *lên men* (fermented), *biến đổi gen* (genetically modified)); a canteen and school trial that logs the dish species replaced; and a chay safety and composition survey that tests borax, preservatives, microbes and protein first, with animal DNA as a cheap PCR screen [@TRU-24] {VN-direct|Medium} ([[ch25-demand-to-frontier]]).
- **Protein quality and zinc, where children actually fall short.** Tofu scores 64 (in vivo) to 98 (in vitro) and extruded soybean 65 to 97 on DIAAS (textured soy protein has a single in-vitro PDCAAS of 65), against 100 or more for pork, chicken, egg and milk [@NQR-05; @NQR-07; @NQR-08; @NQR-09]. Textured soy costs far less per gram of quality-adjusted protein than eggs, and a 20 to 30% soy extender keeps a minced pork dish at a DIAAS of about 97 or more (our calculation, `cost_per_quality_protein.csv` and `protein_quality.csv`) [@COST-41] {general|Medium}. For school-age children protein is not the documented gap; calcium and vitamin A are [@UPL-18], and breakfast is the thin meal (our menu coding, `upland_school_weeks.csv`). Stunting (18% of children under five in 2023, 32% among ethnic minority children) [@APR-27] is a problem of the youngest children, where plant products face the young-child pattern and registration as foods for children under 36 months [@NQR-04] {VN-direct|Medium} ([[ch11-protein-diet]]).

> **Correction.** In v0.6 this said textured soy scores 65 to 97 on DIAAS; the source gives 65 to 97 for extruded soybean and only a single in-vitro PDCAAS of 65 for textured soy protein.

- **Know who pays.** Only 4 of the original 19 demand moves have a funder whose scope fits and that accepts Vietnam (our assessment, `funder_fit.csv`). The Bezos Centre for Sustainable Protein at NUS appears to fit consumer-acceptance and label tests with a Vietnamese institute (our assessment) [@AFN-15]; the chay-day survey question has no philanthropic payer and belongs in national survey budgets [@AFN-05] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Stop running small student surveys** based on intention models; they add little to what is known.

What the actor check changed, and the questions that now need a trial or a quote rather than more reading, are in [[ch29-actor-check]].

{{kn:kn-hybrid-saving}} {{kn:kn-funder-fit}} {{kn:kn-intend-cut-meat}}

## Looking to 2050

- **Vietnam is nearly absent from the frontier fields:** 2 of 494 gas-fermentation protein papers (2016 to 2026), none on mycoprotein or molecular farming. The 2025 to 2026 wave of Vietnamese work is mostly domestic food technology ([[ch21-frontier-technology]]).
- **The futures questions research bodies could answer best:** feed conversion and soybean-meal inclusion by species; EPA plus DHA needs of Vietnamese species; pretreatment of high-silica Mekong straw; life-cycle data for cassava fermentation with biogas; strains that grow at 40 °C; and cell lines from Vietnamese species for the 2040s ([[app-r1-open-questions]]).
- **Public goods:** a yearly national protein and feed balance, and a published tracker of the 16 scenario signposts ([[ch28-robust-moves]]).
- **Foresight capacity:** Vietnam's own foresight studies advise small, high-quality scenario workshops; one on the Part IV scenarios would test our axes and vision ([[app-m2-futures-method]]).

{{kn:kn-vn-gas-protein-papers}}

**Read next:** [[front-exec-summary]] · [[ch06-knowledge-talent]] · [[ch10-technology-fit]] · [[app-s13-science]] · [[app-s7-research]] · [[app-s8-labs-talent]] · [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]] · [[ch29-actor-check]]. Codes such as T1 or PO-017 are decoded in [[front-how-to-read]].

data.title: Brief for international organisations and development finance
data.summary: For development agencies, foundations, NGOs and foreign governments, Vietnam's alternative-protein frontier is held back by public goods, such as a novel-food procedure, trial capacity and shared pilot fermentation, that fit technical assistance, research grants and first-loss development finance. On the demand side, only 4 of the original 19 demand moves have a funder that fits and accepts Vietnam.
data.body:
# Brief for international organisations and development finance

**The short version.** Vietnam is a protein-processing economy that imports its plant protein. It has cheap inputs and a strong feed industry, but ranks joint last in the region on regulatory readiness, has no open pilot fermentation and almost no venture capital for this sector. The leverage points are public goods and first-plant finance. Several can be supported through existing channels (regulator-to-regulator cooperation, research grants, development-finance co-investment) at modest cost. On the demand side, fund what fits your unit and your rules: welfare money fits canteen menus, market-shaping money fits procurement and label rules, and development finance fits import substitution and feed.

## Why Vietnam matters

- About 99% of the soy protein in Vietnamese feed and three-quarters of the maize supply are imported, a feed-ingredient import bill of roughly USD 10 billion in 2025 ([[ch01-why-vietnam]]).
- Vietnam exported USD 11.3 billion of seafood in 2025; aquafeed is where fishmeal prices bite, and where alternative feed proteins have their clearest market ([[ch01-why-vietnam]], [[ch09-economics]]).
- The regional comparison scores Vietnam 100 on labour and 0 on regulatory readiness. Its recommended fix is a published novel-food procedure with statutory timelines ([[ch03-regional]]).

{{chart:chart-hawkwood-scores}}

## Six entry points

| Entry point | What it would do | Channels | Links |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Novel-food drafting support | Help MOH draft the new-food clause (the window runs from first comments in October 2026 to the vote considered in May 2027) and the decree (not-novel determination, reliance lane, recognised assessment units, timelines) | Regulator-to-regulator agreements (Singapore SFA's MOUs), FAO food-safety work | [[ch27-policy-options]] options 1 and 5 |
| 2. Feed-list and trial capacity | Fund public trials of microbial proteins in shrimp, pangasius, pigs and poultry; support the aquafeed-list fix | Agricultural research grants; bilateral programmes | PO-017, PO-018, PO-021 |
| 3. Protein-quality laboratory | Amino-acid and DIAAS testing, with phytate, zinc and iron analysis, at a national reference laboratory | Technical assistance; equipment grants | PO-027 |
| 4. Shared pilot fermentation | Co-fund a food-grade pilot line and tolling programme; broker access to Thailand's EECi pilot plant | Grants; blended finance; bilateral science cooperation | PO-026, PO-033 |
| 5. First-plant finance | A first-loss or co-investment tranche for a first fermentation-feed plant, following the Entobel structure (private equity, DFI, offtake) | IFC, ADB Ventures, Proparco (via local funds), other DFIs | [[ch08-capital]] |
| 6. Open data | A yearly by-product atlas, an open fermentation cost model, a regional Asian fishmeal price series | Research grants; statistical cooperation | PO-028; public goods P5 (by-product atlas) and P6 (open cost model) in [[ch26-plays]] |

## Precedents to build on

- **Entobel:** IFC's USD 2.5 million upstream collaboration alongside Mekong Capital and Dragon Capital, with Vinh Hoan's offtake ([[ch08-capital]]).
- **Decree 43/2026:** Vietnam already fast-tracks GMOs approved by five developed countries; the same reliance logic can apply to novel foods ([[ch07-rules]]).
- **Thailand's recognised assessment units** and **Korea's published review time of about nine to 12 months** ([[ch03-regional]]).

## Motivations and framing

AltProtein Vietnam frames the case around food and feed security, industrial value and trade. Climate and animal welfare are motivations for many international funders; in Vietnam, livestock accounted for about 5.8% of national greenhouse-gas emissions in 2016, and the grid emits about 0.66 kg CO2 per kWh, so climate claims for power-intensive processes need care ([[ch01-why-vietnam]], [[ch09-economics]]). The documented demand routes avoid about 0.01 to 0.05 Mt CO2e a year by 2030 and about 0.14 Mt (0.08 to 0.25) by 2035 on the benchmark path (0.33 to 0.99 Mt on the stretch path), about half of it from displacing beef and buffalo (our estimate) [@FUF-04; @FUF-05; @FUF-07] {general|Low}. Treat climate as a co-benefit, not the case; the welfare impact is overwhelmingly in chickens and ducks.

## Coordination

After the March 2025 mergers, MAE holds feed, aquafeed, GMO biosafety and genetic resources; MOST holds standards, the sandbox, high-tech status and IP; MOH holds food safety. A joint programme across these three ministries is administratively simpler than before ([[ch07-rules]]).

## The demand side

- **Separate the protein problems.** Cities eat far more meat than guidance advises. Stunting (18% of children under five in 2023, 32% among ethnic minority children) is a problem of the youngest children, where plant products face the young-child protein-quality pattern and registration as foods for children under 36 months [@APR-27; @NQR-04] {VN-direct|Medium}. For school-age children protein is not the gap: upland boarding lunches and dinners carried meat, fish or egg in 240 of 242 published meals, and breakfast is the thin meal (our menu coding) [@UPL-01; @UPL-02; @UPL-03; @UPL-04; @UPL-05; @UPL-06; @UPL-07; @UPL-08; @UPL-09; @UPL-10; @UPL-11; @UPL-12; @UPL-13; @UPL-14; @UPL-15; @UPL-16; @UPL-17]; weighed boarding diets met protein and zinc, and the documented shortfalls are calcium and vitamin A [@UPL-18] {VN-direct|Medium}. Fund complementary-food standards for the under-twos, and protein quality, zinc and iron in school food standards ([[ch11-protein-diet]]).
- **In funder units.** On the benchmark path the displacing routes spare about 2.4 to 2.7 million animals a year by 2035, 93 to 94% of them chickens and ducks, and avoid about 0.14 Mt CO2e (0.08 to 0.25). Import substitution, most of the protein delivered, spares none (our estimate) [@FUF-03; @FUF-04] {VN-direct|Low}. The routes deliver about 19,000 t of protein a year by 2035, of which about 11,000 to 17,000 t made in Vietnam for the home market, and displace about 0.2% of meat protein ([[ch18-demand-sizing]]).
- **Match the route to your unit and your rules.** Welfare funders: a canteen trial with Humane World, which trained chefs and nutritionists in Viet Nam in 2025, that logs the dish species replaced; chicken leads only 13% of caterers' sample-menu protein dishes (our calculation, `canteen_dish_summary.csv`) [@UPL-27; @UPL-28; @UPL-29; @UPL-30; @UPL-32]. Market-shaping funders: procurement of a canteen protein ingredient and the naming and GMO rules; Nova Vista's USD 10 million programme funds procurement, advance market commitments and retailer ratio targets, and prioritises policy staff in Japan, South Korea, Germany and the Nordics. R&D funders: ingredient functionality and Vietnamese sensory tests. Development finance: import substitution and feed, on the import bill and jobs. Nutrition agencies: protein quality, zinc and iron in school food standards [@AFN-05; @AFN-23; @UPL-27] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Why the chay route is hard to fund.** Only 4 of the original 19 demand moves have a funder whose scope fits and that accepts Vietnam (our assessment, `funder_fit.csv`). Culture-change and diet-change work is excluded by Nova Vista and now by ACE Movement Grants; ReRoot Asia has no Vietnam track; Lever's Asia expansion names India and Thailand; and we found no Vietnam work by Sinergia or Good Food Fund [@AFN-05; @FUF-01; @AFN-29; @AFN-39; @AFN-26; @AFN-27] {VN-direct|Medium}. Existing chay days already avoid about as much meat protein as the Part IV scenario assumes, but that is in the baseline; the chay-day survey question belongs in national survey budgets (NSO, NIN) or GAIN's Diet Quality Questionnaire ([[ch12-chay-baseline]]).
- **Corporate commitments are a weak lever here.** Accor's target of 50% vegetarian or plant-based dishes by 2030 is the only one we found that binds Vietnamese units (43 hotels; it counts dishes, not protein), we found no Vietnamese protein buyer with a published target, and only 2 of 100 Asian protein buyers have targets to boost plant-protein sales. If you fund commitments work, fund implementation measurement at Accor's Vietnamese hotels and a disclosure ask to Vinamilk, not a new pledge campaign [@AFN-40; @AFN-41; @AFN-18; @AFN-21] {VN-direct|Medium} ([[ch15-channels]]).

What the actor check changed for funders and field-builders, and who could answer the open questions, are in [[ch29-actor-check]].

{{kn:kn-funder-fit}} {{kn:kn-animals-spared-2035}} {{kn:kn-co2e-avoided-2035}} {{kn:kn-chay-days-share}} {{kn:kn-demand-bench-2035}}

## Looking to 2050

- **Where long-horizon support has leverage:** a national protein and feed balance (the EU's new balance-sheet method is a ready template); a review cycle for the vision at each five-year plan; climate-proof siting in a Mekong Delta that sinks about 1.1 cm a year; concessional finance windows ready to open when signposts trip; and Vietnam's part in any ASEAN reliance on novel-food approvals ([[ch28-robust-moves]]).
- **Just transition is about farm incomes, not factory jobs.** A 10 kt a year plant employs 60 to 100 people; the households most affected by a protein shift are the remaining small pig and poultry farms, and the ones who could gain are cassava, rice-straw and brewery-residue suppliers.
- **Climate finance hardly reaches food** (about 7% of climate finance in 2021 and 2022), no approved carbon-credit method exists for protein substitution, and green-bond criteria for alternative proteins appeared in 2025.
- **A jointly authored vision has a precedent:** *Vietnam 2035* was written by the World Bank and the planning ministry. Our Vietnam 2050 protein vision is offered for that kind of discussion ([[ch24-vision-2050]], [[app-f5-targets-hubs]]).

{{kn:kn-no-regret-moves}} {{kn:kn-delta-subsidence}}

**Read next:** [[front-exec-summary]] · [[ch08-capital]] · [[ch03-regional]] · [[ch27-policy-options]] · [[app-s11-capital]] · [[app-s3-regional]] · [[ch25-demand-to-frontier]] · [[ch29-actor-check]]. Codes such as T1 or PO-017 are decoded in [[front-how-to-read]].

data.title: M1. Method, evidence rules and limits
data.summary: How the study was designed around six audiences, how two research waves and a retail audit were run, which tools were and were not available, how evidence was labelled and checked, how earlier drafts were used, and what the limits are. Section M1.10 summarises the futures round added in v0.2; the full futures method is in Appendix M2.
data.body:
# M1. Method, evidence rules and limits

## M1.1 Design: six audiences, eleven questions

The study started from the decisions six groups of readers face, and set a research goal for each:

| Audience | Decision they face | Research goal |
|---|---|---|
| Investors (venture capital, impact investors, development finance) | Is there investable deal flow, and which theses? | Deal history and investors; cost inputs; 4 to 8 evidence-backed theses with what must be true and kill tests |
| Policy makers (Vietnamese ministries and provinces; ASEAN bodies; foreign governments) | What to write, fund or change | Full instrument register; precedents; ranked policy options with owners |
| Startups | What to build, where, with whom, through which legal route | Feedstock, facility, laboratory and programme directories; routes to market by product type |
| Food and feed manufacturers | Whether to add lines, source Vietnamese ingredients or site production | Capacity map; formulation analysis; import dependence; export routes |
| Research bodies | What to research, with whom, with what funding | Bibliometric map; institution directory; gaps Vietnam is placed to fill |
| International organisations | Where programmes can move the frontier | Partner map; fundable public goods |

These goals were turned into eleven macro questions (protein economy, asset map, industrial capacity, the existing market, rules, knowledge base, capital, regional position, economics, technology fit, synthesis), which became the chapters, and a list of micro deliverables (directories, registers, data sheets), which became the appendices and data files.

After the first research wave we re-read the goals and recorded, for each audience, what was still missing. The second wave was designed to close those gaps.

## M1.2 Research waves

Research was carried out by AltProtein Vietnam with AI research assistants organised as parallel research streams (called "agents" in the working papers), each with a written brief, a shared protocol and its own source-ID prefix. Their notes were then consolidated, checked and synthesised into this report.

| Wave | Stream | Prefix | Topic |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Macro | MAC | Protein economy, feed, trade, targets |
| 1 | Feedstock | FS | Crops, residues, side streams, prices |
| 1 | Industry | IND | Fermentation, feed, food and processing capacity |
| 1 | Ecosystem | ECO | Companies and actors |
| 1 | Regulation | REG | Food, feed, GMO, labelling, incentives, sandboxes |
| 1 | Research and development | RD | Institutions, research output, talent, funding |
| 1 | Capital | CAP | Deals, investors, programmes |
| 1 | Regional | RGN | Neighbouring countries, approvals, trade |
| 1 | Costs | COST | Input costs, commodity prices, cost benchmarks |
| 1 | Formulation | FORM | Retail audit analysis and ingredient supply |
| 2 | Science | SCI | State of the science by technology family; checks of earlier claims |
| 2 | Regulation 2 | REG2 | Draft Food Safety Law, aquafeed list, sandbox, tax |
| 2 | Feed market | FM | Fishmeal, inclusion rates, trials, prices to beat |
| 2 | Geography and time | GT | Administrative reforms, milestones, outlook |
| 2 | Company verification | VCO | Checks of company facts and capacities |
| 2 | Infrastructure | INF | Pilot plants, laboratories, parks, talent |
| 2 | Bibliometrics | BIB | Research output counts and comparisons |

In total the streams logged **806 sources** (599 in wave 1, 207 in wave 2): 180 press, 175 peer-reviewed, 133 company, 124 government or statistics, 78 legal texts and the rest from databases, advocacy groups and market research ([[app-r4-sources]]).

{{chart:chart-sources-by-type}}

## M1.3 Tools and their limits

- **Web search** was available for part of the first wave only; the session's search budget ran out part-way through. After that, research used direct reads of known pages, the search functions inside legal databases, scholarly indexes (Scite, and the OpenAIRE research graph) and trade data (World Bank WITS, UN Comtrade). General search engines were not used as a workaround.
- **Bibliometrics.** OpenAlex, the planned bibliometric source, refused requests (HTTP 429) during the run, so counts come from OpenAIRE, with OpenAlex queries saved for a rerun ([[app-s7-research]]). Counts are lower bounds; Vietnamese-language journals are only partly indexed.
- **Unreachable sources** (blocked pages, rate limits, image-only PDFs) are logged in the working papers and in `open_questions.csv`.
- **Language.** Vietnamese legal texts and press were read in Vietnamese.

## M1.4 The retail audit

AltProtein Vietnam recorded 186 alternative-protein and plant-based products (SKUs) in 11 stores: five in Nha Trang on 6 September 2026 and six in Ho Chi Minh City on 16 and 20 September 2026, from hypermarkets to specialty importers. Records include price, pack size, ingredients and label nutrition where legible; low-confidence price reads are flagged. The audit is a convenience sample in two cities, not a national survey ([[app-s2-retail-audit]]). Source ID FORM-01.

## M1.5 Evidence rules

- **Labels.** Every finding carries VN-direct, VN-adjacent (with the transfer stated) or general.
- **Confidence.** High (primary source read), Medium (reputable secondary or primary read in part), Low (single claim, press, company marketing, or our derivation from weak inputs).
- **Measured, estimated, claimed.** Kept distinct; our calculations are marked.
- **Disagreements.** Never averaged. Both values and the position taken are recorded (142 entries, [[app-r2-disagreements]]).
- **Currency.** Regulatory and market claims older than 12 months were re-checked where possible.
- **Earlier drafts are leads, not sources.** This project produced internal scoping drafts before version 0.1. Their claims were listed as leads and each was re-checked against a primary or reputable source before use; several were wrong and are corrected in [[app-m5-changelog]].

## M1.6 Checking

- Every headline number in the chapters was traced to a source ID and checked against the working note that produced it.
- Every citation token in the content resolves to `sources.csv`; cross-links, evidence tags and key-number and chart references were validated by script.
- An independent review pass re-checked the headline numbers against notes and sources before publication.
- Wave 2 re-verified a sample of wave 1 company and regulatory claims; corrections are recorded in the `change_log` fields of the data files.

## M1.7 Synthesis methods

- **Technology fit** ([[ch10-technology-fit]]) rates ten families on seven conditions (strong, moderate, weak).
- **Plays** ([[ch26-plays]]) are scored 1 to 5 on seven criteria, with weight presets per audience in `play_weight_presets.csv`. Scores are judgements based on the cited evidence.
- **Policy options** ([[ch27-policy-options]]) are ranked by impact on investability, feasibility and time-criticality.
- **Scenarios** ([[ch19-outlook-2035]]) are internally consistent pictures with signposts, not forecasts.
- **Cost stacks** ([[ch09-economics]]) combine sourced Vietnamese prices with stated engineering assumptions and are indicative.

## M1.8 Limits

- No interviews in this draft; the remaining gaps need phone calls and letters ([[ch30-unknowns]]).
- Search limits mean some recent press and grey literature were missed; absence in our logs means "not found", not "does not exist".
- Company capacities are often self-reported or old.
- Trade tonnages in some databases are estimated; we use values and mirror data where so.
- Provincial statistics before and after the July 2025 merger need re-aggregation ([[app-s10-admin-map]]).
- The study is not investment, legal or engineering advice.

## M1.9 Data and reuse

All tables are in `data/` with a data dictionary. The unedited research notes are in `working-papers/`. Where notes and report disagree, the report is the current position.

## M1.10 Version 0.2: the futures round

Version 0.2 (September 2026) adds the futures chapters to 2050 (now chapters 20 to 24 and 28) and Appendices M2 and F2 to F6. The futures round followed the same evidence rules as v0.1, with four additions. The full method is in [[app-m2-futures-method]].

- **Scope decisions.** New futures chapters in the same package; evidence-anchored foresight plus one normative vision, clearly labelled; four topics (frontier production technology, drivers and shocks, economy and policy futures, quantitative projections); demand as a macro input only, with no consumer research or market-size forecast. Insects remain a benchmark, not a play.
- **Research waves 3 to 5.** Eight streams in wave 3 (frontier gas fermentation, frontier biology and AI, climate, the balance model, geopolitics and macro drivers, economics and policy, horizon scan, national targets), three gap-closing streams in wave 4 (next-generation feedstocks, aquaculture futures, spatial hubs) after an actor review, and one in wave 5 (vision benchmarks and foresight practice). They added 469 sources (1,275 in all) under the prefixes FTG, FTB, CLM, QNT, GEO, ECF, HSC, NTS, NGF, AQF, HUB and VIS.
- **Tools.** Web search with per-stream caps (about 137 searches in total), direct reading of official texts, OpenAlex for bibliometrics and literature (it worked in this round, unlike wave 2), and a desktop browser as a read-only fallback for pages that direct fetches could not reach. No sign-in, form, download or personal identifier was used in any request.
- **Foresight tags.** Every forward-looking claim carries a foresight type (trend, projection, estimate, signal, wildcard or, in chapter 24 only, vision) and a horizon year ([[front-how-to-read]]).
- **Quantitative model.** A transparent protein and feed balance model (`tools/balance_model.py`) reproduces published outlooks to 2035 within about 2% and extends them to 2050 under four scenarios ([[app-f4-balance-model]]).
- **Checks.** An actor review after wave 3, consolidation of all new sources into `sources.csv`, the extended validator (which now also checks foresight tags) and an independent verification pass on the Part IV numbers and model arithmetic.
- **Corrections to v0.1.** Corrections are listed in section M5.9 of [[app-m5-changelog]]; the new open questions (OQ-128 onwards) and disagreements (DG-143 onwards) are in [[app-r1-open-questions]] and [[app-r2-disagreements]].

## M1.11 Version 0.3: the demand round

Version 0.3 adds Part III on the demand side, built from eight research streams (wave 6, 451 sources), a re-read of the retail audit for demand signals and a reproducible demand sizing model. It introduces a demand evidence tag (stated, revealed, tested or inferred) alongside the evidence and foresight tags. The full method, evidence rules, rejected claims and limits are in [[app-m3-demand-method]].

## M1.12 Version 0.4: the actor check

Version 0.4 checks Part III against 80 named actors and 118 decision questions, then runs sixteen research lines in three waves (waves 7 to 9, 577 sources) and stops when no line changes a Part III conclusion. The method, yield by line, stopping rule and limits are in [[app-m4-actor-check-waves]].

## M1.13 Version 0.5: the prologue

Version 0.5 adds a prologue for readers new to alternative protein ([[front-prologue]], [[front-prologue-vi]]). Three research agents, working from a common brief, gathered facts on definitions and technology families, the general arguments for and against alternative protein, and the international landscape (wave 10, 81 sources). Each reused package sources where they applied and recorded a short verbatim quote for every key number; an independent check compared the prologue with those notes before release. The briefs and notes are in `working-papers/wave10/`. The prologue is background: it adds no finding about Vietnam and changes none.

data.title: M2. Futures method: how the 2050 chapters were built
data.summary: How the futures round behind Part IV was designed, researched and checked: the ten questions it answers, the twelve research streams and their 469 sources, the foresight badges on every forward-looking claim, the two-axis scenario method, the stress test of plays and moves, the vision and backcasting method, and the limits of the work.
data.body:
# M2. Futures method: how Part IV was built

**What this appendix contains.** The method behind the 2050 futures work (chapters 20 to 24 in Part IV and chapter 28 in Part V): the decisions that set its scope, the questions it answers, the twelve research streams and their tools, the evidence and foresight labels, how the scenarios, stress tests and vision were built, how the work was checked, and its limits. It extends the v0.1 method in [[app-m1-method]], which still applies unless this page says otherwise.

**How to use it.** If you meet a foresight badge such as *estimate* in Part IV, start with section M2.4. To rerun or challenge a result, use sections M2.5 to M2.8, which name the data files and scripts.

---

## M2.1 Purpose and scope of the futures round

Version 0.1 (September 2026) describes Vietnam's alternative-protein supply today and its outlook to 2035 ([[ch19-outlook-2035]]). The futures round asked what could change between 2030 and 2050, and what actors should do now while the answer is uncertain. The research ran on 24 September 2026. The project owner took five decisions before it started.

| Decision | What was decided | Consequence in Part IV |
|---|---|---|
| Packaging | New futures chapters in the same package; executive summaries and briefs updated | Chapters 20 to 24 and 28, Appendices M2 and F2 to F6, 33 data files from the streams and 6 synthesis files |
| Stance | Evidence-anchored foresight plus one bold normative vision, clearly labelled | Horizon scan, exploratory scenarios and signposts; one "Vietnam 2050" vision with backcast milestones ([[ch24-vision-2050]]) |
| Topics | All four: frontier technology; drivers and shocks; economy and policy futures; quantitative projections | Chapters 20 to 22, and a transparent protein and feed balance model for 2030 to 2050 ([[app-f4-balance-model]]) |
| Demand | Demand enters only as a macro input (population, income, diet, published outlooks) | No consumer research; no market-size forecast for Vietnamese alternative-protein products |
| Insects | Incumbent and benchmark only | No insect play recommended; insect papers in the bibliometric screen set aside as benchmark material |

Unchanged from v0.1: the supply-side scope; food and feed together; neutral framing led by food and feed security, industry and trade; English text with a Vietnamese summary.

## M2.2 Who Part IV is for, and the questions it answers

### M2.2.1 Actor futures goals

| Actor | What they need from a 2050 view | Futures goal | Main chapters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Investors | Technology readiness and cost paths; when Vietnam's advantages switch on; regional competition; signposts that trigger investment | FG-VC: dated technology and cost trajectories with Vietnam triggers; option-value theses | 16, 18, 20 |
