### S5.2.4 Consolidation and new capacity, 2025 to 2026

- **Exit.** Cargill left aquafeed in May 2025 (trade press) [@IND-43] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Acquisition.** Royal De Heus bought CJ's regional feed business, CJ Feed & Care. The deal was announced on 1 October 2025 and completed on 3 March 2026. It covered Vietnam, Indonesia, Cambodia, South Korea and the Philippines, with 17 feed mills in total across the five countries. The price and the Vietnamese share were not disclosed [@VCO-07; @VCO-08] {VN-direct|High}. De Heus Vietnam now lists 21 plants [@VCO-09] {VN-direct|Medium}; it is not clear whether this includes the former CJ mills.

> **Correction.** Earlier drafts said De Heus gained 17 plants in Vietnam from CJ. The 17 mills are across five countries [@VCO-07; @VCO-08]. The number in Vietnam is not disclosed.

- **New high-protein aquafeed capacity.** C.P. opened a 124,800 t/yr shrimp-feed plant in Ca Mau on 7 August 2026 [@IND-42] {VN-direct|Medium}. De Heus opened a marine and cold-water fish-feed mill in Vinh Long in July 2026, for feeds with 40 to 50% protein [@IND-45; @VCO-10] {VN-direct|Medium}. These plants are the premium buyers for fishmeal substitutes.

> **Correction.** Wave 1 recorded the De Heus Vinh Long mill at 84,000 t/yr (trade press) [@IND-45]. The De Heus global release of 22 July 2026 gives 168,000 t/yr design capacity [@VCO-10]. We use the company figure; 84,000 t/yr may be phase 1. The conflict is logged in [[app-r2-disagreements]].

- **First commercial novel protein in shrimp feed.** Skretting Vietnam and Entobel announced a strategic partnership on 26 November 2025, and commercial production of Skretting shrimp feed containing Entobel's insect meal began that month. This is the first commercial insect-meal shrimp feed in Vietnam (company claim). No inclusion rate or volume was disclosed [@VCO-28] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Prices and tax.** Feed prices rose 10 to 14% between January and April 2026 (a poultry association estimate) [@MAC-24] {VN-direct|Low}, and shrimp-feed makers raised prices by VND 1,200 to 1,500 per kg in early June 2026 [@FM-10] {VN-direct|Medium}. Feed became non-taxable for VAT from 1 July 2025, so mills can no longer deduct the input VAT they pay [@MAC-25] {VN-direct|Medium}; see [[app-s12-costs]].

### S5.2.5 Premix and fishmeal plants

- **Premix.** Cargill Provimi (Dong Nai, 40,000 t/yr) is the only premix plant with a published capacity [@IND-47] {VN-direct|Medium}; De Heus lists one premix plant [@VCO-09]. Premix blenders are a low-volume entry route for functional ingredients such as yeast derivatives and postbiotics.
- **Fishmeal plants.** Not mapped. Vietnam exported USD 430.5 M of fishmeal in 2023, mostly to China, so domestic plants exist at scale [@FM-38] {VN-direct|Medium}; see [[app-s6-feed-market]].

---

## S5.3 Soybean crushing

- **VAL.** Cong ty TNHH Kinh doanh nong san Viet Nam (VAL), a Bunge and Wilmar business at Phu My 1 Industrial Park, Ho Chi Minh City (former Ba Ria-Vung Tau), can crush 2.6 Mt of soybeans a year and make nearly 2 Mt of meal after a USD 100 M second line (December 2025). Ho Chi Minh City officials expect it to reach about 30% of the domestic soybean-meal market. It has no food-grade or protein-isolate line on record [@VCO-16] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **National crush.** 1.9 Mt of soybeans were crushed in 2025, giving 1.48 Mt of meal at 78% extraction; USDA forecasts 2.5 Mt in 2026 and 3.0 Mt in 2027 [@MAC-04] {VN-direct|Medium}. Four crush plants operated in 2025 (one in the north, three in the south), and new lines opened in Q1 2026; USDA does not name the crushers [@MAC-04; @MAC-05] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Reading.** VAL's stated 2.6 Mt is more than the whole 2025 national crush and close to the 2026 forecast, so it is most likely a design capacity after the second line, not 2025 throughput (our reading). The other crushers remain unnamed.
- **Import dependence.** Domestic soybeans (43 kt) could supply only about 2.3% of the 2025 crush (our calculation, 43 / 1,900) [@MAC-04]. Crushing shifts imports from meal to beans; it does not reduce dependence.

---

## S5.4 Soy, dairy, meat and chay processors

| Firm | Location | Capacity and scale | Relevance | Sources | Label |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vinasoy (Quang Ngai Sugar, QNS) | Quang Ngai; Bac Ninh (plants from 2012 and 2013, with a soy research centre); Ho Chi Minh City (former Binh Duong) | 390 million L/yr of soymilk in three plants (2022); the Binh Duong plant was designed for 180 million L/yr, with phase 1 of 90 million L opened December 2017; soymilk revenue over VND 4,100 bn (2024); about 80% of soymilk (company) | Soybean receiving, grinding, UHT and aseptic packing; okara side stream. No 2025 capacity figure found | [@IND-48; @IND-49; @IND-50; @VCO-17] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| ToFu House | Hung Yen (Van Giang) | 150 to 500 t of tofu products a month; ISO 22000 | A rare industrial tofu maker in an artisanal sector | [@IND-51] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Vinamilk | 9 or more plants | Mega factory phase 1, 400 million L/yr (2013) | UHT, spray-dried powder and yoghurt; 17 plant-based products logged in the September 2026 retail audit | [@IND-52; @IND-53] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Vissan | Ho Chi Minh City | Not published; SATRA 67.8%, Masan MEATLife 24.9% (2025 annual report) | Chay spring rolls and canned chay beef-and-tofu on the same lines as meat; plant list not published | [@VCO-13; @VCO-14; @BUY-04; @IND-53] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| CJ Cau Tre (CJ Foods Vietnam) | Ho Chi Minh City headquarters; plants not verified | not published | Frozen foods including chay spring rolls and bibigo lines; the year CJ bought Cau Tre is not verified | [@VCO-12; @IND-53] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Cholimex Foods | Ho Chi Minh City | not published | Frozen dim sum including chay; sauces | [@IND-53; @ECO-37] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| SG Food | Ho Chi Minh City | About 2,000 staff (field log) | Frozen ready meals including chay; supplies 7-Eleven fresh food | [@IND-53; @ECO-29] | {VN-direct\|Low} |

- **Plant milks.** Other brands on shelf include TH true NUT and Vinasoy's Fami and Veyo [@IND-53; @FORM-33] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Chay versus meat.** Field notes say a brand's chay product is often 17 to 38% cheaper than its meat version. Only one pair (Vissan spring rolls, 38% cheaper) is a high-confidence read [@IND-53] {VN-direct|Low}; see [[app-s2-retail-audit]].
- **Do chay specialists.** Capacities are unknown for An Nhien, Au Lac (Anlac Vegan Food), Thoai An, Top.V (Agrex Saigon), Song Huong Foods (Ho Chi Minh City, Binh Chanh) and Saky Foods [@IND-53; @IND-54] {VN-direct|Low}. The retail audit logged more than 20 local chay brands, and none publishes plant capacity [@IND-53]. An Nhien is a registered trading company that sells soy and barley textured-protein chay under its own brand (since late 2014), is Halal-certified and claims exports to Korea, Europe and North America; no factory is disclosed [@VCO-26] {VN-direct|Medium}. An earlier lead listed Xuan Hong as a chay maker. We found a Xuan Hong chay brand on shelf (a dried soy and wheat analogue) with an unidentified maker [@FORM-01], and a cassava starch processor of that name in Tay Ninh [@ECO-39] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Private labels.** Retailer private-label chay exists: Coop Select (reportedly made by GN Foods in Tay Ninh; not re-verified) and Choice L for Lotte [@IND-53] {VN-direct|Low}. Imported Chinese canned "plant based" luncheon meats sit beside Vissan's local canned chay [@IND-53].

---

## S5.5 Starch, glucose and maltodextrin

- **Cassava starch.** 120 to 150 factories (the sources' counts differ), with 11.3 Mt of design and 8.62 Mt of actual root capacity (reported January 2023; data year not stated) [@FS-02; @FS-07] {VN-direct|Medium}. Tay Ninh has 65 to 68 of them and 6.4 Mt/yr of root capacity [@FS-03; @FS-07] {VN-direct|Medium}. Details in [[app-s4-feedstocks]] (sheets C2 to C5).
- **Vedan.** Between 1994 and 2004 Vedan built 140,000 t/yr of glucose syrup, about 216,000 t/yr of native tapioca starch lines (72,000 + 72,000 + 36,000 + 36,000) and 40,000 t/yr of modified starch (nameplates) [@VCO-03] {VN-direct|Medium}. It lists glucose syrup (including an EU-organic grade) for sale to third parties [@IND-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. The Phuoc Long tapioca starch plant, with its native starch lines [@IND-04], is in Dong Nai (former Binh Phuoc) [@IND-02; @IND-66].
- **Daesang.** Starch plant in Tay Ninh (2005); capacity not found [@IND-11] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Maltodextrin.** We found no Vietnamese producer.
- **Reading.** Cassava glucose syrup is the obvious local carbon source for fermentation, and it is already made at scale next to the aerobic fermenters.

---

## S5.6 Extrusion, spray drying and protein isolates: absence findings

| Capability | What we found | Sources | Label |
|---|---|---|---|
| Soy, pea or rice protein isolate or concentrate plant | None. Soybeans are crushed or used whole. VAL has no isolate line on record | [@IND-48; @IND-49; @IND-50; @VCO-16] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Textured vegetable protein (TVP) or wheat-gluten manufacturer | None. An Nhien makes or sells TVP-based chay but is registered as a trader | [@VCO-26] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Food-grade extrusion (low or high moisture) | None found. The only extrusion documented is in aquafeed | [@IND-46] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Spray drying | Dairy powder lines exist (Vinamilk); instant-coffee dryers are candidates for toll drying but were not checked | [@IND-52] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Research on extrusion | At most one Vietnamese extrusion study (2015 to 2026), among about 6 on-topic plant-based meat papers | [@BIB-01] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |

- **Imports fill the gap.** In 2023 Vietnam imported USD 31.06 M of wheat gluten (HS 1109, 59% from China), USD 33.98 M of protein concentrates and textured protein (HS 2106.10; United States 46%, China 27%) and USD 22.18 M of peptones and other protein substances (HS 3504, including some isolates; China 45%) [@COST-36; @COST-37; @COST-38] {VN-direct|Medium}. The quantities in the database look imputed, so we quote values only. MFN import duties in 2023 were 10% (wheat gluten), 5% (HS 2106.10) and 3% (HS 3504) [@REG2-20; @REG2-23] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Equipment makers.** We could not confirm a Vietnamese sales or service entity for Buhler, Clextral, Famsun, GEA or Alfa Laval; their pages failed or gave no Vietnamese detail [@INF-27; @INF-30; @INF-31; @INF-32; @INF-33] {general|Low}.

---

## S5.7 OEM and co-packing

- **Chay OEM already works.** Retailer private labels (Coop Select, Choice L) show that contract manufacture of chay products is an established model [@IND-53] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Frozen formats.** Vissan, CJ Cau Tre, Cholimex, SG Food and GN Foods already make chay on meat or frozen-food lines. They are the most plausible co-packers for plant-based products and first customers for protein ingredients.
- **Plant milks.** Vinasoy and the dairy majors have UHT capacity. We found no evidence that they sell it to others.
- **Aerobic fermentation.** No toll offer exists (S5.1.9). The route is a structured deal with Vedan or Ajinomoto.
- **Feed trials.** Mills run at about half capacity (S5.2.1), so pelleting trial slots should be easy to find.

---

## S5.8 Engineering and equipment

| Firm | Type | Vietnamese presence | Relevance | Sources | Label |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HTG Engineering | Local mechanical, electrical, cleanroom and cold-storage contractor | Ho Chi Minh City | USD 3.88 M of mechanical, electrical, cold-storage (-25 C) and class 10,000 cleanroom work across three Ajinomoto plants; clients include Coca-Cola and PepsiCo. Fermenter fabrication not stated | [@IND-64] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Rieckermann | German process-equipment and turnkey engineer | Lists a project in Vietnam (croissant line) | Turnkey food and pharma process lines, including a croissant line in Vietnam; designed the VNVC vaccine plant | [@INF-24; @IND-31] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| TECOVA | GMP and ISO design, validation and compliance consultancy | Vietnam | GMP design and qualification for food, pharma and biotech | [@IND-65] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Buhler, Famsun, Clextral | Feed, aquafeed and food extrusion | Not verified | Main suppliers of extrusion lines | [@INF-27; @INF-30; @INF-31] | {general\|Low} |
| GEA, Alfa Laval | Separators, decanters, spray dryers, evaporators | Not verified | Downstream processing for single-cell protein and protein isolates | [@INF-32; @INF-33] | {general\|Low} |
| Local tofu and soymilk machine makers (for example Dong Duong Vina) | Small food-machinery fabricators | Vietnam | Small-batch soymilk and tofu equipment for pilot work; not checked | none | {VN-direct\|Low} |

Plants in Vietnam are designed by foreign engineering firms and fitted out by local contractors. We found no local maker of sanitary stainless fermenters, extruders or spray dryers in either research wave.

---

## S5.9 Shared infrastructure (summary)

Saigon Hi-Tech Park covers 913 ha (phase 1 of 300 ha and phase 2 of 613 ha), with 165 projects and USD 14.08 bn of registered capital; it has an incubator (SHTP-IC), an R&D centre (SHTP Labs) and a Biotech Center [@IND-57] {VN-direct|Medium}. FIRI (Hanoi, with a Ho Chi Minh City branch) has an ISO/IEC 17025 lab, a microbial culture collection and an experimental production and technology-transfer centre, and lists C.P., CJ, Habeco and Vissan as clients [@IND-60; @INF-03] {VN-direct|Medium}. The National Institute for Food Control and Eurofins Sac Ky Hai Dang test food and feed; QUATEST 3 tests food [@IND-61; @IND-62; @IND-63] {VN-direct|Medium}. None publishes a food-grade fermentation service of 100 L to 1,000 L or more. Details are in [[app-s8-labs-talent]].

---

## Gaps and how to close them

| # | Gap | Why it matters | Cheapest way to close it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Vedan's current MSG, lysine and fermentation capacity, tank count and idle time | Largest single unknown in the fermentation volume estimate; a tolling partner candidate | Read Vedan's environmental permit on the MAE portal; ask Vedan's starch-derivatives R&D team directly |
| 2 | Whether any incumbent will toll-ferment | Decides whether a first plant needs its own tanks | Direct inquiry to Vedan and to Ajinomoto Vietnam's corporate planning team about the 700 m3 tanks |
| 3 | Ajinomoto fermenter numbers and volumes | Second-largest aerobic base | Find the full 2023 EIA behind permit 379/GPMT-BTNMT |
| 4 | Pilot fermentation access (50 to 3,000 L, food grade) | No public pilot service found | One-page equipment questionnaire to FIRI, the HCMC Biotechnology Center and SHTP Labs |
| 5 | Capacity and processes of do chay and plant-based makers | Co-packer selection | Manufacturer names from product labels (the field photos exist), then company registration and self-declaration records |
| 6 | Extrusion, spray drying, maltodextrin, protein isolates | Absence findings need testing | Customs data for HS 3504 and 2106.10 by importer; ask Vinasoy and instant-coffee dryers (Nestle Tri An, Masan/Vinacafe Bien Hoa, Trung Nguyen) about toll drying |
| 7 | Citric acid, enzymes, threonine and methionine production | Tests the "all imported" assumption | Customs import data for 2024 and 2025; the Vietnam Chemicals Agency plant list |
| 8 | Which Vietnamese mills came with CJ Feed & Care; whether the 21 De Heus plants include them | Buyer concentration | Ask De Heus Vietnam communications |
| 9 | Fishmeal plants and premix makers | Domestic competitor for novel feed protein | MAE livestock department feed-facility registry; VASEP for by-product fishmeal plants |
| 10 | Status of AB Mauri La Nga after the 2019 suspension | The only sizeable yeast plant with a published capacity | Dong Nai Department of Agriculture and Environment, or AB Mauri directly |
| 11 | Local fabricators of stainless fermenters and food machinery; Vietnamese entities of the equipment majors | Capex and service lead times | Vietnam Mechanical Enterprises Association; phone the regional offices of Buhler, GEA, Alfa Laval, Famsun and Clextral |
| 12 | Plant lists for Vissan, CJ Foods Vietnam and Ajinomoto; Vinasoy 2025 capacity | Co-packing and okara | 2025 annual or sustainability reports (Vissan publishes to UPCoM; QNS annual report) |
| 13 | Other soybean crushers | Soybean meal supply and okara-free protein routes | Vietnam Feed Association; the next USDA Oilseeds Annual |

See [[app-r1-open-questions]] for the full register and [[app-r2-disagreements]] for the capacity conflicts (Vedan, De Heus, C.P., ethanol, Carlsberg, VNVC).

## Related data files

- `facilities.csv`: 82 facilities (fermentation, starch, breweries, feed and aquafeed mills, soy, dairy and meat processors, biologics, parks, labs and engineering firms) with capacity, unit, year, relevant capability, whether they serve third parties, province (current and former), sources, label, confidence and a change log of wave 2 corrections.
- `fermentation_volume_estimate.csv`: the modelled vessel-volume estimate by segment, with capacity inputs and productivity assumptions.
- `engineering_suppliers.csv`: nine engineering contractors and equipment vendors with their Vietnamese presence.
- `companies.csv`: the company directory behind [[app-s1-directory]].
- `pilot_labs.csv`: pilot plants, testing labs and parks ([[app-s8-labs-talent]]).
- `feedstocks.csv` and `macro_indicators.csv`: the raw materials and feed volumes these plants use.
- `tariffs.csv`: import duties on protein ingredients.
- `disagreements.csv` and `open_questions.csv`: conflicting capacities and open questions.

data.title: S6. Feed and aquafeed market
data.summary: The feed-protein market a Vietnamese alternative protein would sell into: feed output and imports, aquafeed by species, fishmeal prices to August 2026, the displaceable fishmeal pool, the incumbent substitutes, trial evidence by species, buyer economics, the prices to beat and the Chinese import counterfactual. It includes the revealed price of imported inactive yeast (about 9,200 t in 2025 for food and feed, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg), the ASC feed-mill register and what Vietnamese mills paid for fishmeal.
data.body:
# S6. Feed and aquafeed market

Feed is where a Vietnamese alternative protein is most likely to find its first large buyers. This appendix sets out the market it would enter: how much feed Vietnam makes and imports, how much aquafeed goes to each species, what fishmeal costs, how much fishmeal a novel protein could realistically displace, which substitutes are already in use, what feed trials show, how feed mills decide, and the prices a new product must beat. It ends with the counterfactual: Chinese microbial proteins that can already be imported. It supports [[ch01-why-vietnam]], [[ch09-economics]] and [[ch26-plays]]. Production costs are in [[app-s12-costs]]; the rules for listing a new feed ingredient are in [[app-s9-regulation]].

## How to read this appendix

- **Terms.** FM is fishmeal. SBM is soybean meal. SPC is soy protein concentrate. SCP is single-cell protein (microbial biomass). CAP is *Clostridium autoethanogenum* protein, a bacterial SCP made from steel-mill off-gas. BSF is black soldier fly. CP is crude protein. FCR is feed conversion ratio (kg of feed per kg of animal gained).
- **Protein replacement and functional effects.** "Protein replacement" means a novel ingredient supplies protein in place of fishmeal or soybean meal. A "functional effect" is a benefit such as better survival, immunity or palatability that protein supply does not explain. We keep the two apart, because they support very different prices.
- **Prices.** World Bank prices are nominal USD per tonne. We express them per tonne of protein at 65% CP for fishmeal and 46% CP for soybean meal. VND converts at 26,000 per USD.
- **Years.** USDA's "MY2024/25" for Vietnamese soybeans and soybean meal runs from January to December 2025, so it equals calendar 2025.
- **Our calculations** are marked and show their inputs. Several key inputs (aquafeed volumes by species, inclusion rates) are industry estimates or global averages, so the derived pool is Low confidence.

---

## S6.1 Feed output

| Year | Livestock and poultry compound feed | Aquafeed, USDA | Aquafeed, industry | Total feed demand, USDA | Sources | Label |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | about 20.8 Mt (implied from 2024 growth) | not given | not given | not given | [@MAC-28] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| 2024 | 21.5 Mt (up 3.4%): pig 55.3%, poultry 40.9%, other livestock 3.7% | 6.2 Mt | not given | 27.5 Mt | [@MAC-28; @MAC-02] | {VN-direct\|High} |
| 2025 | about 22 Mt (up about 3%) | 6.5 Mt | 3.9 to 4.8 Mt | 28.6 Mt | [@MAC-01; @MAC-06] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| H1 2026 | 12.43 Mt (up 7.5%) | not given | not given | not given | [@MAC-03] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| 2026 forecast (USDA, April 2026) | 22.77 Mt | 6.73 Mt | not given | 29.5 Mt | [@MAC-01] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| 2027 forecast (USDA, April 2026) | 23.48 Mt | 7.12 Mt | not given | 30.6 Mt | [@MAC-01] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |

USDA's August 2026 quarterly revised the forecasts to 23.6 Mt of livestock and poultry feed, 6.85 Mt of aquafeed and 30.45 Mt in total for 2026, and 24.2 Mt, 7.0 Mt and 31.2 Mt for 2027 [@MAC-03] {VN-direct|Medium}.

- **The 21.5 Mt and 22 Mt figures appear to exclude aquafeed.** The species split (pig 55.3%, poultry 40.9%, other livestock 3.7%) adds to about 100% (99.9%) and leaves no room for aquafeed (our inference) [@MAC-28] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Industry structure.** 269 industrial feed mills had 43.2 Mt/yr of design capacity in 2023 and ran at about half capacity; foreign-invested firms made 62.5% of output in 2022 [@IND-39] {VN-direct|Medium}. More than 260 feed companies operate [@MAC-25]. Details and the main groups are in [[app-s5-facilities]].
- **Feed prices in 2026.** Feed prices rose 10 to 14% between January and April 2026, by the poultry association's estimate. The poultry association chair said they could rise 20 to 25% if the Middle East conflict continued [@MAC-24] {VN-direct|Low}. Live hog prices fell about 20% and broiler prices 11 to 19% in H1 2026, a cost-price squeeze [@MAC-03] {VN-direct|Medium}.

---

## S6.2 Feed-ingredient imports and the feed balance

### S6.2.1 Imports by commodity

| Commodity | 2024 | 2025 | Main origins, 2025 | Share of supply imported | Sources | Label |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corn | 12.52 Mt, USD 3.04 bn (Argentina 51.1%, Brazil 39%) | 11.91 Mt, USD 2.95 bn; average USD 248.1/t | Argentina 46.5%, Brazil 34.8%, United States about 13% | about 74% | [@MAC-11; @MAC-08; @MAC-01] | {VN-direct\|High} |
| Soybeans | 2.22 Mt, about USD 1.12 bn (value derived) | 2.61 Mt, USD 1.21 bn; average USD 465.5/t | Brazil 45.8%, United States 43.6%, Canada 7.3% | 98.4% (derived: imports / (imports + production)) | [@MAC-05; @MAC-09; @MAC-04] | {VN-direct\|High} |
| Wheat (all uses) | about 5.74 Mt customs-implied (USDA 5.5 Mt) | 5.45 Mt, USD 1.46 bn; average USD 267.4/t | Australia 25.4%, Brazil 19.1%, United States 17.5% | 100% | [@MAC-10; @MAC-02] | {VN-direct\|High} |
| of which feed wheat | about 2.5 Mt | about 2.58 Mt | Brazil 29%, Ukraine 24%, Russia 12%, United States 12%, Australia 10% | 100% | [@MAC-01] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Soybean meal | 6.0 Mt (Argentina 69%, United States 14%, Brazil 13%) | 5.70 Mt | Argentina 69%, Brazil 15%, United States 13% (read from the USDA table; re-check in the PDF) | 79% of meal; about 99% of soy protein (our calculation from USDA supply data) | [@MAC-05; @MAC-04] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| DDGS | 1.3 Mt | 1.5 Mt (1.55 Mt in the USDA feed-ingredient table) | United States 72%, Brazil 15%, India 13% | 100% | [@MAC-02; @MAC-01; @FS-23] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Rapeseed meal | not given | 281 kt (up 22%; USDA MY2024/25, October 2024 to September 2025) | India largest | not given | [@MAC-04] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Copra meal | not given | 53 kt | not given | not given | [@MAC-04] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Customs group "animal feed and ingredients" (value) | about USD 4.89 bn (derived) | USD 4.58 bn | Argentina 36.6%, United States 18.8%, Brazil 9.7% | not given | [@MAC-07] | {VN-direct\|High} |
| Fishmeal | not found | not found | see S6.5 | not given | none | {VN-direct\|Low} |

- **H1 2026.** Corn imports were 6.8 Mt (up 49%; Argentina 37%, Brazil 36%, United States 13%), wheat 4.8 Mt (up 58%; Argentina 58%) and DDGS 645 kt (down 24%; United States 81%) [@MAC-03] {VN-direct|Medium}. USDA raised its corn import forecast for MY2026/27 to 15 Mt [@MAC-03] {VN-direct|Medium}. The average corn import unit value in H1 2026 was about USD 251/t (June USD 258/t), derived from customs import value and volume [@COST-34] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Import bill.** The sum of four customs lines (corn USD 2.95 bn, soybeans USD 1.21 bn, wheat USD 1.46 bn and "animal feed and ingredients" USD 4.58 bn) is about USD 10.2 bn for 2025 and about USD 10.6 bn for 2024 (our calculation from [@MAC-07; @MAC-08; @MAC-09; @MAC-10]) {VN-direct|Medium}. It is gross: it includes about 2.85 Mt of milling wheat (USDA food, seed and industrial use, MY2025/26) [@MAC-01] and about 0.54 Mt of food soybeans [@MAC-04]. The physical volume of corn, soybeans, wheat, soybean meal, DDGS and rapeseed meal was about 27.4 Mt in 2025 (our calculation from the table above). The livestock department's narrower 2024 figure is 22.4 Mt and USD 7.7 bn (corn 10 Mt, oil meals 5.5 Mt, wheat and barley 2.36 Mt) [@MAC-28] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Share imported.** Official and industry sources give 65 to 85% of feed raw materials imported, depending on definition [@MAC-25; @MAC-27; @MAC-28] {VN-direct|Low}. We prefer ingredient-specific figures: corn about 74%, soy protein about 99%, wheat and DDGS 100%.
- **Price history.** The average corn import price was about USD 295/t in 2023 (derived), USD 243/t in 2024 and USD 248/t in 2025 [@MAC-11; @MAC-08] {VN-direct|Medium}. Wheat averaged USD 267/t in 2025, about 37% below the September 2022 average of USD 424/t [@MAC-10; @MAC-44] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Tariffs.** Feed protein and energy imports are duty-free. The MFN duty on feed corn (HS 1005.90.99) and on soybean meal (HS 2304.00.29 and 2304.00.90) fell to 0% on 31 March 2025; soybeans (HS 1201.90) and fishmeal (HS 2301.20) were already at 0% in 2023 [@REG2-21; @REG2-23] {VN-direct|Medium}. Wheat has been at 0% since November 2021 [@MAC-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. So domestic novel proteins get no tariff shelter against soybean meal or fishmeal. Nor against imported microbial protein: Chinese and ASEAN yeast and single-cell protein (HS 2102.10 and 2102.20) enter at 0% under ACFTA, ATIGA and RCEP [@FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}.

### S6.2.2 The feed-ingredient balance, 2025

USDA's 2025 feed-ingredient table shows 23.57 Mt imported out of 28.62 Mt, about 82% [@FS-23] {VN-direct|High}.

| Component | Mt, 2025 | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Total feed ingredients | 28.62 | [@FS-23] |
| Domestic supply | 5.05: rice bran and broken rice 2.8, corn 1.7, cassava 0.55 | [@FS-23] |
| Imported | 23.57: corn 9.2, soybean meal 7.2 (including local crush of imported beans), feed wheat 2.58, DDGS 1.55, other about 3.0 | [@FS-23]; "other" is our calculation (23.57 minus the itemised 20.53) |

### S6.2.3 Soybean and soybean-meal balance, 2025

For calendar 2025 (USDA's MY2024/25) [@MAC-04] {VN-direct|Medium}:

- **Soybeans.** Supply: opening stocks 460 kt + production 42 kt + imports 2,609 kt = 3,111 kt. Uses: crush 1,900 kt + food 540 kt + feed and waste 220 kt + closing stocks 451 kt = 3,111 kt. The balance closes.
- **Soybean meal.** Supply: opening stocks 678 kt + production 1,482 kt (78% extraction from 1,900 kt) + imports 5,703 kt = 7,863 kt. Uses: exports 283 kt + food 95 kt + feed 7,200 kt + closing stocks 285 kt = 7,863 kt. The balance closes.
- **Reading.** Even if every domestic soybean were crushed, it would supply only about 2.3% of the crush (our calculation, 43 / 1,900). Domestic crushing shifts imports from meal to beans; it does not reduce dependence. About 99% of the soy protein in Vietnamese feed is imported (our calculation from USDA supply data).

> **Correction.** Earlier drafts mixed years: they combined 2026 soybean forecasts (41 kt produced, 3.2 Mt imported) with a 2025 forecast of 7.0 Mt of soybean-meal feed use. The reconciled 2025 figures are 2.61 Mt of soybeans imported (98.4% of imports plus production, our calculation), 5.70 Mt of soybean meal imported and 7.2 Mt of soybean meal fed [@MAC-04; @MAC-09].

---

## S6.3 Aquafeed volumes by species, and the unresolved gap

### S6.3.1 Two incompatible estimates

| Estimate | 2025 volume | Basis | Source | Label |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| USDA Post | 6.5 Mt (6.2 Mt in 2024; April 2026 forecasts 6.73 Mt for 2026 and 7.12 Mt for 2027, revised in August 2026 to 6.85 Mt and 7.0 Mt) | Method not disclosed | [@MAC-01; @MAC-02; @MAC-03] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Industry, by species | 3.9 to 4.8 Mt (our sum) | Shrimp feed up to 920 kt; fish feed 3.0 to 3.9 Mt | [@MAC-06] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Industry, capacity x utilisation | 3.3 to 3.85 Mt | Up to 5.5 Mt installed at 60 to 70% | [@MAC-06] | {VN-direct\|Low} |

Industry estimates by species, 2025 [@MAC-06] {VN-direct|Low}:

| Species | Feed volume, 2025 | Farmed output, 2025 [@MAC-15] |
|---|---|---|
| Shrimp (mostly intensive whiteleg) | up to 920 kt | whiteleg 994.4 kt; black tiger 296.7 kt |
| Pangasius | 2.0 to 2.5 Mt | 1,938.8 kt |
| Tilapia | 0.4 to 0.5 Mt | not published |
| Snakehead | up to 0.3 Mt | not published |
| Marine fish | 0.08 to 0.10 Mt | not published |
| **Total** | **3.9 to 4.8 Mt** | aquaculture total 6,116.8 kt |

US tariffs on Chinese tilapia have pushed northern feed millers, including Dabaco, into tilapia and carp feed [@MAC-06] {VN-direct|Low}.

### S6.3.2 Why the numbers do not close

- **Shrimp.** The industry source says 920 kt of shrimp feed supported "nearly 800,000 tonnes" of shrimp [@MAC-06]. NSO reports 1,291 kt of farmed whiteleg plus black tiger shrimp (our sum, 994.4 + 296.7) [@MAC-15] {VN-direct|High}. Black tiger shrimp is mostly semi-intensive and uses little pelleted feed. But whiteleg output alone (994.4 kt) would need more than 920 kt of feed at any FCR above 0.93 (our calculation, 920 / 994.4). Feed-based and statistical estimates diverge by about 40%.
- **Pangasius.** 2.0 to 2.5 Mt of feed for 1,938.8 kt of fish implies an FCR of only 1.03 to 1.29 (our calculation).
- **Possible explanations.** The industry feed estimates are low; part of the feed is farm-made; or official output is overstated. We cannot tell which.
- **Sensitivity.** If shrimp feed matched NSO whiteleg output at an assumed FCR of 1.2 to 1.4, shrimp feed would be 1.19 to 1.39 Mt (our calculation, 994.4 x 1.2 and x 1.4), not 920 kt.

> **Correction.** Earlier drafts gave aquafeed as 3.4 to 4.0 Mt. That matches only the capacity x utilisation arithmetic, not a production estimate. We report the sum of industry species estimates (3.9 to 4.8 Mt, our sum) and the USDA estimate (6.5 Mt) side by side and do not average them. The displaceable pool below uses the industry species volumes, because only they give a split by species. Livestock and poultry compound feed was about 22 Mt in 2025 [@MAC-01; @MAC-06].

## S6.5 Vietnam's fishmeal trade and domestic supply

Vietnam is a net exporter of fishmeal by value, mostly to China [@FM-37; @FM-38] {VN-direct|Medium}:

| Flow, 2023 (HS 2301.20) | Value | Reported quantity | Main partners |
|---|---|---|---|
| Imports | USD 260.0 M | 138,676 t | India USD 128.4 M (49%), Korea 25.4 M, Brazil 14.9 M, Chile 12.6 M, Peru 11.9 M |
| Exports | USD 430.5 M | 226,644 t | China USD 402.3 M (93.5%), Korea 6.6 M, Thailand 6.3 M, Japan 6.2 M |

- **Quantities are imputed.** Every partner shows the same unit value (USD 1,875/t for imports, USD 1,899/t for exports), so the database estimated the tonnages. Quote values, not tonnes [@FM-37; @FM-38] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Net position.** About USD 170 M net exports in 2023 (our calculation, 430.5 - 260.0).
- **Reading.** Vietnam makes fishmeal from pangasius by-products, other processing waste and low-value fish, and sells most of it to China [@FM-38]. It imports higher-grade meal, much of it from India [@FM-37], for shrimp and marine feeds. Pangasius processing by-products are 62 to 67% of the whole fish [@MAC-45] {VN-direct|Medium}; by-product fishmeal yields are 35.8% for African catfish waste and 54.8% for tilapia waste [@FM-44] {general|Medium}. See [[app-s4-feedstocks]], sheet C26.
- **Gaps.** Domestic fishmeal production, grade mix and domestic prices (VND/kg by 55%, 60% and 65% CP) for 2024 to 2026 were not found.

## S6.7 The displaceable fishmeal pool

How much fishmeal is in Vietnamese aquafeed that a non-animal protein could, in principle, replace? We count only species with both a sourced feed volume and a sourced inclusion range. Feed volumes are the 2025 industry estimates [@MAC-06; @FM-04]; rates are from S6.6. {VN-direct|Low} for volumes, {general|Medium} for rates; the result is Low confidence.

| Species | Feed volume, kt | Fishmeal inclusion | Fishmeal, kt (our calculation) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shrimp | 920 | 6% (low bound) | 55 |
| Shrimp | 920 | 10% (central low) | 92 |
| Shrimp | 920 | 20% (central high) | 184 |
| Shrimp | 920 | 25% (high bound) | 230 |
| Pangasius | 2,000 to 2,500 | 1% to 2% | 20 to 50 |
| Tilapia | 400 to 500 | 1% to 2% | 4 to 10 |

- **Sourced bounds** (shrimp 6 to 25%): 55 + 20 + 4 = **79 kt** to 230 + 50 + 10 = **290 kt** a year (our calculation).
- **Central case** (shrimp 10 to 20%): 92 + 20 + 4 = 116 kt to 184 + 50 + 10 = 244 kt, which we round to **120 to 245 kt** a year (our calculation).
- **Hypothetical additions** (unsourced rates): snakehead up to 300 kt of feed x 20 to 40% = 60 to 120 kt; marine fish 80 to 100 kt x 15 to 30% = 12 to 30 kt. Even at the top of both hypotheses and the top of the sourced range, the pool is about 440 kt (our calculation, 290 + 120 + 30).
- **Sensitivity to shrimp volume.** If shrimp feed matched NSO whiteleg output (1.19 to 1.39 Mt at FCR 1.2 to 1.4; see S6.3), shrimp fishmeal alone would be 119 to 278 kt at 10 to 20% (our calculation).
- **Comparison.** Our wave 1 macro note gave about 80 to 270 kt, using 23% as the shrimp ceiling [@MAC-06; @MAC-41]. The wave 2 range (79 to 290 kt) allows 25% from trial control diets. The central range (120 to 245 kt) is the better single range to quote.
- **Realistic capture by a novel protein.** Trials show 25 to 60% of fishmeal can be replaced without growth loss (S6.9). Applying 25 to 50% to shrimp fishmeal at 10 to 20% inclusion gives 920 x 10% x 25% = 23 kt to 920 x 20% x 50% = 92 kt, which we round to **25 to 90 kt** a year of novel-protein demand (our calculation). That is 2 to 8 plants of Entobel's design size (11 kt/yr), and it is already contested by Entobel, Chinese SCP and poultry by-product meal.

> **Correction.** Earlier drafts gave a displaceable fishmeal pool of 350 to 450 kt a year. Sourced inputs do not support it. It is reachable only if the unsourced snakehead and marine-fish inclusion rates sit at the top of the hypotheses above. Use a central 120 to 245 kt, sourced bounds of 79 to 290 kt, and a realistic capture by a novel protein of 25 to 90 kt (our calculation in the tables above, from inputs in [@FM-04; @FM-05; @FM-07; @FM-08; @MAC-06]).

### S6.9.2 Functional and immunity effects (separate from protein)

- CAP improved growth and survival after pathogen challenge in whiteleg shrimp across 15 to 45 ppt salinity [@FM-20] {general|Medium}.
- Mealworm meal at 50% replacement cut post-challenge mortality by 76.9% in whiteleg shrimp [@FM-26] {general|Medium}.
- FeedKind raised survival and antioxidant markers in largemouth bass [@FM-16] {general|Medium}.
- BSF protein hydrolysate at 1 to 2% of diet raised palatability in shrimp feed [@FM-45] {general|Medium}.
- Beta-glucan raised striped catfish survival under winter conditions from 78.3% to 95.0% [@FM-31] {general|Medium}. Yeast is broadly reviewed as an immunostimulant [@FM-32] {general|Medium}.

**Reading.** The growth data support partial replacement (about 25 to 60% of fishmeal) in the Vietnamese species that still use fishmeal: shrimp, snakehead and marine fish. Early life stages need their own trials (the barramundi fry result is a warning). In pangasius and tilapia there is little fishmeal left to replace, so a novel ingredient there must sell on function or on soybean-meal parity. A product sold on function can charge far more per tonne than one sold on protein (S6.11).

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shrimp feed, price level | about VND 33,000 to 50,000/kg (USD 1,270 to 1,920/t) | 2025 | Derived: a cut of VND 1,000 to 1,500/kg described as 3% (1,000 / 0.03 and 1,500 / 0.03) | [@FM-04] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Shrimp feed, price increase | VND about +1,200/kg (basic lines) and +1,500/kg (higher-protein or premium lines), about +2.4 to +4.5% on the derived level | 1 to 8 June 2026 | New Hope Vinh Long, Alphafeed, Tongwei, Hai Dai Vinh Long, Thang Long | [@FM-10] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Pangasius and tilapia feed, price level | about VND 10,000 to 20,000/kg (USD 385 to 770/t) | 2025 | Derived: a cut of VND 500 to 1,000/kg described as 5% | [@FM-04] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Pangasius, farm gate | VND 26,500 to 30,000/kg live fish | late 2024 | trade press | [@FM-11] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |
| Compound hog feed | VND 360,000 to 370,000 per bag (bag size not stated) | March 2026 | retail | [@COST-33] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Poultry feed | VND 260,000 to 370,000 per bag, up about 2 to 5% on the previous level | March 2026 | retail | [@COST-33] | {VN-direct\|Low} |
| Live hog | VND 65,000/kg live weight | April 2026 | farm gate | [@COST-35] | {VN-direct\|Medium} |

### S6.10.3 What fishmeal costs a shrimp mill

At 15% inclusion, fishmeal adds USD 256 per tonne of feed at the 2025 average price and USD 375 at the August 2026 price (our calculation, 0.15 x 1,706 and 0.15 x 2,500). That is roughly 13 to 30% of the derived shrimp-feed price of USD 1,270 to 1,920/t (our calculation). At USD 2,500/t, each percentage point of fishmeal removed saves about USD 25 per tonne of feed before paying for the replacement (our calculation, 0.01 x 2,500). This is why mills want to cut fishmeal.

### S6.10.4 Who buys

- **Shrimp feed.** Sheng Long, C.P. Vietnam, Uni-President Vietnam, Tongwei, Grobest and Gromax made a combined 640 kt in 2025, about 70% of shrimp feed [@FM-04; @IND-41] {VN-direct|Medium}. New high-protein capacity (C.P. Ca Mau, 124,800 t/yr; De Heus Vinh Long, 84,000 t/yr, opened July 2026 for marine fish whose feeds need 40 to 50% protein) adds premium buyers [@IND-42; @IND-45; @VCO-10] {VN-direct|Medium}. See [[app-s5-facilities]].
- **Pangasius.** Vertically integrated groups; Vinh Hoan has contracted to buy at least 15,000 t of insect meal over 2025 to 2027 [@ECO-05] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Livestock feed.** De Heus, GreenFeed, Cargill and Japfa top Vietnam Report's 2025 reputation ranking of feed companies [@MAC-25] {VN-direct|Low}. C.P. Vietnam, with 21 plants, is another major feed group [@IND-43] {VN-direct|Low}. De Heus's purchase of CJ Feed & Care (closed 3 March 2026) concentrates buying power further (our inference) [@VCO-08] {VN-direct|High}.
- **Integrated pangasius groups own certified mills.** Feed One, 75% owned by Vinh Hoan, has been ASC-certified since July 2024; Nam Viet and Sao Mai feed companies were certified in 2026 (group ownership not verified) and Godaco is in audit [@FBA-15; @FBA-04] {VN-direct|High}.
- **Certification pull, and its limits.** On 25 September 2026 the ASC register listed 15 certified Vietnamese feed mills, the most of any country (15 of 114 worldwide), and 6 more in initial audit; they include C.P. Vietnam, De Heus, Grobest, Skretting, BioMar Viet Uc, GreenFeed and Feed One [@FBA-04] {VN-direct|High}. From 1 May 2028 all ASC farm audits use the new Farm Standard, which requires compound feed from ASC-certified mills [@FBA-02; @FBA-03] {general|Medium}. The pull is for traceable soy and marine inputs, not for microbial protein. ASC Feed Standard v1.2 (in force from 2 February 2026) treats feed stuffs (if due diligence indicates low risk) and any ingredient under 1% of a mill's aquafeed intake as eligible without credit; BAP counts only ingredients from algae and other aquatic microorganisms towards its marine target; neither standard, nor GLOBALG.A.P., requires or rewards yeast, fungal or bacterial biomass [@FBA-01; @FBA-05] {general|High}. A supplier should expect a request for due-diligence data, a GHG factor and strain GMO status, not a premium (our inference). Nutreco reached 0.6% novel ingredients in 2025 against a 5 to 10% target (Skretting 1.5%) [@FBA-07] {VN-adjacent|High}, and we found no named Vietnamese mill that has published a purchase of microbial protein.

### S6.10.5 How a mill qualifies a new ingredient

A typical sequence, drawn from the trial literature and the published local cases (it is not a Vietnamese standard procedure):

1. Specification and safety data: proximate analysis, amino acids, contaminants.
2. Digestibility trial in the target species.
3. Dose-response growth trial in tanks, usually 8 to 12 weeks.
4. Pond or farm trial, with a lab such as ShrimpVet, which ran an additive challenge trial in Ho Chi Minh City [@ECO-70].
5. Legal listing as a feed ingredient in Vietnam. For a new substance in livestock feed this means a feed trial under the Law on Animal Husbandry Art 37 and Circular 94/2025, with about 40 working days of agency steps (protocol approval 15 + 5 days, recognition 15 + 5 days) plus the trial itself [@REG2-08; @REG-29; @REG-32] {VN-direct|Medium}. Our estimate of the total is 6 to 18 months. For aquafeed, the documented steps are about 20 days of appraisal, the trial, then 10 working days (Decree 26/2019/ND-CP Art 32, as amended) [@REG-38; @REG2-02] {VN-direct|Medium}. Whether an aquafeed trial is required for a new raw material is ambiguous (S6.8). See [[app-s9-regulation]].
6. Supply-security and price agreement. The Entobel and Vinh Hoan offtake (at least 15,000 t over 2025 to 2027) is the local precedent [@ECO-05] {VN-direct|Medium}.

---

## S6.11 The price to beat

**Assumptions.** Fishmeal at 65% CP: USD 1,706/t (2025 average) to USD 2,500/t (August 2026). Soybean meal at 46% CP: USD 366/t (2025) to USD 403/t (August 2026) [@FM-01] {general|High}. Novel products: SCP at 70% CP; fungal biomass at 50% CP. Indicative Vietnamese production cost from the fungal feed-protein cost stack in [[app-s12-costs]]: USD 2,227 to 6,612 per tonne of product, or USD 4,050 to 14,700 per tonne of protein (modelled, Low).

| Target | Price to beat, USD per t of protein | Parity price, USD per t of product | Indicative Vietnamese cost, USD per t of protein | Gap at the low-cost end | Plausible? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Fishmeal replacement in shrimp feed (protein basis) | 2,625 to 3,846 | SCP at 70%: 1,837 to 2,692. Fungal at 50%: 1,312 to 1,923 | 4,050 to 14,700 | 1.54 times (2025 price) to 1.05 times (August 2026 price) | Marginal. Needs low capex, near-free carbon and a lasting fishmeal spike. Imports of Chinese SCP probably undercut it |
| 2. Functional ingredient in pangasius feed (1 to 2% inclusion) | Not a protein price: about USD 1,000 to 4,250 per t of product if it delivers a 3 to 5% gain in feed efficiency or survival | as left | 4,050 to 14,700 (USD 2,227 to 6,612 per t of product) | Overlaps at the low end | Plausible with repeatable functional data. Small: 2,000 to 2,500 kt of feed x 1 to 2% = 20 to 50 kt a year at full uptake |
| 2b. Functional-plus-protein ingredient in shrimp feed (2 to 5%) | Fishmeal parity plus USD 1,280 to 4,800 per t for a 5% performance gain | SCP at 70%: about 3,100 to 7,500 | as above | Overlaps | The most plausible entry point |
| 2c. Revealed price: imported bulk inactive yeast, which mills already buy for the same functional role | Not a protein price: USD 1,100 per t of product (2025, 8,729 t); specialty yeast products USD 8,550 per t (464 t) | as left | 4,050 to 14,700 (USD 2,227 to 6,612 per t of product) | 2.0 times the bulk price at the low end | Only with head-to-head trials that show a gain worth the difference (table below); the specialty tier leaves headroom but is small |
| 3. Soybean-meal replacement in pig and poultry feed | 796 to 876 | SCP at 70%: 557 to 613. Fungal at 50%: 398 to 438 | 4,050 to 14,700 | 4.6 to 5.1 times | Not plausible for fermentation protein |

All values in this table are our calculation from [@FM-01; @FM-04; @FM-10; @FBA-17] and the cost stack; {VN-direct|Low}.

**Arithmetic for targets 2 and 2b (our calculation).** Maximum ingredient price = soybean-meal price + (performance gain x feed price) / inclusion rate. Inputs: soybean meal USD 403/t [@FM-01]; feed price levels derived in S6.10.2 [@FM-04]; performance gains of 3 to 5% are assumptions.

- Pangasius feed at USD 385/t, 5% gain, 2% inclusion: 403 + (0.05 x 385) / 0.02 = USD 1,366/t.
- Pangasius feed at USD 770/t, 5% gain, 1% inclusion: 403 + (0.05 x 770) / 0.01 = USD 4,253/t.
- Pangasius feed at USD 385/t, 3% gain, 2% inclusion: 403 + (0.03 x 385) / 0.02 = about USD 980/t.
- Shrimp: 5% of USD 1,280 to 1,920/t of feed, divided by 2 to 5% inclusion, gives USD 1,280 to 4,800/t above the fishmeal-parity value.

**The head-to-head test.** Mills already buy a functional yeast at about USD 1,100 per t, so the right comparison for a new microbial ingredient is that yeast, not a diet without it. The gain a trial must show is (ingredient cost minus yeast price) times inclusion, divided by the feed price (our calculation; `t2_price_per_performance.csv`):

| Species (feed price) | Ingredient cost case | Inclusion | Extra cost, USD per t of feed | Gain needed, % of feed cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shrimp (USD 1,270 to 1,920 per t) | Low (USD 2,227 per t) | 2% | 22.5 | 1.2 to 1.8 |
| Shrimp | High (USD 6,612 per t) | 2% | 110.2 | 5.7 to 8.7 |
| Pangasius (USD 385 to 770 per t) | Low (USD 2,227 per t) | 2% | 22.5 | 2.9 to 5.9 |
| Pangasius | High (USD 6,612 per t) | 2% | 110.2 | 14.3 to 28.6 |

Our calculation from [@FBA-17; @FM-04; @COST-43; @COST-44] {VN-direct\|Low}. Shrimp is the only plausible first market for a purpose-grown product; in pangasius only a by-product yeast priced near USD 1.1 per kg works.

**Reading.** A Vietnamese feed protein sold on protein price alone does not clear fishmeal at 2025 prices and cannot touch soybean meal. At the August 2026 fishmeal price, the low end of the indicative cost comes within about 5% of parity, but that depends on the spike lasting. The investable thesis is a functional shrimp or pangasius ingredient with trial data, or a very low-cost by-product route. Pig and poultry feed (about 22 Mt) is ruled out by price, not by volume.

---

## S6.12 Outlook to 2030

- **Vietnamese feed demand.** USDA's April 2026 annual report expected total feed demand (animal plus aquafeed) to rise from 28.6 Mt (2025) to 29.5 Mt (2026) and 30.6 Mt (2027), with aquafeed at 6.73 Mt (2026) and 7.12 Mt (2027) on its own, higher aquafeed basis [@MAC-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. Its August 2026 quarterly raised these to 30.45 Mt (2026) and 31.2 Mt (2027), with aquafeed at 6.85 Mt and 7.0 Mt [@MAC-03] {VN-direct|Medium}. USDA's April 2026 forecasts put soybean-meal feed use at 7.4 Mt (2026) and 7.8 Mt (2027) [@MAC-04], revised in August to 8.1 Mt for 2027; USDA expects corn imports of 15 Mt in MY2026/27 [@MAC-03] {VN-direct|Medium}. Every increment of demand growth is met by imports (our inference).
- **The 2030 target.** Decision 1520/QD-TTg targets 30 to 32 Mt of industrial feed output from 40 to 45 Mt of capacity by 2030 [@MAC-23; @REG-54] {VN-direct|High}. The extract does not say whether aquafeed is included. The feed scheme, Decision 1625/QD-TTg, sets the same 30 to 32 Mt for industrial *livestock* feed, so the target appears to exclude aquafeed [@NTS-23] {VN-direct|Medium}; see [[ch22-protein-balance-2050]]. From about 22 Mt of livestock and poultry feed in 2025, the target needs 6.4 to 7.8% growth a year (our calculation, (30/22) and (32/22) to the power 1/5). Growth was about 3% in 2025 and 7.5% in H1 2026 [@MAC-01; @MAC-03]. Reaching the target would add 8 to 10 Mt of feed a year compared with 2025 (our calculation), a large protein-input requirement that imports or domestic novel inputs would have to meet.
- **Shrimp feed.** Sheng Long expects feed sales to rise about 15% in 2026 (as quoted) [@FM-04] {VN-direct|Low}.
- **Price forecasts.** The World Bank's April 2026 forecasts stop at 2027: soybean meal USD 359/t (2026) and USD 363/t (2027); maize USD 211/t and USD 214/t. Maize had already reached USD 224/t by August 2026. There is no World Bank fishmeal forecast [@GT-14; @GT-15] {general|High}. Any 2030 feed-price path is therefore a scenario assumption; see [[app-f1-outlook]].
- **Global fishmeal supply.** About 4.5 Mt of fishmeal was made in 2016, 69% of it used in aquafeed; global aquafeed was projected to grow from 49.7 Mt (2015) to 87.1 Mt (2025) [@FM-06] {general|Medium}. Aquaculture now takes about 87% (about 4 Mt a year), citing FAO 2024, and trimmings are a major source of fishmeal [@FM-35] {general|Medium}. Supply is flat and demand is rising, which supports structurally high fishmeal prices, but prices also swing with Peruvian anchovy seasons.
- **Leading indicator.** The fishmeal to soybean-meal price ratio (3.8 in 2024, 4.7 in 2025, 6.2 in August 2026) is the signpost to track monthly on the Pink Sheet [@GT-15] {general|High}.

---

## S6.13 The Chinese counterfactual

- **China is pushing soybean meal out of its own feed.** MARA issued a "Three-Year Action Plan" to reduce and substitute soybean meal in feed (2023), and a 2025 review reports that soybean-meal use in Chinese feed fell 8.0% in 2024 [@FM-36] {general|Low}. We could not read the plan's numeric targets. A 2021 MARA plan to reduce corn and soybean meal in feed also named single-cell protein [@RGN-56] {general|Medium}. Earlier, China's fishmeal imports held at 1.0 to 1.5 Mt a year while its aquafeed grew to 19 Mt (2014) [@FM-09] {general|Medium}.
- **Commercial-scale Chinese microbial protein plants exist.** Calysseo runs a 20,000 t/yr FeedKind plant in China, and CAP from steel-mill gas has been used in fish and shrimp diets [@FM-13; @FM-15] {general|Medium}. Angel Yeast has 11,000 t/yr of yeast-protein capacity in Yichang [@RGN-24; @HSC-14] {general|Low}. Chinese glutamic-acid biomass is already sold in Vietnam [@FM-12] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **The trade link runs both ways.** Vietnam sends 93.5% of its fishmeal exports (USD 402.3 M in 2023) to China [@FM-38] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **What it means for price (our reasoning, not a finding).** Chinese by-product SCP has near-zero marginal feedstock cost, so it can price anywhere between soybean-meal and fishmeal parity. The realistic landed price for a Vietnamese feed SCP is therefore at or below fishmeal-protein parity. A Vietnamese producer should plan for a realised price of 70 to 90% of fishmeal-protein parity: about USD 1,840 to 2,360 per tonne of protein at the 2025 average fishmeal price and USD 2,690 to 3,460 at the August 2026 price (our calculation, 0.7 and 0.9 x 2,625 and x 3,846).
- **Test.** Any Vietnamese feed-SCP business plan should be tested against a quote for Chinese SCP delivered to a Mekong Delta mill, not against fishmeal list prices. The revealed benchmark exists: China shipped 4,236 t of HS 2102.20 to Vietnam in 2025 at about USD 1.27 per kg, duty-free under ACFTA and RCEP; the share that is bacterial biomass rather than yeast is unknown [@FBA-17; @FTR-32] {VN-direct|Medium}.

---

## Gaps and how to close them

| # | Gap | Why it matters | Cheapest way to close it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Vietnamese commercial fishmeal inclusion by species | Swing factor in the displaceable pool (shrimp 6 to 25%) | One call each to the technical managers of Sheng Long, Uni-President Vietnam, Grobest and the Vinh Hoan feed division; or the Vietnam Feed Association |
| 2 | Aquafeed volume by species consistent with NSO output | USDA (6.5 Mt) and industry (3.9 to 4.8 Mt) disagree | Ask MAE's Department of Fisheries and Fisheries Surveillance for the feed chapter of its annual review |
| 3 | Domestic fishmeal production, grades and prices (VND/kg at 55, 60 and 65% CP) | The real local price to beat | Kien Giang (now An Giang) and Ca Mau fishmeal plants; AgroMonitor weekly feed report; monthly customs data for HS 2301.20 |
| 4 | Absolute shrimp and pangasius feed prices | Our price levels are derived from percentage changes | A current dealer price list from the Mekong Delta, or VASEP's cost-of-production series |
| 5 | Partly closed (HS 2102.20 trade, S6.8). Still open: the bacterial share of Chinese 2102.20 and the price of glutamic-acid biomass | The counterfactual price | Ask V-Group / CK Vietnam for a quote; declaration-level customs data for HS 2309.90 and 2102.20 |
| 6 | CAP capacity and price; FeedKind price | Regional competitor economics | Company investor materials; GFI APAC China team |
| 7 | MARA soybean-meal reduction targets and SCP approvals | Size of the Chinese home market | Read the MARA notice on moa.gov.cn directly |
| 8 | Tilapia and pangasius SCP or yeast replacement thresholds | No tilapia threshold retrieved | Targeted literature search; Can Tho University and Nong Lam University aquaculture faculties |
| 9 | FAO SOFIA 2024 fishmeal figures read directly | Global supply context is secondhand | FAO Open Knowledge repository PDF |
| 10 | Skretting's insect-meal inclusion rate and volumes; Entobel's realised output and price | The only local price signal for a novel protein | Ask Skretting Vietnam and Entobel |
| 11 | Soybean-meal origin shares for 2025 | Argentina 69% or Brazil 69% depends on the table reading | Re-read the USDA VM2026-0006 PDF |
| 12 | Whether the 2030 feed target includes aquafeed | Changes the implied growth rate | Read Decision 1520/QD-TTg in full |

See [[app-r1-open-questions]] for the full register and [[app-r2-disagreements]] for the conflicts on aquafeed volume, shrimp output, fishmeal prices, inclusion rates and the pool.

## Related data files

- `feed_imports.csv`: feed-ingredient imports by commodity and year (2023 to H1 2026), with value, origins and the derived totals.
- `macro_indicators.csv`: feed output, aquafeed estimates, fisheries output by species, feed shares of cost and the 2030 target.
- `feed_benchmarks.csv`: fishmeal (2020 to August 2026), soybean meal and other World Bank prices, Vietnamese feed price levels, and incumbent novel proteins, with price per tonne of protein.
- `inclusion_rates.csv`: fishmeal inclusion ranges by species with basis and confidence.
- `replacement_trials.csv`: maximum replacement without growth loss by species and ingredient.
- `commodity_prices.csv`: wave 1 commodity prices, including Vietnamese corn import values and retail feed prices.
- `outlook.csv`: World Bank forecasts and the fishmeal to soybean-meal ratio.
- `tariffs.csv` and `routes.csv`: import duties (MFN and preferential) and routes to market for feed ingredients.
- `inactive_yeast_trade.csv`, `asc_feed_mills.csv`, `feed_buyer_register.csv` and `t2_price_per_performance.csv`: HS 2102.20 trade by year, the Vietnamese ASC feed-mill register, the feed-buyer register and the head-to-head price-per-performance calculation.
- `facilities.csv`: feed and aquafeed mills.
- `disagreements.csv` and `open_questions.csv`: conflicting numbers and open questions.

data.title: S7. Research landscape and bibliometrics
data.summary: How much alternative-protein research Vietnam publishes, topic by topic and against its neighbours, which groups and institutions hold the relevant skills, who funds them, and the 11 research gaps Vietnam is well placed to fill.
data.body:
# S7. Research landscape and bibliometrics

This appendix maps Vietnam's published research relevant to alternative protein: how much there is, where it sits, who does it, who pays for it, and where the gaps are. It combines two passes:

- **Wave 1 (Scite):** 30 searches in the Scite literature database, more than 150 Vietnam-affiliated records from 2015 to 2026 screened, and 76 papers tabulated with a key result each [@RD-01] {VN-direct|Medium}.
- **Wave 2 (OpenAIRE):** country-tagged counts for 20 topics in Vietnam and 3 topic groups in five comparison countries, with every query URL stored so that the counts can be re-run [@BIB-01] {VN-direct|Medium}.

`publications.csv` (103 rows) merges the wave 1 list with 40 top-cited wave 2 records, deduplicated on DOI. The technology science itself (titres, costs, safety) is in [[app-s13-science]]; pilot plants, laboratories and graduates are in [[app-s8-labs-talent]].

Terms: *VN-affiliated* means at least one author works at a Vietnamese institution. *VN-tagged* means OpenAIRE links the record to Vietnam through its country code. *Per 10k* means topic records per 10,000 of the country's total OpenAIRE publication records in the same window. *DIAAS* and *PDCAAS* are protein-quality scores that correct amino-acid content for digestibility.

## S7.1 Key findings

1. **Vietnam's output on food-facing alternative protein is small.** Records tagged to each country for plant-based or cultivated meat, 2015 to September 2026: Vietnam 9, Philippines 10, Indonesia 47, Thailand 49, Malaysia 61, Singapore 112 [@BIB-01] {VN-adjacent|Medium}. Vietnam has about 5 to 12 times fewer records than Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore (our calculation: 47 / 9 = 5.2; 112 / 9 = 12.4).
2. **The gap remains after adjusting for research size.** Per 10,000 publications: Vietnam 0.37, Philippines 0.62, Malaysia 1.02, Thailand 1.58, Singapore 2.94 [@BIB-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. Vietnam's intensity is about a quarter of Thailand's and an eighth of Singapore's (our calculation from the same counts). A second database, on a broader core basket, OpenAlex gives 4.1 works per 10,000 national publications for Vietnam against 13.4 for Thailand (2015 to 2025), about 31% [@HSC-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. We therefore say "about a quarter to a third of Thailand's".
3. **In feed-side protein, Vietnam is at the regional level.** Fishmeal-replacement records per 10,000: Vietnam 0.42, Thailand 0.45, Malaysia 0.47, Philippines 0.68 [@BIB-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. The Vietnam figure is an undercount: a broader wave 1 search found about 20 Vietnamese aquafeed replacement papers [@RD-01] {VN-direct|Medium}.
4. **Vietnam has zero or near-zero records in six core technologies** after reading the titles: precision fermentation (0), mycoprotein (0 to 1), fish or shrimp cell lines for food (0), cultivated meat (1, a legal analysis), texturised or extruded protein (1, a 2026 review) and mung bean protein (0 to 1) [@BIB-01; @RD-01] {VN-direct|Medium}.
5. **Plant-based meat research is about 6 on-topic papers from 2015 to 2026, with one extrusion study, Taiwan-led with a first author also at Can Tho University of Technology** (see the corrections below) [@BIB-01; @HSC-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. A 2026 high-moisture meat analogue paper from the Industrial University of Ho Chi Minh City (IUH), found later, is not in these counts [@TIC-21] {VN-direct|Medium}.
6. **Vietnam's real strengths sit next to alternative protein:** aquafeed nutrition trials (Can Tho University, Nha Trang University), *Pichia pastoris* expression (VNU-HCM University of Science), human stem-cell culture including serum-free media (Vinmec, VNU-HCM Stem Cell Institute), fungal genetic tools for koji mould and *Cordyceps* (VNU Hanoi University of Science) and microalgae cultivation (Institute of Biotechnology VAST, VNUA) [@RD-01] {VN-direct|Medium}.
7. **Spirulina is Vietnam's biggest topic (87 records, 3.62 per 10,000), but the most-cited papers are about wastewater, diesel-engine fuel and nanoparticles**; only one surfaced paper extracts spirulina protein as an ingredient [@BIB-01] {VN-direct|Medium}.
8. **Output is rising from a very low base:** 7 records in 2015 to 2019, 14 in 2020 to 2022 and 21 in 2023 to September 2026, across the topic sets read in full [@BIB-01] {VN-direct|Low}.
9. **No Vietnamese DIAAS or PDCAAS study was found**, although Vietnamese groups do measure in vitro digestibility, RNA reduction and aflatoxin [@RD-01; @RD-23; @RD-31; @RD-61] {VN-direct|Medium}.
10. **Research money is national and small-grant based.** NAFOSTED is a leading acknowledged funder; international money (ACIAR, SATREPS, EU, Dutch) is present but not aimed at alternative protein; no GFI grantee in Vietnam was found [@RD-06; @RD-12; @RD-04; @RD-11; @RD-56; @RD-57; @RD-58; @RD-03] {VN-direct|Medium}.

> **Correction.** In v0.6 finding 5 said about 5 on-topic plant-based meat papers and no Vietnamese extrusion study; the source shows about 6, and the one extrusion study found has a first author also at Can Tho University of Technology [@HSC-01] {VN-direct|Medium}.

## S7.2 How the counts were made

> **Method note.** All Vietnam counts are **lower bounds**. Scite's affiliation data are incomplete, and OpenAIRE's country tagging misses at least one Vietnamese paper found in wave 1 (HUST's rice distillers' grain protein preprint) [@RD-01; @BIB-01] {VN-direct|High}. Both databases index Vietnamese-language journals only in part. OpenAIRE counts also contain false positives: in the Vietnam sets read in full, about 3 in 10 records were off-topic or had a doubtful Vietnam link [@BIB-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. Compare countries by order of magnitude, not to the decimal.

> **Correction.** The brief for wave 2 asked for OpenAlex counts. OpenAlex returned HTTP 429 ("too many requests") on all 4 attempts between 15:52 and 15:58 UTC on 23 September 2026; users without an API key now get a budget of USD 0.10 a day, most likely already used by the shared connection [@BIB-02; @BIB-03] {general|High}. Europe PMC was also refused (our run log, `working-papers/wave2/biblio/bibliometrics.md`) {general|High}. Wave 2 therefore used the OpenAIRE Graph API [@BIB-01] {general|High}. Wave 1's Scite counts should not be used for country benchmarking: a Scite query for cultivated meat with the affiliation "Thailand" returned 1 paper, while OpenAIRE returned 49 Thai records for a comparable query [@BIB-05; @BIB-01] {general|High}. Section S7.13 gives the full method notes.

## S7.3 Topic-by-topic depth

Depth scale: *none*; *thin* (a few isolated papers, no sustained group); *moderate* (one or more groups publishing repeatedly); *strong* (several groups, international-level output). Wave 1 counts are Vietnam-affiliated papers found and screened in Scite; wave 2 counts are OpenAIRE VN-tagged records from 1 January 2015 to 23 September 2026, with records per 10,000 of Vietnam's 240,387 publications [@RD-01; @BIB-01] {VN-direct|Medium}.

| Topic | Wave 1 (Scite, screened) | Wave 2 (OpenAIRE raw count, per 10k) | Wave 2 after reading titles | Depth | Leading Vietnamese groups |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## S7.6 Vietnam's adjacent strengths

**Aquafeed protein replacement** is the deepest applied field, with measured results from laboratory or tank trials [@RD-46; @RD-47; @RD-48] {VN-direct|High}:

- soy protein concentrate replaced 40% of fishmeal protein in snakehead with no loss of growth; 60 to 100% replacement reduced growth (2016);
- fermented soybean meal had 88.8% crude protein digestibility in whiteleg shrimp, with an optimum fishmeal replacement of 253.6 g/kg (2018);
- spent brewer's yeast replaced up to 60% of fishmeal protein in giant freshwater prawn without loss of growth or survival (2019).

**Food-grade side-stream protein (HUST)** [@RD-22; @RD-23; @RD-32] {VN-direct|Medium}:

- rice-based dried distillers' grains from Vietnamese ethanol plants hold 50 to 80% protein (dry matter); cassava distillers' grains only 13 to 16% (preprint, 2024);
- alkaline extraction recovered 90% of the protein, and enzymatically extracted protein was 77.1% digestible in vitro (2025);
- spent brewer's yeast protein was recovered at 84.9% and made into an energy bar with 14.9 g protein (2024).

**Recombinant growth factors and serum-free culture** [@RD-36; @RD-37; @RD-38; @RD-39] {VN-direct|Medium}. VNU-HCM groups expressed FGF-2, KGF/FGF7 and PDGF-BB in *Pichia* (2020 to 2021). Vinmec tested serum- and xeno-free media for cord-blood stem cells; only 1 of 4 commercial kits (StemMACS) worked (2022). These are the costliest ingredients of cultivated-meat media, made here for medicine, not food.

**Fungal genetic tools** [@RD-33; @RD-34] {VN-direct|Medium}. VNU Hanoi University of Science built an *Agrobacterium*-mediated transformation system with dual auxotrophic markers in *A. oryzae* (2021) and reached 100% *pyrG* deletion efficiency in five *Cordyceps militaris* strains, the base for a food-grade expression platform (2024).

**Microalgae cultivation** [@RD-21; @RD-20] {VN-direct|Medium}. A salt-tolerant Spirulina strain reached 48.73% protein (dry weight) in a 42 ppt medium (2023). VNUA published a review of Arthrospira production in Vietnam (2021).

**Mid-sized clusters that sit next to alternative protein** (OpenAIRE, VN-tagged): black soldier fly 34 records (the three most cited are about biodiesel from larval fat), *Pichia* 25 (mostly vaccine antigens and enzymes), *A. oryzae* 23 (mostly fungal genetic tools), duckweed 23 (mostly genomics and taxonomy) and "alternative protein" 20 (mostly feed) [@BIB-01] {VN-direct|Medium}. None of the ten most-cited papers in the *Pichia*, *A. oryzae* or duckweed clusters produces a food protein.
